questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following features will not be manifested in an infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following features will not be manifested in an infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trismus

Trismus is not a feature of infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space. Trismus is seen in pre-styloid abscess due to the involvement of the medial pterygoid muscle.

The parapharyngeal space is divided into two compartments by the styloid process and its attachments. Clinical features depend on the compartment involved.

In post-styloid abscess, there is a bulge of the pharynx behind the posterior pillar, accompanied by paralysis of cranial nerves IX, X (resulting in vocal cord paralysis), XI, XII, and the sympathetic chain, which can manifest as Horner's syndrome. Torticollis might be present due to the involvement of prevertebral muscles. Swelling in the parotid region may also be present. Notably, trismus, the inability to fully open the mouth, is usually absent in this type of abscess.

The pre-styloid abscess exhibits distinct features, including the prolapse of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa, along with trismus caused by the spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle. Marked odynophagia is also common. Additionally, an external swelling can be observed behind the angle of the jaw.

Diagnosis can be established using a contrast-enhanced CT scan (CECT). If there is suspicion of thrombosis of the internal jugular vein or an aneurysm of the internal carotid artery, magnetic resonance arteriography (MRA) can be useful.

Patients require intravenous antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, carbapenem antibiotics, plus drugs that target anaerobic organisms, such as clindamycin or metronidazole. A parapharyngeal abscess is drained by an external horizontal incision made on the skin a few centimeters below the angle of the mandible.

The image attached below shows the components of both spaces:

Pearl: Compartments of the parapharyngeal space

  Prestyloid Poststyloid
Relation to styloid Anterior Posterior
Relations

Medially: Tonsillar fossa

Laterally: Medial pterygoid muscle

Medially: Posterior part of the lateral pharyngeal wall

Laterally: Parotid gland
Contents Medial pterygoid muscle

Carotid artery

Jugular vein, IXth, Xth, XIth, XIIth cranial nerves

Sympathetic trunk
Presentation

Prolapse of tonsil and tonsillar fossa,

Spasm of medial pterygoid muscle leading to trismus

The pharynx bulging behind the posterior pillar

Injury to of CN IX, X, XI, and XII leading to vocal cord paralysis

Sympathetic chain injury leading to Horner’s syndrome

Swelling of the parotid region

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While collecting blood for samples, you have spilled some on the floor. What would be the immediate next step?
questions.raw_text: While collecting blood for samples, you have spilled some on the floor. What would be the immediate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Call the infection control team of the hospital

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clean with absorbable material

The immediate next step in this scenario is to clean the spilled blood with absorbable material.

This absorbable material is then discarded in the yellow bin. Following this, sodium hypochlorite solution is used to decontaminate the surface. The concentrations of sodium hypochlorite used are: 

  • < 10 mL blood spill - 1:100 dilution to decontaminate non-porous surfaces
  • > 10 mL blood spill or culture spill - 1:10 dilution for the first application, followed by 1:100 dilution

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: For hypertrophic non-union following a fracture, the most appropriate treatment would be __________
questions.raw_text: For hypertrophic non-union following a fracture, the most appropriate treatment would be __________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stabilization

In cases of hypertrophic non-union following a fracture, stabilization alone has the potential to induce union.

Non-union following a fracture occurs when the healing process fails to progress, resulting in a failure to unite. There are two primary types of non-union:

  • Hypertrophic - where callus formation is present but does not bridge the fracture site
  • Atrophic - characterized by minimal or no attempt at callus formation

For hypertrophic non-union without deformity, conservative treatment using functional bracing or rigid fixation alone (internally or externally) can promote union. However, in cases of atrophic non-union, fixation alone is insufficient, requiring the excision of fibrous tissues in the fracture gap and sclerotic bone ends, followed by the application of bone grafts around the fracture.

questions.text: Identify the given bone marrow biopsy instrument.
questions.raw_text: Identify the given bone marrow biopsy instrument.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Klima needle

The given instrument is a Klima needle.

Klima and Salah's needles are reusable bone marrow aspiration & biopsy needles, both are made of stainless steel. Klima needle has a guard that screws along the length of the needle. It has no side screw. Whereas, Salah's needle has a guard situated 2 cm from the tip and has a side screw.

The image below shows Salah's needle.

 

Islam and Jamshidi needles have a t-bar at the end for easier maneuvering. Jamshidi needle has a tapering end to reduce the crush artefacts in the sample. Islam needle has a core securing device, i.e., its cutting edge is shaped to hold the core of the bone during the procedure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A patient presented with ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensations in the face, vertigo with numbness and loss of sweating and dysarthria on the ipsilateral side. All these symptoms are caused due to a lesion in:

A. Medial medulla
B. Lateral medulla
C. Ventromedial medulla
D. Lateral medulla including nucleus ambiguus and spinothalamic tract
questions.raw_text:
A patient presented with ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensations in the face, vertigo with numbness and loss of sweating and dysarthria on the ipsilateral side. All these symptoms are caused due to a lesion in:

A. Medial medulla
B. Lateral medulla
C. Ventromedial medulla
D. Lateral medulla including nucleus ambiguus and spinothalamic tract
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. B and D

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lateral medullary syndrome/Wallenberg syndrome. This may result from a stroke affecting the ipsilateral vertebral artery.

Lateral medullary syndrome: The clinical findings correspond to the neuroanatomical structures affected in the lateral portion of the medulla:

  • Descending tract and nucleus of CN V (trigeminal)- loss of pain and sensation over the ipsilateral half of the face.
  • Inferior cerebellar peduncle – ipsilateral ataxia (gait and limb)
  • Lateral spinothalamic tract – loss of pain and temperature sensation over the contralateral half of the body. 
  • IX and X CN - ipsilateral paralysis of palate, vocal cord, diminished gag reflex giving rise to dysphagia, dysarthria.
  • Vestibular nucleus - Nystagmus, diplopia, vertigo, nausea
  • Descending sympathetic tract – ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome (miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following marked structure is damaged in respiratory distress syndrome?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following marked structure is damaged in respiratory distress syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

Type II pneumocytes, which are marked as 2 in the above image, are damaged in respiratory distress syndrome.

The cells forming the lining epithelium of alveoli (also called pneumocytes) are mainly of the following types:

  • Type I pneumocytes - large flattened cells which present a very thin diffusion barrier for gases. These cells have large cytoplasmic extensions and form the primary lining cells of the alveoli. They are connected to each other by tight junctions.
  • Type II pneumocytes (granular pneumocytes) - These are rounded secretory cells bearing microvilli on their free surfaces. These cells secrete the surfactant which decreases the surface tension between the thin alveolar walls and thus prevents alveoli from collapsing during respiration. Type II cells are important in alveolar repair as well.

The below image shows the pneumocytes lining the alveoli:

The alveoli are surrounded by pulmonary capillaries. The alveoli also contain other specialized cells, including pulmonary alveolar macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, neuroendocrine cells, and mast cells. 

Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) is seen in premature infants due to the reduction in production and secretion of the lung surfactant. The surfactant reduces the alveolar surface tension. This phospholipid is synthesized in type II pneumocytes (also called granular pneumocytes) in the endoplasmic reticulum.

The surfactant appears in the amniotic fluid between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation. Mature levels of the pulmonary surfactant are present usually after 35 weeks of gestation. Therefore, respiratory distress syndrome is seen in premature infants due to the immaturity of surfactant

Administration of antenatal glucocorticoids to mothers who deliver at 24 to 34 weeks can increase surfactant production and reduce the risk of RDS. It includes either giving 2 doses of betamethasone 12mg/dose with 24 hours between each dose, or 4 doses of dexamethasone 6mg/dose, with 12 hours between each dose.

Mild to moderate RDS can be managed with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). CPAP is a noninvasive modality of support where a continuous distending pressure (5-7 cm H20) is applied at the nostril level to keep the alveoli open in a spontaneously breathing baby. Severe cases will require mechanical ventilation.

Surfactant administration is reserved for severe cases and moderate cases not improving even with fiO2> 40% in CPAP.

With treatment, it rarely leads to respiratory failure and has a good prognosis.

Pearl: Pulmonary surfactant

It lowers the surface tension of the water layer at the alveolar surface, which increases lung compliance, thereby making it easier for the lungs to expand. It is secreted by type II alveolar cells. It is a mixture of phospholipids and protein.

4 unique apoproteins of surfactant: Surfactant proteins are (SP)-A, SP-B, SP-C, and SP-D.

  • SP-A - Regulation of the feedback uptake of surfactant by the type II alveolar epithelial cells that secrete it.
  • SP-B & SP-C - Key protein members of the monomolecular film of surfactant.
  • SP-D - Organization of SP-B and SP-C into the surfactant layer.

A deep breath increases its secretion by stretching the type II cells. Its concentration decreases when breaths are small.

In the fetus, surfactant synthesis is variable. The surfactant may be present as early as gestational week 24 and is almost always present by gestational week 35.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the correct order of using eye drops and eye ointment?
questions.raw_text: What is the correct order of using eye drops and eye ointment?

options.label: A
options.text: Eye drops first,  ointment 15 min later

options.label: B
options.text: Ointment first, eye drops 15 min later

questions.correct_answer: A. Eye drops first,  ointment 15 min later
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Eye drops first, ointment 15 min later

Eye drops first followed by ointment 15 minutes later is the correct way of usage.

An ointment is thicker in consistency and needs to stay on the eyes for a longer time for absorption of the medication. Hence, it is generally put in the eyes at bedtime.

Eyedrops are watery thin and can be absorbed faster. Hence eyedrops are put first, and after 10-15 minutes, once they are completely absorbed, eye ointment can be applied.

Eye ointments are usually avoided during the daytime as they cause marked blurring of vision.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
Which of the following is correct about the drugs used in Gout?

A. Aspirin is not used as it decreases the uric acid excretion
B. Diclofenac is used as it concentrates in the joint
C. Indomethacin is used as it acts by multiple pathways
D. Aspirin is used as it is most powerful NSAID
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following is correct about the drugs used in Gout?

A. Aspirin is not used as it decreases the uric acid excretion
B. Diclofenac is used as it concentrates in the joint
C. Indomethacin is used as it acts by multiple pathways
D. Aspirin is used as it is most powerful NSAID
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A, B & C

Gout is a metabolic disease associated with hyperuricemia.

The drug of choice is an acute attack of gout is NSAIDs (Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) like indomethacin or the drug colchicine, but they are poorly tolerated and should not be used in elderly patients with chronic kidney disease.

Indomethacin is commonly used in the initial treatment of gout. In addition to inhibiting prostaglandin synthase, indomethacin and other NSAIDs also inhibit urate crystal phagocytosis

Intraarticular steroids like triamcinolone or methylprednisolone can also be given.

Aspirin is not used because it causes renal retention of uric acid at low doses. It is uricosuric only at higher doses that are poorly tolerated.

 

Pearl: Drugs precipitating Gout

Drugs that precipitate gout are-

Cyclosporine or cancer drugs
Aspirin (low dose)
Niacin
Thiazide
Lasix (furosemide)
Ethambutol
Alcohol
Pyrazinamide

Mnemonic for drugs precipitating gout is 'CANT LEAP'

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man who had undergone an exploratory laparotomy 6 months ago came for a follow-up visit. Which of the following statements about healed incision is false?
questions.raw_text: A man who had undergone an exploratory laparotomy 6 months ago came for a follow-up visit. Which of the following statements about healed incision is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Disorganized collagen fibers become aligned along stress lines

options.label: B
options.text: Strength of the scar is in their weave rather than in their amount

options.label: C
options.text: By the first week it is held by sutures and type I collagen

options.label: D
options.text: Tensile strength is about 60-80% of normal skin by  3 months

questions.correct_answer: C. By the first week it is held by sutures and type I collagen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. By the first week it is held by sutures and type I collagen

By the first week, a surgical wound has minimal inherent strength because the dermal edges are held together by hemostatic plug, sutures and a weak type III collagen.

During postoperative weeks 2-3 (remodelling phase), fibroblasts proliferate rapidly and begin to replace weak type III collagen with stronger type I collagen. The strength of the wound is still limited to less than 10% of its final strength. By week 6, the concentration of strong collagen fibers begins to resemble that of intact skin.

As the collagen matures and becomes denser, the scar becomes almost acellular as the fibroblasts and blood vessels reduce.The disorganized collagen fibers become aligned along stress lines with their strength being in their weave rather than in their amount.

Most of these changes occur over the first three months but a scar will continue to mature for 1 to 2 years. Tensile strength will continue to increase but would not be expected to exceed 60–80% of that of normal skin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fibers from the marked structure terminate at which of the following?
questions.raw_text: Fibers from the marked structure terminate at which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Red nucleus

The peduncle highlighted in the image is the superior cerebellar peduncle. The superior cerebellar peduncle includes fibers from deep cerebellar nuclei that project to the brainstem, red nucleus, and thalamus. It also contains the ventral spinocerebellar tract fibers.

The superior cerebellar peduncle contains all the efferent fibers from the dentate, emboliform, and the globose nuclei, and a small fascicle from the fastigial nucleus. Its fibers decussate in the caudal mesencephalon and are destined to synapse in the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus. The middle cerebellar peduncle contains only afferent fibers from the contralateral pontine nuclei. The inferior cerebellar peduncle is a mixture of afferent fibers from the brainstem and spinal cord and efferent fibers to the vestibular nuclei.

The image below summarizes the various tracts in the cerebellar unit.

The cerebellum consists of two hemispheres (right and left) joined by a median vermis. It is divided into three lobes:-

  • Anterior lobe - lies superiorly above the primary fissure
  • Middle lobe - lies inferiorly below the primary fissure. It is the largest lobe. It is also called the posterior lobe.
  • Flocculonodular lobe - lies posterior to the uvulonodular fissure

It has two surfaces - superior and inferior separated by a horizontal fissure. It is connected to the other parts of the central nervous system via three peduncles

  • Superior cerebellar peduncle -connecting to the midbrain
  • Middle cerebellar peduncle - connecting to the pons
  • Inferior cerebellar peduncle - connecting to the medulla oblongata

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy had received a full course rabies vaccine taken in December 2018. His pet dog which has been fully vaccinated now (November 2019) bit him on the toe. Bleeding was present at the site of the bite. What would be the line of treatment?
questions.raw_text: A 5-year-old boy had received a full course rabies vaccine taken in December 2018. His pet dog which has been fully vaccinated now (November 2019) bit him on the toe. Bleeding was present at the site of the bite. What would be the line of treatment?
questions.correct_answer: B. 2 doses of vaccine on Day 0 & 3
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 doses of vaccine on Day 0 & 3

This boy should receive 2 doses of vaccine on days 0 & 3 as he has received a prior course of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) > 3 months ago.

Management of a new dog bite in a previously immunized individual with either pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is as follows:

  • Category I: Wound treatment only
  • Category II/ III:
    • Wound treatment with soap and running water for 15 min and apply antiseptic
    • Anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) -on days 0 and 3, 2 doses ID (0.1 ml, 1 site)/ 2 doses IM (1 VIAL, 1 site)

*Note: In developing countries like India, the vaccination status of animals alone, doesn't play a significant role in determining the initiation of prophylaxis in humans.

Pearl: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted). There are no contraindications to post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies. It can be safely administered to pregnant women, infants, and immunocompromised individuals.

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG): 

  • Passive immunization
  • Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine
  • Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight
  • Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.
  • Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

  • RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.
  • The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.
  • RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

  1. Multiple bites
  2. Deep wounds
  3. Bites to head, neck, and hands
  4. Patients with severe immunodeficiency
  5. Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal
  6. Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

  • High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.
  • Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult
  • Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year
  • Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of 3 intramuscular (IM) or 3 intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0, 7 and 21 or 28.

  • Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm
  • Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.
  • Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.
  • High-risk individuals who receive pre-exposure prophylaxis should have their neutralising antibody titres checked every six months during the first 2 years following immunisation, and every 2 years thereafter. If the levels fall below 0.5 IU/ml, a booster dose of vaccine is recommended. 

Management of re-exposure to rabies virus

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

  • Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency
  • Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment 

For any exposed or re-exposed patient who has received and can document previous completion of PEP or PrEP:

  • Proper wound management
  • One site ID / IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3
  • RIG not given

Only in case of exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP or PrEP within the last three months, adequate wound washing alone is required.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following has the least risk of perinatal transmission?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following has the least risk of perinatal transmission?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rubella

Rubella has the least risk of perinatal transmission. 

Rubella or German measles has an intrauterine transmission that causes serious infection in pregnancy which results in abortions or severe fetal defects if infection occurs in the first trimester. The classical triad of congenital rubella syndrome is deafness, cataract, and congenital heart disease.

Other options- 

Option A: Herpes simplex infection can be acquired in utero, intrapartum/perinatally, or during the neonatal period. The intrauterine infection causes skin vesicles, eye findings (chorioretinitis, keratoconjunctivitis), and microcephaly/hydranencephaly. Intrapartum infection presents with either:

  • Skin, eye, and mouth disease
  • Encephalitis
  • Disseminated disease with sepsis-like presentation

Option B: Cytomegalovirus, the most common congenital infection with perinatal transmission presents with hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. One of the long-term sequelae is hearing loss. 

Option D: Hepatitis B virus is associated with significant perinatal transmission. The most important risk factor that determines perinatal transmission is HBeAg.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Systematic desensitisation is based on the principle of counter conditioning and reciprocal inhibition

options.label: B
options.text: When flooding, the patient is exposed to the fear according to a hierarchy

options.label: C
options.text: In therapeutic graded exposure, relaxation training is not involved

options.label: D
options.text: Eye movement desensitisation is used in post traumatic stress disorder and phobias

questions.correct_answer: B. When flooding, the patient is exposed to the fear according to a hierarchy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. When flooding, the patient is exposed to the fear according to a hierarchy

In flooding, the patient is exposed to their fear, but without any hierarchy i.e, there is no gradual exposure as in systematic desensitization. Patients learn to remain in the feared situation until they feel calm.

Systematic desensitization - employs counter conditioning and reciprocal inhibition. It is used in the treatment of OCD and phobias.

Therapeutic graded exposure - similar to systematic desensitization, but there is no relaxation training. The treatment is carried out in a real-life context.

Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) - inducing saccades (quick, simultaneous movement of both eyes between two or more phases of fixation) when a person is imagining an anxiety-producing event. The saccades can yield a positive thought which decreases anxiety. It is used in PTSD and phobias.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a random sample of 5000 corporate workers, the correlation coefficient of work satisfaction and life expectancy was found to be +0.7 with a p-value of 0.01. What is your interpretation?
questions.raw_text: In a random sample of 5000 corporate workers, the correlation coefficient of work satisfaction and life expectancy was found to be +0.7 with a p-value of 0.01. What is your interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Work satisfaction does not improve life expectancy

options.label: B
options.text: Strong statistically significant positive association between the variables

options.label: C
options.text: 70% people who enjoy work will live longer

options.label: D
options.text: 30% people who do not enjoy work will have a shorter life expectancy

questions.correct_answer: B. Strong statistically significant positive association between the variables
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strong statistically significant positive association between the variables

The above study is statistically significant (p-value = 0.01) and indicates a strong positive correlation (correlation coefficient = +0.7) between work satisfaction and life expectancy.

Correlation is a measure of the statistical association of the variables, not a causal relationship.

Here, the coefficient of determination (r2) = 0.7 x 0.7 = 0.49. This means that 49% of the variation in life expectancy can be explained by satisfaction at work. 

Pearl: Correlation

Correlation expresses the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables in terms of a correlation coefficient. It is represented by r.

  • Values of r vary from -1 (perfect negative correlation) to +1 (perfect positive correlation).
  • Value (size) of the coefficient: Indicates the strength of relationship
  • Sign of the coefficient: Indicates direction of relationship

Coefficients between ±0.5 and 1 are regarded as strong whereas those between ±0.5 and 0 are regarded as weak.

The data is plotted in a scattergram as shown in the examples given below

Examples:

Types of correlation coefficients

  1. Pearson coefficient
  2. Spearman coefficient

Coefficient of Determination (CD) =  r2

It is simply the percentage variability in one factor due to change in another variable.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female came to OPD with complaints of backache. On examination, Schober test was positive and her eyes and nose were hyperpigmented. Probable diagnosis is
questions.raw_text: A 30-year-old female came to OPD with complaints of backache. On examination, Schober test was positive and her eyes and nose were hyperpigmented. Probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ochronosis

Given X-ray shows intervertebral disc calcification and hyperpigmentation of nose and eyes are present. Both features are indicative of ochronosis as diagnosis.

  • Ochronosis also known as alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder.
  • It is due to deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase leading to accumulation of homogentisic acid.
  • Clinical features: Triad of
    • Homogentisic aciduria (urine turns dark color on standing due to oxidation or alkalinisation)
    • Eumelanin like pigmentation of skin, sclera, cartilages etc.
    • Degenerative chronic arthropathies especially of spine, hip, knees.

Option a: Hypoparathyroidism doesn't explain hyperpigmentation and other clinical features of hypoparathyroidism aren't mentioned.

Option b: Fluorosis - dental symptoms are not mentioned and osteoporosis will be marked in case of fluorosis. Also, hyperpigmentation is not a typical feature of fluorosis.

Option d: Ankylosing spondylitis – females are unlikely to be affected and it doesn’t explain hyperpigmentation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient was planned for surgery under general anaesthesia. During induction of anaesthesia, rocuronium 85 mg was given and the patient was tried to be intubated. It resulted in a failed intubation. Which of the following drugs can be given for immediate reversal of the drug?
questions.raw_text: A patient was planned for surgery under general anaesthesia. During induction of anaesthesia, rocuronium 85 mg was given and the patient was tried to be intubated. It resulted in a failed intubation. Which of the following drugs can be given for immediate reversal of the drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sugammadex

Sugammadex is used for immediate reversal of rocuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade/relaxant in the given scenario.

Sugammadex is a modified γ-cyclodextrin and the first selective relaxant–binding agent based on an encapsulating principle for inactivation of nondepolarising neuromuscular blocking drugs, mainly rocuronium and vecuronium. This principle of complex formation of sugammadex and rocuronium or vecuronium in a 1:1 ratio occurs at all levels of neuromuscular blockade, resulting in a faster-acting pharmacologic reversal when compared with anticholinesterase drugs like neostigmine. 

The stability of the rocuronium-sugammadex complex is a result of Van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonds, and hydrophobic interactions. There is some binding affinity with pancuronium, but this interaction is too low to have a significant clinical effect. 

Other options:

Option A: Neostigmine is used to reverse depolarising neuromuscular blockade such as succinylcholine, especially in the phase II block(fade of the train-of-four response), and sufficient time has passed for the circulating concentration of succinylcholine to be negligible. Therefore, neostigmine is slow-acting compared to sugammadex, but the agent is preferred in the case of succinylcholine. 

Neostigmine administration during phase I block increases neuromuscular Ach concentration and inhibits pseudocholinesterase (plasma cholinesterase) activity, which can prolong the action of succinylcholine; hence, it is given after some time during the phase II block. 

Option B: Glycopyrrolate is given alongside neostigmine in a 1:5 ratio to counteract its cholinergic adverse effects. Atropine is an alternative, but glycopyrrolate is preferred due to the incidence of tachycardia associated with atropine.

Option D: Edrophonium is a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor preferred in the case of mivacurium reversal since it does not show plasma cholinesterase inhibition present in neostigmine, which can prolong mivacurium action.

questions.text: Which of the following is not true regarding the procedure done using the instrument given in the image below?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not true regarding the procedure done using the instrument given in the image below?

options.text: Diagnosing an infiltrative or granulomatous disease

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Contraindicated if platelet count <40,000

The image shows a bone marrow biopsy needle. Thrombocytopenia is not in itself a contraindication for bone marrow biopsy. However, a platelet count >20,000 is ensured for safety purposes.

Indications of bone marrow biopsy:

  • Evaluation of unexplained anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and pancytopenia
  • Evaluation of polycythemia, thrombocytosis, and leukocytosis
  • Diagnosis, evaluation, and staging of lymphoma or solid tumors
  • Evaluation and diagnosis of plasma cell disorders and leukemias
  • Evaluation of suspected infiltrative and storage diseases
  • Assessment of pyrexia of unknown origin

Contraindications of bone marrow biopsy:

  • Severe hemophilia
  • Severe disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
  • Severe bleeding disorders

Procedure for bone marrow biopsy:

The prone or lateral position is chosen for the procedure. Posterior superior iliac spine is identified. After disinfection and local anesthesia, the patient is asked to inhale slowly through the nose and exhale slowly through the mouth to relieve anxiety. The needle is inserted and rotated on its axis.

On reaching the desired depth, the stylet is removed and the needle is advanced. The needle is rotated in the opposite direction to loosen the specimen. It is then withdrawn using the same rotational movement.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3 year old child is brought to the hospital with complaints of multiple episodes of loose stools and progressive weight loss. She was found to have a mid-upper arm circumference of 10.5 cm. Which of the following is true regarding the management of this child?
questions.raw_text: A 3 year old child is brought to the hospital with complaints of multiple episodes of loose stools and progressive weight loss. She was found to have a mid-upper arm circumference of 10.5 cm. Which of the following is true regarding the management of this child?

options.label: B
options.text: Administer 10 mL of 50% glucose IV, if unconscious

options.label: C
options.text: Continue aggressive hydration, even after dehydration resolves

options.label: D
options.text: Use ReSoMal for rehydration 5 mL/kg every 30 min for the first 2 hours

questions.correct_answer: D. Use ReSoMal for rehydration 5 mL/kg every 30 min for the first 2 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Use ReSoMal for rehydration 5 mL/kg every 30 min for the first 2 hours

Progressive weight loss and mid-upper arm circumference of <11.5 cm denote severe acute protein-energy malnutrition (PEM). When accompanied by loose stools, management includes the use of low sodium ORS for rehydration of 5ml/kg every 30 min for the first 2 hours.

Management of fluid/electrolyte status in SAM:

  1. Do not give IV fluids unless the child is in shock.
  2. Give ReSoMal (low-sodium rehydration solution for malnutrition) 5 mL/kg every 30 min for the first 2 hr orally or NG tube.
  3. Then give 5-10 mL/kg in alternate hours for up to 10 hour. The amount depends on stool loss and eagerness to drink. Feed every other alternate hour.
  4. Give ReSoMal after each watery stool as a prevention strategy.
  5. Do not continue aggressive hydration even after dehydration resolves.

Treatment of hypoglycemia in malnutrition:

  • If conscious: 10% glucose (50 mL) orally or 1 teaspoon sugar under the tongue, whichever is the quickest.
  • If unconscious: Immediately give sterile 10% glucose (5 mL/kg) by IV.

Note:

50% glucose is never used in children as it is extremely viscous and concentrated. This could lead to injection site pain, severe thrombophlebitis, and irritation. Also, this can cause osmotic overload in a three-year-old.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An 8-year-old child diagnosed to have focal seizures was initiated on oxcarbazepine. Which of the following would be incorrect regarding the agent being used?
questions.raw_text: An 8-year-old child diagnosed to have focal seizures was initiated on oxcarbazepine. Which of the following would be incorrect regarding the agent being used?

options.label: B
options.text: Enzyme induction potency is less when compared to carbamazepine

options.label: D
options.text: Hyponatremia risk is less when compared to carbamazepine

questions.correct_answer: D. Hyponatremia risk is less when compared to carbamazepine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyponatremia risk is less when compared to carbamazepine

The risk of hyponatremia with oxcarbazepine is higher when compared to carbamazepine. 

The possible proposed mechanisms of oxcarbazepine-induced hyponatremia include either a direct effect of this drug on the renal collecting tubules or an enhancement of their responsiveness to circulating vasopressin, which promotes aquaporin channel migration to the apical membrane, thereby increasing water permeability. As a result, it leads to greater water retention, reduced plasma osmolality and decreased serum sodium concentration. 

Other options: 

Option A: Oxcarbazepine is a keto analogue of carbamazepine. It is a prodrug. The mechanism of action of oxcarbazepine is by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels (same as carbamazepine).

Option B: Oxcarbazepine does not cause auto-induction of metabolizing enzymes. It can induce CYP enzymes, but is less potent when compared to carbamazepine.

Option C: The active form is metabolized by glucuronide conjugation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following features can be seen in patients with restless leg syndrome, except:
questions.raw_text: All of the following features can be seen in patients with restless leg syndrome, except:

options.label: A
options.text: Symptoms worsen during the evening or night

options.label: B
options.text: Accompanied by an unpleasant sensation in the legs

options.label: C
options.text: Symptoms that begin or worsen with activity

options.label: D
options.text: Partial or complete relief by movement

questions.correct_answer: C. Symptoms that begin or worsen with activity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Symptoms that begin or worsen with activity

In restless leg syndrome (RLS), symptoms begin or worsen with rest. It is also called as Willis-Ekbom disease.

The four core symptoms required for the diagnosis of RLS are:

  • An urge to move the legs
  • Usually caused or accompanied by an unpleasant sensation in the legs (creepy-crawly feeling, paresthesia, or burning)
  • Symptoms that begin or worsen with rest and partial or complete relief by movement
  • Worsening during the evening or night

Restless leg syndrome is a typical sensory-motor disorder that generally affects the legs during rest periods, especially sleep. There is an irresistible urge to shake the legs associated with burning sensation, itching, and cramps of the legs. In idiopathic cases, dopaminergic hypofunction is postulated.

In patients with restless legs syndrome, iron stores are initially repleted, and the aggravating factors are eliminated. If RLS still persists, initial therapy with a gabapentinoid (pregabalin, gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil) is preferred, rather than a dopamine agonist (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine). This is due to the high frequency of intermediate and long-term augmentation with dopamine agonists, as well as their risk of impulse control disorders.

FDA-approved drugs for the treatment of restless leg syndrome: 

  • Gabapentin
  • Ropinirole
  • Pramipexole
  • Rotigotine 

A dopamine agonist is used as an alternative in patients with increased risk for side effects from gabapentinoids, such as those with obesity and its complications, a past or present history of moderate to severe depression, a disorder causing gait instability or respiratory failure, and a history of substance use disorder.

Non-pharmacological treatments that can be used in restless leg syndrome are:

  • Avoiding alcohol at bedtime
  • Massaging affected legs
  • Hot baths
  • Applying hot or cold to the affected area
  • Engaging in moderate exercises
subtopics: Willis - Ekbom Disease / Restless Leg Syndrome

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Langerhans cell histiocytosis

The given electron microscopy image shows tennis racket shaped Birbeck granules. These granules are characteristic of Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

These granules are pentalaminar tubules with dilated terminal ends. This gives a characteristic tennis racket appearance on electron microscopy. They contain the protein langerin (CD207).

The image given below shows the Birbeck granules as seen on electron microscopy.

On peripheral smear, the proliferating Langerhans cells are characterised by:

  • Abundant vacuolated cytoplasm
  • Vesicular nuclei containing linear grooves or folds - coffee bean nuclei

The image given below shows Langerhans cells with coffee bean nuclei and moderately abundant pale cytoplasm mixed with a few eosinophils.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Soft tissue damage is maximal in MIPO technique

In MIPO (minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis) technique, soft tissue damage is minimal.

MIPO is a type of bridge plating or biological fixation (option C). Here, the plate is fixed proximally and distally and the central fracture area is rendered untouched. Hence, fracture hematoma and soft tissue damage are minimised.

Option A: Gallow's traction, hip spica and Russel traction are measures commonly used in children. But Russell's traction can also be used in adults as a first-aid measure. 

Option B: Metaphyseal fractures or fractures extending intra-articularly are indications for primary plating.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Which of the following are the objective tests for the hearing?
  1. BERA (Brainstem evoked response audiometry)
  2. OAE (Otoacoustic emission)
  3. PTA (Pure tone audiometry)
  4. Tympanometry
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following are the objective tests for the hearing?
  1. BERA (Brainstem evoked response audiometry)
  2. OAE (Otoacoustic emission)
  3. PTA (Pure tone audiometry)
  4. Tympanometry
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 4

BERA, OAE, and tympanometry are the objective tests for hearing. PTA (pure tone audiometry) is a subjective test for hearing as it relies on patient responses to pure tone stimuli. Other examples of subjective tests include tuning fork tests and speech audiometry.

Tympanometry is an objective test of the middle ear and eustachian tube functions (conductive compartment of hearing). Here, the compliance of the TM, i.e., how much it moves to the pressure differentials applied from the external ear is measured. 

The image below shows the types of tympanogram:

Pearl: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) or ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response)

It is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway.

Normally, 7 waves are produced in the first 10ms. 

  • Wave I – distal part of the cochlear nerve
  • Wave II –proximal part of the cochlear nerve
  • Wave III – cochlear nucleus
  • Wave IV – superior olivary complex
  • Wave V – lateral lemniscus
  • Wave VI & VII – inferior colliculus

Findings:

  • Conductive or cochlear pathology- delayed wave-I but inter-peak latency of I-V is normal
  • Retrocochlear pathology- wave-I present, rest of the waves absent
  • Acoustic neuroma or vestibular schwannoma- increased inter-peak latency of wave I-V and increased inter-aural latency of wave V > 0.2ms.

Uses:

  • To objectively find hearing threshold- wave-V appears 10dB above the hearing level obtained through PTA
  • Best audiometric test for:
    • Confirming hearing loss in infants
    • Diagnosing acoustic neuroma
    • Differentiating cochlear and retro-cochlear hearing loss
    • Diagnosing non-organic hearing loss.

Pearl: OAEs - Otoacoustic emissions

It is an objective test that records the low-intensity sounds produced by the outer hair cells of a normal cochlea.

It is of two types:

  • Spontaneous type- it is generated spontaneously and is present in 50% of normal individuals.
  • Evoked types- also called Kemp echoes or cochlear echoes, are generated in response to sound stimulus and found in all individuals with normal hearing. The two subtypes are transient evoked and distortion product.

The applications are as follows:

  • Screening test for neonates, infants, and small children for deafness due to inner ear causes.
  • Helps to differentiate cochlear and retrocochlear hearing loss- normal OAE indicates normal cochlea and hence retrocochlear pathology in a patient with sensorineural deafness.
  • Early detection of noise-induced hearing loss- since it is generated by outer hair cells that are prone to damage by noise trauma.

Pearl: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its intensity can be increased or decreased by 5dB.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:
  • For AC: 15 dB
  • For BC: 25 dB

Symbols used in pure tone audiometry:

 

Disease Findings in PTA audiogram
Conductive hearing loss AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present
Sensorineural hearing loss Both AC and BC are abnormal and no air-Bone gap
Mixed hearing loss Both AC and BC abnormal and air-bone gap present
Presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise-induced hearing loss (higher frequencies affected first) Downsloping or descending audiogram 
Early stages of Meniere's disease (lower frequencies affected first) Upsloping or ascending audiogram
Congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis (mid-frequency hearing loss) U-shaped or trough-shaped or cookie bite shaped audiogram
Early cases of noise-induced hearing loss

Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz
Otosclerosis  Carhart's notch- dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Seman's technique is used for which of the following conditions?
questions.raw_text: Seman's technique is used for which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Premature ejaculation

Seman's stop-start technique is used for premature ejaculation, to prolong the time period until ejaculation. 

Seman's technique (stop-start technique): A man approaches the point close to climax and then stops and relaxes before starting again. This method prolongs the time before ejaculation by relying on behaviour modification. 

Other treatments for premature ejaculation:

  • Squeeze technique (by Master and Johnson's)- as a man approaches a climax, he squeezes the tip of the penis just below the head of the penis. The pressure is held there until the sensation of impending orgasm diminishes. The process can then be started over again so that over time a man prolongs the time period until he reaches ejaculation.
  • Sensate focusing - refocussing on the non-coital aspects of sexual activity.
  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) - delays ejaculation. e.g.- dapoxetine, paroxetine.

questions.text: A patient from a North-Eastern state was diagnosed to have an infection with P. falciparum malaria. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Artemether plus lumefantrine

The most appropriate treatment for Plasmodium falciparum infection in North-Eastern states is artemether (20 mg) plus lumefantrine (120 mg).

As per National Vector Borne Disease Control Program (NVBDCP): 

  • Plasmodium malariae: treat as Plasmodium falciparum
  • Plasmodium ovale: treat as Plasmodium vivax
  • Severe and complicated malaria

            -Initial parenteral treatment x 24-48 hr:  quinine/artemether/artesunate/arteether

            -Oral treatment after 48 hrs-after parenteral quinine: quinine + doxycyclinex 7 days or quinine + clindamycin x 7 days (pregnancy and chidren<8yrs)

            -After parenteral artemisinin derivates: in NE states: ACT -AL X 3 days+primaquine (day2), in other states: ACT-SPX 3 days+primaquine (day 2) 

  • Chemoprophylaxis

                       Short-term, less than or equal to 6 weeks: Doxycycline OD (start one day before travel and continue for 4 weeks after return)

                        Long-term, more than 6 weeks: mefloquine weekly (start 2 weeks before travel and 4 weeks after return).

Correct answer: D. None of them is a conclusive evidence

None of the options are considered as conclusive evidence of drowning.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman underwent an emergency LSCS under general anesthesia to deliver a term, healthy infant. Two hours later, she developed sudden tachypnea, cyanosis, and massive pulmonary edema and died despite resuscitative measures. The histopathological picture of her lung is shown below.  What is the likely cause of death?
questions.raw_text: A 28-year-old woman underwent an emergency LSCS under general anesthesia to deliver a term, healthy infant. Two hours later, she developed sudden tachypnea, cyanosis, and massive pulmonary edema and died despite resuscitative measures. The histopathological picture of her lung is shown below.  What is the likely cause of death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mendelson’s syndrome

The given scenario and image showing massive neutrophilic infiltration are suggestive of Mendelson’s syndrome or aspiration pneumonitis.

Mendelson's syndrome is a chemical pneumonitis caused by the aspiration of sterile gastric contents during general anesthesia, especially during pregnancy. The most common cause of maternal mortality associated with general anesthesia is either due to a pulmonary aspiration or a failed endotracheal intubation. 

The risk factors for Mendelson's syndrome include:

  • Gastric volume > 25 mL (0.4 mL/kg)
  • Gastric pH < 2.5

Incidence of aspiration can be reduced by the administration of:

  • Non-particulate antacids like sodium citrate 30-45 minutes before intubation
  • H2 receptor antagonists like intravenous ranitidine 
  • Metoclopramide 1-2 hours before induction

Other options:

Option B: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia is a type of ILD associated with Masson bodies and plugs of loose connective tissue on histology.

Option C: CMV pneumonia is associated with the owl's eye appearance on histology.

Option D: Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia is associated with black-walled cysts on silver staining.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the dose of carbetocin used in the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.raw_text: What is the dose of carbetocin used in the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 100 mcg

100 mcg of carbetocin is used in the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH).

The use of carbetocin (100 µg, IM/IV) is recommended for the prevention of PPH. It is a long-acting synthetic analog of oxytocin with agonist properties. By binding to oxytocin receptors on the uterine smooth muscle, oxytocin produces rhythmic muscle contractions, heightens the rate of contraction, and increases the baseline tone of the uterus.

To effectively prevent PPH, the use of only one of the following uterotonic agents is recommended as per the WHO 2025 guidelines:

  • Oxytocin (10 IU - IM/IV)
  • Carbetocin (100 μg - IM/IV) - Recommended when cold chain for oxytocin is not guaranteed.
  • Misoprostol (400 μg or 600 μg, per-oral)

Of these, oxytocin is used as the first-line agent in preventing postpartum hemorrhage. When oxytocin is not available, the other drugs mentioned above can be used based on the clinical condition and availability of the drug.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient of blunt chest trauma has been started on mechanical ventilation. Which of the following is not correct about the initial setting?
questions.raw_text: A patient of blunt chest trauma has been started on mechanical ventilation. Which of the following is not correct about the initial setting?
questions.correct_answer: D. Tidal volume - 12ml/kg of actual BW
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tidal volume - 12ml/kg of actual BW

The tidal volume of 12ml/kg of actual body weight is an incorrect initial setting for mechanical ventilation. 

Initial ventilatory settings are as given below:

  • Tidal volume - 4-6 ml/kg of IBW (Ideal Body Weight)
  • Respiratory rate - 12 Breaths/ min
  • FiO2 - 100% to begin with and titrated to lesser values to prevent oxygen toxicity
  • PEEP - Begin with 5 cm H2O, titrate to 10 cm H2O (Carefully increased as high PEEP may impair ventricular filling in a patient with blunt chest trauma)

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is defined as the emotional release and discharge after consciously reliving a painful experience that has been repressed?
questions.raw_text: What is defined as the emotional release and discharge after consciously reliving a painful experience that has been repressed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Abreaction

Abreaction is a psychoanalytical term for reliving an experience to release it emotionally. It is a specific type of catharsis done by becoming conscious of repressed traumatic events.

Catharsis is a general term for the process of releasing strong or repressed emotions. It can be done through various mediums, like expressing emotions through art. When the unconscious repressed memories are consciously recalled and relived, this technique specifically is called abreaction.

questions.text: Which of the following is typically not seen in allergic rhinitis?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is typically not seen in allergic rhinitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Otto Veraguth folds

Otto Veraguth folds are not seen in allergic rhinitis.

Otto Veraguth fold is a physical sign of depression wherein there is a triangular fold in the nasal corner of upper eyelid.

Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated immunological response of the nasal mucosa to allergens in the environment.

Patients typically present with recurrent bouts of sneezing, nasal obstruction, watery nasal discharge, and itching.

Clinical signs include:

  • Allergic shiners: dark circles around the eyes.
  • Allergic salute: black transverse nasal crease on the dorsum of the nose due to repeated upward rubbing.
  • Dennie-Morgan lines - transverse skin creases in the infraorbital area.

Allergic rhinitis can be classified into intermittent and persistent, based on the duration of the disease:

  • Intermittent- Symptoms are present for less than 4 days a week, or less than 4 weeks
  • Persistent- Symptoms are present for more than 4 days a week, or more than 4 weeks

It can be classified as mild, moderate, or severe based on the severity of the disease:

  • Mild- None of the following symptoms are present- sleep impairment, impairment of daily activities, school, or work, troublesome symptoms.
  • Moderate- severe: If at least one of the symptoms mentioned above are present.

A step-care approach is recommended for allergic rhinitis and its impact on asthma (ARIA) for the treatment of allergic rhinitis includes the following:

  • Oral antihistamines or intranasal cromolyn sodium are recommended for mild, intermittent disease. (option A).
  • Intranasal corticosteroids are used for moderate disease as monotherapy. (option B).
  • Oral antihistamines and intranasal steroids can be used in combination to treat severe diseases. (option C).
  • A short course of oral corticosteroids and immunotherapy can be used for severe, persistent disease in case the above intervention fails

In the given image, Otto Veraguth's sign or Veraguth's fold is shown, a diagonal palpebral fold running from the lateral corners of the eyes, medially upward to the medial end of the eyebrows. It is a physical sign of depression.

Another physical sign of depression is the Omega sign. In this, there is vertical wrinkling between the eyebrows joined at the top by a horizontal crease.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What could be the diagnosis of a woman with this appearance on x-ray?
questions.raw_text: What could be the diagnosis of a woman with this appearance on x-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Multiple enchondromas

The diagnosis of the woman is multiple enchondromas. The X-ray shows multiple calcified lesions in the fingers. 

Multiple enchondromatosis is also known as Ollier disease. It is a tumor in the metaphysis of long bones. There is a failure of bone formation and broadening of unossified cartilage within the bone. This results in shortening and angular deformity of the affected bones with an increased risk of pathological fractures. Enchondromas are also known as Maffucci syndrome if it is associated with overlying soft tissue hemangiomas. 25% of the patients with Ollier's disease will develop sarcomas by 40 years of age. 

X-ray shows intralesional calcifications with a popcorn appearance. Histologically, enchondromas consist of hyaline cartilage with cytologically benign chondrocytes. Treatment of multiple enchondromas includes correction by osteotomy if the deformities are obvious. 

Given below is an X-ray showing calcifications:

Other options:

Option A: Multiple brown tumors are caused secondary to hyperparathyroidism and resemble a giant-cell tumor. It can be diagnosed by estimating the levels of calcium, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone levels. The bone surrounding the lesion shows peritrabecular fibrosis.

The image below shows a brown tumor on the left hand:

Option B: Fibrous dysplasia is a condition characterized by the replacement of bone with fibrous tissue. The X-ray shows a ground-glass appearance with a well-defined sclerotic rim. It is seen in association with McCune-Albright syndrome. Shepherd’s crook deformity in the proximal femur is characteristic of fibrous dysplasia. 

The image below shows a child with McCune-Albright syndrome:

Option D: Multiple exostoses is an autosomal dominant type of osteochondroma that affects the phalanx, scaphoid, and metacarpals. The X-ray shows bony erosions and is excised. 

The image below shows exostoses at the base of the thumb:

A 29-year-old lady presented with polydipsia and polyuria. Her symptoms started soon after a road traffic accident 6 months ago. Her blood pressure was recorded at 120/80 mmHg with no postural drop. K = 3.5 mEq/ L

Urea = 15 mg/dl

Sugar = 65 mg/ dl

Plasma osmolality = 268 mOsm/L

Urine osmolality = 45 mOsm/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Psychogenic polydipsia

The most likely diagnosis for the given clinical scenario would be psychogenic polydipsia.

The normal range of urine osmolality is 500-850 mOsm/L and that of plasma osmolality is 280-295 mOsm/L. Hence in the given scenario, both urine and plasma osmolality are low, along with hyponatremia suggestive of psychogenic polydipsia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and was discharged after removing the drain tube on the first postoperative day. On day three, the patient came back to the hospital and was febrile. On ultrasound examination, there was a 5 x 5 cm collection in the subhepatic space. What is the next best step?
questions.raw_text: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and was discharged after removing the drain tube on the first postoperative day. On day three, the patient came back to the hospital and was febrile. On ultrasound examination, there was a 5 x 5 cm collection in the subhepatic space. What is the next best step?

options.label: A
options.text: To give oral antibiotics since the given accumulation is normal

options.label: B
options.text: To re-explore the wound and insert a T-tube

questions.correct_answer: C. Insert pigtail catheter for drainage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Insert pigtail catheter for drainage

The given clinical situation suggests a bile duct injury following laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The next best step after imaging would be to control inflammation by drainage of fluid collections by pigtail insertion and administration of broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-month-old baby was brought to the OPD with complaints of irritability, stiffness, and weakness of limbs. On examination, there was hypertonia of limbs. After a few months, the baby died due to the rapid progression of the disease. A brain autopsy was done and the following cells were seen. What are these cells?
questions.raw_text: A 5-month-old baby was brought to the OPD with complaints of irritability, stiffness, and weakness of limbs. On examination, there was hypertonia of limbs. After a few months, the baby died due to the rapid progression of the disease. A brain autopsy was done and the following cells were seen. What are these cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Macrophages

The clinical scenario showing motor symptoms and rapid progression to death, an autopsy of the brain showing globoid cells is highly suggestive of Krabbe's disease. The globoid cells are macrophages.

Krabbe's disease or globoid cell leukodystrophy is a neurodegenerative disorder with severe myelin destruction due to a deficiency of galactocerebroside β-galactosidase.

The onset of symptoms is between 3 to 6 months of age, dominated by motor signs such as stiffness and weakness. Survival beyond the age of 2 years is uncommon. The brain shows loss of myelin and oligodendrocytes with a similar process affecting the peripheral nerves.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the principle behind the wound-healing procedure shown in the image below?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is the principle behind the wound-healing procedure shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Negative pressure wound therapy

The given image shows negative pressure wound therapy using a vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) device to promote healing in chronic wounds.

Principle: An intermittent negative pressure of -125 mmHg hastens debridement and formation of granulation tissue in chronic wounds.

Indications: Chronic wounds (such as diabetic foot ulcers, stage III and IV pressure ulcers), traumatic wounds, flaps and grafts, and dehisced incisions.

Contraindications:

  1. Exposed vital structures (organs, blood vessels, or vascular grafts) 
  2. Preexisting infection 
  3. Inadequate debridement of devitalized soft tissue or bone increases the risk of infection.
  4. The presence of malignancy (Marjolin’s ulcer).
  5. An allergic reaction towards the adhesive used to maintain the vacuum seal.

Though not an absolute contraindication, there is no appreciable benefit for ischemic wounds.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The pelvic ultrasound of a 35-year-old woman is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: The pelvic ultrasound of a 35-year-old woman is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Monochorionic twins

The pelvic ultrasound in a 35-year-old woman shows the 'T-sign' seen in a monochorionic twin pregnancy.

In monochorionic pregnancy, the chorion does not extend between the layers of the intertwin membrane. Thus, the inter-twin membrane comes to an abrupt halt in a T-configuration at the edge of the amniotic sac. 

In contrast, in a dichorionic pregnancy, the sonographic image depicts a  'twin-peak' sign or the 'lambda sign" as the chorion is present between the intertwin membrane. A triangular portion of the placenta is seen inserted between the amniochorion layers.

The type of twin pregnancy is best diagnosed by transabdominal ultrasound at 11-14 weeks of gestation as the chorion and amnion are not yet fused. At 11-14 weeks, the intervening membranes are clearly visualized at the site of insertion of the amniotic membrane into the placenta. If not visualised transabdominally, transvaginal ultrasound is done.

Sonographic assessment is done by observing the following:

  Monochorionicity  Dichorionicity
Placental mass 1 2
Presence of intervening membrane T sign twin peak/ lambda/ delta sign
Thickness of intervening membrane <2mm ≥ 2mm

Pearl: Twinning

Pearl: Radiological Signs in Obstetrics

Bagel Sign (USG)

It is seen in unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy. It is also known as the tubal ring sign or the blob sign. It refers to the appearance of an anechoic gestational sac in the adnexa surrounded by a hyperechoic ring.

 

Twin Peak Sign/ Lambda Sign (USG)

Chorionicity of the placenta is best diagnosed by ultrasound at 10–13 weeks of gestation. In dichorionic twins, there is a thick triangular projection of placental tissue between the two gestational sacs. This is known as the lambda sign or twin peak sign.

 

T Sign (USG)

The T sign which is seen in monochorionic diamniotic gestation is thin and T-shaped because there is no extension of placental tissue or chorion in between the amniotic membranes.

 

Double Decidual Sac Sign (USG)

It is seen in early intrauterine pregnancy as two concentric echogenic rings surrounding the gestational sac.

 

Lemon Sign (USG)

At the level of the lateral ventricles, there is inward bowing or scalloping of frontal bones giving rise to the lemon sign. It is suggestive of spina bifida. It is also characteristically associated with Chiari II Malformation.

 

Banana Sign (USG)

Anterior curvature of the cerebellum with effacement of the cisterna magna in the posterior fossa is seen as banana sign. 

 

Spalding sign (USG)

It usually appears 7 days after intrauterine death and is caused by liquefaction of the brain matter and softening of the ligamentous structures supporting the vault, leading to irregular overlapping of the cranial bones on one another.

 

Frog Eye Sign (USG)

It is seen in anencephaly. Due to the absence of calvaria, the orbits appear more prominent. This is known as the "frog-eye sign". 

 

Omphalocele (USG)

It is a congenital midline abdominal wall defect at the base of the umbilical cord insertion, with herniation of the solid abdominal viscera and/or bowel out of the fetal abdomen  (indicated with an asterisk). The extruded abdominal contents are covered in a sac.

 

Double Bubble Sign (USG)

Dilatation of stomach and first part of duodenum due to duodenal atresia.

 

Bunch of grapes sign or Snowstorm appearance (USG) 

The appearance of multiple cystic spaces or lesions in a complete mole.

 

Ball sign (X-ray)

It is due to the crumpled up spine of the fetus seen in case of intrauterine death.

 

Robert’s sign (X-ray)

The presence of gas in the fetal great vessels in case of intrauterine fetal demise is known as Robert's sign.

 

Stuck twin sign (USG)

Smaller twin is held in a fixed position along the uterine wall due to the severe oligohydramnios. It is seen in twin-twin transfusion syndrome.

 

Butterfly sign (USG)

Normal appearance of the choroid plexuses on axial imaging of the fetal brain. An absence of this sign suggests holoprosencephaly.

 

Cloverleaf skull (USG)

Seen in craniosynostosis

 

Empty amnion sign (USG)

Visualization of an amniotic sac without concomitant visualization of an embryo. It is an indicator of pregnancy failure.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young girl presented to the OPD for examination. She is tall and thin with slender fingers, and dislocated lenses. Workup revealed cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. Which amino acid supplement is required in this case?
questions.raw_text: A young girl presented to the OPD for examination. She is tall and thin with slender fingers, and dislocated lenses. Workup revealed cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. Which amino acid supplement is required in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cysteine

The clinical picture of a tall and thin young girl with slender fingers, dislocated lenses, and cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is suggestive of classic homocystinuria. The amino acid supplement required in this scenario is cysteine.

Classic homocystinuria is a metabolic disorder of methionine metabolism, due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. It is an autosomal recessive condition.

Cystathionine beta-synthase is a pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme that condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine. The absence of this enzyme will cause cysteine deficiency, hence cysteine needs to be supplemented in the diet.

Clinical features:

  • Affected children are initially asymptomatic. 
  • Ectopia lentis (subluxation of the lens) is seen first, after 3 years of age.
  • Intellectual disability and psychiatric and behavioral disorders.
  • Thromboembolic episodes.
  • Skeletal abnormalities resembling those of Marfan syndrome: They are tall and thin with elongated limbs and arachnodactyly (slender fingers).

Elevations of both methionine and homocysteine in body fluids are the diagnostic laboratory findings. The diagnosis is established by molecular analysis of cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) or by assay of the enzyme in cultured fibroblasts, phytohemagglutinin-stimulated lymphocytes, or liver biopsy specimens. Treatment includes restriction of methionine intake and supplementation with cysteine, betaine, vitamins B6, B12, and folate.

 

The image below shows arachnodactyly. 

 Methionine supplementation is required in non-classical homocystinuria. It is due to impaired re-methylation of homocysteine to methionine. This can be caused by defective methionine synthase or reduced availability of two essential cofactors, 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, and methylcobalamin.

Elevated homocysteine levels with low levels of methionine will be seen. Treatment includes methionine supplementation and administration of methyl folate, hydroxocobalamin, and betaine.

Pearl: Homocystinuria

The concept for treatment:

  • Since homocysteine is produced from methionine, decreased dietary intake of methionine decreases the formation of homocysteine.
  • As the end product of this cycle is cysteine, increased dietary intake of cysteine will decrease the conversion of methionine to homocysteine through negative feedback.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In death due to firearm injury, the entry wound shows only an abrasion collar. The range of the firearm is:
questions.raw_text: In death due to firearm injury, the entry wound shows only an abrasion collar. The range of the firearm is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Distant range

The entry wound shows only an abrasion collar when the range of the firearm is distant. 

To determine the range of firing, the following parameters are used:

  • The entry wound size and shape
  • Blast effect – Muzzle end imprint and edge eversion
  • Blackening, Tattooing, Singeing of hair, Abrasion collar, and Grease collar
  • Hair should be preserved to determine the range of firing which can be examined for carbonization/desiccation in close range, also from lead deposition around the wound to assess the range of firing.

Abrasion collar: Gyroscopic movement of the bullet, the skin's elasticity, and the grease and dirt particles on the bullet's surface are the major causative factors of abrasion and grease collar. They are seen on the skin around the wound of entry at all ranges. Depending on the angle of entry made by the bullet, i.e.

  • A perpendicular entry of the bullet develops the abrasion collar of rounded shape.
  • An acute angular entry of the bullet develops the abrasion collar of an oblique or oval shape.
  • Some contusion present in the abraded collar is known as contusion collar

Grease collar: Mostly seen on the clothing and is seen as a black deposit, sharply outlined as if printed (better-seen on light color clothes and on fair-skinned individuals).

Medicolegal importance: Helpful in deriving information such as wound of entry and direction of firing

Note: A grease collar need not always be present. Hard metal jacketed bullets are associated less commonly with soiling. Often, the ring is not appreciable during gross inspection and may only be demonstrable on microscopic examination or other laboratory tests.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: You are conducting the routine newborn assessment of a 2.3 kg baby born 10 minutes back. You would classify the neonate as having cold stress if you notice the body temperature to be:
questions.raw_text: You are conducting the routine newborn assessment of a 2.3 kg baby born 10 minutes back. You would classify the neonate as having cold stress if you notice the body temperature to be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 36.0-36.4 °C

A temperature of 36.0 to 36.4°C categorizes a neonate as having cold stress.

An infant’s normal body temperature is 36.5 to 37.5 °C. It is measured in the apex of the baby's axilla by holding the thermometer for at least 3 minutes.

Hypothermia is an axillary temperature of <36.5 °C.

  • Cold stress: 36.0 to 36.4 °C
  • Moderate hypothermia: 32 to 35.9 °C
  • Severe hypothermia: <32 °C

Hyperthermia is an axillary temperature of >37.5 °C.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The type of hypoxia based on the graph is_____
(Consider the plot in red as normal)
questions.raw_text:
The type of hypoxia based on the graph is_____
(Consider the plot in red as normal)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anemic hypoxia

In the given graph, the X-axis represents the partial pressure of oxygen (PO2), and the Y-axis represents the blood oxygen content (ml/dl). The graph represents the curve that would be seen in anemic hypoxia and the normal oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.

The graph indicates two lines: a red line representing normal hemoglobin and a purple line representing reduced hemoglobin levels. The red line corresponds to an arterial blood oxygen content of approximately 19 mL/dL, and venous blood oxygen content of 14 mL/dL. On the other hand, the purple line represents an arterial blood oxygen content of 9 mL/dL and venous blood oxygen content of 4 mL/dL.

This scenario demonstrates a 50% decrease in blood oxygen content due to a decrease in the hemoglobin level, while the partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) remains within the normal range. This condition is characterized as anemic hypoxia.

The patients might not experience any difficulty during rest because 2,3-DPG increases in the red blood cells. However, they may have difficulty during exercise because of a limited ability to increase O2 delivery to the active tissues. 

Conditions that cause a right shift in the oxygen hemoglobin curve are: (Conditions with the increased requirement of O2 - metabolically active tissues)

  • Hypoxia
  • Hypercarbia
  • Decreased pH
  • Increased temperature
  • Increased 2,3-biphosphoglycerate

Conditions that cause a left shift in the oxygen hemoglobin curve 

  • Increased oxygen
  • Decreased carbon dioxide
  • Increased pH
  • Decreased temperature
  • Decreased 2,3-biphosphoglycerate
  • Fetal hemoglobin.

Pearl: Factors affecting 2,3 -DPG

↑ in 2, 3-DPG ↓ in 2, 3-DPG

  • Acclimitization (high altitude)
  • Thyroid hormone
  • Growth hormone

Pearl: P50

P50= the partial pressure of oxygen at which Hb is 50% saturated. Its value is about 26mmHg

When the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the right, P50 increases.

Or in other words, higher the P50, lower is the affinity of Hemoglobin for O2.

questions.text: A 54-year-old woman was diagnosed with advanced cervical cancer. She has a 14-year-old daughter. What advice would you give her daughter?
questions.raw_text: A 54-year-old woman was diagnosed with advanced cervical cancer. She has a 14-year-old daughter. What advice would you give her daughter?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Advise HPV vaccine

The patient's 14-year-old daughter should be advised to take the HPV vaccine.

The patient's daughter is not at a higher risk for developing cervical cancer because it does not run in families. The etiology of cervical cancer is related to human papilloma virus (HPV) infection, and immunization against the virus is protective. 

There are three types of available HPV vaccines, Cervarix, Gardasil, and Gardasil-9.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a village, it is observed that several farmers have crossed gait and use a stick for support to stand up and walk. Due to poor yield from farms, they consume meals containing rice and pulses only. Supplementing their diet with which of the following vitamins could have prevented this?
questions.raw_text: In a village, it is observed that several farmers have crossed gait and use a stick for support to stand up and walk. Due to poor yield from farms, they consume meals containing rice and pulses only. Supplementing their diet with which of the following vitamins could have prevented this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

The likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is neurolathyrism.  Administration of vitamin C at doses of 500-1000 mg is beneficial for this.

Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals. It is due to the consumption of khesari dal or Lathyrus sativus. When the husk is removed, it looks similar to red gram or Bengal gram. It is mostly consumed by poor agricultural laborers because it is relatively cheap. Lathyrism is more prevalent in parts of Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, and Bihar. The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act in India has banned Lathyrus sativus in all forms (whole/ split/ flour). 

In humans, it is referred to as neurolathyrism because it affects the nervous system, leading to progressive spastic paralysis of the lower limbs. Beta-oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA) is the toxic compound causing this disease. It is water-soluble and can be removed by the following methods:

  • Soaking pulses in hot water and discarding the water 
  • Overnight soaking in lime water, followed by boiling 
  • Parboiling - for large-scale detoxification
