questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a patient with thrombocytopenia, platelet transfusion is done when the platelet level drops below a threshold. To proceed with surgery, platelet transfusion is done to achieve a platelet level of?
questions.raw_text: In a patient with thrombocytopenia, platelet transfusion is done when the platelet level drops below a threshold. To proceed with surgery, platelet transfusion is done to achieve a platelet level of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 50,000

In an otherwise healthy patient, surgery can safely be performed in patients with platelet counts higher than 50,000/mm3. The risk of bleeding increases significantly if the platelet count is below this level. When platelet transfusions are used to treat thrombocytopenia, the platelet count rises by 10,000/mm3 for every unit transfused.

Thrombocytopenia is defined as a platelet count less than 1,50,000/mm3. It may be the result of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), drug-induced thrombocytopenia, rheumatological diseases (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis), pregnancy and chronic liver disease. The initial step if the patient has low platelet count is to repeat the test and examine the peripheral smear. 

Anemia is also a common preoperative hematological disorder. The optimal preoperative hemoglobin concentration varies between 7.5 to 10 g/dL across the individuals, with inter-individual differences due to co-morbid conditions in the patients. Patients with anemia or suspected anemia must undergo a battery of investigations to determine the type of anemia and how best to correct it. Preexisting anemia is a risk factor for postoperative death and complications such as AKI, stroke and infections.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with cyanosis. His chest radiograph is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A child presents with cyanosis. His chest radiograph is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

The given clinical scenario and chest X-ray showing a "coeur en sabot" or boot-shaped heart are suggestive of tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). 

TOF is a cyanotic congenital heart disease with the following four components:

  • Obstruction to right ventricular outflow (pulmonary stenosis)
  • Malalignment type of ventricular septal defect (VSD)
  • Dextroposition of the aorta so that it overrides the ventricular septum (overriding of the aorta), and
  • Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

In TOF, the enlarged right ventricle pushes the heart's apex upward, causing the cardiac shadow on an X-ray to appear as a boot-shaped heart or coeur en sabot as shown below:

 

Option B: Ebstein anomaly is a rare cyanotic congenital heart disease with diminished pulmonary blood flow due to abnormality of the tricuspid valve. 

In the Ebstein anomaly, there is severe right-sided cardiomegaly due to an elongated and enlarged right atrium, which leads to an elevated apex giving a box-shaped heart, as shown below:

 

Option C: Transposition of great arteries (TGA) can present from birth to infancy with cyanosis, decreased exercise tolerance, and poor physical development TGA is the most specific heart disease in infants of diabetic mothers. 

The following is a radiograph of TGA showing the egg-on-a-string appearance/egg-on-side appearance of the heart:

 

Option D: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVC) occurs due to the anomalous connection of pulmonary veins instead of joining to the left atrium resulting in pulmonary venous blood reaching the right atrium. 

In the supracardiac type of TAPVC, the configuration of the heart and the superior mediastinal borders resemble a snowman. It is also referred to as the figure of 8 sign, as shown below:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about retrosternal goitre?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements is true about retrosternal goitre?

options.label: A
options.text: Operated in all patients regardless of symptoms

options.label: B
options.text: Sternal incision is always required to operate

options.label: C
options.text: It receives blood supply from the thoracodorsal artery

options.label: D
options.text: Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision

questions.correct_answer: D. Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision

Most of the retrosternal goiters can be removed by neck incision (transcervical approach).

Retrosternal goitre is defined as having >50% of the goiter below the suprasternal notch. It can be either primary or secondary.

  • Primary: rare and arises from ectopic thyroid tissue in the mediastinum; receives blood supply from intrathoracic blood vessels. It is not related to thyroid tissue in the neck.
  • Secondary: they are the most common type; an extension of enlarged thyroid from the neck, usually arising from the lower pole of nodular goitre. It receives its blood supply from superior and inferior thyroid vessels.

The majority of patients are asymptomatic or have minimal symptoms. If the gland enlarges within the thoracic inlet, the pressure may lead to dysphagia, tracheal compression, and eventually airway symptoms. Pemberton sign can be positive (facial flushing and dilatation of cervical veins upon raising the arms above the head).

CECT neck and thorax is the investigation of choice.

Over 95% of retrosternal goiters can be removed via a transcervical incision since they are an extension from thyroid tissue in the neck.

Other options:

Option A: Surgical removal of the retrosternal goiter is indicated in patients with significant airway compression, and in young patients who have symptoms such as dyspnoea or dysphagia. 

Option B: Median sternotomy approach is indicated in:

  • Primary mediastinal goiter
  • Malignant retrosternal goitre
  • Very large retrosternal goiter
  • Recurrence in the mediastinum

For a primary mediastinal goiter whose boundaries are completely within the chest, resection is often achieved through median sternotomy or thoracotomy to ensure that the vessels supplying the tumor are properly ligated. Removing the tumor through a cervical approach can result in uncontrolled bleeding and is generally avoided. 

Option C: Blood supply to the retrosternal goiter is from the thyroid vessels (secondary retrosternal goiter).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the eye.
questions.raw_text: Identify the marked structure in the eye.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Canal of Petit

The marked structure represents the Canal of Petit. 

In front of the anterior hyaloid membrane and behind the ciliary body and zonule is the capsulohyaloid sinus (or space), or Petit's canal. This is one of the sites of retrolental hemorrhages. This is also the route along which blood sometimes enters the lens, through some rupture in the posterior lens capsule. 

Other options- 

Option A: Posterior capsule of lens has circular adhesions with anterior hyaloid surface called as the hyaloideocapsular ligaments of Weiger or retrolental ligament. The circular attachment is known as Egger's line. The potential space between the anterior hyaloid face and the posterior lense capsule with the circular attachment is referred to as the Berger's space.

Option B: Lens capsule is a thin, transparent, hyaline membrane surrounding the lens which is thicker over the anterior than the posterior surface

Option C: The canal of Hannover lies between orbiculo-anterocapsular and orbiculo-posterocapsular parts of zonular fibers.

questions.text: A 24-year-old patient comes to you with the following lesions. He tells you that he used to develop similar lesions since childhood but they always heal without scarring. His father also suffers from a similar condition. Which protein is defective in this patient?

This clinical scenario and the image showing superficial blisters are suggestive of epidermolysis bullosa simplex, which is an autosomal dominant condition associated with a defect in K5/K14 proteins.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study, first schools were sampled, then sections and finally students. What is this type of sampling known as?
questions.raw_text: In a study, first schools were sampled, then sections and finally students. What is this type of sampling known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Multistage sampling

Multistage sampling is the taking of samples in stages using smaller and smaller sampling units at each stage. It involves dividing the population into groups (or clusters). Then, one or more clusters are chosen at random and everyone within the chosen cluster is sampled.

Snowball sampling is a type of non-random sampling preferred in case of diseases with social stigma (eg., alcoholism, iv drug abuse etc).

Pearl: Sampling

1. Simple random sampling

  • In simple random sampling, samples are drawn in such a way that every element in a population has equal chances of being included.
  • Randomness refers to the method of picking the sample and not the outcome.

2. Stratified random sampling

  • In stratified random sampling, the population is first divided into homogeneous groups, or strata. From these strata, random samples are drawn.
  • For example, dividing a population into the strata of men, women, and children and then picking samples randomly from these strata.

3. Cluster sampling

  • In cluster sampling, the population is divided into internally heterogeneous groups. Then a simple random sampling is done of these clusters and taken as the samples.
  • In other words, the clusters are the sampling unit.
  • This is usually done when large-scale simple random sampling or stratified sampling is laborious or expensive.
  • This is the method used in assessing the immunization status of children.
  • Cluster sampling involves a design effect, which is an adjustment to allow for design structure. It aids in the correlation between clusters.
  • Multistage sampling is a form of cluster sampling, where sampling clusters are chosen from the already divided clusters.

4. Systematic random sampling

  • In systematic sampling, there is a systematic pattern to selecting the elements of a sample.
  • For example, every 3rd baby to be born can be selected.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with glaucoma presents with a bulging cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A patient with glaucoma presents with a bulging cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Staphyloma

High intraocular pressure leads to the thinning of the outer tunics of the eyeball such as cornea and sclera, thereby resulting in their ectasia (bulging) which is known as staphyloma. Ciliary and equatorial staphylomas are most commonly associated with glaucoma.

Staphyloma is an abnormal protrusion of the uveal tissue through a weak and thin portion of the cornea or sclera. So, staphyloma is lined internally by uveal tissue and externally by weak cornea or sclera.

Keratoconus (Option A) is a progressive bilateral corneal ectatic disorder due to defective synthesis of mucopolysaccharide and collagen tissue. It usually starts at puberty and progresses slowly, not associated with risk factors like glaucoma. Therefore, we can rule out keratoconus in this patient.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following diseases should healthcare workers involved in handling biomedical waste be vaccinated against?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following diseases should healthcare workers involved in handling biomedical waste be vaccinated against?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatitis B and tetanus

Healthcare workers involved in handling biomedical waste should be vaccinated against hepatitis B and tetanus.

These are most likely to be transmitted by the handling of biomedical waste. Yearly health check-ups should be done, and a booster dose should be given if needed.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding adipocere formation?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is false regarding adipocere formation?

options.label: A
options.text: Facial features are not preserved making identification difficult

options.label: B
options.text: It inhibits growth of putrefactive bacteria

options.label: C
options.text: It is commonly seen in bodies immersed in water

options.label: D
options.text: It has distinct offensive or sweetish smell

questions.correct_answer: A. Facial features are not preserved making identification difficult
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Facial features are not preserved making identification difficult

When the process involves the face, the features are well preserved, which helps to establish the identity.

Adipocere is a modification of putrefaction. In this, the fatty tissues of the body change into a substance known as adipocere. The change is due to the gradual hydrolysis and hydrogenation of fats forming insoluble soaps. These soaps are acidic, which prevents the growth of putrefactive bacteria.

Adipocere has a distinct offensive or sweetish smell, but during the early stages of its production, a penetrating ammoniacal odor is also noticed. A warm, moist, anaerobic environment favors adipocere formation e.g., bodies immersed in water.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a seizure. On evaluation, urine osmolality is 1000 mOsm/Kg and serum osmolality is 270 mOsm/Kg. Which electrolyte abnormality can be expected in this patient?
questions.raw_text: A patient presents with a seizure. On evaluation, urine osmolality is 1000 mOsm/Kg and serum osmolality is 270 mOsm/Kg. Which electrolyte abnormality can be expected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyponatremia

This patient has high urine osmolality of 1000 mOsm/kg (normal 500-800 mOsm/kg) and low plasma osmolality of 270 mOsm/kg (normal 285-295 mOsm/kg). This is seen in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone synthesis (SIADH) and hyponatremia is the most common electrolyte abnormality seen.

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone ADH release (SIADH) is a condition where there is an unsuppressed release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the pituitary gland or nonpituitary sources or its continued action on vasopressin receptors.

ADH promotes the reabsorption of water from the collecting duct. Excessive secretion of ADH in SIADH results in enhanced water reabsorption. Therefore, only water is reabsorbed and not the solutes resulting in concentrated urine. This is depicted as high urine osmolality. The excess of water reabsorbed from the tubules expand and dilute the extracellular fluid leading to dilutional hyponatremia. This is depicted as low plasma osmolality. 

Since there is an increase in body water with little or no change in body sodium in SIADH, this is known as euvolemic hyponatremia.

Patients may be asymptomatic or present with headache, confusion, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, seizures, and coma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida at 33 weeks of gestation was rushed to the hospital with recurrent seizures. Her husband says that prior to the seizures, she had complained of a headache and visual disturbances. She was on antihypertensives from the first trimester and there is no history of neurological disease. Which of the following is true regarding her management?
questions.raw_text: A primigravida at 33 weeks of gestation was rushed to the hospital with recurrent seizures. Her husband says that prior to the seizures, she had complained of a headache and visual disturbances. She was on antihypertensives from the first trimester and there is no history of neurological disease. Which of the following is true regarding her management?

options.label: A
options.text: First step of management is intravenous MgSO4

options.label: B
options.text: Diazepam is recommended as an anticonvulsant if MgSO4 fails

options.label: C
options.text: Treatment may be based on recommendations from the Magpie trial

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal alkalosis commonly occurs and needs correction

questions.correct_answer: C. Treatment may be based on recommendations from the Magpie trial
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Treatment may be based on recommendations from the Magpie trial

The clinical scenario is suggestive of eclampsia and management may be based on recommendations from the Magpie trial.

The advantage of the prophylactic use of magnesium sulfate in lowering the risk of eclampsia was given by the Magpie trial. Based on this recommendation, MgSO4 is administered to women having eclampsia to control the seizures and prevent further convulsions.

The following are the steps taken in the management of eclampsia:

  • The first step is maintaining the airway and ensuring oxygen delivery to both mother and fetus.
  • The next step is to administer MgSO4 to control seizures.
  • Antihypertensives are given to lower the blood pressure.
  • Finally, the pregnancy is terminated and the fetus is delivered.

Thiopentone > phenobarbitone may be used to control seizures. No attempt should be made to shorten the convulsion using diazepam as it often leads to thrombophlebitis and respiratory depression. 

Maternal acidosis usually occurs and is corrected when present.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text:
Arrange the following anesthetic agents on the basis of their potency.

Nitrous oxide

Halothane

Isoflurane

Methoxyflurane
questions.raw_text:
Arrange the following anesthetic agents on the basis of their potency.

Nitrous oxide

Halothane

Isoflurane

questions.correct_answer: A. Methoxyflurane> Halothane> Isoflurane> Nitrous oxide
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methoxyflurane> Halothane> Isoflurane> Nitrous oxide

The potency of the inhaled anesthetics given above can be arranged as methoxyflurane> halothane> isoflurane> nitrous oxide. It is due to the change in the agents' minimum alveolar concentration (MAC).

The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of an inhaled anesthetic is the lowest concentration required to prevent movement in response to a defined noxious stimulus in 50% of subjects. It is a measure of the potency of inhalational anesthetics. So, the lower the MAC value, the lower the concentration of anesthetic drug required, implying the drug is more potent.

MAC values (expressed as a '%' of 1 atmosphere) of some anesthetic agents:

  • Nitrous oxide with a MAC value of 104 is the least potent inhaled anesthetic
  • Methoxyflurane – MAC- 0.2 (most potent)
  • Desflurane: 6.0 
  • Sevoflurane– 2.05
  • Isoflurane – 1.28
  • Halothane – 0.75

Pearl: Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC)

Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) is the minimum concentration of an inhaled anesthetic at 1 atm of pressure that prevents skeletal muscle movement in response to a surgical incision in 50% of patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A lady presents with abdominal pain. USG reveals multiple gall stones with no wall thickening. CBD diameter is 12 mm and serum bilirubin was 0.8. Alkaline phosphatase is 380 and GGT is raised by 5 times. What is the next best step of management?
questions.raw_text: A lady presents with abdominal pain. USG reveals multiple gall stones with no wall thickening. CBD diameter is 12 mm and serum bilirubin was 0.8. Alkaline phosphatase is 380 and GGT is raised by 5 times. What is the next best step of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRCP

In this clinical scenario, a patient with gallstones, a dilated common bile duct, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase level raises suspicion for common bile duct stones. The next best step would be to perform magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) to confirm their presence.

A dilated common bile duct (>8 mm) detected on ultrasound in a patient with gallstones, jaundice, biliary pain and an abnormal liver function panel (elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases; but these can be normal in some cases) strongly indicates the presence of common bile duct stones (choledocholithiasis).

If there is uncertainty regarding the presence of bile duct stones, as in this case where bilirubin levels are normal, MRCP offers precise anatomical visualization and exhibits high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing choledocholithiasis.

While endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is also highly effective in diagnosing choledocholithiasis, due to its invasive nature and the risks associated with the procedure, it is rarely used as a purely diagnostic modality. Instead, it is reserved for cases in which a therapeutic intervention, such as stone extraction or sphincterotomy, is planned.

Treatment options:

  • ERCP along with sphincterotomy and stone removal.
  • Laparoscopic common bile duct exploration
  • Open common bile duct exploration is only done when endoscopic and laparoscopic methods are not feasible or when concomitant biliary drainage is needed.

Pearl: Diagnostic Evaluation of the Bile Ducts

Diagnostic Evaluation of the Bile Ducts

  • Hepatobiliary ultrasound: Initial procedure of choice in investigating possible biliary tract obstruction
  • CT scan: Procedure of choice in investigating possible biliary obstruction if diagnostic limitations prevent HBUS
  • MRCP: Useful modality for visualizing pancreatic and biliary ducts
  • ERCP: Best visualisation of distal biliary tract
    • Endoscopic sphincterotomy and stone removal can also be done
  • PTC(Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography): Best visualisation of proximal biliary tract
    • Indicated when ERCP is contraindicated or failed
  • EUS: Most sensitive method to detect ampullary stones

Pearl: Diagnostic Evaluation of the Gall Bladder

  • Gallbladder Ultrasound: Investigation of choice for detection of gall stones
  • Abdominal X-ray: Useful in 
    • Calcified gall stones
    • Emphysematous cholecystitis
    • Porcelain gallbladder
    • Limey bile
    • Gallstone ileus
  • Radioisotope scans (HIDA/DIDA/DISIDA)
    • Indicated for confirmation of suspected acute cholecystitis
    • Useful in diagnosis of acalculous cholecystopathy

Abbreviations:

  • HIDA: Hepatobiliary IminoDiacetic Acid scan
  • DIDA/DISDA: Di-isopropyl IminoDiacetic Acid - Dynamic Tc99m DIDA Cholescintigraphy

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is not associated with autism spectrum disorder?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not associated with autism spectrum disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Early development of handedness

Children with autism spectrum disorder do not show early handedness and lateralization and remain ambidextrous at an age when cerebral dominance is established in most children.

Other findings that may be present in autism spectrum disorders (not core diagnostic criteria) include:

  • Higher incidence of abnormal dermatoglyphics (e.g., fingerprints)
  • Deficits in language development
  • Intellectual disability
  • Hypo/hyper-response to sensory stimuli (e.g., no response to loud sound/ keen response to ticking of a watch)
  • Hyperactivity and inattention
  • Precocious skills (e.g., prodigious route memories or calculating abilities)
  • Insomnia

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which serotype of HPV is responsible for carcinoma cervix?
questions.raw_text: Which serotype of HPV is responsible for carcinoma cervix?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 16, 18, 31, 33

HPV serotypes 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 52, 56, 58, 59, 68 are associated with carcinoma cervix.

Risk factors for carcinoma cervix include:

  • Human Papilloma virus (most important)
  • Sexual intercourse before 18 years
  • Multiple sexual partners
  • Multiparity
  • Poor personal hygiene
  • Smoking and drug abuse
  • Women with STD, HIV, HSV 
  • Immune suppression

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or southern blot or Hybrid capture technique is used for HPV DNA detection.

questions.text: The inclusion body rickettsial morula is found in neutrophils during infection caused by:
questions.raw_text: The inclusion body rickettsial morula is found in neutrophils during infection caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anaplasma phagocytophilum

The inclusion body rickettsial morula is found in granulocytes (neutrophils) during infection caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum. 

Anaplasma causes human granulocyte anaplasmosis. It is transmitted by ticks. Clinical features are fever, headache, confusion, vomiting and myalgia. Inclusions in granulocytes are seen. The image below shows a morula of Anaplasma in a neutrophil:

Ehrlichia chaffeensis is a gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium that is transmitted by hard ticks such as the lone star tick. Clinical presentation of Ehrlichia chaffeensis infection is similar to that of Anaplasma infection. Severe human monocytic ehrlichiosis is characterized by meningoencephalitis, renal failure, respiratory failure, and shock. The treatment of choice for human monocytic ehrlichiosis is doxycycline. 

The image below shows a morula of Ehrlichia in a monocyte:

Note: Infection by both Anaplasma and Ehrlichia can lead to the formation of rickettsial morulas in leukocytes. However, Anaplasma leads to the formation of morulas predominantly in the granulocytes, whereas Ehrlichia predominantly affects the monocytes.

Other options:

Option A: Rickettsia rickettsii causes rocky mountain spotted fever. It is transmitted by ticks. Patients present with fever, headache, and rash.

Option B: Rickettsia conorii causes Mediterranean spotted fever. The parasite is transmitted by ticks, and the patients present with fever, headache, rash, and eschar (tache noire).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An infant has a congenital bronchopulmonary malformation as shown in the CT scan given below. Which of the following is most likely to supply the marked structure?
questions.raw_text: An infant has a congenital bronchopulmonary malformation as shown in the CT scan given below. Which of the following is most likely to supply the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thoracic aorta

The given CT shows an intralobar pulmonary sequestration of the left lung. The thoracic aorta commonly supplies the sequestered lobe of the lung.

Pulmonary sequestration is an area of embryonic lung tissue, separate from the lung. It receives blood supply from an anomalous systemic artery from the aorta. It is of two types:

  • Intralobar sequestration: Located within normal lung tissue (usually lower lobes, >95%), shares the same pleura, and receives blood from the descending thoracic aorta with pulmonary venous drainage.

  • Extralobar sequestration: Lies outside the normal lung, enclosed in its own pleura, usually left-sided (66%), with systemic arterial supply from the thoracic or upper abdominal aorta and venous drainage to systemic veins (azygos/hemiazygos).

Treatment involves resection of the pulmonary sequestration.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study, two groups of newborns are checked for differences in their birth weights based on whether mothers received supplements or not. Which of the following would be most appropriate test of significance?
questions.raw_text: In a study, two groups of newborns are checked for differences in their birth weights based on whether mothers received supplements or not. Which of the following would be most appropriate test of significance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Un-paired t test

The unpaired t-test is used to test the difference between two groups of parametric variables or means when the samples are independent of each other. Here, birth weights (quantitative variable) of the two groups of newborns are being compared, which are independent of each other.

Pearl: Tests of Significance

How to choose which test to use?

  • See the variable. Are the variables quantitative or qualitative?
    • If the variables are qualitative (nominal), then Chi square test is used.
    • If the variables are quantitative, then see whether 2 groups or more than 2 groups .
      • If 2 groups are being tested, then T tests are used. In that, if the same group is tested before and after, paired T test is used. Otherwise, unpaired T test is used.
      • If more than 2 groups are being tested, then use ANOVA.

1. T Tests

  • Unpaired t tests
    • Also known as the student’s t test, independent t test, two-samples t test.
    • It's the most commonly used t test and it tests the difference between two groups (the means of 2 groups) independent of each other and indicates how significant the differences are.
  • Paired t tests
    • "Pairs before marriage are not the same after!"
    • So remember the paired test is mainly used in the comparison of a before and after scenario 
    • Also known as correlated t test, dependent samples t test.
    • It is mainly used on dependent samples. For example, the cholesterol level of a person before and after using a specific drug.
    • It can also be used when you put the same condition under test using different items or things. For example, same crash safety tests for different cars.
  • T scores 
    • The t score is referred to as the ratio of the difference between two groups and the difference within the groups.
    • The smaller the t score, the more similarity there is between two groups and vice versa.

 

2. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)

  • The analysis of variance test (ANOVA) is used to test the difference between two or usually more than two groups (means) and here the inferences are made by analyzing the variances.

 

3. Chi-Square Test

  • The Chi-Square test (χ2) is a non-parametric(non-numeric) test and it is used to test hypotheses in relation to nominal scale data or categorical data.
  • It is a test of proportions and associations.
  • A Chi-square distribution is usually positively skewed but it approaches a normal distribution as its degrees of freedom increases.
  • If the frequency of any of the cells of the categorical table is <5, then Fisher’s exact test is used.

Tafenoquine is used in the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax. Total eradication of the Plasmodium species, which includes the clinical curative and hypnozoites phase, is called a radical cure.

questions.text: An HIV-positive patient on ART with zidovudine, lamivudine, and indinavir develops pulmonary tuberculosis. Which of the following anti-tubercular drugs should be avoided in him?
questions.raw_text: An HIV-positive patient on ART with zidovudine, lamivudine, and indinavir develops pulmonary tuberculosis. Which of the following anti-tubercular drugs should be avoided in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rifampicin

Rifampicin should be avoided as it is a potent inducer of CYP enzymes, including CYPs 1A2, 3A4, 2C9, and 2C19, which in turn can induce the metabolism of indinavir and result in therapeutic failure of ART.

Rifabutin causes the least induction of cytochrome enzymes and is therefore preferred in HIV patients who are on protease inhibitors/NNRTIs.

Cytochrome enzyme-inducing potency of rifamycins is: rifampicin > rifapentine > rifabutin.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant lady of 49 kg is in her first trimester. What are her additional calorie requirements in this trimester?
questions.raw_text: A pregnant lady of 49 kg is in her first trimester. What are her additional calorie requirements in this trimester?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Continue same diet

The pregnant lady can continue the same diet since there are no additional calorie requirements in the first trimester.

Pregnancy requires an additional 80,000 kcal, mostly during the last 20 weeks. To meet this demand, a caloric increase of 100 to 300 kcal/d is recommended during pregnancy. This greater intake, however, should not be divided equally during the course of pregnancy. The Institute of Medicine (2006) recommends adding 0, 340, and 452 kcal/d to the estimated nonpregnant energy requirements in the first, second, and third trimesters respectively. 

Whenever caloric intake is inadequate, protein is metabolized rather than being spared for its vital role in fetal growth and development.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An old lady slipped and fell at home. She was diagnosed with a Colles' fracture and managed with a POP cast. What is the correct sequence of reduction?
questions.raw_text: An old lady slipped and fell at home. She was diagnosed with a Colles' fracture and managed with a POP cast. What is the correct sequence of reduction?

options.label: A
options.text: Traction, POP, palmar flexion, ulnar deviation

options.label: B
options.text: Traction, palmar flexion, ulnar deviation, POP

options.label: C
options.text: Traction, ulnar deviation, palmar flexion, POP

options.label: D
options.text: Palmar flexion, ulnar deviation, traction, POP

questions.correct_answer: B. Traction, palmar flexion, ulnar deviation, POP
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Traction, palmar flexion, ulnar deviation, POP

The correct order of reduction of Colles' fracture is traction, palmar flexion, ulnar deviation, POP.

Colle's fracture refers to the extra-articular fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation of the distal bone fragment.

Displacements that may be seen in Colles' fracture are:

  • Impaction of fragments
  • Dorsal tilt
  • Dorsal displacement
  • Lateral tilt (radial tilt)
  • Lateral displacement (radial displacement)
  • Supination

The patient usually presents with pain, swelling, and deformity of the wrist. There may be a typical 'dinner-fork deformity' where the radial styloid process comes to lie at the same level or a little higher than the ulnar styloid process. A dorsal tilt is characteristic and is seen on a lateral x-ray.

Management of Colles' fracture:

  • Undisplaced fractures: immobilization in a below-elbow plaster cast for 6 weeks
  • Displaced fractures: closed manipulative reduction and immobilization in Colles' cast. The technique of reduction of Colles' fracture is as follows: 
    • Dis-impaction of the fracture fragments by longitudinal traction against counter traction provided by the assistant. 
    • The distal fragment is then pressed into palmar flexion followed by ulnar deviation.
    • The patient's hand is drawn into pronation, palmar flexion, and ulnar deviation.
    • A Colles' cast is then applied, extending from below the elbow to the metacarpal heads, with the wrist in palmar flexion and ulnar deviation. 
    • Surgical correction is advisable for comminuted fractures, especially in young adults where the dominant hand is involved. It can be with percutaneous K-wire fixation, external fixators, or locking compression plates.

Complications:

  • Stiffness of joints - finger stiffness is commonly seen
  • Malunion - can produce dinner-fork deformity
  • Subluxation of the inferior radio-ulnar joint
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome - uncommon
  • Sudek's osteodystrophy - Colles' fracture is the commonest cause of this condition in the upper limb.
  • Rupture of extensor pollicis longus tendon - extremely rare

Pearl: Named fractures of the upper limb

Colle's fracture: Extra-articular fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation of the distal bone fragment.

 

Galeazzi fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the lower third of the radius and subluxation of the distal radio-ulnar joint.

 

Monteggia fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the shaft of the ulna with dislocation of a proximal radio-ulnar joint.

 

Barton’s fracture: Intra-articular fracture of the distal radius. Barton's fracture can be dorsal or volar (reverse Barton's).

 

Rolando's fracture: Intra-articular comminuted fracture of the base of the first metacarpal with a T or Y configuration.

 

Smith's fracture: Reverse Colles' fracture. Extra-articular fracture of the distal one-third of the radius with palmar or ventral displacement (Image below).

 

Chauffeur's fracture or the Hutchinson fracture: Fracture of the radial styloid.

Essex–Lopresti lesion: Fracture of the radial head with disruption of the interosseous membrane and distal radial ulnar joint ligaments.

Nightstick fracture: Isolated fracture of radial or ulnar bone.

questions.text: A woman presents with impaired hearing. Her audiogram findings are given below. Pick the right combination of tuning fork test results that would be seen in this patient.
questions.raw_text: A woman presents with impaired hearing. Her audiogram findings are given below. Pick the right combination of tuning fork test results that would be seen in this patient.

options.label: A
options.text: Left Rinne's test negative, Weber's test lateralized to right ear

options.label: B
options.text: Left Rinne's test negative, Weber's test lateralized to left ear

options.label: C
options.text: Left  Rinne's test positive, Weber's test lateralized to right ear

options.label: D
options.text: Left Rinne's test positive, Weber's test lateralized to left ear

questions.correct_answer: C. Left  Rinne's test positive, Weber's test lateralized to right ear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left Rinne's test positive, Weber's test lateralized to right ear

The given audiogram findings indicate sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear. Tuning fork tests in this patient would show left Rinnie's positive and Weber lateralized to the right ear.

In left sensorineural hearing loss, Rinne's test will be positive on both left and right ears, and Weber's test will be lateralized to the better ear, which is the right.

Tuning fork tests are performed commonly with tuning forks of frequencies such as 128, 256, 512, 1024, etc. The tuning fork of 512 Hz is considered ideal as forks of lower frequencies produce a sense of bone vibration, while those of higher frequencies have a shorter decay time.

Rinne’s test is done by placing a vibrating tuning fork on the patient’s mastoid and when he/she stops hearing, it is brought beside the external auditory meatus (EAC). If he/she still hears the sound, air conduction (AC) is better than bone conduction (BC).

Weber test is done by placing a vibrating tuning in the middle of the forehead or the vertex and the patient is asked in which ear the sound is better heard.

Pearl: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its intensity can be increased or decreased by 5dB.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:
  • For AC: 15 dB
  • For BC: 25 dB

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who is on treatment for hyperlipidemia develops gallstones. What is the mechanism of action of the causative drug that was given to this patient?
questions.raw_text: A patient who is on treatment for hyperlipidemia develops gallstones. What is the mechanism of action of the causative drug that was given to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Activates PPAR alpha

The antilipidemic drugs likely to cause gallstones are the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) that act by activating PPAR alpha.

PPARs are a superfamily of nuclear receptors involved in the regulation of energy homeostasis and metabolic function. It has three subtypes:

  • PPARα - reduces triglyceride level 
  • PPARγ - causes insulin sensitization 
  • PPARδ - enhances fatty acids metabolism

Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) is a key enzyme in the degradation of VLDL. Fibrates bind to PPAR alpha and cause stimulation of lipoprotein lipase enzyme. Increased LPL synthesis enhances the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Additionally, fibrates also stimulate fatty acid oxidation and reduce the expression of apo C-III (inhibitor of lipolysis). All fibrates increase the lithogenicity of bile, thereby increasing the risk of gall stones

Other options: 

Class HMG- CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) Niacin Bile acid-binding resins

Colestipol,
colesevelam

Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase

Reduces LDL levels

  • Significant increase HDL levels

  • Elevations of serum amino-transferase activity

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the function of the proteasome?
questions.raw_text: What is the function of the proteasome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Protein degradation

The proteasome takes part in protein degradation. 

The proteasome is a cylindrical structure in the cytosol that degrades polyubiquitinated proteins. It has a central core with proteolytic enzymes. Proteins that are tagged by ubiquitin to be degraded enter the core through regulatory rings on either side of the cylinder.

Clinical relevance: It plays an important role in antigen presentation to T lymphocytes as it degrades viruses and other molecules to small peptides.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presented to the OPD with long hands and feet, and a protruding lower jaw. Which of the following genes is most likely implicated in this scenario?
questions.raw_text: A patient presented to the OPD with long hands and feet, and a protruding lower jaw. Which of the following genes is most likely implicated in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PIT1

Mutations of the pituitary-specific gene PIT-1 can lead to the development of a somatotroph adenoma which produces elevated levels of GH Growth hormone (and IGF-1) which can lead to acromegaly as given in the clinical scenario above.

Somatotrophs, mammosomatotrophs, and lactotrophs are derived from stem cells that express the pituitary transcription factor, PIT-1.

If the increased levels of GH are present after closure of the epiphyses, acromegaly develops. In this condition, growth is most conspicuously seen in

  • Skin and soft tissues, viscera (thyroid, heart, liver, and adrenals).
  • The bones of the face, hands, and feet are thickened and enlarged.
  • Bone density may increase (hyperostosis) in both the spine and the hips.
  • Enlargement and protusion of the jaw is seen (prognathism), and broadening of the lower face.
  • The feet and hands are enlarged, and the fingers become thickened and sausage-like.

GH excess can also be associated with a variety of other manifestatiions, like gonadal dysfunction, diabetes mellitus, generalized muscle weakness, hypertension, arthritis, congestive heart failure, and an increased risk of gastrointestinal cancers.

Other options:

Steroidogenic factor -1 (SF-1) and GATA-2 are factors that are required for gonadotroph differentiation.

questions.correct_answer: A. Gross Domestic Product- gross income generated only from within the country
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gross Domestic Product- gross income generated only from within the country

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the income generated only from within the country and does not include income received from abroad.

Pearl: Economics

  • Gross National Income (GNI):
    • It is also known as the gross national product (GNP). It is the gross income generated from within the country as well as the income received from abroad. It is expressed as either ‘at current prices’ or ‘at constant prices’.
  • Per capita income:
    • It is arrived at by dividing the GNP by the total population of a country. It is a general indicator of national wealth.
  • Gross Domestic Product (GDP):
    • It is the gross income generated only from within the country. It doesn’t include income from abroad.
  • Net National Product (NNP):
    • It is the market value of all final goods and services in a country during a year after depreciation has been allowed for.
  • Net Domestic Product (NDP):
    • It is gross domestic product (GDP) minus the depreciation of a country’s capital goods.
  • Purchasing Power Parity (PPP):
    • It is an economic theory that compares the currencies of different countries through a market basket of goods approach. According to this concept, two currencies are in equilibrium when a market basket of goods is priced the same in both countries.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of triazoles?
questions.raw_text: What is the mechanism of triazoles?

options.label: A
options.text: Interferes with DNA and RNA synthesis

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibits epoxidation of squalene in fungi

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of ergosterol synthesis

Triazoles act by inhibiting ergosterol synthesis.

The azole group inhibits the fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme called 14-α-sterol demethylase and results in an impairment of the conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol. This results in the depletion of membrane ergosterol.

Azole antifungals are of two types:

  • Imidazoles - clotrimazole, ketoconazole, luliconazole
  • Triazoles - itraconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole and isavuconazole

Pearl: Mechanism of action of Antifungal drugs

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: ETDRS study was related to?
questions.raw_text: ETDRS study was related to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetic macular edema

Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) was a randomized clinical trial that studied the effect of photocoagulation on diabetic macular edema. 

The results of the study demonstrated the beneficial effects of focal photocoagulation on diabetic macular edema. The study resulted in the recommendation that all eyes with clinically significant diabetic macular edema should be considered for focal photocoagulation. 

Pearl: Early treatment diabetic retinopathy study (ETDRS) classification

Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR):

  • Mild NPDR
    • At least one microaneurysm must be present
  • Moderate NPDR
    • Microaneurysms/intraretinal hemorrhage in 2 or 3 quadrants
    • Early mild intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA)
    • Hard exudates and cotton-wool spots may or may not be present
  • Severe NPDR - any one of the following (4-2-1 rule)
    • 4 quadrants of microaneurysms and extensive intraretinal hemorrhages
    • 2 quadrants of venous beading
    • 1 quadrant of IRMA changes
  • Very severe NPDR - any two of the following (4-2-1)
    • 4 quadrants of microaneurysms and extensive intraretinal hemorrhages
    • 2 quadrants of venous beading
    • 1 quadrant of IRMA changes

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR):

  • PDR without high-risk characteristics (Early PDR)
    • Early neovascularization at the optic disc (NVD) or neovascularization elsewhere (NVE)
  • PDR with high-risk characteristics as follows
    • NVD < 1/4 disc area with vitreous hemorrhage (VH) or preretinal hemorrhage (PRH)
    • NVD 1/4 to 1/3 of disc area with or without VH or PRH
    • NVE > 1/2 disc area with VH or PRH

Clinically significant macular edema: 1 of the following 3 criteria are present on slit-lamp examination with 90D lens

  • Thickening of the retina at or within 500 micron of the center of the fovea.
  • Hard exudates at or within 500 micron of the centre of fovea associated with adjacent retinal thickening.
  • Development of a zone of retinal thickening one disc diameter or larger in size. At least a part of this should be within one disc diameter of the foveal center.

Advanced diabetic eye disease:

  • Persistent vitreous hemorrhage
  • Tractional retinal detachment
  • Neovascular glaucoma

With regard to forced alkaline diuresis, which of the following pairs is true?
  Type of poison ingested Reagent used
1 Weak acids Acetazolamide
2 Weak bases Acetazolamide
3 Weak bases Sodium bicarbonate
4 Weak acids Sodium bicarbonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

Urinary alkalinization (forced alkaline diuresis) is most effective for weak acids, primarily eliminated by the renal tract. It is performed with sodium bicarbonate.

Acetazolamide should not be used to produce alkaline urine, because it may worsen toxicity by causing a concomitant systemic acidosis. It results in an increase in the amount of the unionized drug in the blood and enhanced tissue distribution. It may also compete with acidic drugs for tubular secretion and thereby inhibit their elimination.

Drugs most commonly treated with forced alkaline diuresis are salicylates and phenobarbital.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The most appropriate expansion of Apgar is:
questions.raw_text: The most appropriate expansion of Apgar is:
questions.correct_answer: C. Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration

The parameters to consider while calculating APGAR score in newborn babies are:

  1. Appearance
  2. Pulse rate
  3. Grimace
  4. Activity(muscle tone)
  5. Respiratory effort

The Apgar score is a systematic way of assessing the infant after birth at 1 and 5 minutes of life. It gives a maximum score of 10 which indicates the newborn is in the best possible condition.

Changes in the Apgar scores denote the response of the infant to resuscitation. Apgar scores should not be used to determine the need for resuscitation or to guide the steps of resuscitation. Apgar score alone should not be interpreted as evidence of asphyxia.

A score from 7-10 is considered normal. Scores between 0-3 require immediate resuscitation. If the score at 5 minutes remains less than 7, the infant should be assessed again every 5 minutes for the next 20 minutes.

Causes for false positive APGAR score are:

  • Prematurity
  • Drugs like analgesics, narcotics, sedatives, magnesium sulfate
  • Acute cerebral trauma
  • Precipitous delivery
  • Airway obstruction (choanal atresia)  
  • Congenital pneumonia or sepsis
  • Hemorrhage- hypovolemia

False-negative Apgar score is seen in maternal acidosis and high fetal catecholamine levels.

Pearl: APGAR score

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following agents cause hydrops fetalis?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following agents cause hydrops fetalis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parvovirus

Parvovirus B19 is the most common infectious cause of nonimmune hydrops fetalis. Parvovirus B19 infects fetal erythroid progenitor cells and causes anemia. Severe anemia leads to high-output cardiac failure and nonimmune hydrops fetalis. 

Hydrops is diagnosed by identifying two or more fetal effusions, such as pleural, pericardial, or ascitic effusions, or the presence of one effusion along with anasarca. Hydrops can be seen in association with red cell auto immunization, which is termed immune hydrops. Otherwise, it is nonimmune. 

Nonimmune hydrops is more common than immune hydrops. Causes of nonimmune hydrops include cardiac pathology (Ebstein anomaly), chromosomal (Turner's syndrome), hematological (hemoglobinopathies), lymphatic abnormalities (cystic hygroma), and thoracic abnormalities. 

Infectious causes of nonimmune hydrops are parvovirus B19 (most common), syphilis, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella, enterovirus, varicella, herpes simplex, coxsackievirus, listeriosis, leptospirosis, Chagas disease, and Lyme disease.

options.label: D
options.text: Bone Marrow biopsy with reticulin stain

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Erythropoietin levels

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of polycythemia (Hb>16 g/dL). Hence, erythropoietin levels (EPO) are estimated next, to differentiate between primary or secondary polycythemia. Based on EPO levels:

  • Primary polycythemia - normal/ decreased
  • Secondary polycythemia - increased

Options A and B: JAK 2 mutation and Philadelphia chromosome analysis is only done as a last resort.

Option D: Bone marrow estimation with reticulin is done for myelofibrosis which can be seen in the spent/ late stage of the disease. However, peripheral smear findings are not suggestive of primary myelofibrosis. Leukoerythroblastic reaction with dacrocytes is seen in myelofibrosis.

Major criteria:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which statement regarding HIV infection is true?
questions.raw_text: Which statement regarding HIV infection is true?

options.label: A
options.text: HIV-2 is more pathogenic than HIV -1

options.label: B
options.text: HIV-1 subtype C is the most common form worldwide

options.label: D
options.text: Donated blood is not screened for HIV- 2

questions.correct_answer: B. HIV-1 subtype C is the most common form worldwide
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HIV-1 subtype C is the most common form worldwide

HIV-1 subtype C is the most common form worldwide.

Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has two serotypes HIV-1 and HIV- 2 based on differences in the env (envelope) gene. 

HIV-1 is further divided into 4 distinct groups, group M (major)/N/O/P. The M group comprises nine subtypes A, B, C, D, F, G, H, J, and K.

  • Subtype C is the most common form worldwide & is more associated with heterosexual transmission.
  • Subtype B is more associated with spread through blood and homosexual contact.

Options A, C: HIV- 2 is less pathogenic than HIV-1 and is predominantly confined to Africa.

Option D: Donated blood is screened for both HIV -1 & HIV-2.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant female with known cardiac disease presents in the first trimester with history of warfarin embryopathy. What should be advised now?
questions.raw_text: A pregnant female with known cardiac disease presents in the first trimester with history of warfarin embryopathy. What should be advised now?

options.label: B
options.text: Replace warfarin with heparin in first trimester

questions.correct_answer: B. Replace warfarin with heparin in first trimester
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Replace warfarin with heparin in first trimester

In the first trimester, warfarin has to be replaced with heparin due to its potential teratogenic effects such as miscarriage, stillbirths, achondroplasia and stippled epiphyses.

Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) must replace warfarin and shouldn’t be added along with the warfarin (Option D).

The detailed guideline for anticoagulation in pregnancy is as follows:

Period of pregnancy Anticoagulation of choice
First trimester

If dose of warfarin < 5mg/day– continue warfarin till 36 weeks

If dose of warfarin > 5mg /day or warfarin embryopathy – replace it with heparin / LMWH
From 12 weeks to 36 weeks warfarin
At 36 weeks Switch to LMWH
1 week before EDD / 3 days before EDD Switch to UFH (as LMWH have longer T1/2– chances of PPH)
On the day of delivery Stop all anticoagulantS
6 hrs after vaginal delivery / 6-12 hrs after cesarean   Restart UFH and warfarin.When INR is 2.5 to 3 withdraw UFH & continue warfarin

  • EDD: expected date of delivery
  • UFH: unfractionated heparin
  • PPH: postpartum hemorrhage

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3, 6

A child presenting with abrasion with slight oozing after a dog bite comes under category III. The correct statements are 1, 2, 3, and 6.

The following measures should be taken immediately to stop the contraction of rabies:

  • Cleansing: The most important step in the prevention of rabies is washing the affected area with plenty of soap and water under a running tap for 15 minutes. This is a standard procedure that minimizes the contraction of rabies.
  • Chemical treatment: After washing and drying the wound, disinfectants like povidone-iodine and spirit can be applied.
  • Suturing: Bite wounds are not sutured generally. If suturing is unavoidable, rabies immunoglobulin should be infiltrated in the depth and around the wound, and suturing should be delayed by a few hours.
  • In unavoidable situations, minimal loose sutures may be applied to arrest bleeding.
  • Other measures: Local antibiotics and tetanus toxoids should be given.

Post-exposure prophylaxis regimen for rabies:

Intramuscular regimen: In this regimen, 1 ml or 0.5 ml of vaccine is injected into the deltoid in patients with category II and III wounds.

  • Essen regimen: A 5-dose regimen in which 1 dose of vaccine is given on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28.
  • Zagreb regimen: A 4-dose multisite regimen in which 2 doses of vaccine are given on day 0, followed by 1 dose on days 7 and 21.

Intradermal regimen: In this regimen, 0.1 ml of injection is given at 2 sites on days 0, 3, 7, and 28.

Equine Rabies Immunoglobulin at a dose of 40 IU/kg (a maximum of 3000 IU) body weight is given once. It is given to all Category III bites and also Category II bites in the case of immune-compromised persons.

Pearl: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted). There are no contraindications to post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies. It can be safely administered to pregnant women, infants, and immunocompromised individuals.

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG): 

  • Passive immunization
  • Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine
  • Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight
  • Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.
  • Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

  • RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.
  • The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.
  • RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

  1. Multiple bites
  2. Deep wounds
  3. Bites to head, neck, and hands
  4. Patients with severe immunodeficiency
  5. Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal
  6. Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

  • High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.
  • Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult
  • Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year
  • Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of 3 intramuscular (IM) or 3 intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0, 7 and 21 or 28.

  • Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm
  • Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.
  • Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.
  • High-risk individuals who receive pre-exposure prophylaxis should have their neutralising antibody titres checked every six months during the first 2 years following immunisation, and every 2 years thereafter. If the levels fall below 0.5 IU/ml, a booster dose of vaccine is recommended. 

Management of re-exposure to rabies virus

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

  • Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency
  • Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment 

For any exposed or re-exposed patient who has received and can document previous completion of PEP or PrEP:

  • Proper wound management
  • One site ID / IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3
  • RIG not given

Only in case of exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP or PrEP within the last three months, adequate wound washing alone is required.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presented with complaints of dyspnea on exertion for 1 month. Echocardiography showed the presence of mitral stenosis and left ventricular hypertrophy. Identify the histopathological finding given below and the probable diagnosis.
questions.raw_text: A patient presented with complaints of dyspnea on exertion for 1 month. Echocardiography showed the presence of mitral stenosis and left ventricular hypertrophy. Identify the histopathological finding given below and the probable diagnosis.
questions.correct_answer: A. Aschoff body; Rheumatic heart disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aschoff body; Rheumatic heart disease

The lesion shown in the histopathological slide is Aschoff's body and the most probable diagnosis is rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

Aschoff's bodies are the lesions found in the heart during acute rheumatic fever. They are composed of foci of T lymphocytes, activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells, and occasional plasma cells. Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and central round-to-ovoid nuclei with chromatin that is centrally condensed into a slender, wavy ribbon. Hence, they are also called caterpillar cells.

Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis. During acute rheumatic fever, Aschoff bodies may be found in any of the three layers of the heart that results in pericarditis, myocarditis, or endocarditis. 

Chronic inflammation leads to diffuse thickening and fibrosis of the valve leaflets, often with calcific deposits. Fibrinoid necrosis occurs due to inflammation of the endocardium and the left-sided valves. Over these areas of necrosis, small vegetations called verrucae develop along the lines of closure. Irregular thickenings present in the subendocardium are called MacCallum plaques.

In chronic RHD, the mitral valve leaflet is thickened, with commissural fusion and shortening. There is thickening and fusion of the tendinous cords. This can lead to narrowing the mitral orifice, leading to a fish mouth appearance (button hole).

Some major manifestations of rheumatic Fever are:

  • Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints 
  • Pancarditis (myocarditis, pericarditis, or endocarditis)
  • Subcutaneous nodules (typically on extensor surfaces of extremities)
  • Erythema marginatum, an irregular circinate skin rash 
  • Sydenham chorea, a neurologic disorder with involuntary rapid movements

Image showing button hole appearance seen in mitral stenosis in case of rheumatic heart disease.

Image show Aschoff bodies seen in RHD.

Other options:

Option B: Degenerative calcific deposits in the mitral valve typically develop in the fibrous annulus. They are seen grossly as irregular, stony hard, occasionally ulcerated nodules at the base of the leaflets. Usually, it does not affect valvular function. However, occasionally it can lead to regurgitation, stenosis, or arrhythmias.

The image below shows severe calcification of the mitral valve annulus with focally thickened shortened and fused chordae.

Option C: In sarcoidosis, the involved tissues contain well-formed non-necrotizing granulomas. They are composed of aggregates of tightly clustered epithelioid macrophages, often with giant cells, usually without central necrosis. As the lesions become chronic, fibrous rims or hyaline fibrous scars enclose the granulomas.

The image below shows non-necrotizing granulomas in the wall of a bronchiole in sarcoidosis.

Option D: In tuberculosis, sites of active involvement of tuberculosis are marked histologically by a characteristic granulomatous inflammatory reaction composed of both caseating and non-caseating tubercles. Usually, granuloma shows central granular caseation surrounded by multinucleate giant cells. Central caseation may be absent in non-caseating granulomas. Staining should be done to detect acid-fast bacilli when granulomas are present. 

The image below shows a caseating granulomatous lesion with areas of caseation (on the right half) bordered by collections of epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes.

Image showing non-necrotizing granuloma seen in pulmonary tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The given peripheral smear is associated with which of the following leukemias?
questions.raw_text: The given peripheral smear is associated with which of the following leukemias?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

The peripheral smear findings point toward a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

The peripheral smear shows smudge cells, increased lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm, and round to slightly irregular nuclei containing clumped chromatin. This large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes is often described as a "convent-girl" appearance.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)/ Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is the most common leukemia among adults in the western world. The differentiating point between CLL and SLL is that the absolute lymphocyte count is >5000/mm³ in CLL and <5000/mm³ in SLL.

 The chromosomal defects:

  • Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis)
  • Deletion of 11q
  • Trisomy 12q
  • Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis)

It is usually asymptomatic at diagnosis but can present with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are usually seen.

Total blood count: 

  • Total leukocyte count is highly variable; leukopenia is seen when the marrow is involved. 
  • Hypogammaglobulinemia is common and contributes to increased susceptibility to infections.
  • 10% to 15% of patients develop hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells.

Findings of peripheral smear:

  • Predominantly shows small lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm.
  • Contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is often described as a convent-girl appearance.
  • Smudge cells or basket cells or parachute cells - artifacts of the lymphocytes which are disrupted during the process of making smears.
  • Spherocytes (due to coexisting autoimmune hemolytic anemia) and nucleated RBCs (due to premature release of progenitors in face of severe anemia, marrow infiltration by the tumor, or both)

Lymph node biopsy: Diffuse effacement of lymph node architecture is seen. Small lymphocytes admixed with variable numbers of larger activated lymphocytes that often gather in loose aggregates. Proliferation centers containing mitotically active cells are pathognomonic for CLL / SLL.

The histopathological image shows small, darker staining lymphocytes with prominent nucleoli, which are typically seen in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

AML is a hematopoietic progenitor malignancy that causes immature myeloblast accumulation in the bone marrow. Incidence increases with age and peaks after 60 years of age.

Clinically, the patients present with symptoms resulting due to pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia). There is generalized fatigue, bone pain, bleeding tendencies, and an increased risk of recurrent infections. For acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML) diagnosis, the blast cell count should be ≥20% in the peripheral blood or bone marrow.

Other distinctive features of AML:

  • Bone marrow/ smear shows a large, uniform population of cells (myeloblasts) with prominent nucleoli (yellow arrow). It shows the presence of primary cytoplasmic granules.
  • Auer rods: needle-shaped azurophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies formed by the fusion of lysosomes. (black arrow)
  • Multiple Auer rods clustered together within a single cell resembling a bundle of sticks known as faggot cells (seen in peripheral smear).

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) arises from immature B (pre-B) or T (pre-T) cells called lymphoblasts. Immunohistochemistry for terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is positive in pre-B and pre-T lymphoblasts.

Peripheral smear shows lymphoblasts that have condensed chromatin, less conspicuous nucleoli, and smaller amounts of cytoplasm which lacks granules as shown below.

Chronic myeloid leukemia is characterized by the presence of a Philadelphia chromosome resulting from reciprocal translocation t(9;22) forming the BCR-ABL fusion gene. They have hypercellular marrow due to a massively increased number of maturing granulocytic precursors.

The image below shows peripheral smear findings of CML with neutrophils, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and band cells.

Pearl: WHO classification of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)

The 5th edition of WHO (2022) classification classifies acute myeloid leukemia (AML) as follows:

AML with defining genetic abnormalities (gene or chromosome changes):

  • Acute promyelocytic leukemia with PML::RARA fusion
  • AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 fusion
  • AML with CBFB::MYH11 fusion
  • AML with DEK::NUP214 fusion
  • AML with RBM15::MRTFA fusion
  • AML with BCR::ABL1 fusion
  • AML with KMT2A rearrangement*
  • AML with MECOM rearrangement
  • AML with NUP98 rearrangement
  • AML with NPM1 mutation
  • AML with CEBPA mutation
  • AML, myelodysplasia-related#
  • AML with other defined genetic alterations

 AML, defined by differentiation:

  • AML with minimal differentiation
  • AML without maturation
  • AML with maturation
  • Acute basophilic leukaemia
  • Acute myelomonocytic leukaemia
  • Acute monocytic leukaemia
  • Acute erythroid leukaemia
  • Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia

Most AML with defining genetic abnormalities are diagnosed with < 20% blasts except AML with BCR: ABL1 and AML with CEBPA mutation that require at least 20% blasts for diagnosis.

*AML with KMT2A rearrangement is the new term that replaces “AML with t(9;11)(p22;q23); KMT2A-MLLT3

#AML with myelodysplasia-related changes has been renamed as AML, myelodysplasia-related (AML-MR).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Identify the incorrect statement in rapid sequence intubation?
questions.raw_text: Identify the incorrect statement in rapid sequence intubation?

options.label: A
options.text: Preoxygenation with 100% oxygen  for 3 min is done.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the method of choice in cardiac arrest patient.

options.label: D
options.text: Induction agent and muscle relaxant are given simultaneously.

questions.correct_answer: C. It is the method of choice in cardiac arrest patient.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is the method of choice in cardiac arrest patient.

The incorrect statement regarding rapid sequence intubation (RSI) is that it is the method of choice in cardiac arrest patients.

RSI is a technique of anesthesia induction in patients who are at an increased risk of gastric regurgitation and pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents. Common cases include pregnancy, full stomach, intestinal obstruction, poorly controlled gastroesophageal reflux disease, morbid obesity, and diabetic gastroparesis. The goal is to intubate rapidly to minimize the time between the loss of consciousness and securing of the airway with a cuffed endotracheal tube.

It is achieved by pre-oxygenating the patient with 100% oxygen for 2-3 minutes. An inducing agent is administered, which is immediately followed by a muscle relaxant succinylcholine or rocuronium. The trachea is intubated without any prior bag and mask ventilation using a high-volume and low-pressure cuff which adequately cuffs the airway and prevents aspiration.

Cardiac arrest is an emergency condition with importance given to start chest compressions, defibrillation, or drugs to restore perfusion. The airway is commonly blocked by posterior displacement of the tongue which can be managed by head tilt and chin lift or giving jaw thrust. In case of airway blockade or to prevent aspiration, the airway is maintained by emergency tracheal tube intubation and does not involve the procedure that is followed in RSI. Endotracheal tube placement is commonly done during post-cardiac arrest care.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents with mental confusion, visual and auditory hallucinations, perceived changes of body shape, swelling of the tongue and a fear of impending death after he was treated for primary chancre of syphilis with an intramuscular injection. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A patient presents with mental confusion, visual and auditory hallucinations, perceived changes of body shape, swelling of the tongue and a fear of impending death after he was treated for primary chancre of syphilis with an intramuscular injection. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hoigne syndrome

The development of acute psychotic symptoms after intramuscular administration of penicillin G points to a diagnosis of Hoigne syndrome. It may also be seen after benzathine administration also. 

Hoigne syndrome:

  • Acute psychotic symptoms are seen such as mental confusion, visual and auditory hallucinations, and perceived changes of body shape.
  • The patient may also present with swelling of the tongue and a fear of impending death.
  • These are usually embolic toxic reactions, possibly due to vascular occlusion by large crystals of the penicillin salts. 
  • It is due to a pseudoanaphylactic or pseudoallergic reaction, not penicillin allergy.

A Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction is a transient clinical phenomenon that occurs in patients infected with spirochetes like syphilis, leptospirosis, Lyme disease, and relapsing fever, who are treated with antibiotics. The reaction occurs within 24 hours of antibiotic therapy. It generally manifests as fever, chills, rigors, nausea and vomiting, headache, tachycardia, hypotension, hyperventilation, flushing, myalgia, and exacerbation of skin lesions. It is an acute, self-limiting condition.

questions.text: An intravenous pyelogram done for evaluation of recurrent UTI in a  child is shown below. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?
questions.raw_text: An intravenous pyelogram done for evaluation of recurrent UTI in a  child is shown below. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Associated with an increased incidence of renal cell carcinoma

options.label: C
options.text: Lies just below the origin of inferior mesenteric artery

options.label: D
options.text: Division at the level of the isthmus improves function

questions.correct_answer: D. Division at the level of the isthmus improves function
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Division at the level of the isthmus improves function

The given scenario with intravenous pyelogram showing flower vase sign points to a diagnosis of horseshoe kidney. Division of the relatively avascular isthmus between the kidneys is usually not indicated. This is because it can lead to an increased risk of urinary fistula.

Horseshoe kidneys are the most common fusion defects of the kidney, characterized by abnormalities in the position, rotation, and vascular supply of the kidney.

The fused portion lies adjacent to the L3 or L4 vertebra just below the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery. Ascent of the fused kidneys is prevented by the inferior mesenteric artery. Adrenal glands remain in the normal position. 

There is a 2:1 male predominance. It is also commonly associated with renal cell carcinoma, Wilms tumor, multicystic dysplastic kidney, and Turner’s syndrome.

Patients may be asymptomatic or may present with:

  • Dull renal pain
  • Abdominal lump
  • Urinary tract infections
  • Increased angulation of ureters resulting in - 
    • Nephrolithiasis
    • Hydronephrosis

Radiological diagnosis is by intravenous pyelogram which shows flower vase sign or handshake sign.

Symptomatic management is preferred. Heminephrectomy is usually not indicated for horseshoe kidneys with unilateral RCC/ Wilms tumor. This is because it can result in devascularisation due to the unpredictable blood supply of the horseshoe kidney from nearby major vessels.

Note: Division of the relatively avascular isthmus between the kidneys is only indicated in the course of surgery for abdominal aortic aneurysm.
