questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the immunological abnormality that is seen with the lack of CD40 in B cells is?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the immunological abnormality that is seen with the lack of CD40 in B cells is?

options.label: A
options.text: Total lack of natural killer cells

options.label: C
options.text: Decrease in IgG and increase in IgM

options.label: D
options.text: Inability of neutrophils to fight against infections

questions.correct_answer: C. Decrease in IgG and increase in IgM
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decrease in IgG and increase in IgM

The deficiency of the CD40 and its absence in B cells leads to Hyper IgM syndrome. A decrease in IgG and an increase in IgM is seen in this syndrome.

The patients most often have loss-of-function mutations involving either CD40 or activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), a DNA-editing enzyme expressed in B cells that are required for Ig class switching and affinity maturation.

The deficiency of the CD40 and its absence in B cells interferes with class switching and the production of memory cells. The B-cell response to antigens, is unaffected, accounting for the presence of increased IgM antibodies. Hence, the condition is known as Hyper IgM syndrome.

The IgM levels can be seen to have an increased or normal serum values while that of IgG shows to be extremely low with no IgA or IgE. Clinical features are recurrent pyogenic infections because of low levels of opsonizing IgG antibodies. They are highly susceptible to pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii.

 

Pearl: Primary immunodeficiency disorders

Affected component of the immune system

Disorder

Humoral immunity: Problems with B cells and their antibody production
  • Common variable immunodeficiency
  • Selective immunoglobulin deficiency, such as IgA deficiency
  • Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
  • X-linked agammaglobulinemia

Cellular immunity: Problems with T cells 
  • Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis
  • DiGeorge syndrome
  • X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome

Combined humoral and cellular immunity: Problems with B and T cells
  • Ataxia-telangiectasia
  • Hyperimmunoglobulinemia M syndrome
  • Severe combined immunodeficiency
  • Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

Phagocytes: Problems with the movement or killing 
  • Chronic granulomatous disease
  • Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (rare)
  • Tuftsin deficiency
  • Cyclic neutropenia
  • Leukocyte adhesion defects

Complement proteins: 

Deficiency of complement proteins
  • Complement component 1 (C1) inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angioedema)
  • Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9): Recurrent Neisseria infections

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Most specific indicator of alcohol-induced liver dysfunction is _____
questions.raw_text: Most specific indicator of alcohol-induced liver dysfunction is _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GGT

Among the given options, the most specific indicator of alcohol-induced liver dysfunction is gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT).

GGT is commonly used in patients with alcoholic liver disease as a marker of excessive alcohol intake. GGT is present in many tissues, including the kidneys, pancreas, and liver. It is mainly derived from the liver and this is often used as a marker of hepatobiliary diseases. Chronic alcohol consumption leads to the induction of hepatic microsomal GGT which leads to a rise in GGT  in alcoholics.

Laboratory investigations in patients with alcohol-induced liver dysfunction:

  • AST (SGOT) and ALT (SGPT) elevations that do not exceed 400 IU/L.
  • AST/ALT ratio of >1.5.
  • Serum bilirubin >3 mg/dL. 

Note that while GGT is a sensitive marker for alcohol-induced liver disease, it is not completely specific to this condition. Other conditions such as biliary obstruction or use of certain medications can also elevate GGT levels.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about blood products?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements is true about blood products?

options.label: A
options.text: Platelets is stored between 20°C to 24°C with a shelf life of 5 days.

options.label: B
options.text: Cryoprecipitate is stored at -20°C with a shelf life of 6 months

options.label: C
options.text: Packed red cells stored with adenine, glucose, mannitol and saline is stored between -5°C to -15°C with a shelf life of 5 weeks

options.label: D
options.text: Fresh frozen plasma is stored between -5°C to -15°C with a shelf life of 2 years

questions.correct_answer: A. Platelets is stored between 20°C to 24°C with a shelf life of 5 days.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Platelets is stored between 20°C to 24°C with a shelf life of 5 days.

The statement that is true about blood products is platelets can be stored between 20°C to 24°C with a shelf life of 5 days.

Platelet concentrates can be stored for up to 5 days at +20°C to +24°C, with agitation. It is used in thrombocytopenia, platelet function defects, disseminated intravascular coagulation, during massive blood transfusion to prevent dilutional thrombocytopenia, and in bone marrow failure. Agitation during storage is necessary to maintain their viability and function. This is because platelets are stored at room temperature, where they continue to metabolize glucose and produce lactate. Agitation helps to maintain a uniform distribution of platelets, prevent their clumping together, and facilitate gas exchange.

Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate are generally stored at a temperature of –30 °C. They are thawed at temperatures between +30 °C and +37 °C in the blood bank before issue and transported to the ward at ambient temperature. They must be used immediately and should never be refrozen.

Whole blood and packed red cells are always stored at +2 °C to +6 °C and transported between +2 °C and +10 °C. Packed red cells stored with SAGM (sodium, adenine, glucose, and mannitol as components) provide a shelf-life of up to 42 days.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a 100-m dash, most of the energy consumed by skeletal muscles to replenish ATP is derived from _______
questions.raw_text: In a 100-m dash, most of the energy consumed by skeletal muscles to replenish ATP is derived from _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phosphocreatine

In a 100-m dash that takes 10 s, 85% of the energy consumed is derived anaerobically by phosphocreatine, which is hydrolyzed to creatine and phosphate groups with the release of considerable energy.

The ATP concentration in a muscle is low enough (4 millimolar) to sustain contractions for 1-2 seconds after which ATP is dephosphorylated into ADP. The ADP is re-phosphorylated by phosphocreatine for the next 5 to 8 seconds.

ADP is re-phosphorylated by 3 sources.
  • Phosphocreatine after 2 seconds upto 10 seconds.
  • Glycolysis (anaerobic) after 10 seconds upto a minute
  • Oxidative metabolism - after a minute upto 2-4 hours.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure being performed in the image given below.
questions.raw_text: Identify the procedure being performed in the image given below.

options.label: C
options.text: Intraosseous route access for giving IV fluids

questions.correct_answer: C. Intraosseous route access for giving IV fluids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intraosseous route access for giving IV fluids

The procedure being performed in the above image is intraosseous route access for transfusing IV fluids in the anterior proximal tibia.

The intraosseous route is an alternative to the intravenous (IV) route in the transfusion of fluids in shock. The marrow of long bones has a rich network of vessels that drain into a central venous canal, emissary veins, and ultimately the central circulation. So, the bone marrow functions as a non-collapsible venous access route.

Intraosseous cannulation is recommended for patients in whom IV access proves difficult or unattainable. (e.g., in cardiopulmonary arrest). In such a case, if venous access is not available within 1 min, an intraosseous needle should be placed in the anterior proximal tibia. During a resuscitation procedure, all anesthetic drugs and fluids can be administered through intraosseous cannulae.

Insertion sites for intraosseous infusion: 

  • In the proximal tibia, 1-2 cm anteromedial from the tibial tuberosity
  • Distal tibia at the junction of the medial malleolus and the shaft of the tibia
  • Distal one-third of the femur

The response time to drug administration in intraosseous infusion is close to the IV route. Fluids should be given as boluses using a 50 mL syringe.

The image below shows the procedure of intraosseous cannulation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following substances inhibits aconitase enzyme?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following substances inhibits aconitase enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fluoroacetate

Flouroacetate is an inhibitor of the aconitase enzyme.

Fluoroacetate combines with Co-A to form fluoroacetyl-CoA. Fluoroacetyl-CoA then condenses with oxaloacetate to form Fluorocitrate. Fluorocitrate then inhibits the enzyme aconitase.

Pearl: Steps involved in TCA cycle

Step 1

Acetyl CoA + Oxaloacetate → Citrate

     (2C  + 4C  =   6C)

Enzyme: Citrate Synthase

Irreversible, Exothermic reaction
Step 2

Citrate → Cis –aconitate  → Isocitrate 

( 6C    →          6C →             6C)

Enzyme:   Aconitase

Cofactor:   Fe2+

The Reaction occurs in 2 steps:         

1st step:  Dehydration      

2nd step:  Rehydration

Inhibited by: Fluoroacetate (Non- Competitive)
Step 3

Isocitrate →[Oxalosuccinate]→α- Keto glutarate

        (6C) →         [6C]         →         (5C)

Enzyme:  Isocitrate Dehydrogenase

Cofactor:   Mn2+ or Mg2+

Reaction:  Oxidative  Decarboxylation

Intermediate:   Oxalosuccinate [ Unstable]

Release:    1 NADH and CO2
Step 4

α- Keto glutarate → Succcinyl Co A 

       (5C             →         4C)

Enzyme: α- Ketoglutarate Dehydrogenase(Multienzyme complex)

Reaction:  Oxidative Decarboxylation

Inhibited by: Arsenite  (Non – Competitive)

Physiologically unidirectional step.

Release: 1 NADH and CO2
Step 5

Succinyl- CoA  → Succinate

      ( 4C          →         4C )

Enzyme:  Succinate Thiokinase

Cofactor: Mg2+

Release:  1 ATP / GTP

Substrate level phosphorylation
Step 6

Succinate  →   Fumarate

( 4C          →         4C )

Enzyme:  Succinate Dehydrogenase (Part of 2nd complex ETC)

Cofactor:  FAD and Fe-S protein 

The only enzyme of TCA cycle attached to the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Inhibited by: Malonate ( competitive)

Release: FADH2
Step 7

Fumarate  →   Malate

( 4C         →     4C )

Enzyme:  Fumarate Hydratase

Reaction: Hydration
Step 8

Malate  →  Oxaloacetate  

( 4C     →        4C )

Enzyme:  Malate Dehydrogenase

Release:  1 NADH

Oxaloacetate is regenerated.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The following diagram charts the population change over years from 1983 to 1989 in a given place. What is the statistical diagram used here?
questions.raw_text: The following diagram charts the population change over years from 1983 to 1989 in a given place. What is the statistical diagram used here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Component bar graph

The given image shows a component bar graph. 

A bar chart or bar graph is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data. They can be simple, multiple or component bar graphs.

A component bar graph is used to represent data in which the total magnitude is divided into different subsets or components. A simple bar graph is used to represent a single variable across different categories.

A bar chart can be distinguished from a histogram because the rectangles are separated by the spaces. This indicates that the data forms discrete categories.

In a histogram, the rectangles are not separated by spaces as the data represented forms a continuous set instead of discrete groups.

Pearl: Graphical Representation of Data

1. Histogram

  • A histogram, by definition, is a graphical representation of frequency distribution that contains rectangles and shows the underlying frequency of a set of continuous, quantitative data.
  • The X or horizontal axis is called the abscissa which usually has the group scores or class intervals of the variables/data and the Y or vertical axis is called the ordinate which usually shows the frequencies at which these variables appear.
  • The following image shows a histogram.

2. Bar Chart

  • It is also called a bar graph.
  • It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data as they are not quantitative and usually qualitative.
  • The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups.
  • Bar graphs can be simple, multiple or component bar graphs.

3. Pie Charts

  • Pie charts are also used for nominal or ordinal data.
  • The categorical data are represented as segments of a circle.

4. Frequency polygons

  • Frequency polygons are used for mainly ratio and interval scale data.
  • In a frequency polygon, the mid-points of each class interval are joined together by straight lines.

5. Ogive

  • A frequency polygon which is drawn to represent cumulative frequency distributions form a typical S-shaped curve which is called an ogive. It referred to as a cumulative frequency diagram.

6. Line chart

  • It is also called a line diagram or line graph.
  • Its best use is to show the trend of events or change over passage of time.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about the Chi-square test?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not true about the Chi-square test?

options.label: A
options.text: Tests the significance of difference between two proportions

options.label: B
options.text: Tells about the presence or absence of an association between two variables

options.label: C
options.text: Directly measures the strength of association

options.label: D
options.text: It is usually used for skewed data

questions.correct_answer: C. Directly measures the strength of association
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Directly measures the strength of association

A Chi-square test does not directly measure the strength of association. It merely tells about the presence or lack of association.

Pearl: Tests of Significance

How to choose which test to use?

  • See the variable. Are the variables quantitative or qualitative?
    • If the variables are qualitative (nominal), then Chi square test is used.
    • If the variables are quantitative, then see whether 2 groups or more than 2 groups .
      • If 2 groups are being tested, then T tests are used. In that, if the same group is tested before and after, paired T test is used. Otherwise, unpaired T test is used.
      • If more than 2 groups are being tested, then use ANOVA.

1. T Tests

  • Unpaired t tests
    • Also known as the student’s t test, independent t test, two-samples t test.
    • It's the most commonly used t test and it tests the difference between two groups (the means of 2 groups) independent of each other and indicates how significant the differences are.
  • Paired t tests
    • "Pairs before marriage are not the same after!"
    • So remember the paired test is mainly used in the comparison of a before and after scenario 
    • Also known as correlated t test, dependent samples t test.
    • It is mainly used on dependent samples. For example, the cholesterol level of a person before and after using a specific drug.
    • It can also be used when you put the same condition under test using different items or things. For example, same crash safety tests for different cars.
  • T scores 
    • The t score is referred to as the ratio of the difference between two groups and the difference within the groups.
    • The smaller the t score, the more similarity there is between two groups and vice versa.

 

2. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)

  • The analysis of variance test (ANOVA) is used to test the difference between two or usually more than two groups (means) and here the inferences are made by analyzing the variances.

 

3. Chi-Square Test

  • The Chi-Square test (χ2) is a non-parametric(non-numeric) test and it is used to test hypotheses in relation to nominal scale data or categorical data.
  • It is a test of proportions and associations.
  • A Chi-square distribution is usually positively skewed but it approaches a normal distribution as its degrees of freedom increases.
  • If the frequency of any of the cells of the categorical table is <5, then Fisher’s exact test is used.
subtopics: Chi Square Test / Non Parametric Tests

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with foul-smelling bloody discharge per vagina mixed with mucous. On examination, a necrotizing growth is seen in the cervix with lateral parametrium involvement. What is the management for this patient?
questions.raw_text: A 50-year-old woman presents with foul-smelling bloody discharge per vagina mixed with mucous. On examination, a necrotizing growth is seen in the cervix with lateral parametrium involvement. What is the management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chemoradiation

This patient with a cervical tumor involving the parametrium has stage IIB cervical carcinoma, which is treated primarily with chemoradiation. 

Stage IIB cervical cancer refers to cancer that has extended beyond the cervix and upper vagina to the parametrial tissue. It has not spread to the pelvic sidewall or the lower third of the vagina. The primary management for stage IIB cervical cancer is concurrent chemoradiation therapy. This involves the combination of external beam radiation therapy, brachytherapy, and chemotherapy (usually with cisplatin). This approach has been shown to improve overall survival and reduce the risk of local and distant recurrence compared to radiation therapy alone.

Following chemoradiation, patients should be closely monitored for treatment response and potential side effects or complications. This includes regular physical examinations, Pap tests, and imaging studies as needed. The prognosis for stage IIB cervical cancer depends on various factors, such as the size of the tumor, lymph node involvement, and the patient's overall health. With appropriate treatment, the 5-year survival rate for stage IIB cervical cancer is around 58-63%.

Other options:

Option A: Chemotherapy alone: Chemotherapy alone is not the primary treatment for stage IIB cervical cancer. It may be used as an adjunct to other treatments, such as radiation therapy, but is not sufficient on its own. 

Option B - Brachytherapy: Brachytherapy is a form of internal radiation therapy, in which a radioactive source is placed close to the tumor. While it is an important component of the treatment for cervical cancer, it is typically not used as a standalone treatment.

Option D - Surgery: Surgery is not the primary treatment option for stage IIB cervical cancer. In some rare cases, pelvic exenteration may be performed, but this is typically reserved for patients with recurrent or persistent disease after chemoradiation.

Pearl: Staging of Carcinoma Cervix

Stage I - limited to the cervix

  • A: Microscopic lesion
    • A1 - stromal invasion ≤3mm depth
    • A2 - a stromal invasion of >3 and ≤5mm depth
  • B: Macroscopic lesion
    • B1 - stromal invasion >5mm depth & tumor size ≤2cm 
    • B2 - tumor size >2cm to ≤4cm 
    • B3 - tumor size >4cm 

Stage II - involves upper 2/3 of vagina

  • A: Extends to the upper two-thirds of the vagina without parametrial involvement
    • A1 - tumor size ≤4cm 
    • A2 - tumor size >4cm 
  • B: Extends to parametrium but not upto the pelvic wall.

Stage III - spreads to lower 1/3 of vagina

  • A: Extends to lower 1/3 of the vagina
  • B: Extends to the pelvic wall (hydronephrosis/non-functioning kidney)
  • C: Involvement of the pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes, irrespective of the tumor size and extent
    • C1: pelvic lymph node involved
    • C2: para-aortic lymph node involved

Stage IV - metastasis

  • A: Bladder/bowel involvement (adjacent pelvic organs)
  • B: Distant metastasis

Note: The involvement of vascular/lymphatic spaces does not change the staging. The lateral extent of the lesion is no longer considered.

Stage IIIB is the most common stage of presentation.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25 year old man involved in a fight, injured his finger and the deformity is shown in the following image. X-ray is normal. The most appropriate management at this stage is:
questions.raw_text: A 25 year old man involved in a fight, injured his finger and the deformity is shown in the following image. X-ray is normal. The most appropriate management at this stage is:

options.label: C
options.text: Surgical repair of the flexor tendon

questions.correct_answer: D. Splint the finger in hyperextension
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Splint the finger in hyperextension

Based on the mechanism of injury and the deformity characterized by flexion at the distal interphalangeal joint, along with a normal radiograph, the likely diagnosis is mallet finger, which is managed by splinting the finger in hyperextension.

Mallet finger, also known as baseball finger, occurs when there is a sudden passive flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint, causing avulsion of the extensor tendon from its insertion at the base of the distal phalanx.

Surgery is considered only if there is a large fragment (>50%) and subluxation of the DIP joint.

Pearl: Important Injuries of the Hand

Gamekeeper's thumb: It is an injury of the thumb leading to avulsion, rupture or damage of the ulnar collateral ligament. It is commonly seen in gamekeepers and following a fall on an outstretched hand.

 
Mallet finger/baseball finger: It is a disruption to the extensor tendon over the DIP joint. It occurs when a collision with a hard object (e.g., a ball) forces it to flex more than its normal range of motion.
 

 

Jersey finger: It is an avulsion injury of the flexor digitorum profundus at the insertion of the base of the distal phalanx. The ring finger most commonly involved.

 

Trigger finger: A nodule on the flexor tendon prevents it from moving along the A1 pulley. This causes the finger to be stuck in a flexed position.

 

Boxer's fracture: It is a break in the neck of the metacarpal. It is caused by striking an object with a closed fist, as seen in boxing. The little finger is the most commonly affected.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which fixation technique is used for fat in the histopathological examination?
questions.raw_text: Which fixation technique is used for fat in the histopathological examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Frozen section

A frozen section is done for the fixation of fats. This ensures that the tissue need not go through routine processing, which can remove lipids.

Routine paraffin embedding uses solvents that dissolve lipids, so fat is lost. To see fat, you need frozen sections and special stains (Oil Red O, Sudan stains) that preserve and highlight lipids. When the tissue sample goes through rapid freezing, it becomes firmer. The ice acts as an embedding medium, allowing the tissue to be sectioned. 

The temperature range in the cryostat machine usually ranges from 0⁰C to -35⁰C. The majority of the tissue can be appropriately sectioned between -15⁰C to -25⁰C. Tissue samples that contain water can be sectioned at a higher temperature. The tissues that contain more fat will need to be cut at a lower temperature.

The stain used for fat is the oil red O stain. It can identify neutral lipids and fatty acids in smears and tissues. It is used in the following conditions:

  • Fat embolism in lung tissue
  • Renal cell carcinoma
  • Sebaceous gland tumors of the skin
  • Lipid-rich carcinomas

Fixatives containing alcohols, or routine processing with clearing, will remove lipids. Fixation can be achieved by the following methods:

  • Physical methods - heating, microwaving, cryopreservation
  • Chemical methods - immersion of specimen in fixative, perfusing vascular system with a fixative

 Given below are a few fixatives with their uses:

Technique/Tissue Fixative
Electron microscopy Glutaraldehyde
Trephine biopsy-bone marrow Zenker's fluid (AZF fixative)
GI biopsies Bouin's fixative
Brain Formalin ammonium chloride
Adrenal biopsy Orth's fluid
Pap smear Ethanol

 The most commonly used fixative is 10% neutral buffered formalin.

questions.text: A 58-year-old man died 24 hours after the onset of substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm. On autopsy, an atheromatous plaque was seen obstructing the left anterior descending artery. Which type of calcification is most likely to be seen in this condition?
questions.raw_text: A 58-year-old man died 24 hours after the onset of substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm. On autopsy, an atheromatous plaque was seen obstructing the left anterior descending artery. Which type of calcification is most likely to be seen in this condition?
questions.correct_answer: C. Dystrophic with normal serum calcium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dystrophic with normal serum calcium

Atheromatous plaques are associated with dystrophic calcification. This is seen in the presence of normal calcium levels in the serum.

The deposition of calcium in dead or dying tissues is called dystrophic calcification. Although it occurs in the presence of normal serum calcium, it can be worsened by hypercalcemia.

Dystrophic calcification is seen in areas of necrosis of any type. Some examples include atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis and areas of caseous necrosis in tuberculosis.

Note :

Dystrophic calcification: Deposition of calcium at sites of cell injury and necrosis

Metastatic calcification: Deposition of calcium in normal tissues, caused by hypercalcemia 

Pearl: Types of calcifications

  Dystrophic calcification Metastatic calcification
Location Dead and dying tissues Normal interstitial tissues of the vasculature, kidneys, lungs, and gastric mucosa.
Calcium metabolism Normal deranged causing hypercalcemia
Examples

Calcific valvular stenosis

Advanced Atheromatous plaque

Monckeberg medial sclerosis

Parathyroid tumors

Hypercalcemia of malignancy

Paget disease

vitamin D intoxication

Sarcoidosis

Renal failure

questions.text: In a 46XY female complete gonadal dysgenesis was noted. Complete gonadal dysgenesis is caused by what in the SRY gene?
questions.raw_text: In a 46XY female complete gonadal dysgenesis was noted. Complete gonadal dysgenesis is caused by what in the SRY gene?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Point mutation

Amongst the given options, a point mutation in the SRY gene is most likely to result in complete gonadal dysgenesis but this answer remains controversial as some other sources mention SRY deletion is more commonly associated. The most common cause attributable to about 85% of cases is still idiopathic. 

 Pure gonadal dysgenesis results from a point mutation in SRY/ SRY deletion or point mutations in another gene with testis-determining effects (DAXJ, SF-1, CBX2). This leads to underdeveloped dysgenetic gonads that fail to produce androgens or AMH. This is characterized by a normal prepubertal female phenotype and a normal mullerian system due to absent AMH.

The child usually presents with failure in the development of secondary sexual characteristics at puberty and amenorrhea. Investigations reveal the absence of estrogen production and they have elevated levels of FSH (>40 miU/mL) and low oestradiol levels (<25 pg/mL).

Women with streak ovaries are infertile, but they can bear children with oocyte donation. They must be treated with cyclic estrogen and progestogen to promote feminization and secondary sexual characteristics and prevent osteoporosis.

Pearl: Sexual Differentiation

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mitochondrial

The type of inheritance in MELAS is mitochondrial, which manifests as mitochondrial myopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes.

Mitochondrial inheritance:

  • Inherited exclusively from the affected mother (ovum) as an individual’s mitochondrial genome is entirely derived from the mother because sperms contain few mitochondria, which are typically shed upon fertilization.
  • Both male and female children born to an affected mother will inherit the disease.
  • 80% of mitochondrial DNA codes for mitochondrial RNA, and therefore most mitochondrial DNA mutations lead to functional problems, which may be manifested as muscle disorders.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What formula is the dosing rate of a drug based on?
questions.raw_text: What formula is the dosing rate of a drug based on?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clearance x plasma concentration

The formula for drug dosing rate is clearance x plasma concentration.

The equation for dose rate given here is based on steady-state concentration. When a drug is given repeatedly at short intervals it will accumulate in the body until the elimination of the drug matches its input. So steady-state concentration is the plasma concentration at which the drug elimination and drug input balance each other.

Steady-state concentration(Cpss) = Dose rate / Clearance

From this equation dose rate for a target steady-state plasma concentration is calculated as 

Dose rate = Clearance(CL) x target plasma concentration(Cpss)

Pearl: Zero order vs First order kinetics of drugs

Zero order

First order

Constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time

 Constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit time

Rate of elimination is independent of plasma concentration

 Rate of elimination is proportional to the plasma concentration

Clearance is more at low concentration and less at high concentration

 Clearance remains constant 

Half-life is less at low concentration and more at high concentration

 Half-life remains constant

Very few drugs follow zero-order kinetics, e.g.(WATT Power)

  • Warfarin
  • Alcohol, Aspirin
  • Tolbutamide
  • Theophylline 
  • Phenytoin

 

 Most of the drugs follow first order kinetics

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a false statement regarding contrecoup injuries?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is a false statement regarding contrecoup injuries?

options.label: A
options.text: Fracture of the skull may not occur, even in the presence of severe coup and contrecoup injuries

options.label: B
options.text: A fall on the frontal region will produce an occipital contrecoup

options.label: C
options.text: A fall on the temporal region will produce a contrecoup in the ipsilateral lobe

options.label: D
options.text: The most common site for contrecoup injury is frontal and temporal lobes

questions.correct_answer: B. A fall on the frontal region will produce an occipital contrecoup
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A fall on the frontal region will produce an occipital contrecoup

A fall on the frontal region will not produce occipital contrecoup injuries. This is due to the relatively smooth internal surface of the posterior cranial fossa.

Coup injury is damage that occurs on the same side of the direct trauma. Contrecoup injuries are present opposite to the site of trauma and is due to shear strain.

Fracture of the skull may not occur, even in the presence of severe coup and contrecoup injuries (option A). The skull's anterior and middle cranial fossae have sharp edges. This makes the temporal and frontal lobes highly prone to contrecoup injuries (option D). 

A fall on the temporal region can produce a contrecoup injury on the ipsilateral lobe due to the presence of the falx cerebri (option C).
During the impact, the ipsilateral lobe moves in the opposite direction striking the falx cerebri, resulting in contrecoup injury on the same lobe (as the impact) but opposite to the site of initial trauma.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: During your rounds in the neonatal ward, you see a 2-week-old neonate with the following skin finding. It is a disorder of which of the following glands?
questions.raw_text: During your rounds in the neonatal ward, you see a 2-week-old neonate with the following skin finding. It is a disorder of which of the following glands?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eccrine glands

The image shows clear, thin‐walled, superficial vesicles 1–2 mm in diameter, without associated erythema, resembling drops of water in a newborn. It is suggestive of miliaria, a disorder of eccrine sweat glands. 

Pearl: Different types of miliaria

Miliaria is a common acute or subacute skin condition that arises due to the occlusion or disruption of eccrine sweat ducts in hot humid conditions.

Based on the level of blockade it is differentiated into

  • Miliaria Crystallina- Stratum corneum
  • Miliaria Rubra - Malpighian Layer
  • Miliaria profunda - Dermoepidermal junction

Pathophysiology:

  • The first event may be an increase in the skin flora, perhaps with Staphylococcus epidermidis being responsible for producing an extracellular polysaccharide substance or slime that blocks the lumen of the sweat duct.
  • The parakeratotic plugs, a notable feature of the later stages of the disease, are not the primary cause of the obstruction but arise in the repair process, and further aggravate the obstruction.
  • Leakage of sweat into the epidermis is responsible for the final production of the lesions, and for their further aggravation.
  • Miliaria crystallina occurs commonly in infants due to a delay in the development of patency in the sweat ducts.

Clinical features:

  • Miliaria crystallina: Clear, thin‐walled vesicles, 1–2 mm in diameter without an inflammatory areola, are usually symptomless and develop in crops, mainly on the trunk. In persistent febrile illnesses, recurrent crops may occur. The vesicles soon rupture and are followed by superficial, branny desquamation.

 

  • Miliaria rubra: Typical lesions develop on the body, especially in areas of friction with clothing, and in flexures. The lesions are uniformly minute erythematous papules, which may be present in very large numbers. Characteristically, the lesions produce intense discomfort in the form of an unbearable pricking sensation. Relief is often instantaneous when the stimulus to sweating is abolished by a cool shower. In infants, lesions commonly appear on the occluded skin of the neck, groins and axillae, but also occur elsewhere.

 

 

  • Miliaria profunda: This nearly always follows repeated attacks of miliaria rubra, and is common only in the tropics. The lesions are easily missed. The affected skin is covered with pale, firm papules 1–3 mm across, especially on the body, but sometimes also on the limbs. There is no itching or discomfort from the lesions.

 

Treatment:

  • First line
    • Control local environment (remove excess bedding, fans, air
    conditioning)
    • Cool the skin (damp compresses, cool showers)
    • Avoid tight or excessive clothing
  • Second line
    • Menthol (e.g. 0.5% menthol in aqueous cream)
    • Topical antibiotics if there is secondary infection
    • Mild topical steroids
  • Third line
    • Removal to cooler climate
    • Prophylactic oral vitamin C

questions.text: The given USG of lung shows:
questions.raw_text: The given USG of lung shows:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sea shore sign

The given image shows the seashore sign seen in M-mode imaging of the normal lung.

The ultrasound image shows a linear pattern on the top depicting the chest wall and a sandy appearance below indicating normal lung tissue, resembling the waves and the sand at the seashore.


On M-mode ultrasound of a normal lung, the motionless chest wall appears as a linear pattern above the pleural line resembling horizontal "waves". Below the pleural line, a granular, sandy pattern appears due to lung sliding.  Together, this resembles waves meeting sand at the seashore.

Stratosphere/Barcode sign refers to M-mode showing a linear pattern below the pleural line due to loss of normal lung sliding. It is seen in pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Paradoxical response of GH release to thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) is seen in all of the following conditions except______
questions.raw_text: Paradoxical response of GH release to thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) is seen in all of the following conditions except______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malnutrition

The paradoxical response of GH release to TRH is not seen in malnutrition patients.

In normal individuals, GH doesn't respond to TRH stimulation, but paradoxically, the GH levels may increase in response to TRH stimulation in the following conditions:

  • Acromegaly
  • Prolactinoma
  • Anorexia nervosa

The exact mechanism underlying this paradoxical GH response is poorly understood.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Rhinosporidium seeberi belongs to which group of organisms?
questions.raw_text: Rhinosporidium seeberi belongs to which group of organisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aquatic protista

Rhinosporidium seeberi is an aquatic protista.

It was long considered a fungus due to its morphological and staining characteristics, but it could not be cultured like other fungi. Molecular studies have since reclassified it as a protistan parasite, belonging to the Mesomycetozoea, linked to 
a novel clade of organisms called DRIP (Dermocystidium, Rosette agent, Ichthyophonus, and Psorospermum). 

 

Pearl: Rhinosporidiosis

  • It is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi which is recently reclassified as a member of the protistan Mesomycetozoa
  • It is more common in the southern states of India
  • It affects immunocompetent individuals
  • Most commonly a waterborne disease
  • Clinical features: Blood tinged nasal discharge, frank epistaxis, nasal stuffiness
  • Findings: 
    • Leafy, polypoidal mass, pink to purple in color and attached to the nasal septum or lateral wall
    • Sometimes, it extends into the nasopharynx and may hang behind the soft palate
    • The mass is very vascular and bleeds easily on touch
    • Its surface is studded with white dots representing the sporangia
  • Diagnosis: Biopsy which shows sporangia

Histologic section showing sporangium (arrow) which is fully packed with immature sporoblasts at the periphery and mature ones at the center

Treatment: Complete excision of the mass with diathermy knife and cauterization of its base. Recurrence may occur after surgical excision. Dapsone is also used.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions do you see punched-out lesions of the retina?
questions.raw_text: In which of the following conditions do you see punched-out lesions of the retina?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis characteristically causes punched-out lesions in the retina.

Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infestation due to Toxoplasma gondii. It primarily affects the central nervous system and retina. In humans, it occurs as congenital, acquired, or recurrent.

Congenital toxoplasmosis is acquired by the transplacental route. Infants are usually born with inactive disease. Bilateral healed punched-out chorioretinal lesions in the macular area are usually seen. In acquired toxoplasmosis, punched-out lesions similar to congenital toxoplasmosis are seen. In addition, punctate outer retinal toxoplasmosis (PORT) may also be seen. 

Other options:

Option A - Posterior staphyloma is used to describe a bulge in the sclera with the choroid behind the equator. On ophthalmoscopy, there is an excavated area with retinal vessels dipping in it. 

Option B - Fundal coloboma occurs due to a defect in the closure of the embryonic cleft. It appears as a comet-shaped defect with the apex towards the disc which may or may not be involved. A few choroidal or retinal vessels may also be seen on the surface. 

Option C - Congenital rubella typically produces a salt and pepper appearance of the fundus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman with Grave's disease was taking antithyroid medication throughout her pregnancy. The baby was born with aplasia cutis congenita. Which drug could have caused this condition?
questions.raw_text: A woman with Grave's disease was taking antithyroid medication throughout her pregnancy. The baby was born with aplasia cutis congenita. Which drug could have caused this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carbimazole

Carbimazole intake during the first trimester of pregnancy is associated with aplasia cutis congenita.

Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with teratogenic effects such as:

  • Aplasia cutis congenita: Congenital absence of scalp hair and skin along with calvarial defects
  • Choanal atresia
  • Tracheoesophageal fistula
  • Fetal goiter

The drug of choice for the treatment of hyperthyroidism during the first trimester of pregnancy is propylthiouracil (PTU). It is because it has lower teratogenic effects than carbimazole or methimazole.

However, propylthiouracil use is limited to the first trimester due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. It is replaced with methimazole (or carbimazole) in the second and third trimesters of the pregnancy.

Radioiodine therapy is contraindicated during pregnancy and lactation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Cancer that least commonly spreads by lymphatic route is ______.
questions.raw_text: Cancer that least commonly spreads by lymphatic route is ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Basal Cell Carcinoma

Basal cell carcinoma is a locally aggressive tumor that rarely spreads by the lymphatic route.

Mutations in sonic hedgehog pathway are associated with it. 

It presents as small, slowly growing pearly nodule, often with tortuous telangiectatic vessels on its surface, rolled borders, and a central crust (nodular BCC).

The occasional presence of melanin in this variant of nodular BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

The most common site is the inner canthus of the eye.

Basal cell carcinoma does not show lymphatic or hematogenous metastasis. It is primarily locally invasive.

After the delivery of the placenta, she started to bleed profusely.  Which among the following is absolutely contraindicated for use in controlling bleeding?
questions.raw_text: A 32-year-old primigravida delivered a full-term male baby by vaginal delivery.  She is a known case of rheumatic mitral stenosis for 4 years. After the delivery of the placenta, she started to bleed profusely.  Which among the following is absolutely contraindicated for use in controlling bleeding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methyl ergometrine

The given scenario indicates postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) in a primigravida with rheumatic mitral stenosis. Methyl ergometrine is contraindicated in patients with organic heart disease.

Contraindications of methyl ergometrine are:

  • Twin pregnancy - Second baby gets compromised by tetanic contractions of uterus if given after delivery of first baby
  • Organic cardiac disease - Causes overloading of right heart by squeezing blood from uterine circulation.
  • Severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
  • Rh negative mother -  Increases chance of fetomaternal transfusion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency room with loss of consciousness, chest pain, and diaphoresis. On examination, she was grossly unstable and the bilateral pulses were unequal. ECG showed nonspecific ST-T changes. What is the next best investigation?
questions.raw_text: A 45-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency room with loss of consciousness, chest pain, and diaphoresis. On examination, she was grossly unstable and the bilateral pulses were unequal. ECG showed nonspecific ST-T changes. What is the next best investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Transesophageal echocardiography

The clinical presentation of acute onset of chest pain, loss of consciousness, and diaphoresis, with bilaterally unequal pulses and ECG showing nonspecific ST-T changes, is highly suggestive of aortic dissection. The next best investigation in this patient is transesophageal echocardiography, since she is hemodynamically unstable.

The symptoms of loss of consciousness, chest pain, and diaphoresis with a history of hypertension can also point towards the diagnosis of myocardial infarction, but the presence of unequal bilateral pulses and non-specific ECG changes are against the diagnosis of MI and point towards aortic dissection; hence cardiac enzymes are not preferred as they are specific only to MI and not diagnose other diseases (Option C). 

Aortic dissection occurs when a defect or flap occurs in the intima of the aorta. It results in blood tracking into the aortic tissues and splitting of the medial layer of the aorta.

Predisposing factors:

  • Age
  • Hypertension
  • Marfan syndrome
  • Pregnancy
  • Other connective tissue disorders, for example, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, giant cell arteritis, systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Coarctation of the aorta
  • Turner or Noonan syndromes
  • Aortic cannulation site (iatrogenic)

Clinical features:

The most typical presentation of aortic dissection is a tearing interscapular pain. It is associated with diaphoresis. Other symptoms are syncope, weakness, and dyspnea. On examination, there can be hypertension or hypotension, loss of pulses, findings of aortic regurgitation, pulmonary edema, or neurological manifestations. Unequal pulses or blood pressure in the extremities may be seen due to changes of flow in the true and false lumens. 

ECG findings: An ECG that shows no findings of acute myocardial infarction helps to differentiate aortic dissection from myocardial infarction.

Imaging: 

  • In hemodynamically stable patients, the diagnosis is established with a contrast-enhanced CT scan. The characteristic diagnostic finding is a double-lumen aorta.
  • In hemodynamically unstable patients, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is the investigation of choice.
  • MRI and X-ray are not preferred in the evaluation of aortic dissection.

Treatment:

The initial management is with beta-blockers to control hypertension, along with pain management. The preferred beta-blocker is esmolol. These reduce cardiac contractility and blood pressure.

Isolated use of a direct vasodilator such as hydralazine is contraindicated in acute dissection because these agents can increase hydraulic shear and worsen the dissection. CCBs like verapamil and diltiazem may be used intravenously if nitroprusside or beta-blockers cannot be employed.

Once hypertension is controlled, definitive surgical repair of aortic dissection is done. Treatment options depend on the classification.

  • Stanford Type A (DeBakey types I and II) requires surgical intervention once the patient's blood pressure is stabilized.
  • Stanford Type B (DeBakey type III) is best managed by antihypertensive drugs. Surgical intervention is indicated in complicated cases if the pain increases (signaling impending rupture) or when there is evidence of malperfusion of organs or neurological symptoms.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 28-yr old man has recently finished a half- marathon. He complains of pain along the anterior and medial aspect of the tibia which increases on jogging & walking for a long time. Plain X-Ray radiograph of the leg was found to be normal. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 28-yr old man has recently finished a half- marathon. He complains of pain along the anterior and medial aspect of the tibia which increases on jogging & walking for a long time. Plain X-Ray radiograph of the leg was found to be normal. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Shin splint

The given clinical scenario, with a history of lower limb overuse (marathon running) and pain along the medial tibial border, which increases with activity (jogging and long walks), along with a normal radiograph, suggests medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS), also known as shin splints.

MTSS is a stress injury of the tibia that occurs due to the frequent overuse of the lower limbs. It is commonly seen in athletes and military personnel.

Exercise-induced pain along the distal two-thirds of the medial tibial border is typical. Since it is a stress injury, the radiograph of the leg appears normal.

Management is mainly conservative with rest and activity modification, with less repetitive and load-bearing exercises.

Other options :

Option A: A Jones fracture is a transverse fracture at the base of the 5th metatarsal, occurring at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction. It typically results from a strong abduction force applied to the forefoot, which creates a bending moment at this junction, leading to the fracture.

Option C:  Lisfranc fracture refers to a fracture of the metatarsal bases associated with dislocation of the tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joints. The Lisfranc articulation includes the tarsometatarsal joints, which consist of the first, second, and third metatarso-cuneiform joints, along with the fourth and fifth metatarso-cuboid joints.

Option D: Nutcracker fracture refers to a compression fracture of the cuboid bone, typically caused by forceful abduction of the forefoot.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presented with overfamiliarity, flight of ideas, elevated mood, increased sexual desire, and pseudohallucination. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 16-year-old girl presented with overfamiliarity, flight of ideas, elevated mood, increased sexual desire, and pseudohallucination. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mania

In the given clinical scenario, history of overfamiliarity, elevated mood, flight of ideas, and increased sexual desire are suggestive of mania.

The diagnostic criteria for mania are:

A. Distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated/irritable mood, and abnormally and persistently increased activity/energy, lasting at least 1 week.

B. During the period of mood disturbance and increased energy/activity, three (or more) of the following symptoms are present to a significant degree:

1. Increased self-esteem or grandiosity

2. Decreased need for sleep

3. More talkative than usual or a pressure to keep talking

4. Flight of ideas

5. Distractibility

6. Increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation

7. Excessive involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful consequences (unrestrained buying sprees, sexual indiscretions)

C. The mood disturbance is severe enough to cause marked social or occupational impairment or to necessitate hospitalization.

D. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (e.g., a drug of abuse, a medication, other treatment) or to another medical condition.


Other options: 

Option B - Hypomania is a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated/irritable mood, abnormally and persistently increased activity/energy, lasting for at least 4 days. It is similar to a manic episode but it is not severe enough to cause impairment in social or occupational functioning. No psychotic features are present.

Option C - Cyclothymia is a mild, chronic mood disorder with numerous depressive and hypomanic episodes over the course of at least 2 years.

Option D - Schizomania is an old term in DSM III, used to describe schizophrenic and manic symptomatology occurring in one episode, classified under schizoaffective disorder. Schizoaffective disorder is characterized by active phase symptoms of schizophrenia, like delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms. Additionally, there is a presence of manic/depressive syndrome that is not brief relative to the duration of the psychosis. The delusions or hallucinations are present for at least 2 weeks without coexisting mood symptoms.

 

Pearl: Bipolar disorder

Bipolar & related disorders

Manic episode

  • Symptoms more severe
  • 1 week unless hospitalized
  • Marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or hospitalization necessary
  • May have psychotic features; makes episode manic by definition

Hypomanic episode  

  • Symptoms less severe
  • 4 days to less than 7 days
  • Unequivocal, observable change in functioning from patient's baseline
  • Symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment or necessitate hospitalization
  • No psychotic features

Bipolar I

  • Manic episode(s)
  • Depressive episodes common (but not required for diagnosis)

Bipolar II

  • Hypomanic episode(s)
  • Major depressive episodes (required for diagnosis)

Cyclothymic disorder

  • At least 2 years of fluctuating, mild hypomanic & depressive symptoms that
    do not meet criteria for hypomanic episodes or major depressive episodes

Pearl: Patterns of Mood Disorders

Pearl: Psychotic disorders

Differential diagnosis of DSM-5 psychotic disorders

Psychotic disorder

 Criteria for diagnosis

Sudden onset and a full return to function

Duration: > 1 day and < 1 month
Schizophreniform disorder

Same symptoms as schizophrenia and functional decline not required

Duration: > 1 month & < 6 months
Schizophrenia

Requires functional decline

At least 6 months (includes at least 1 month of active symptoms, can include prodromal and residual periods)
Schizoaffective disorder

With concurrent mood episode. Active-phase symptoms of schizophrenia with at least a 2 weeks of lifetime history of delusions or hallucinations in absence of prominent mood symptoms
Delusional disorder

One or more delusions for > 1 month

No other psychotic symptoms and normal functioning apart from the direct impact of delusions
Shared psychotic disorder (folie a deux)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about hair cycle?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not true about hair cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: Anagen is responsible for final hair length

options.label: B
options.text: 50% of hair is in anagen at any point in time

options.label: C
options.text: Lower part of the follicle involutes during catagen

options.label: D
options.text: Kenogen is a state of latency

questions.correct_answer: B. 50% of hair is in anagen at any point in time
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 50% of hair is in anagen at any point in time

80-90% of hair follicles at a given time are in the anagen phase.

The hair cycle has three phases:

Anagen:

It refers to the period of active hair growth. Anagen can continue for several years and the duration of this phase is responsible for determining the final length of the hair. Normally, 80–90% of hair follicles on the human scalp are in anagen at any one time. It can be identified by the presence of angulated roots.

Catagen:

At the end of anagen, epithelial cell division slows and stops, and the follicle enters an involutionary phase known as catagen. The proximal end of the hair shaft keratinizes to form a club-shaped structure and the lower part of the follicle involutes by apoptosis. It lasts for about 3 weeks.

Telogen:

It is the resting phase between catagen and the next anagen. Clubbing becomes more prominent. It lasts for about 3 months. Club hair is eventually shed through an active process called exogen.

In the human scalp, hair follicles may remain in a state of latency, also known as kenogen, for a pro­longed period after the club hair is shed.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following is true regarding the vaccine vial monitor (VVM)?
  1. It is used for monitoring heat exposure of the vaccine by healthcare workers in primary healthcare.
  2. It shows cumulative exposure of the vaccine to the heat.
  3. It can be used to assess the potential efficacy of the vaccine.
  4. Calculation of the expiry date can be done using VVM.
  5. The expiry date of the vaccine can be relaxed if VVM is in an acceptable range.
  6. If the square and the circle are the same in color, then the vaccine can be safely used.
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following is true regarding the vaccine vial monitor (VVM)?
  1. It is used for monitoring heat exposure of the vaccine by healthcare workers in primary healthcare.
  2. It shows cumulative exposure of the vaccine to the heat.
  3. It can be used to assess the potential efficacy of the vaccine.
  4. Calculation of the expiry date can be done using VVM.
  5. The expiry date of the vaccine can be relaxed if VVM is in an acceptable range.
  6. If the square and the circle are the same in color, then the vaccine can be safely used.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1,2

The correct statements are 1 and 2.

Vaccine vial monitors (VVM) are heat-sensitive indicators routinely used to monitor heat exposure of the vaccine and determine vaccine viability as the vaccine vial moves across the supply chain. It records cumulative heat exposure through a gradual change in color.

If the color of the inner square is the same or is darker than the outer circle, it indicates that the vaccine has been exposed to high temperatures and should be discarded.

A VVM can be used to assess vaccine potency and not vaccine efficacy. Vaccine potency is the ability of the vaccine to provide adequate immunity to the patient. Vaccine potency is irreversibly lost when the vaccine is exposed to unfavorable temperatures; hence, VVM indicating heat exposure can be used to assess whether the vaccine potency is likely to be intact or not. Vaccine efficacy, on the other hand, is a measure of the immunity conferred by the vaccine or the ability of the vaccine to prevent the disease in a vaccinated person under ideal conditions, such as clinical trials. The term vaccine efficacy is used in relation to findings of clinical trials, whereas the term vaccine potency is used for regular usage of the vaccine. Vaccine efficacy is determined only during clinical trials, whereas vaccine potency is tested for every batch of the vaccine that is manufactured.

There are currently 4 types of VVMs; they are chosen to match the heat sensitivity of the vaccines based on the VVM number: 

  • VVM 30: High stability
  • VVM 14: Medium stability
  • VVM 7: Moderate stability
  • VVM 2: Least stable

Purpose of VVMs:

  • Ensures that vaccines damaged by heat are not administered.
  • Decision on which vaccines to be kept after a cold chain break occurs, minimizing unnecessary vaccine wastage.
  • Decision on which vaccine is to be used first. Vaccines showing significant heat exposure should be used before those that show lower heat exposure, even if their expiry date is longer.

The expiry date of a vaccine cannot be relaxed even if VVM is in an acceptable range. Expired vaccines must be discarded. The expiry date of a vaccine cannot be determined using a VVM as it does not monitor the vaccine components. It only ensures that the vaccines have been exposed to the required temperatures and are viable for use. 

There are two different locations for VVMs:

  • On the label of the vaccine: The vaccine vial, once opened, can be kept for subsequent immunization sessions for up to 28 days, regardless of the formulation of the product.
  • In a location other than on the label (e.g., cap or neck of ampoule): The vaccine vial, once opened should be discarded at the end of the immunization session or within six hours of opening, whichever comes first, regardless of the formulation of the product.

Pearl: Vaccine Vial Monitors

  • Vaccine vial monitors are used to monitor heat exposure of vaccines.
  • It is a chemical indicator that records the cumulative heat exposure through a gradual change in color.
  • If the color of the inner square is the same color or darker than the outer circle, it indicates that the vaccine has been exposed to too much heat and it must be discarded.
  • Currently, there are four types of VVMs (VVM2, VVM7, VVM14, and VVM30). They are chosen to match the heat sensitivity of the vaccine.
  • The VVM can be located on the label of the vaccine or on the neck or cap of the ampule/vial.
  • VVMs also help in reduction of vaccine wastage by indicating which batch of vaccines can be used first.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The upstroke of action potential (phase 0) in the sinoatrial node is due to ______________ ?
questions.raw_text: The upstroke of action potential (phase 0) in the sinoatrial node is due to ______________ ?

options.label: A
options.text: Sodium influx via voltage gated sodium channels

options.label: D
options.text: Influx of both sodium and calcium

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcium currents only

The upstroke of action potential (phase 0) in the sinoatrial node is due to calcium currents only. It occurs due to the influx of Ca2+ ions by the opening of voltage-gated L-type channels.

The action potential of the SA node differs from that of the atria, ventricles, and Purkinje fibres in the following ways: (1) In the absence of neural input, the SA node demonstrates automaticity and the ability to produce its own action potentials. (2) It has an unstable resting membrane potential. (3) It has no sustained plateau. 

The resting membrane potential (RMP) of the SA node is -55 to -60 millivolts. Phases of this potential are: 

  • Phase 0 (Upstroke wave)-  This is due to the influx of Ca2+ ions by the opening of voltage-gated L-type channels.
  • Phase 3 (Downstroke wave)- This is due to the efflux of K+ leading to repolarization. (Option C)
  • Phase 4 (Prepotential)- Because of ongoing K+ efflux, hyperpolarization sets in. This makes the channel more permeable to Na+ ions and since these Na+ channels are activated during hyperpolarization they are referred to as funny currents (Ih/ If). They form the first half of the pre-potential. The second half of the prepotential is completed by the opening of the voltage-gated T-(transient) type Ca2+ channel. The slope of Phase 4 in the SA node determines the heart rate.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Combination of appearance in CTEV
questions.raw_text: Combination of appearance in CTEV
questions.correct_answer: B. Equinus, inversion, forefoot adduction, cavus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Equinus, inversion, forefoot adduction, cavus

In congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), or idiopathic clubfoot, the deformity is equinus, inversion, forefoot adduction, and cavus. CTEV is a congenital malformation of the foot. It is predominately seen in male children. Calf and medial foot tissues are underdeveloped. 

Components of deformity:

  • Cavus - This deformity occurs due to exaggerated arching of the foot at the mid-tarsal joint.
  • Adduction - This deformity occurs at the talonavicular joint.
  • Inversion - This deformity occurs at the subtalar joint. The calcaneum is inverted, and along with it, the whole foot is inverted. This leads to a medially facing sole. 
  • Equinus - This deformity occurs at the ankle joint and tarsal joints.

Equinovarus deformity causes inward twisting of the foot (shown below), with the sole facing posteromedially in severe cases. Associated disorders like congenital hip dislocation and spina bifida should be evaluated. 

 Ponseti's method is a successful method of manipulation in CTEV. It should begin as early as the first 2 weeks after birth. Weekly manipulation of the foot is done with the help of plaster casts. The order of correction according to Ponseti's method is cavus-adduction-varus-equinus (CAVE).

The first metatarsal is elevated initially to correct the cavus. This creates a flat longitudinal medial border of the foot. Then, the forefoot is abducted in the plane of the metatarsals. This everts the hindfoot and corrects the forefoot out of supination. Finally, the equinus is corrected by dorsiflexing the foot at the ankle joint. In most cases, a percutaneous Achilles' tenotomy is required later for complete correction of the equinus deformity. 

Typically, five casts are required for correction, followed by a cast for 3 weeks. After correction, a foot abduction brace (FAB) is used to maintain the corrected position, initially full-time (for 3 months) and then night-time and nap-time for 4 years. This helps prevent relapse of the deformity. CTEV shoes are worn during the day once the child starts walking for up to 5 years. 

Pearl: Age wise management of CTEV

Initial treatment starts with Ponseti's POP cast as early as possible, but within 1 year of age.

If deformity gets corrected:

  • Dennis Brown splint is used till 1 year of age
  • After 1 year upto 5 years CTEV shoes are used in day, and Dennis Brown splint is used at night

If deformity is not corrected or untreated previously:

  • 1-3 years: Posteromedial soft tissue release (PMSTR) 
  • 3-5 years: Dillwyn Evans procedure
  • 5-8 years: Dwyer osteotomy
  • 8-10 years: Wedge tarsectomy
  • >10 years: Triple arthrodesis, external fixators

Which of the following are risk factors for calcium stone formation?
  1. Hypercalciuria
  2. Hypercitraturia
  3. Hyperoxaluria
  4. Hyperuricosuria
  5. Hypermagnesuria
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 & 4

Hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, and hyperuricosuria are risk factors for calcium stone formation. 

Risk factors for calcium stone formation include:

  • High urine concentration of calcium, oxalate, or uric acid
  • Low urine concentration of renal stone inhibiting factors such as citrate and magnesium
  • Abnormal urine pH

Renal stone formation is governed by factors promoting and inhibiting stone formation. Stone formation occurs when the concentration product is more than the formation product i.e., CP > FP, where:

  • Concentration product (CP) - the amount of solute in solution
  • Formation product (FP) - maximum concentration of solute in solution after taking into account stone inhibiting factors.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with hypotonia and seizures. It was confirmed to be cerebrohepatorenal syndrome. Which of the following is accumulated in the brain in cerebrohepatorenal syndrome?
questions.raw_text: A child presents with hypotonia and seizures. It was confirmed to be cerebrohepatorenal syndrome. Which of the following is accumulated in the brain in cerebrohepatorenal syndrome?
questions.correct_answer: A. Very long chain fatty acid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Very long chain fatty acid

Very long-chain fatty acids are accumulated in cerebrohepatorenal syndrome.

Cerebrohepatorenal syndrome, also known as Zellweger's syndrome, is a rare inherited disorder characterised by the absence of peroxisomes in all tissues. It is caused by mutations in the genes encoding peroxins, which take part in peroxisome biosynthesis. There is accumulation of C26-C38 polyenoic acids in brain tissues along with generalised loss of peroxisomal functions. Patients present with severe neurological symptoms and most die within a year. Other biochemical findings include abnormalities in the bile acid synthesis and a decreased plasmalogens.
subtopics: Fatty Acid Oxidation and Its Disorders

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents with muscle aches, hypotonia and poor exercise tolerance. Further investigation reveals myoglobinuria and elevated creatine kinase enzyme level in blood. Which transporter deficiency is responsible for the pathophysiology of the disease?
questions.raw_text: A 6-year-old boy presents with muscle aches, hypotonia and poor exercise tolerance. Further investigation reveals myoglobinuria and elevated creatine kinase enzyme level in blood. Which transporter deficiency is responsible for the pathophysiology of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carnitine

A young boy with muscle aches, hypotonia, poor exercise tolerance, myoglobinuria and elevated creatine kinase suggests a deficiency of carnitine.

Carnitine is a key transporter needed for beta-oxidation of fatty acids. It binds to acyl-CoAs to form acylcarnitine. This helps in the transfer of fatty acids across the impermeable inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation. Thus, carnitine deficiency results in impaired beta-oxidation of fatty acids. There will be inadequate ATP production in response to increased demands (e.g. exercise) with excess fatty acid accumulation in muscle cells. This results in muscle breakdown. 

Patients with carnitine deficiency present with hypoglycemia, muscle aches, hypotonia and poor exercise tolerance (myopathy). They have high levels of serum creatine kinase. Treatment includes carnitine supplementation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with redness and pain in the eye. Examination revealed an IOP of 38 mm of Hg, aqueous flare, and corneal precipitates. Which of the following drugs must be avoided in her?
questions.raw_text: A 30-year-old female presents with redness and pain in the eye. Examination revealed an IOP of 38 mm of Hg, aqueous flare, and corneal precipitates. Which of the following drugs must be avoided in her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prostaglandin analogs

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of anterior uveitis with a raised intraocular pressure. Among the given options, latanoprost is the least suited for use in this patient as it can result in worsening of the anterior uveitis.

Latanoprost is a PGF 2 alpha analog that acts by increasing the uveoscleral outflow and thereby lowers the intraocular pressure. Latanoprost is a prodrug and gets activated during its passage through the cornea. It acts by stimulating the prostanoid receptors on the ciliary muscles. This leads to the release of matrix metalloproteinases, which act to increases the uveoscleral outflow. It should be used with caution in those with uveitis, iritis, cystoid macular edema, and herpes simplex keratitis. 

Topical prostaglandins like latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost, and tafluprost are now used as first-line agents to lower IOP.  The most common ocular side effects are conjunctival hyperemia, eyelash thickening, iris hyperpigmentation, and loss of periorbital fat (bimatoprost). The systemic side effects are uncommon and include occasional headache, malaise, myalgia, skin rash, and mild upper respiratory infections.

questions.text:
Which of the following is the most common complication following ligation of the first vessel during abdominoperineal resection for rectal carcinoma?

(APR - Abdominoperineal resection)
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following is the most common complication following ligation of the first vessel during abdominoperineal resection for rectal carcinoma?

(APR - Abdominoperineal resection)

options.label: A
options.text: Parasympathetic - bladder dysfunction and retrograde ejaculation.

options.label: C
options.text: Sympathetic -  retrograde ejaculation and  bladder dysfunction.

options.label: D
options.text: Sympathetic - Impotence and loss of cutaneous sensation in perineal region

questions.correct_answer: C. Sympathetic -  retrograde ejaculation and  bladder dysfunction.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sympathetic - retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction.

The first vessel that is usually ligated during abdominoperineal resection (APR) is the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). A high inferior mesenteric artery ligation during abdominoperineal resection can injure the superior hypogastric nerve, resulting in sympathetic dysfunction and leading to retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction.

Abdominoperineal resection is the complete excision of the rectum, anal canal, and sphincter apparatus. This is done with the creation of a permanent colostomy. This is commonly preferred in elderly patients with distal rectal cancer with poor sphincter function. In these patients, the end colostomy offers a better quality of life.

Complications:

  • Higher recurrence rates compared to low anterior resection.
  • Anastomotic leaks or dehiscences
  • Necrosis of the transposed colon
  • Bleeding
  • Strictures  

The sympathetic innervation of the rectum is from L1, L2, and L3, which together form the superior hypogastric plexus. They divide into left and right hypogastric nerves at the level of the sacral promontory supplying the rectum and the genitourinary system. A high IMA ligation during surgery can result in sympathetic dysfunction causing retrograde ejaculation.

Injury to the pelvic plexus and nervi erigentes, during the division along the pelvic side wall, can cause erectile dysfunction, impotence, and atonic bladder. Injury to the periprostatic plexus can lead to sexual and bladder dysfunction.

questions.text: The half-life of letrozole is:
questions.raw_text: The half-life of letrozole is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 45 hours

The half-life of letrozole is 45 hours.

Letrozole is a reversible aromatase inhibitor. It is a non-steroidal compound that inhibits the aromatization of estrogen thereby causing estrogen depletion. Letrozole is rapidly absorbed with 99.9% oral bioavailability and has a t½ of around 41 hours.

Letrozole is used as the first-line drug for estrogen-positive breast cancer following mastectomy in post-menopausal women.

Adverse effects of letrozole are due to the depletion of estrogen. The commonly seen adverse effects are hot flashes, vaginal dryness, nausea, diarrhea, dyspepsia, accelerated bone loss, and thinning of hair.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of melancholia?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not a feature of melancholia?

options.label: D
options.text: Profound feelings of guilt over trivial events

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sleep-onset insomnia

Sleep-onset insomnia is a characteristic feature of anxiety disorder, not melancholia.

Melancholia is one of the oldest terms used in psychiatry, to describe the dark mood of depression. It is still used to refer to a state of depression characterized by:

  • Severe anhedonia
  • Early morning awakening (terminal insomnia)
  • Weight loss
  • Profound feelings of guilt (often over trivial events)

Melancholia is sometimes referred to as "endogenous depression" or depression that arises in the absence of external life stressors or precipitants.

questions.text:
While conducting a study on the age at death in males of a population Y, the distribution curve given below is obtained. Which of the following is true?
  1. It is a positively skewed distribution
  2. It is a left skewed distribution
  3. Mean > median > mode
  4. It is a bimodal distribution
  5. Mean < median < mode
questions.raw_text:
While conducting a study on the age at death in males of a population Y, the distribution curve given below is obtained. Which of the following is true?
  1. It is a positively skewed distribution
  2. It is a left skewed distribution
  3. Mean > median > mode
  4. It is a bimodal distribution
  5. Mean < median < mode
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 & 5

The given image shows a negatively skewed or a left-skewed distribution curve. Here, mean < median < mode.

Mode is the most frequently occurring value in the distribution and is given by the highest point of the graph. Since the given graph has only one peak, it is unimodal.

A positively skewed distribution refers to a right-skewed distribution. In such cases, mean > median > mode.

Pearl: Mean, Median, Mode in Different Distribution Shapes

  • The relationship between the mean, median and mode depends upon the distribution.
  • In a unimodal symmetrical distribution like a normal distribution, all the three measures are approximately the same, as shown in Figure (2) in the following image, i.e., mean = median = mode.
  • Figure (3) in the following image shows a positively skewed distribution in which the longer tail is towards the positive direction. In this, the mean will be larger than the median and mode, i.e., mean > median > mode.
  • Figure (1) in the following image shows a negatively skewed distribution in which the longer tail is towards the negative direction. In this, the mean will be smaller than the median, i.e., mean < median < mode.

Unimodal symmetrical distribution

Mean = Median = Mode

Positively (right) skewed distribution

Mean > Median > Mode

Negatively (left) skewed distribution

Mean < Median < Mode
  • As seen in the figures above, in any distribution curve, the mode is generally the highest point. The mean will be pulled up or down based on the values in the distribution. The median will lie between the mode and mean and divide the distribution in two equal halves under the curve.
  • A bimodal distribution will have two high points as shown in the image below.
  • Mathematically, the relationship between mode, median and mean in asymmetrical distributions can be given as:
    Mode = 3 median – 2 mean (or) Mean = ½ (3 median – mode).
  • Outlier is the statistical term used for an observation or value that is very distant from other observations in the distribution.
  • In a distribution with outliers, preferred measure of central tendency is the median.
  • Mode is least affected by outliers but mean is the most affected out of all the measures of location.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: In case of a meniscal tear repair, which of the following zones heals best?
questions.raw_text: In case of a meniscal tear repair, which of the following zones heals best?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Red zone

The red zone heals best in case of a meniscal tear due to its rich blood supply.

The menisci are divided into three zones depending on the perfusion of blood. The menisci are supplied by perimeniscal blood vessels from superior and inferior branches of medial and lateral genicular vessels.

Following birth, the menisci become increasingly avascular. By adulthood, only the peripheral 10% to 25% of the tissue is perfused. This gives rise to 3 distinct regions of the menisci:

  • The peripheral relatively vascularised region called the red-red zone (Zone 1)
  • A zone of transition between the 2 zones, which is called the red-white zone (Zone 2)
  • The completely avascular inner zone known as the white-white zone (Zone 3)

There is a direct relationship between the vascularization and capacity of the tissue to heal, predisposing the white-white zone to permanent post-traumatic and degenerative lesions.

Kaposi varicelliform eruption or eczema herpeticum is a widespread viral skin infection that causes localized or mild vesicular eruptions in a patient with pre‐existing skin disease (most commonly in atopic dermatitis).

Oral or intravenous acyclovir is used for the treatment depending on the severity of the infection.
