questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A preterm baby who was delivered at 28 weeks developed respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following is true about surface tension and compliance in this baby?
questions.raw_text: A preterm baby who was delivered at 28 weeks developed respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following is true about surface tension and compliance in this baby?

options.label: C
options.text: Both surface tension and compliance decreased

options.label: D
options.text: Both surface tension and compliance increased

questions.correct_answer: B. Surface tension - increased; Compliance - decreased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Surface tension - increased; Compliance - decreased

This preterm baby who developed respiratory distress syndrome has surfactant deficiency. In case of surfactant deficiency, the surface tension increases and compliance decreases.

Surfactant is secreted by the type 2 pneumocytes in the alveoli. Dipalmitoyl lecithin/dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) is a major component of lung surfactant. It reduces surface tension inside the alveoli, as shown below.

Compliance is defined as the extent of lung expansion for each unit increase in pressure. An important factor that affects lung compliance is surface tension. As surface tension increases, the pressure required to keep the alveoli open also increases. As more pressure is required to expand the alveoli, lung compliance will be reduced. 

Pearl: Pulmonary surfactant

It lowers the surface tension of the water layer at the alveolar surface, which increases lung compliance, thereby making it easier for the lungs to expand. It is secreted by type II alveolar cells. It is a mixture of phospholipids and protein.

4 unique apoproteins of surfactant: Surfactant proteins are (SP)-A, SP-B, SP-C, and SP-D.

  • SP-A - Regulation of the feedback uptake of surfactant by the type II alveolar epithelial cells that secrete it.
  • SP-B & SP-C - Key protein members of the monomolecular film of surfactant.
  • SP-D - Organization of SP-B and SP-C into the surfactant layer.

A deep breath increases its secretion by stretching the type II cells. Its concentration decreases when breaths are small.

In the fetus, surfactant synthesis is variable. The surfactant may be present as early as gestational week 24 and is almost always present by gestational week 35.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the true statement regarding the given nerve action potential curve.
questions.raw_text: Identify the true statement regarding the given nerve action potential curve.

options.label: B
options.text: At point 5, the nerve is more excitable

options.label: C
options.text: Point 3 to 4 is due to opening of Na+ and closure of K+ channels

questions.correct_answer: D. Point 2 to 4 is refractory period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Point 2 to 4 is refractory period

The correct statement regarding the given nerve action potential curve is point 2 to 4 is the refractory period.

The sequence of events occurring during an action potential is shown below 

  • Point 1 represents the resting state where both channels are closed. 
  • Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus and sodium enters the cell. The initiation of action potential occurs only after a certain potential is reached, which is called the threshold potential represented by point 2. (Option A)
  • After this, the sodium influx causes the opening of more Na+ channels through a positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs to reach point 3.
  • At point 3, Na+ channels close and K+ channels open, causing repolarization due to K+ efflux. (Option C)
  • Point 4 represents continued repolarization due to potassium efflux.
  • At point 5, Na+ channels are reset and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus. During this phase, the K+ channels remain open and slowly return to the closed state, causing after-hyperpolarization. As a stronger stimulus is required to reach the threshold potential, the excitability of nerve fiber is reduced at point 5. (Option B)
  • As both channels close, the membrane returns to resting membrane potential back to point 1.

The refractory period is divided into an absolute refractory period (from point 2 upto most of the repolarisation curve) and a relative refractory period. During the absolute refractory period, the nerve will not be excited no matter how strong a stimulus is given. However, during the relative refractory period, stronger than normal stimuli can cause excitation.

Pearl: Seddon's classification of nerve injuries

Seddon's classification includes 3 groups:

  • Conduction is lost but the nerve is in continuity and neural tubes are intact

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A child with loose stools for one day presented to your OPD. On examination,  signs of dehydration were present and the child was given ORS. It facilitates glucose absorption through which of the following receptors?
questions.raw_text: A child with loose stools for one day presented to your OPD. On examination,  signs of dehydration were present and the child was given ORS. It facilitates glucose absorption through which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. SGLT1

ORS facilitates glucose absorption through SGLT 1 (Sodium-dependent glucose co-transporter - 1). In a child with diarrhea, when oral rehydration solution is given, there is coupled absorption of sodium and glucose through SGLT -1.

Glucose transport may be active or passive.

Active transport of glucose takes place through Sodium dependent glucose transporter (SGLT 1 and 2). SGLT 1 helps in glucose absorption in both the small intestine and the renal tubules. SGLT 2 primarily facilitates glucose absorption in the renal tubules. 

Passive absorption of glucose occurs through facilitated diffusion. This is carried out by Glucose transporters (GLUT) 1 -7.

questions.text: A body fluid sample is being studied and has Na: 10 mEq/L, K: 140 mEq/L, CI: 4 mEq/L. Identify the compartment from which the sample has been obtained.
questions.raw_text: A body fluid sample is being studied and has Na: 10 mEq/L, K: 140 mEq/L, CI: 4 mEq/L. Identify the compartment from which the sample has been obtained.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intracellular fluid

The sample obtained is from the intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment. The ICF contains large quantities of potassium (K+) ions - 140 mEq/L . The ICF also has lesser amounts of sodium (Na+) and Chloride (Cl-) ions.

The extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment includes interstitial fluids and plasma. In contrast to the ICF, the ECF has an abundance of sodium, chloride, calcium and bicarbonate ions, and lesser amounts of potassium, phosphate and magnesium ions.

questions.text: A 30-year-old man weighing 70 kg had a sodium level of 120 mEq/L. Calculate the sodium deficit.
questions.raw_text: A 30-year-old man weighing 70 kg had a sodium level of 120 mEq/L. Calculate the sodium deficit.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 840 mEq

The sodium deficit in the given scenario is 840 mEq.

Sodium deficit is calculated as 0.6 x body weight x (target plasma sodium concentration - starting plasma sodium concentration).

Substituting the given values in the formula :

Sodium deficit = 0.6 x 70 x (140 - 120) = 840 mEq.

questions.text: A 20-year-old was brought to the ER after falling off his bicycle. His vitals were stable, but he had a bruise over the perineum and he has not passed urine yet. Blood was seen at the meatus and the bladder was not palpable. What will be the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.raw_text: A 20-year-old was brought to the ER after falling off his bicycle. His vitals were stable, but he had a bruise over the perineum and he has not passed urine yet. Blood was seen at the meatus and the bladder was not palpable. What will be the next step in the management of this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for bladder to fill and urge to urinate

questions.correct_answer: D. Wait for bladder to fill and urge to urinate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wait for bladder to fill and urge to urinate

The clinical features such as perineal bruise and blood at the urethral meatus following a fall from the bicycle are suggestive of a bulbar urethral injury. In this case, as the bladder is not palpable the best option would be to wait for the bladder to fill and urge to urinate. Once the bladder is full the urine should be drained by a suprapubic catheter.

Foleys catheter insertion should not be done in cases of suspected urethral injury, as it can convert a partial tear into a complete tear.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the fluid shown below.
questions.raw_text: Identify the fluid shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ringer lactate

The fluid shown in the image is ringer lactate or Hartmann's solution.

Ringer lactate, or Hartmann's solution, is a crystalloid made up of sodium 131 mEq, chloride 112 mEq, potassium 5 mEq, bicarbonate (as lactate) 29 mEq, and 2 mEq of calcium. It is devoid of glucose.

It is useful in the following conditions: 

  • Correction of severe hypovolemia
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Postoperative period, burns, diarrhea
  • Correction of hypokalemia
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis.

It should be avoided in severe shock, liver diseases, vomiting, nasogastric aspiration, and metabolic alkalosis. It cannot be used along with blood transfusion since calcium in the ringer lactate can bind with citrate in the transfused blood leading to clot formation. 

Other options:

Option A: Haemaccel is a colloid and contains 145 mmol of sodium, 6.25 mmol of calcium, and 5.1 mmol of potassium. It is mainly used for rapid volume replacement in circulatory shock, burns, and trauma. These release histamine and hence, H2 blocker has to be supplemented. It is also used in heart-lung machines.

Options C and D: Isolyte P and Isolyte M are crystalloids. Isolyte P is commonly used in fluid therapy for pediatrics. One liter contains 50 grams of glucose, 25 mEq of sodium, 22 mEq of potassium, 3 mEq of magnesium, and 23 mEq of acetate. Hyponatremia, renal failure, hyperkalemia, and hypovolemic shock are some of the contraindications.

Isolyte M is used for maintenance. It mainly contains 50 grams of glucose, 40 mEq sodium, 38 mEq chloride, 35 mEq potassium, 15 mEq phosphate, and 20 mEq acetate. It is useful in correcting hypokalemia in patients with good renal function, and acidosis. It is contraindicated in hyponatremia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A young teenage boy with a history of drug abuse had been instilled with a shot of intravenous cocaine at a party. He is rushed to the emergency room by his friends. Some of the symptoms were diaphoresis, headache, and acute coronary spasm. Which of the following symptoms noted would go against the likely diagnosis of cocaine poisoning?
questions.raw_text: A young teenage boy with a history of drug abuse had been instilled with a shot of intravenous cocaine at a party. He is rushed to the emergency room by his friends. Some of the symptoms were diaphoresis, headache, and acute coronary spasm. Which of the following symptoms noted would go against the likely diagnosis of cocaine poisoning?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bradycardia

Cocaine intoxication presents with tachycardia and not bradycardia. Thus, the presence of bradycardia would go against the diagnosis of cocaine intoxication.

Cocaine is an alkaloid deliriant extracted from Erythroxylum coca.

Acute intoxication with cocaine leads to symptoms spanning 2 stages-

  1. Stage of excitement/euphoria - associated with hypervigilance, anxiety, hyperactivity along with hyper-adrenergic signs of mydriasis, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, hyperthermia, and cardiac arrhythmias. 
  2. Stage of depression - associated with loss of reflexes, muscle paralysis, circulatory and respiratory failure, and coma. 

Chronic intoxication is characterized by toxic delirium and tactile hallucination of bugs (cocaine bugs) or vermin crawling under the skin (formication).

Common complications include cerebrovascular accidents and myocardial ischemia. 

Treatment includes intravenous diazepam for controlling seizures. For ventricular arrhythmias, propranolol may be given intravenously. If the patient has psychosis, haloperidol may be given. Treatment of chronic cocaine abuse requires psychiatric support. 

Cocaine withdrawal is a triphasic syndrome that presents after the sudden stoppage of chronic cocaine use. The phases are as follows - 

  1. Crash phase (9 hours - 4 days): Anorexia, depression, excessive craving, hypersomnia, fatigue.
  2. Normal mood, anxiety, and anhedonia (4 - 7 days)
  3. Extinction phase (7 - 10 days): Absence of withdrawal symptoms but increased susceptibility to relapse.

Treatment for withdrawal includes bromocriptine and amantadine. They are useful in reducing cocaine craving.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the given cross-section of a muscle spindle, the structure marked below is innervated by which of the following motor nerve fibres?
questions.raw_text: In the given cross-section of a muscle spindle, the structure marked below is innervated by which of the following motor nerve fibres?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gamma

In the given cross-section of a muscle spindle, the structure marked shows intrafusal muscle fibres, which are innervated by gamma(γ) motor neurons. 

Each muscle spindle is 3 to 10 mm long and consists of 3 to 12 tiny intrafusal muscle fibers that are pointed at their ends and attached to the glycocalyx of the surrounding large extrafusal muscle fibers. There are two kinds of sensory endings in each spindle, a single primary (group Ia) ending and up to eight secondary (group II) endings.

Intrafusal fibers are of 2 types: (1) nuclear bag fibers - subdivided as dynamic and static nuclear bag fibers and (2) nuclear chain fibers.

Each intrafusal muscle fiber is a tiny skeletal muscle fiber. Since there are either few or no actin and myosin filaments in the centre of each of these fibres, the centre does not contract when the ends do. It performs the role of a sensory receptor instead. The end portions that do contract are excited by small gamma(γ) motor nerve fibers which help control basic muscle tone. 

There are two types of γ motor neurons- (a) dynamic that supplies dynamic nuclear bag fibers and (b) static that supply static nuclear bag fibers and nuclear chain fibers.

Other options:

Option B: Alpha (α) motor fibers supply the extrafusal muscle fibers which are the regular contractile units of the muscle. They are on an average 14 micrometers in diameter and these fibers branch many times after they enter the muscle and innervate the large skeletal muscle fibers at the motor endplate. A single alpha nerve fibre can stimulate anywhere between three to several hundred skeletal muscle fibres, which are collectively called the motor unit.

Option C: Beta (β) fibers are for touch and pressure.

Option D: Delta (δ) fibers are for pain and temperature.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 69-year-old man who is a chronic smoker, hypertensive, and has a BMI of 35 kg/m2 complains of diminished vision in the right eye. His visual acuity is 6/36 BE and the anterior segment appears normal. His fundus is as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.correct_answer: B. Age related dry macular degeneration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Age related dry macular degeneration

The clinical scenario along with the image which shows drusen (druplets) are a feature of dry or non-exudative age-related macular degeneration (ARMD). 

Drusen are the earliest visible clinical signs of ARMD. They are composed of lipid, amyloid, complement factors, and associated cellular components.

There are two types of ARMD:

  • Dry (non-exudative, non-neovascular) ARMD is the most common form, comprising around 90% of the diagnosed cases. Initially characterized by macular Drusens, which later progress to geographical atrophy. Geographic atrophy (GA) is the advanced stage of dry ARMD. Antioxidants like the AREDS2 supplements have proven effective.
  • Wet (exudative, neovascular) ARMD is much less common than the dry type, but it is associated with more rapid progression to advanced sight loss.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is the test for immediate memory?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is the test for immediate memory?

options.label: A
options.text: Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed

options.label: B
options.text: Serial (100-7) subtraction test up to 5 steps

options.label: C
options.text: Digit span backwards up to 5 digits with 2 skips allowed

options.label: D
options.text: Serial (20-1) subtraction test up to 5 steps

questions.correct_answer: A. Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed

Forward digit span test is the best test among the given options.

Memory is of 3 types:

  • Immediate
  • Recent
  • Remote

Immediate memory is attention dependent. Tests of attention and memory include

  • Digit span test: Most important and best test for immediate memory
  • Serial (100-7) subtraction test is the best for concentration
  • Days of the week backwards
  • Spell WORLD backwards
  • (20–3) test

Digit span test

The examiner recites numbers randomly without any sequence and asks the patient to repeat the same. The examiner starts with a 2-number sequence and the digit span increases from 2 numbers to 3 numbers and so on. The patient is asked to repeat until he/she fails to repeat all numbers correctly. 

Digit forward

  • Normally a person can repeat up to 7 digits (+/- 2)
  • E.g., Examiner says 2 - 4 –8 –1 –5 –7 - 9. The person has to repeat in the same order 2 – 4 – 8 –1 –5 –7 –9.

Digit backward

  • Reproduction of longer digits in backward direction.
  • Normally a person can repeat up to 5 digits (+/- 1) in backward direction (making option C wrong)
  • Eg : Examiner says 2 - 4 –8 –1 –5 –7 - 9. The person has to repeat it backwards. 9 -7 -5 -1 -8- 4- 2.

 

Serial (100-7) subtraction test

  • 5 scores / steps are taken in to account
    • 1st score – When the patient tells 93 (100 - 7 = 93)
    • 2nd score - When the patient tells 86 (93 – 7 = 86)
    • And so on . . 100 , 93 , 86 , 79 , 72 , 65

Hence among the given options :

Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed would be the answer of choice as it is the best test for immediate memory

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient who is a known case of hypertension on multiple anti-hypertensive medications came to OPD. His ECG finding is given below. Which of the following drugs is responsible for the ECG finding?
questions.raw_text: A patient who is a known case of hypertension on multiple anti-hypertensive medications came to OPD. His ECG finding is given below. Which of the following drugs is responsible for the ECG finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spironolactone

Based on the ECG findings (tall T waves), the most likely diagnosis is hyperkalemia, and among the given drugs, spironolactone is the drug that is most likely to cause hyperkalemia.

Spironolactone is a potasium-sparing diuretic. It is a competitive inhibitor of the mineralocorticoid receptor in the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidneys. It causes a decrease in sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal tubule. As a result, spironolactone promotes sodium diuresis but maintains body potassium levels.

Hyperkalemia is defined as a serum potassium level of more than 5.5 mEq/L. 

Hyperkalemia can cause drastic conduction changes. It can be diagnosed by a sequence of changes affecting the ST-T segments and QRS complex. ST-T segment changes reflect a change in repolarization while QRS complex changes reflect a change in depolarization.

The ECG changes that can be seen in hyperkalemia depend on the extent of hyperkalemia. 

S. No. Serum potassium level ECG change
1 5.5-6.5 mEq/L Tall, peaked T waves with 'tented' or 'pinched' shape
2 6.5-7.5 mEq/L loss of P waves
3 7.0-8.0 mEq/L widened QRS complex
4 > 8.0 mEq/L Sine wave

 

  • Drugs that cause hyperkalemia include:

    • Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
    • Angiotensin receptor blockers eg. Losartan
    • Mineralocorticoid receptor blockers like spironolactone, eplerenone, drospirenone
    • Epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) blockers like amiloride and triamterene
    • Others: Trimethoprim, pentamidine, nafamostat

Treatment of hyperkalemia involves the following:

  1. Administer intravenous calcium gluconate, which raises the threshold and reduces excitability. It is cardioprotective
  2. Administer regular insulin with dextrose. The insulin will reduce the serum potassium concentration by causing an intracellular shift. The dextrose will counteract the hypoglycemic effects of insulin.
  3. Salbutamol nebulization will also shift potassium inside the cell.
  4. Remove potassium with calcium-based resins, diuretics, or hemodialysis.

Other options:

Option A: The major potential side effect of prazosin is postural hypotension and syncope.

Option B: Metoprolol is a cardioselective beta blocker. Cardioselective beta blockers are less likely to cause hyperkalemia as an adverse effect. The risk of metoprolol-induced hyperkalemia is increased if the patient is also diabetic.

Option C: Hydrochlorothiazides increase the renal excretion of potassium and thus cause hypokalemia if the dietary intake of potassium is less.

  • B: Bisoprolol
  • A: Acebutolol
  • A: Atenolol
  • N: Nebivolol ( III )
  • B: Betaxolol ( III )
  • M: Metoprolol
  • E: Esmolol

questions.text: Which is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults?
questions.raw_text: Which is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) in adults and children over the age of 15 years, worldwide and in India.

Burkitt's lymphoma is the most common NHL in children under the age of 15 years.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following agents is to be avoided in a hypertensive patient?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following agents is to be avoided in a hypertensive patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ketamine

Ketamine is avoided in a hypertensive patient as it has intrinsic sympathomimetic properties and hence can aggravate hypertension.

Ketamine increases arterial blood pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output. This is due to central stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system and inhibition of the reuptake of norepinephrine. And hence it should be cautiously used in patients with uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure and arterial aneurysms.

Its stimulatory effects may be beneficial to patients with acute shock. All other intravenous induction agents like propofol, thiopentone and etomidate produce a fall in blood pressure.

Correct answer: B. Vitamin H

Biotin (Vitamin H or Vitamin B7) deficiency can cause alopecia, dermatitis (periorificial), and thinning of hair. It is commonly seen in individuals who are on long term valproate therapy.

Scarring alopecia with islands of dense hair referred to as intermittent constrictions is classically seen in biotin deficiency.

  3. Splinting
  4. Antibiotic coverage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 only

Emergency management of open fractures is mainly focused on the prevention of infection by providing antibiotic coverage and splinting (statements 3 and 4). Reduction of the fracture (statement 1) can be done in the emergency room. Internal fixation is not done on an emergency basis for an open fracture due to the risk of infection (statement 2). It is a part of definitive management and is done after the patient is stabilized.

Open fractures are characterized by a break in the overlying skin and soft tissues. Hence, the fracture fragment is exposed to the external environment. There are more prone to be infected. 

The major components of the management of open fractures:

  • Antibiotic prophylaxis - It should be given as early as possible (within 3 hours of injury). Amoxiclav is commonly used. 
  • Early debridement of the wound and fracture - This includes the following steps:
    • Excision of the wound margins
    • Extension of the wound if required
    • Delivery of the fracture outside the wound for proper examination
    • Removal of the devitalized tissue
    • Cleansing of the wound to remove all the foreign materials
    • Nerves and tendons are usually left alone, but if the wound is clean, a repair can be considered
  • Wound cover:
    • In Gustilo Type I and II fractures, wound cover can be done at the time of debridement (early wound cover)
    • Delayed wound cover is usually practiced in Type III fractures
  • Fracture stabilization: External fixators are used to stabilize the fractures in the emergency room. Definitive management is later done by open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A young child presented with mild intermittent upper abdominal pain. X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A young child presented with mild intermittent upper abdominal pain. X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Morgagni hernia

The clinical features and the chest X-ray showing an opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle are suggestive of Morgagni hernia.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia(CDH) of anteromedial location is the Morgagni hernia. Here the defect is anterior and retrosternal. It is rarer than bochdalek hernia and accounts for only 2-5% of CDH. About 90% of the cases occur on the right side.

It is less symptomatic than bochdalek hernia and the diagnosis is usually delayed until childhood. The patient presents with respiratory or upper GI symptoms. Respiratory symptoms like distress, tachypnea, and recurrent pulmonary infections are common in children. Other symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspnea, flatulence, and indigestion.

Radiographic findings:

  • Radiolucent paracardiac shadow may be seen retrosternally on lateral chest x-ray if there is bowel herniation.
  • Rounded opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle may be seen if there is herniation of omentum or solid organs.
  • A CT scan may be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Surgical repair is indicated in all cases either by a thoracic or abdominal approach.

Other options:

Bochdalek hernia: It is more common than Morgagni hernia. Here the defect is posterolateral in location. Respiratory distress is experienced by most infants. In the pediatric age group, symptoms are predominantly respiratory due to pulmonary hypoplasia. In adults, it is usually asymptomatic and is incidentally found. About 85% of the cases are left-sided.

Gastric volvulus: This is an uncommon condition and presents with the characteristic Borchardt triad which includes:

  • Sudden-onset severe upper abdominal pain
  • Recurrent retching with the production of little vomitus
  • Inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube

It can be organoaxial or mesentroaxial. Chest X-ray may show intrathoracic upside-down stomach and retrosternal or mediastinal air-fluid level.

Image showing intrathoracic gastric volvulus with mediastinal gastric bubble-

Eventration of the diaphragm: It refers to the abnormal contour of the dome of the diaphragm without any disruption to the diaphragmatic continuity. It usually involves a segment of the hemidiaphragm. It can cause respiratory distress in newborns and is usually asymptomatic in adults.

Radiographic findings: The affected portion of the hemidiaphragm is elevated and is seen as a smooth hump, while the normal contour is seen in the remaining part. 'Double diaphragmatic contour' may be seen in frontal view and is confirmed with a lateral X-ray.

Image showing eventration of the right dome of the diaphragm-

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true regarding sodalime?

  1. 100 g of sodalime can absorb 15 liters of CO2

  2. The end product of the reaction of sodalime and CO2 is Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2

  3. The major constituent of sodalime is Ca(OH)2

  4. Water content of sodalime is 5%

  5. KOH is one of the components of sodalime
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following statements is true regarding sodalime?

  1. 100 g of sodalime can absorb 15 liters of CO2

  2. The end product of the reaction of sodalime and CO2 is Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2

  3. The major constituent of sodalime is Ca(OH)2

  4. Water content of sodalime is 5%

  5. KOH is one of the components of sodalime
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 and 5

Statement 1: 100 g of sodalime can absorb 23 liters of CO2

Statement 2: The end product of the reaction of soda lime with CO2 is CaCO3+NaOH. Reaction end products include heat (the heat of neutralization), water, calcium carbonate, and sodium hydroxide.

Its reactions are as follows:

  1. CO2 + H2O → H2CO3
  2. H2CO3 + 2NaOH → Na2CO3 + 2H2O + Heat (a fast reaction)
  3. Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3 + 2NaOH + Heat (a slow reaction)

Note that the water and sodium hydroxide initially required are regenerated.

Statement 3: The major constituent of soda lime is Ca(OH)2 - 80%

Statement 4: Water content of sodalime is 15%

Statement 5: KOH is one of the components of sodalime - 2%

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient presents with severe restlessness, palpitations, and tremors to the emergency department. She is a known case of bronchial asthma. On examination, the neck looks swollen. Blood pressure is elevated, and tachycardia is noted. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Which of the following drugs is used for immediate management in this patient?
questions.raw_text: A female patient presents with severe restlessness, palpitations, and tremors to the emergency department. She is a known case of bronchial asthma. On examination, the neck looks swollen. Blood pressure is elevated, and tachycardia is noted. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Which of the following drugs is used for immediate management in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diltiazem

The given clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis of thyroid storm/thyroid crisis presenting with atrial fibrillation, and the immediate management in this patient is to rate control the arrhythmia with diltiazem (calcium channel blocker).

Thyroid storm/Thyrotoxic crisis is a rare but severe life-threatening complication of hyperthyroidism induced by the release of excessive thyroid hormones.

It is caused by abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications, infection, inadequately prepared hyperthyroid patient for thyroidectomy, amiodarone administration, exposure to iodinated contrast agents, and following radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy.

Features:

  • Fever and severe dehydration
  • Cardiovascular: Circulatory collapse, palpitations, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, and cardiac failure
  • GI symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice
  • Neurological symptoms: Restlessness, irritability, delirium, tremor, convulsions, and coma 

Treatment:

  • If the patient presents with atrial fibrillation, the first step in the management is to do rate control using beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, or amiodarone. Since this patient is a known asthmatic, beta-blockers (propranolol and esmolol) are contraindicated. So, a calcium channel blocker (diltiazem) is the preferred drug for immediate management in this patient.
  • Supportive measures – rehydration by proper fluid therapy, tepid sponging, and cooling blankets.
  • Thionamides like propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole, or carbimazole can be used. PTU (Option D) is the drug of choice in thyroid storm, but it is given only after controlling atrial fibrillation.
  • Lugol’s iodine suppresses thyroid hormone release via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect. It is administered one hour after the first dose of propylthiouracil or methimazole
  • Glucocorticoids help decrease the conversion of T4 to the more active T3 in peripheral tissues and also aid in managing shock.
  • Digoxin and cardiac monitoring are crucial.

Other options:

Options B & C: Beta-blockers like propranolol and esmolol are contraindicated in bronchial asthma patients.

Pearl: Thyroid storm / Thyrotoxic crisis:

It is an emergency caused by an acute exacerbation of hyperthyroidism. 

Precipitating factors:

  • When a thyrotoxic patient has been inadequately prepared for thyroidectomy
  • Abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications
  • Stress
    • Infection
    • Thyroid or non-thyroid surgery
    • Trauma in patients with untreated thyrotoxicosis
  • Acute iodine load
    • Amiodarone administration 
    • Exposure to iodinated contrast agents
    • Following RAI therapy

Clinical features:

  • Fever
  • Tachycardia
  • Altered mentation (delirium, psychosis, coma)
  • GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea)
  • Atrial fibrillation and cardiac failure - most common causes of death

Treatment of thyroid storm:

Treatment modality Effect
IV Fluids, ice packs Rehydration and external cooling
Propylthiouracil
(DOC)

Reduces peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
Propranolol

Block adrenergic effects

Reduces peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
Corticosteroids

Inhibits the release of thyroid hormone from the gland

Reduces peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
Lugol’s iodine/ sodium ipodate Inhibits the release of thyroid hormone from the gland
Digoxin Controls the associated atrial fibrillation
Diuretics and administration of oxygen

To manage cardiac failure

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Peripheral smear of a patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia shows myeloblasts with the following finding. What are these made of?
questions.raw_text: Peripheral smear of a patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia shows myeloblasts with the following finding. What are these made of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lysosomes

The image shows Auer rods in myeloblasts. These are needle-shaped azurophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies formed by the fusion of lysosomes.

Auer rods contain peroxidase and lysosomal enzymes. Myeloblasts with bundles of Auer rods are called faggot cells and are seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia.

questions.text: An elderly patient who presented with abdominal discomfort and weight loss was diagnosed with type I gastric cancer according to Lauren’s classification. Which of the following is not true regarding this condition?

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lymphatic spread

Type I gastric cancer is associated with hematogenous spread. 

Lauren's system classifies gastric cancer pathology as either type I (intestinal) or type II (diffuse), based on differences in etiology, epidemiology, and pathology. Intestinal type of gastric cancer shows hematogenous spread, whereas diffuse-type shows transmural and lymphatic spread.

questions.text: A scattergram was plotted as shown below to study the relationship between two variables. What is the correct interpretation?
questions.raw_text: A scattergram was plotted as shown below to study the relationship between two variables. What is the correct interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: There is correlation between both variables and the Pearson’s coefficient is 1

options.label: B
options.text: There is correlation between both variables and the Pearson’s coefficient is – 1

options.label: C
options.text: There is non-linear correlation between both variables

options.label: D
options.text: There is no association between both variables

questions.correct_answer: C. There is non-linear correlation between both variables
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. There is non-linear correlation between both variables

The given scattergram depicts a non-linear correlation between the two variables. 

Correlation expresses the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables in terms of a correlation coefficient. There are two types of correlation coefficients:

Pearson coefficient Spearman coefficient
Used for data with continuous intervals Used for data with discrete ordered intervals

Used to find linear relationships

(e.g. salt intake vs blood pressure)

Used to find linear or non-linear relationships

(e.g. socioeconomic status vs parity)

Pearl: Correlation

Correlation expresses the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables in terms of a correlation coefficient. It is represented by r.

  • Values of r vary from -1 (perfect negative correlation) to +1 (perfect positive correlation).
  • Value (size) of the coefficient: Indicates the strength of relationship
  • Sign of the coefficient: Indicates direction of relationship

Coefficients between ±0.5 and 1 are regarded as strong whereas those between ±0.5 and 0 are regarded as weak.

The data is plotted in a scattergram as shown in the examples given below

Examples:

Types of correlation coefficients

  1. Pearson coefficient
  2. Spearman coefficient

Coefficient of Determination (CD) =  r2

It is simply the percentage variability in one factor due to change in another variable.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents to the OPD with complaints of amenorrhoea for the past year. She has a history of postpartum hemorrhage and lactational failure. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A woman presents to the OPD with complaints of amenorrhoea for the past year. She has a history of postpartum hemorrhage and lactational failure. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sheehan's syndrome

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Sheehan's syndrome. 

Sheehan's syndrome (SS) is postpartum hypopituitarism secondary to the necrosis of the pituitary gland. It usually results from severe hypotension or shock caused by massive hemorrhage during or after delivery. Patients with SS have varying degrees of anterior pituitary hormone deficiency. The hyperplastic enlargement of the pituitary, which occurs normally during pregnancy, increases the risk of infarction. 

Affected women may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent symptoms are lactation failure (due to a deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to a deficiency of gonadotropins). Because deficiencies of some or all pituitary-responsive hormones may develop after the initial insult, Sheehan syndrome can be heterogeneous and may not be identified for years.

It can present acutely as pituitary apoplexy, an endocrine emergency, characterized by a sudden onset of headache, nausea, visual deficits, and in severe cases, severe hypoglycemia, hypotension and shock, CNS hemorrhage, and death.

Also, it can present late with the following features:

  • Loss of pubic and axillary hair
  • Hypothyroidism due to decreased TSH secretion 
  • Adrenal insufficiency due to low ACTH

Treatment is by hormone replacement - first glucocorticoids, later - thyroid hormone, sex steroids, vasopressin and growth hormones are given. If there is evidence of progressive visual loss, cranial nerve involvement or loss of consciousness, immediate surgical decompression must be carried out. Fertility can be achieved in these women with hMG and hCG. Clomiphene is ineffective. 

Option B: Rotor syndrome is a type of hereditary hyperbilirubinemia with autosomal recessive inheritance. Affected individuals have mild jaundice and hyperbilirubinemia. 

Option C: Prolactinoma or pituitary adenoids is the condition of hyperprolactinemia diagnosed by a prolactin level >200 μg/L. It usually presents with infertility, amenorrhea, and galactorrhea.

Option D: Acromegaly is characterized by the signs and symptoms pertaining to excessive growth hormone secretion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In which condition does the hemithorax typically appear opaque on chest X-ray?
questions.raw_text: In which condition does the hemithorax typically appear opaque on chest X-ray?

options.label: A
options.text: Middle aged man with Macleod syndrome

questions.correct_answer: C. Patient who has undergone pneumonectomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Patient who has undergone pneumonectomy

The hemithorax typically appears opaque in a patient who has undergone pneumonectomy.

After pneumonectomy, the operated hemithorax gradually fills with fluid, which eventually undergoes fibrous tissue replacement, making it completely opaque. In the immediate post-operative period, some air may remain in the space, so it can appear lucent initially before the fluid accumulates.

The below image shows a chest X-ray of a person who has had their right lung removed.

Causes for hypertranslucency/hypertransradiancy of hemithorax:

  • Pneumothorax
  • Pulmonary embolism
  • Air trapping—small airways disease, constrictive obliterative bronchiolitis
  • Emphysema

Causes of opacification of a hemithorax:

  • Pleural effusion
  • Consolidation
  • Collapse
  • Massive tumour
  • Fibrothorax
  • Combination of above lesions
  • Pneumonectomy
  • Lung agenesis

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs gets deposited in cornea?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following drugs gets deposited in cornea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chloroquine

Chloroquine, an anti-malarial drug, may get deposited in the cornea, leading to corneal opacity.

Ocular toxicity of chloroquine:

  • Short-term therapy - blurring of vision and diplopia, reversible on stoppage of the drug.
  • Long-term use (high-dose): 
    • Keratopathy
    • Pigmentary retinopathy
    • Optic atrophy

Hydroxychloroquine has lower ocular toxicity compared to chloroquine. 

Drugs causing corneal opacity:

  • Amiodarone
  • Phenothiazine
  • Indomethacin
  • Chloroquine

Long-term treatment with these drugs can cause a whorl-like opacity in the corneal epithelium called cornea verticillata. It is also seen in Fabry's disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young male patient with a history of a motor vehicle accident is unable to pass urine. Blood is seen at the meatus. What is the most likely site of urethral injury?
questions.raw_text: A young male patient with a history of a motor vehicle accident is unable to pass urine. Blood is seen at the meatus. What is the most likely site of urethral injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Membranous urethra

In the given scenario of a young patient with urinary retention, blood at the meatus, and a history of a motor vehicle accident, the most likely site of injury is the membranous urethra. The given retrograde urethrogram shows contrast leakage at the membranous urethra. 

Urethral injuries in men usually occur after catheterization or during cystoscopy. Injuries following external trauma are rare, but mainly affect the bulbar or the membranous urethra. 

Membranous urethral rupture usually occurs following a road traffic accident, crush injury, or a fall. It is associated with pelvic fracture and extraperitoneal bladder rupture. Clinical features include urinary retention, blood at the meatus, and a high riding prostate on digital examination. Bruising is seen over the pubic area, scrotum, and penis.

Management is by inserting a suprapubic catheter. If there is an associated bladder rupture, the bladder will not be seen on the ultrasound, and management in such a case is by exploration, repair, and placement of a suprapubic catheter.

Other options:

Option A: Bulbar urethral injury occurs following a blow to the perineum with a fall astride injury during cycling or gymnasium accidents. A typical feature is a butterfly-shaped hematoma in the perineum. Other features such as urinary retention and meatal bleeding can also be present. Analgesia, antibiotics, and suprapubic catheterization are needed. The patient should be discouraged from passing urine. Definitive management is delayed urethroplasty after 8-12 weeks.

Options B and D: Spongy and penile urethral rupture can occur following a penile fracture during coitus. Hematuria and difficulty in voiding can be present in spongy urethral injury. A pop sound followed by severe penile pain and penile deformity is characteristic of penile urethral injury. Hematoma, blood at the meatus, and voiding difficulties are also seen.  

Retrograde urethrogram shows loss of smooth contour of the urethra with extravasation of the dye in case of a spongy urethral rupture. Surgical repair is needed in both.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient who underwent an IUD insertion is most likely to develop which of the following in the future?
questions.raw_text: A patient who underwent an IUD insertion is most likely to develop which of the following in the future?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vaginal bleeding

Patients who underwent IUD insertion are most likely to develop vaginal bleeding in the future.

Side effects and complications of IUDs include:

  • Vaginal bleeding – most common
  • Abdominal pain – second most common
  • Pelvic infection
  • Uterine perforation
  • Pregnancy - due to failure of contraception
  • Ectopic pregnancy
  • Expulsion of the IUD
  • Cancer and teratogenicity

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Given below is an electron microscopy image showing deposits in the kidney. What could be the diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: Given below is an electron microscopy image showing deposits in the kidney. What could be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Membranous nephropathy

The given electron microscopy image shows subepithelial deposits in the kidney which is suggestive of membranous nephropathy.

The following electron microscopy image shows subepithelial deposits in the kidney.

Membranous nephropathy is characterized by the diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall. It is due to the accumulation of deposits containing Ig along the subepithelial side of the basement membrane.

Other options:

Option A: Goodpasture syndrome is a glomerular basement membrane defect due to antibodies against type IV collagen. It shows linear deposits along the basement membrane on electron microscopy (EM).

Option B: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is caused due to immune-mediated injury, often presenting with a nephritic-nephrotic picture. It is characterized by the proliferation of cells predominantly in the mesangium and the capillary loops. MPGN type I presents with subendothelial deposits in EM, whereas type II presents with intramembranous dense deposits in EM. 

Option D: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. It is characterized by the absence of deposits. The EM image would reveal podocyte effacement.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 3-year-old girl presents with a mass protruding from the anterior vaginal wall that appears like grape clusters. Histopathological examination reveals tadpole cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 3-year-old girl presents with a mass protruding from the anterior vaginal wall that appears like grape clusters. Histopathological examination reveals tadpole cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma

The most likely diagnosis is embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides).

It is an uncommon vaginal tumor composed of malignant embryonal rhabdomyoblasts. It is most frequently found in infants and in children < 5 years of age. They are locally invasive tumors that cause death by penetration into the peritoneal cavity or by obstruction of the urinary tract.

Grossly, polypoid, rounded, bulky masses that appear like grape clusters can be seen. On microscopy, small tumor cells with oval nuclei, and small protrusions of cytoplasm from one end resembling a tennis racket (tadpole cells) can be seen. Beneath the vaginal epithelium, the tumor cells are crowded in a cambium layer, in the dermis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A patient comes to ED with fever and headache. On examination he has neck stiffness. CSF analysis was done and it shows the following findings. Most likely diagnosis is:

Opening pressure – Increased

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Coxsackie

The given symptoms cluster of fever, vomiting, and neck stiffness is suggestive of meningitis. A CSF analysis showing increased opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly increased protein, and normal glucose is suggestive of viral meningitis. Among the given options, Coxsackie (Option D) is the only viral cause of meningitis. 

Other options:

Option A: Tuberculous meningitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose.

Option B: Bacterial meningitis shows neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose.

Option C: Fungal meningitis shows lymphocytic/neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following anti-diabetic drugs should be stopped in a patient with a creatinine of 5.6 mg/dL?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following anti-diabetic drugs should be stopped in a patient with a creatinine of 5.6 mg/dL?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metformin

Metformin should be stopped in case of elevated creatinine levels (renal insufficiency) > 1.5 mg/dl in men and >1.4 mg/dl in women.

Metformin acts by reducing hepatic glucose production and improves peripheral glucose utilization. Lactic acidosis and Vitamin B12 deficiency are specific adverse effects of metformin. It is not used in patients with a glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min (moderate renal insufficiency), acidosis, unstable congestive cardiac failure, liver disease, severe hypoxemia, and patients undergoing contrast studies.
subtopics: Oral Anti Diabetic Drugs - Adverse Effects

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A morbidly obese diabetic woman is not responsive to metformin therapy. She has a history of pancreatitis and family history of bladder cancer. She does not want to take injections. Which of the following would be suitable to reduce her glucose levels?
questions.raw_text: A morbidly obese diabetic woman is not responsive to metformin therapy. She has a history of pancreatitis and family history of bladder cancer. She does not want to take injections. Which of the following would be suitable to reduce her glucose levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Canagliflozin

Among the given options, canagliflozin (Option C) is the most suitable treatment. It is an oral drug belonging to the class SGLT-2 inhibitors and causes weight loss. Although it increases the risk of urogenital infections, it has no risk of pancreatitis or bladder cancer.

Option A: Sitagliptin, a DPP-IV inhibitor, is associated with the risk of acute pancreatitis.

Option B: Pioglitazone, a thiazolidinedione, can increase the risk of bladder cancer and can cause weight gain and congestive cardiac failure.

Option D: Liraglutide is an injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist. Pancreatitis is a serious adverse effect of this drug. Hence, it is contraindicated in individuals with a history of pancreatitis and should be permanently discontinued if pancreatitis develops.
subtopics: Oral Anti Diabetic Drugs - Adverse Effects

questions.text: Sentinel lymph node biopsy is most useful in which of the following gynecological malignancies?
questions.raw_text: Sentinel lymph node biopsy is most useful in which of the following gynecological malignancies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carcinoma vulva

Among the given gynecological malignancies, sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is most useful in vulval carcinomas.

This is because women with earlier stages of vulval cancer can have diseased lymph nodes even without palpable enlargement of nodes. Hence, sentinel lymph node biopsy helps in early diagnosis lymph node spread which can be managed by lymph node dissection.

A sentinel lymph node is a physiologically, the first lymph node to receive tumor lymphatic drainage.

Malignancies where sentinel lymph node biopsy is commonly done are :

  • Vulval carcinoma
  • Breast carcinoma
  • Penile carcinoma
  • Malignant melanoma

Lymphatic mapping is similar technique to SLNB that can also be used in vulval cancers.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: The memory disorder correctly matched with the pathology is?
questions.raw_text: The memory disorder correctly matched with the pathology is?

options.label: A
options.text: Korsakoff syndrome -  hyperactivation of mammillary bodies

options.label: C
options.text: Alzheimer's disease - early degeneration of frontal lobe

options.label: D
options.text: Frontotemporal dementia - mesial temporal lobe atrophy

questions.correct_answer: B. Alzheimer's disease - loss of synapses
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alzheimer's disease - loss of synapses

The cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease is due to the loss of synapses and neuronal degeneration.

Microscopically, the following are seen:

  • Neuritic plaques - containing amyloid-β
  • Neurofibrillary tangles - containing abnormally phosphorylated tau proteins
  • Amyloid-β accumulation in the blood vessel walls of the cortex and leptomeninges.

Option A: In Korsakoff syndrome, there is inactivation (not hyperactivation) of mammillary bodies due to thiamine deficiency.

Option C: Alzheimer's disease initially affects the parietal and temporal lobe, followed by the frontal lobe in the later stages. Hence personality changes are a late feature of Alzheimer's. 

Option D: Mesial temporal lobe atrophy is very sensitive to Alzheimer's disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The dose at which dopamine acts on beta 1 receptors is ____.
questions.raw_text: The dose at which dopamine acts on beta 1 receptors is ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2-10 mcg/kg/min

The dose at which dopamine acts on β-1 receptors is 2-10 mcg/kg/min.

The systemic effects of dopamine vary with its concentration in the body.

When administered at an infusion rate of 2-5 mcg/kg/min, it directly stimulates cardiac β receptors. This enhances myocardial contractility and is useful in the management of cardiogenic shock.

At doses of 5-15 mcg/kg/min and above, it stimulates α adrenergic receptors. This causes peripheral arterial and venous vasoconstriction.

At lower doses of <2 mcg/kg/min, it directly stimulates both D1 and D2 receptors. The D1 receptors in renal and mesenteric blood vessels are the most sensitive: i.v. infusion of low dose of DA dilates these vessels subsequently, causing increased renal blood flow and increased urine output.

The clinical indications of dopamine include cardiogenic and vasodilatory shock, congestive cardiac failure and symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine or pacing.

The major side effects are: 

  • Severe hypertension (especially when taken with nonselective β-blockers)
  • Ventricular arrhythmias
  • Cardiac ischemia
  • Tissue ischemia/gangrene (high doses/extravasation into tissues)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the first external sign of putrefaction?
questions.raw_text: What is the first external sign of putrefaction?

options.label: A
options.text: Greenish discoloration of skin over caecum

options.label: C
options.text: Bloating of abdomen and external genitalia

options.label: D
options.text: Reddish brown discoloration of inner surface of vessels

questions.correct_answer: A. Greenish discoloration of skin over caecum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Greenish discoloration of skin over caecum

The first external sign of putrefaction is the greenish discoloration of the skin over the region of the caecum.

The disintegration of body tissues is known as putrefaction. It is one of the late signs of death.

Enzyme lecithinase produced by Clostridium welchii plays an important role in putrefaction. Sulphmethaglobin is the agent imparting greenish color.

The earliest internal change is reddish-brown discoloration of the inner surface of vessels, especially of the aorta.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient was intubated for surgery by a final-year resident. Which of the following is the best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube?
questions.raw_text: A 30-year-old male patient was intubated for surgery by a final-year resident. Which of the following is the best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. End-tidal CO2 concentration

The best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube is the end-tidal CO2 concentration assessed by capnography. 

Capnography is a non-invasive method of measurement and graphical display of partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2) in exhaled breath or the end-tidal CO2. Capnograph is the device used for measurement and capnogram is the CO2 waveform that is displayed. It is the most reliable indicator of endotracheal tube placement.

The proper placement of the endotracheal tube is indicated by a normal CO2 waveform for at least three breaths.

 

Other signs to confirm proper endotracheal intubation are:

Symmetrical chest rise, presence of equal bilateral breath sounds, absent breath sounds over the epigastrium, visible condensation in the ETT, large exhaled tidal volume, and appropriate compliance of the reservoir bag during manual ventilation.

Absent CO2 waveform tracing despite correct ETT intubation is seen in the following conditions:

  • Severe bronchospasm,
  • Equipment malfunction,
  • Cardiac arrest, or hemodynamic collapse 

Clinical relevance:

  • Capnography does not differentiate endotracheal from endobronchial intubation. Signs of endobronchial intubation include increased peak expiratory pressure, hypoxemia, increased airway pressures, asymmetric chest expansion and the absence of breath sounds over one lung, generally the left.  
  • In esophageal intubation, the capnograph can initially detect some CO2 in the stomach from swallowing expired air. But after a few breaths, this CO2  will be washed out and ETCO2 will become zero. 
  • The most sensitive and earliest indicator of malignant hyperthermia is a persistent increase in ETCO2.

Pearl: Signs of correct endotracheal intubation

  • Detection of end-tidal CO2 by capnography (Surest confirmation)
  • Symmetric chest rise
  • Bilateral breath sounds
  • Absence of breath sounds in the epigastrium
  • Visible condensation in the endotracheal tube
  • Large exhaled tidal volumes
  • Appropriate compliance of the reservoir bag during manual ventilation

Pearl: Various capnography waveforms:

A- Obstructive airway or bronchospasm
B- Expiratory valve malfunctioning
C- Inspiratory valve malfunction
D- Normal physiological variant seen in pregnant subjects under GA
E- Curare cleft
F- Rebreathing
G- Esophageal intubation
H- Spontaneous breathing
I-Dual capnogram in one lung transplantation patient. The first peak in phase III is from the transplanted normal lung, whereas the second peak is from the native disease lung. A variation of dual capnogram (steeple sign capnogram – dotted line) is seen if there is a leak around the sidestream sensor port at the monitor
J- Malignant hyperthermia
K- Classic ripple effect during the expiratory pause showing cardiogenic oscillations
L- Sudden rise of baseline and end-tidal PCO2 (PETCO2) due to contamination of the sensor with secretions or water vapor.
The gradual rise of baseline and PETCO2 occurs when soda lime is exhausted. 
M -Intermittent mechanical ventilation (IMV) breaths in the midst of spontaneously breathing patient.
N -Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: capnogram showing positive waveforms during each compression. 
O-Capnogram showing rebreathing during inspiration. This is normal in rebreathing circuits such as Mapleson D or Bain circuit.

questions.text: The flipped LDH ratio implies  _______.
questions.raw_text: The flipped LDH ratio implies  _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LDH 1 > LDH 2

The flipped lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio is LDH 1 > LDH 2.

Under normal conditions, LDH 2 is predominantly present in the blood and LDH 1 is predominantly present in the heart. When cardiac tissue is damaged LDH 1 is released into the bloodstream.

LDH 1 > LDH 2 (flipped pattern) in the blood is suggestive of myocardial infarction.

LDH is a tetrameric enzyme with 4 subunits. It has four subunits with two isoforms: H isoform (heart) and M isoform (muscle)

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 55 year old female complains of lower backache. The radiographic image of her lumbosacral spine is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 55 year old female complains of lower backache. The radiographic image of her lumbosacral spine is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Osteoporosis

The radiographic image of an elderly female's lumbosacral spine shows ballooning of disc spaces, resulting in the characteristic biconcave appearance of vertebral bodies known as the 'codfish' appearance, typically seen in osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is a common metabolic bone disease characterised by a diffuse reduction in bone density due to a decrease in bone mass.

Risk factors for osteoporosis include:

  • Increasing age
  • Female sex
  • Alcohol
  • Smoking
  • Previous history of fragility fractures
  • Family history of hip fracture
  • Low body mass index- less than 18.5 kg/m2
  • Excessive usage of glucocorticoids

Osteoporosis presents with fractures that occur without any trauma or as a result of low-impact trauma. The commonly associated fractures are fractures of the distal part of the radius (Colle's fracture), fractures of the hip, and fractures of the vertebrae. In severe cases, the fracture of vertebrae can cause kyphosis.

Radiological findings:

  • A decreased vertical height of the vertebra due to collapse
  • Ground glass appearance - especially in bones like pelvis
  • Codfish appearance - it occurs due to bulging of the disc into the adjacent vertebral bodies so that it becomes biconcave.

DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of osteoporosis. T-score less than -2.5 in the lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip indicates osteoporosis.

Pearl: Risk factors for osteoporosis:

Risk factor for osteoporosis
Low BMI
Family history of osteoporosis
Old age
Previous fragility fracture
Chronic use of glucocorticoids
Family history of hip fractures
Smoking and alcohol intake
Drugs like anticonvulsants, anticoagulants and thyroid replacement therapy
Hyperparathyroidism, multiple myeloma, and malabsorption syndrome

Pearl: Z-score and T-score for osteoporosis:

Z-score:

It is the number of standard deviations a patient’s BMD(bone mass density) differs from the average BMD of their age, sex, and ethnicity.

A Z-score of -2 or below should trigger investigations for underlying disease.

T-score:

It is the BMD at the site when compared to the young normal reference mean. It is a comparison of a patient’s BMD to that of a healthy 30-year old.

  • Normal is a T-score of -1 or higher.
  • Osteopenia is defined as a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5.
  • Osteoporosis is defined as a T-score less than -2.5, that is a BMD which is two and a half standard deviations below the mean of a 30-year old man/woman.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient is started on HAART treatment for HIV. Her CD4 count is 150 cells/μl. She developed a fever and her symptoms worsened during her first week of treatment. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A patient is started on HAART treatment for HIV. Her CD4 count is 150 cells/μl. She developed a fever and her symptoms worsened during her first week of treatment. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome

Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is characterized by an increased inflammatory response to subclinical opportunistic infections after initiating retroviral therapy.

Features seen are fever, worsening of opportunistic infections, new manifestations like lymphadenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates. It typically occurs within 1st few weeks of starting therapy. It commonly occurs in patients with progressive disease, or severe CD4 + T-lymphocyte depletion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: On neurologic examination, a patient is not able to identify an object but is able to recognize the object from its texture, colour and pattern. Which of the following is likely to have been affected?
questions.raw_text: On neurologic examination, a patient is not able to identify an object but is able to recognize the object from its texture, colour and pattern. Which of the following is likely to have been affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inferior temporal lobe

The clinical scenario suggests that the patient has visual agnosia and the likely site of involvement would be the inferior temporal lobe.

  • Agnosia refers to the inability to visually identify objects and is also called optic aphasia. According to De Jong, visual agnosia is further classified into:
    • Apperceptive visual agnosia - the visual image appears distorted to the patient and hence they are unable to recognise it. This occurs due lesions in the parieto-occipital region
    • Associative visual agnosia - inability to visually identify objects in the absence of visual impairment, with ability to identify the object using other sensory modalities (as suggested in the scenario). This occurs due to lesions of occipito-temporal junction, which is present in the inferior temporal lobe. Prosopagnosia is a type of associatetive visual agnosia which refers to the inability to visually identify faces. 

The occipital lobe acts as the primary visual area and a lesion in this region would result in cortical blindness and achromatopsia, which is the inability to visualise colour. In the given scenario, as the patient is also able to identify colour, it indicates that the occipital lobe (Option A) is unaffected and (hence inferior temporal lobe is the better answer). 

Stereognosis is the ability to identify an object by a perception of the form and nature of an object without looking at it. In the given scenario, the patient is able to recognize the object from its texture and pattern which indicates that stereognosis is intact. Loss of this ability is known as astereognosis which occurs in lesions of the superior parietal lobule (Options B and C) and dorsal column pathways.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 36-year-old male with skin-colored umbilicated papules. Microscopy is as shown below. The most likely diagnosis is______.
questions.raw_text: A 36-year-old male with skin-colored umbilicated papules. Microscopy is as shown below. The most likely diagnosis is______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Molluscum contagiosum

The given microscopic image shows large, ellipsoid, homogeneous, cytoplasmic inclusion in cells of the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum classically seen in molluscum contagiosum.

Molluscum contagiosum is a common, self-limited viral disease of the skin caused by a poxvirus. Poxvirus is brick-shaped and is about 300 nm in size, the largest pathogenic poxvirus in humans

Tzanck smear shows intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies (Henderson–Patterson bodies), the largest known inclusion bodies (30–35 μm).

Individual lesions are firm, pruritic, pink to skin-colored umbilicated papules (shown below). A curd-like material can be expressed from the central umbilication

Citrated plasma generated from whole blood is commonly utilized in laboratory testing for hemostasis. The recommended procedure involves the collection of specimens in tubes that are filled with a solution containing 3.2% sodium citrate (109 mM). The appropriate ratio for this collection is 9 parts blood to 1 part anticoagulant. The primary objective of citrate is to effectively eliminate calcium ions, which play a crucial role in the process of blood coagulation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following serotypes are present in the bivalent vaccine against the human papillomavirus?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following serotypes are present in the bivalent vaccine against the human papillomavirus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 16 and 18

Cervarix is the bivalent vaccine given against the human papillomavirus (HPV) and serotypes 16 and 18 are present in it. It is administered at 0, 1 and 6 months.

The quadrivalent vaccine against HPV is named Gardasil or Silgard. Serotypes 6, 11, 16 and 18 are present in it and is given at 0, 2 and 6 months.

The nonavalent HPV vaccine, Gardasil 9, provides protection against nine different HPV serotypes: 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58.
In 2020 it has received an expanded indication which now includes the prevention of oropharyngeal and head and neck cancers.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common cutaneous manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is the most common cutaneous manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Photosensitivity

The most common cutaneous manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus is photosensitivity.

In decreasing order, the cutaneous manifestations in SLE are:

  1. Photosensitivity
  2. Raynaud's phenomenon 
  3. Malar rash
  4. Chronic urticaria >36 hrs
  5. Non-scarring alopecia 
  6. Mouth ulceration
subtopics: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus / SLE - Clinical Features

questions.text: The flow-volume curve after spirometry in patient 1 is given below. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is:
questions.raw_text: The flow-volume curve after spirometry in patient 1 is given below. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Myasthenia gravis

The given flow-volume curve shows decreased lung volumes (total lung capacity, vital capacity, and residual volume) with normal shape, suggestive of a restrictive pattern. The curve is a miniature version of the normal curve with shift towards the right. It is seen in myasthenia gravis.

Myasthenia gravis presents with ventilatory restriction due to reduced respiratory muscle strength.

Asthma, emphysema, and endobronchial neoplasms present with obstructive flow patterns.

questions.text: Identify the following line shown in the below picture:
questions.raw_text: Identify the following line shown in the below picture:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ohngren line

The given image shows Ohngren's line. It is an imaginary line passing through the medial canthus of the eye and the angle of the mandible. It is used for the classification of maxillary carcinoma.

Growth situated above the plane (supra structure) tends to be more aggressive and poorly differentiated and has a poor prognosis. Growth situated below the plane (infrastructure) is more amenable to treatment and has a better prognosis.

Other options:

Option A: Proper alignment of the face is determined by the Frankfort plane, a horizontal line bisecting the inferior border of the infraorbital rim and the superior border of the external auditory canal.

Option B: Donaldson's line passes through the horizontal semicircular canal and bisects the posterior canal. It is the landmark for the endolymphatic sac which lies anterior and inferior to it. 

ELS: Endolymphatic sac, HSCC: Horizontal semicircular canal, PSCC: Posterior semicircular canal, PF dura: Posterior fossa dura

Option C: Ledermann’s classification uses two horizontal lines of Sebileau, one passes through the floor of the orbit and another passes through the floor of the maxillary antra dividing the face into supra structure (ethmoid, sphenoid, frontal sinuses, and the olfactory area of nose), mesostructure (maxillary sinus and respiratory part of nose) and infrastructure (alveolar process). It is used to classify maxillary carcinoma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A woman presents at 8 weeks of gestation. Which of the following signs can be elicited at this gestation?

1. Goodell's sign
2. Osiander's sign
3. Internal ballottement
4. Lightening
questions.raw_text:
A woman presents at 8 weeks of gestation. Which of the following signs can be elicited at this gestation?

1. Goodell's sign
2. Osiander's sign
3. Internal ballottement
4. Lightening
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1,2

The signs that can be elicited at 8 weeks of gestation are Goodell's sign and Osiander's sign.

Goodell’s sign is a sign of early pregnancy, which describes the marked softening of the cervix in contrast to the non-pregnant state. It is seen as early as the 6th week. 

Osiander's sign describes the pulsations felt in the lateral fornix due to increased vascularity. It is seen around 8 weeks of gestation.

Internal ballottement can be elicited between 16–28th weeks of gestation, before which the fetus is too small and after which it is too large to displace. It may not be elicited in cases with scanty liquor amnii, or when the fetus is transversely placed.

Lightening is a sense of relief of the pressure symptoms due to the engagement of the presenting part. It is felt at about 38 weeks of gestation.

Pearl: Uterine Signs in Pregnancy
subtopics: Antenatal Care - Normal Parameters & Clinical Signs

3. Risk of developing blindness increases with age.
4. Illiteracy leads to increased risk of developing blindness.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3 and 4

The correct statements drawn from the values given in the table are 3 and 4.
 
An odds ratio is a measure of the association between an exposure and an outcome. It represents the odds that an outcome will occur given a particular exposure in comparison to the odds of the outcome occurring in the absence of that exposure.

An odds ratio of 1 indicates that the risk factor is not related to the disease.

An odds ratio of less than 1 indicates that a person with the disease is less likely to have been exposed to the factor, implying that the factor may be a protective factor against the disease.

An odds ratio greater than 1 indicates that the odds ratio is significant, and the factor can be ascertained as a risk factor.

The p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one that was actually observed in the biological or clinical experiment. A p-value of less than 0.05 indicates that the test result is statistically significant.
 
Other options:
Statement 1: Female population is at greater risk of developing blindness is a false statement; since the odds ratio is <1, the female population will be at lesser risk of developing blindness than the male population.
 
 Statement 2: People dwelling in rural areas are at increased risk of developing blindness is also false; a p-value of >0.05 means that this association is not statistically significant. 

Pearl: Odds Ratio

  • Odds ratio is a measure of the strength of association between risk factor and outcome in case control studies.
  • Odds ratio can be arrived at from case control studies.
  • It is also known as cross product ratio.
  • A representation of the odds ratio (OR) is given in the picture below:

Calculation of odds ratio (OR) = (a/b)/(c/d) = ad/bc where, 

  Cancer
Exposure   Yes No
Yes a b
No c d
  • OR < 1 indicates possible protection (negative association) as the frequency of exposure is lower among cases than controls.
  • OR = 1 indicates no association of risk with exposure, or that the event is equally likely in both groups.
  • OR > 1 indicates increased risk (positive association) as the frequency of exposure is greater among cases than controls.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which immunoglobulin is elevated in a case of chronic allergy?
questions.raw_text: Which immunoglobulin is elevated in a case of chronic allergy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. IgE

IgE is elevated in cases of chronic allergy.

Pearl: Properties of immunoglobulin classes

IgG:

  • Half-life- 23 days
  • Appears late, indicates chronic infection
  • It is the only maternal Ig to cross the placenta.
  • Has 4 subclasses.
  • Facilitates opsonization (via Fc receptor binding)
  • Causes complement fixation, precipitation, and neutralization of toxins and viruses.

IgM:

  • Half-life- 5 days
  • Has the highest molecular weight and is a pentamer.
  • Polysaccharides and lipids mainly stimulate IgM secretion.
  • Intravascular distribution.
  • Appears early, indicates recent infection.
  • Acts as a surface immunoglobulin on the B cells.
  • It causes agglutination, hemolysis, complement fixation and opsonization.

IgD:

  • Half-life- 2-8 days.
  • Acts as a surface immunoglobulin on the B cells.
  • Serves as recognition receptors for antigens.

IgE:

  • Half-life- 1-5 days
  • Causes type I hypersensitivity.
  • It is the only heat-labile antibody.
  • Levels are raised in helminthic infections.

IgA:

  • Half-life- 6 days
  • It is of 2 types- Serum IgA and Secretory IgA 
  • Secretory IgA (A dimer) results in mucosal immunity.
