questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Study A(red) and Study B(blue) done in a given population yields two different distribution curves as shown below. Comparing both the curves, which of the following will be true?
questions.raw_text: Study A(red) and Study B(blue) done in a given population yields two different distribution curves as shown below. Comparing both the curves, which of the following will be true?

options.label: B
options.text: Mean = median, not equal to mode

options.label: D
options.text: Mode = median, not equal to mean

questions.correct_answer: B. Mean = median, not equal to mode
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mean = median, not equal to mode

On comparing the 2 graphs, we can say mean=median for both study A and B but the mode is different.

Study A is a unimodal symmetrical distribution, so mean=median=mode.

Study B is a bimodal distribution. Here, mean=median, but the curve has two highest points, therefore it has 2 modes. 

Pearl: Mean, Median, Mode in Different Distribution Shapes

  • The relationship between the mean, median and mode depends upon the distribution.
  • In a unimodal symmetrical distribution like a normal distribution, all the three measures are approximately the same, as shown in Figure (2) in the following image, i.e., mean = median = mode.
  • Figure (3) in the following image shows a positively skewed distribution in which the longer tail is towards the positive direction. In this, the mean will be larger than the median and mode, i.e., mean > median > mode.
  • Figure (1) in the following image shows a negatively skewed distribution in which the longer tail is towards the negative direction. In this, the mean will be smaller than the median, i.e., mean < median < mode.

Unimodal symmetrical distribution

Mean = Median = Mode

Positively (right) skewed distribution

Mean > Median > Mode

Negatively (left) skewed distribution

Mean < Median < Mode
  • As seen in the figures above, in any distribution curve, the mode is generally the highest point. The mean will be pulled up or down based on the values in the distribution. The median will lie between the mode and mean and divide the distribution in two equal halves under the curve.
  • A bimodal distribution will have two high points as shown in the image below.
  • Mathematically, the relationship between mode, median and mean in asymmetrical distributions can be given as:
    Mode = 3 median – 2 mean (or) Mean = ½ (3 median – mode).
  • Outlier is the statistical term used for an observation or value that is very distant from other observations in the distribution.
  • In a distribution with outliers, preferred measure of central tendency is the median.
  • Mode is least affected by outliers but mean is the most affected out of all the measures of location.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient on prolonged antibiotic therapy for pneumonia develops persistent diarrhoea. Stool examination is positive for toxins A and B. Which of the following findings is most likely seen on CT abdomen and pelvis?
questions.raw_text: A patient on prolonged antibiotic therapy for pneumonia develops persistent diarrhoea. Stool examination is positive for toxins A and B. Which of the following findings is most likely seen on CT abdomen and pelvis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Accordion sign

The given clinical scenario of a patient developing persistent diarrhoea following prolonged antibiotic therapy for pneumonia is suggestive of pseudomembranous colitis. The Accordion sign is seen in pseudomembranous colitis.

Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) is commonly caused by the disruption of the commensal colonic microflora due to prolonged antimicrobial use, especially antibiotics like cephalosporins, ampicillin, clindamycin, and fluoroquinolones. The more severe form of CDI is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC).

Toxigenic Clostridium difficile produces toxin A (an enterotoxin) and toxin B (a cytotoxin), damaging the epithelial-cell barrier function and causing diarrhoea and pseudomembrane formation, which initially appear as small whitish-yellow plaques and later coalesce to involve the entire colon wall. The patient also presents with fever, abdominal pain, and leukocytosis.

On CT imaging, the accordion sign, also referred to as the concertina sign, may be seen.  These terms refer to a harmonica-like musical instrument. The thickened edematous bowel resembles the folds of an accordion. The hyperaemic-enhancing mucosa stretches over the thickened submucosal folds, producing this appearance. This is also seen when the contrast gets trapped between oedematous haustral folds and pseudomembranes of the colon. 

The accordion sign is typical for pseudomembranous colitis, but can also be seen in:

  • ischemic colitis
  • AIDS-related colitis
  • severe edema from cirrhosis

The CT image below depicts the accordion sign:

Pearl: Diagnostic criteria for Clostridium difficile infection

 

The diagnosis of CDI is based on a combination of clinical criteria:

1.Diarrhea (≥3 unformed stools per 24 h for ≥2 days) with no other recognized cause      

2.Detection of toxins A or B in the stool by PCR or culture

               or               

 Detection of pseudomembranes in the colon

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, what is the finding shown in the image given?
questions.raw_text: In a patient with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, what is the finding shown in the image given?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Putty kidney

A patient with abdominal pain with sterile pyuria and the abdominal X-ray showing homogenous ground glass-like calcification is suggestive of a putty kidney.

The putty kidney is a characteristic finding of genitourinary tuberculosis (GUTB). It is caused by the dissemination of the organism through the bloodstream and is always a secondary TB (reinfection or reactivation of old TB). Genitourinary TB usually presents as sterile pyuria.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen is the most sensitive modality and is the preferred means of visualizing renal calcifications. Microbiological diagnosis is confirmed by at least 3 consecutive early-morning urine samples showing acid-fast bacilli using Ziehl–Neelsen (ZN) stain and subsequently cultured (gold standard).

GUTB is treated with a short course of anti-tubercular therapy (ATT). Ureteric strictures require double J stenting or percutaneous nephrostomy. Definitive treatment is after 3-6mn of ATT, where a reconstructive procedure (open surgical repair > balloon dilatation) is performed. In case the kidney is poorly functioning, a nephrectomy is done.

Option B: Nephrocalcinosis is the deposition of calcium in the kidney parenchyma or tubules, seen in hypercalcemic conditions like hyperparathyroidism.

Option C: Staghorn calculus (a triple phosphate stone) is found in urinary tract infections (UTI) by urease-producing pathogens like proteus and is not a cause of sterile pyuria.

Option D: Psoas calcification is a muscle calcification that develops after acute renal failure and rhabdomyolysis. It is not associated with sterile pyuria.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 75-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension has a biopsy of her heart that is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 75-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension has a biopsy of her heart that is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Restrictive cardiomyopathy

The hyaline, eosinophilic deposits seen on the biopsy point to a diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis, which most commonly leads to restrictive cardiomyopathy. 

Transthyretin is the major component of senile cardiac amyloid deposits. It is a normal serum protein synthesized in the liver that transports thyroxine and retinol-binding protein. The deposits may accumulate subendocardially, and slowly expand - compressing the myocardial fibres - leading to pressure atrophy of myocaridial fibres. The stain used for amyloid deposits is congo red staining, which imparts pink to red color to the amyloid under ordinary light and apple-green birefringence under polarised microscopy.

Presentation of cardiac amyloidosis:

  • Restrictive cardiomyopathy- most common
  • Asymptomatic
  • Dilation
  • Arrhythmias
  • Ischemic disease

The echocardiographic findings in cardiac amyloidosis may include a distinctive granular, sparkling appearance of the thickened cardiac walls, representative of the infiltrative process. Despite the thickened ventricular walls, the ECG in cardiac amyloidosis typically demonstrates low limb lead voltage, often accompanied by ventricular conduction delay and pseudoinfarction patterns. Suspect cardiac amyloidosis when there is thickened ventricular walls with an ECG that shows low voltage. Amyloid infiltration can be detected with gadolinium enhancement on MRI.

A. Dilated cardiomyopathy/DCM is a condition in which the heart muscle becomes enlarged and weakened. This makes it difficult for the heart to pump blood effectively. DCM can be caused by a variety of factors, including coronary artery disease, high blood pressure, and diabetes. 

B. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy/HOCM is a condition in which the IV septum becomes thickened and is typically genetic. On biopsy, myocardial disarray would be noted.

D. Atrial fibrillation by rapid, irregularly irregular contractions of the atria that can lead to tachycardia induced cardiomyopathy. AF can be caused by a variety of factors, including heart disease, high blood pressure, and diabetes.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is the drug of choice for preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in a patient undergoing cardiac surgery?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is the drug of choice for preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in a patient undergoing cardiac surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cefazolin

First- and second-generation cephalosporins (cefazolin) are the drugs of choice for preoperative prophylaxis for cardiac surgery. Clindamycin is reserved for cases of allergy to beta-lactams and vancomycin is recommended for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

Preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis is essential in reducing the risk of surgical site infections, particularly in cardiac surgery, where the consequences of infection can be severe. The choice of antibiotic depends on the patient's medical history, allergies, and the most common pathogens involved in surgical site infections for the specific surgery. In addition to cefazolin, other cephalosporins, such as cefuroxime, can also be used for prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. The timing of antibiotic administration is crucial, with the first dose typically given within 60 minutes before the incision.

Other Options:

Option A: Penicillin G is not the drug of choice for preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. It is mainly used to treat infections caused by susceptible gram-positive bacteria, such as Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and some strains of Staphylococcus aureus.

Option B: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic and is not the drug of choice for preoperative prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. It is typically used to treat respiratory tract infections, skin infections, and other infections caused by susceptible gram-positive bacteria.

Option C: Azithromycin, another macrolide antibiotic, is also not the drug of choice for preoperative prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. It is commonly used to treat respiratory tract infections, sexually transmitted infections, and other infections caused by susceptible gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.

Correct answer: C. Female patients should avoid getting pregnant for 6 months after therapy

Female patients should avoid conception for 3 years after receiving acitretin treatment to prevent retinoid-induced embryopathy.

Acitretin is approved for use in the cutaneous manifestations of psoriasis.

Absolute contraindications:

  • Pregnant women
  • Women who are planning to get pregnant
  • Breastfeeding

Relative contraindications:

  • Leukopenia
  • Alcoholism
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Hypercholesterolemia
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Significant hepatic or renal disease

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An 86-year-old woman presented with sepsis and a massive right pleural effusion. She developed a chylous effusion 2 days after a chest tube insertion. An injury to the thoracic duct is suspected. Which of the following parts is not drained by it?
questions.raw_text: An 86-year-old woman presented with sepsis and a massive right pleural effusion. She developed a chylous effusion 2 days after a chest tube insertion. An injury to the thoracic duct is suspected. Which of the following parts is not drained by it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right upper limb

The right upper limb is drained by the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.

The filtered lymph passes through larger lymphatics and eventually collect into two large trunks, the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, which in turn drain into the brachiocephalic veins.

  • Thoracic duct - drains both lower limbs, left upper limb, abdomen, left halves of thorax, and left side of the head and neck regions (areas shaded green in the image).
  • Right lymphatic duct - drains right upper limb, and right halves of thorax, and right side of the head and neck regions (areas shaded blue in the image).

Injury to the thoracic duct is a rare complication of traumatic chest tube insertion.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the elimination and eradication of lymphatic filariasis is true?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements regarding the elimination and eradication of lymphatic filariasis is true?

options.label: A
options.text: It will be considered as eliminated when the number of microfilaria carriers are less than 5 percent

options.label: B
options.text: It will be considered as eliminated when children born after initiation of the programme are free from antigenemia

options.label: C
options.text: India has set the target of eliminating lymphatic filariasis by 2025

options.label: D
options.text: WHO recommends dual therapy with diethylcarbamazine and albendazole for elimination of transmission

questions.correct_answer: B. It will be considered as eliminated when children born after initiation of the programme are free from antigenemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It will be considered as eliminated when children born after initiation of the programme are free from antigenemia

Lymphatic filariasis will be considered eliminated when the children born after the initiation of the programme are free from antigenemia. Antigenemia refers to the presence of adult filaria worms in the human body.

According to the Elimination of Lymphatic Filariasis (ELF) Programme, there are two criteria to consider elimination of lymphatic filariasis:

  • Children born after the initiation of the elimination programme are free from circulating antigenemia.
  • The number of microfilaria carriers is <1%.

Following the failure to achieve ELF by 2015, the target set to eliminate lymphatic filariasis by WHO was 2020. To achieve the same WHO recommended the use of triple therapy for lymphatic filariasis. It incorporated ivermectin along with diethylcarbamazine (DEC) and albendazole instead of the traditional DEC and albendazole therapy, for the elimination of transmission of lymphatic filariasis.

In 2021, WHO released the 'Road Map for Neglected Tropical Diseases (2021–2030)'. Under this, lymphatic filariasis is targeted for elimination as a public health problem by 2030.

In February 2023, the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare in India launched a nationwide Sarva Dawa Sevan or Mass Drug Administration (MDA) campaign to eliminate LF by 2027, aiming to achieve this goal three years ahead of the global target.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following causes prerenal AKI?
  1. Myeloma light chains
  2. Snakebite
  3. ACE inhibitors
  4. Rhabdomyolysis
  5. NSAIDs
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following causes prerenal AKI?
  1. Myeloma light chains
  2. Snakebite
  3. ACE inhibitors
  4. Rhabdomyolysis
  5. NSAIDs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3, 4 and 5

NSAIDs, Rhabdomyolysis and ACE inhibitors cause prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI). 

The use of NSAIDs causes reduced production of vasodilatory prostaglandins. This leads to decreased renal perfusion and glomerular capillary pressure. NSAIDs can also lead to acute interstitial nephritis, a cause of renal AKI. However, this is relatively uncommon.

ACE inhibitors cause inhibition of efferent arteriole vasoconstriction, leading to reduced renal perfusion.

Rhabdomyolysis causes AKI by both prerenal mechanisms (due to volume sequestration) and ATN (due to precipitation of myoglobin in the renal tubules). 

Nephrotoxins like myeloma light chains, snake venom, myoglobin (due to rhabdomyolysis) cause acute tubular necrosis (ATN). This leads to renal or intrinsic AKI.
subtopics: Acute Kidney Injury / AKI - Pathophysiology & Clinical Features

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old female, who is a known case of sickle cell anemia, comes to the casualty with a history of severe eye pain, redness, and diminution of vision. On examination, the visual acuity is 6/60, and there is circumcorneal congestion, corneal edema, and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the drug of choice from the given options?
questions.raw_text: A 55-year-old female, who is a known case of sickle cell anemia, comes to the casualty with a history of severe eye pain, redness, and diminution of vision. On examination, the visual acuity is 6/60, and there is circumcorneal congestion, corneal edema, and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the drug of choice from the given options?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intravenous mannitol

This patient with complaints of severe ocular pain, corneal congestion, and edema with a shallow anterior chamber most likely has acute angle closure glaucoma. Since this patient has a past history of sickle cell disease, intravenous mannitol is the drug of choice for this patient

Acetazolamide is contraindicated in cases of sickle-cell anemia since these drugs tend to increase sickling of erythrocytes.

  • Apraclonidine

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old male patient presents with midline swelling in the neck.  The swelling moves with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 23-year-old male patient presents with midline swelling in the neck.  The swelling moves with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroglossal cyst

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a thyroglossal cyst. It moves with deglutition, protrusion of the tongue, and side-to-side movement is also possible.

A thyroglossal duct cyst is a congenital midline neck swelling that typically presents during childhood often noticed after an upper respiratory infection.

A thyroglossal cyst represents the persistence of the track of the thyroid gland and can be found adjacent to the midline. The thyroid gland descends early in fetal life from the base of the tongue towards its position in the lower neck. At the time of descent, the hyoid bone has not been formed and the track of the thyroid gland is variable, passing in front, through, or behind the eventual position of the hyoid body. 

It can occur anywhere along the migratory course of the duct:

    • Infrahyoid (most common site)
    • Region of thyroid cartilage
    • Suprahyoid
    • Floor of mouth
    • Beneath foramen cecum

Clinical features of thyroglossal cyst:

  • Classically the cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion. This indicates attachment to the hyoid bone. 
  • Swelling is smooth, soft, fluctuant (cystic), nontender, mobile, and shows transillumination.
  • Thyroid fossa is empty, if there is no thyroid in the normal location.

Complications of thyroglossal cyst:

  • The most common complication is infection.
  • Thyroglossal fistula is an acquired condition that either follows infection of the cyst which bursts open or due to inadequate removal of the cyst.
  • 1% of thyroglossal duct cysts are found to be malignant of which the most common type of cancer is papillary (85%).

However, only the thyroglossal cyst moves with tongue protrusion. This is because the duct extends from the foramen cecum of the tongue to the isthmus of the gland. 

Sistrunk’s operation is performed to excise the cyst and prevent a recurrence. It involves excision of the whole thyroglossal tract, involving removal of the body of the hyoid bone, and suprahyoid tract through the tongue base to the vallecula at the site of the primitive foramen cecum along with the core of tissue on either side.

Features of hoarseness of voice, cough, neck swelling that increases in size on coughing/Valsalva maneuver, and a gurgling sound heard on pressing the swelling are suggestive of laryngocele.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and was discharged after removing  the drain tube on the first postoperative day. On day three, the patient came back to the hospital and was febrile. On ultrasound examination, there was a 5 x 5 cm collection in the subhepatic space. Next best step is ______.
questions.raw_text: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and was discharged after removing  the drain tube on the first postoperative day. On day three, the patient came back to the hospital and was febrile. On ultrasound examination, there was a 5 x 5 cm collection in the subhepatic space. Next best step is ______.

options.label: A
options.text: To give oral antibiotics since the given accumulation is normal

options.label: B
options.text: To re-explore the wound and insert a T-tube

questions.correct_answer: C. Insert pigtail catheter for drainage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Insert pigtail catheter for drainage

The given clinical situation suggests a bile duct injury identified on post-op day 3 following laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The next best step after imaging would be to control inflammation by drainage of fluid collection (pigtail insertion and drainage) and administration of parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Bile duct injury

  • Usually is manifested in the postoperative period
  • Clinical features include fever, increasing abdominal pain, jaundice and bile leakage from an incision.

Imaging: Ultrasonography is done to assess for fluid collection and to evaluate the biliary tree.

Treatment Strategy

  • Control of infection, limiting inflammation
    • Percutaneous drainage of periportal fluid collections
    • Parenteral antibiotics (option A)
  • Clear and thorough delineation of entire biliary anatomy
    • Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) or percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC)
    • Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), especially if a cystic duct stump leak is suspected
  • Re-establishment of biliary-enteric continuity (surgery)
    1. Tension-free, mucosa-to-mucosa anastomosis
    2. Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy

Other options:

Option B: Re-exploration and repair in indicated for biliary leaks identified in within 48 hours post cholecystectomy.

Option D: ERCP would be indicated if drainage using a pigtail catheter fails.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the recommended weight gain during pregnancy in Indian women who are obese or overweight at the time of conception?
questions.raw_text: What is the recommended weight gain during pregnancy in Indian women who are obese or overweight at the time of conception?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 5 - 9 kg

The recommended weight gain during pregnancy in Indian women who are overweight (BMI 23-27.5 kg/m2) or obese (BMI > 27.5 kg/m2) at the time of conception is 5-9 kg. 

For Indian women who have a normal BMI (18.5-23kg/m2) at the time of conception, a weight gain of 10-12kg is recommended. Underweight women (BMI <18.5 kg/m2) should increase their dietary intake during pregnancy, and close monitoring of weight is required. These values are based on the ICMR-NIN guidelines 2024.
subtopics: Antenatal Care - Normal Parameters & Clinical Signs

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radioactive isotopes is not used for brachytherapy?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following radioactive isotopes is not used for brachytherapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iodine-131

I-131 is a beta-emitting radioisotope used in systemic radiotherapy, not in brachytherapy. 

Systemic radiotherapy involves administering a radioactive substance orally or parenterally, allowing it to accumulate in a specific organ or a tumour site. Once concentrated, the material emits beta particles, delivering high-dose localised radiation to abnormal tissues while exposing the surrounding healthy organs to minimal radiation.

This approach is commonly used in radioactive iodine (I-131) therapy for hyperthyroidism and differentiated thyroid cancers. 

In contrast, brachytherapy is a type of radiotherapy where radioactive sources are placed inside or close to the target area. It delivers radiation over short distances using interstitial, intracavitary, or surface placement techniques. The following isotopes are used in brachytherapy:

  • For permanent low-dose-rate implants, isotopes such as Iodine-125 and Palladium-103 are most frequently used, while Gold-198 is used less often
  • Temporary low-dose-rate applications may involve sources like Iridium-192, Cesium-137, and Cobalt-60
  • High-dose-rate procedures predominantly rely on Iridium-192 as the radiation source.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the most frequent site of ectopic gastric mucosa?
questions.raw_text: What is the most frequent site of ectopic gastric mucosa?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Upper esophagus

The most frequent site of the ectopic gastric mucosa is the upper third of the esophagus, where it is referred to as an inlet patch.

It is congenital and mostly asymptomatic. Occasionally, it can release acid, which can result in dysphagia, esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, or, rarely, adenocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 29-year-old primigravida is diagnosed with chlamydial cervicitis. What is the drug of choice?
questions.raw_text: A 29-year-old primigravida is diagnosed with chlamydial cervicitis. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Azithromycin

A single dose of azithromycin 1g is the drug of choice in pregnant women with uncomplicated chlamydial infection. 

The drug of choice for chlamydia infection in adults and adolescents is doxycycline 100 mg orally BD for 7 days. It is contraindicated in pregnancy.

Alternative regimens are: 

  • Azithromycin 1g orally, single dose 
  • Levofloxacin 500mg OD for 7 days

Azithromycin is preferred due to its greater effectiveness and lower cost. 

Option A: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy as it causes depression of bone growth and enamel hypoplasia in the fetus.

Option B: Ceftriaxone is used for the treatment of gonococcal infections.

Option D: Amoxicillin is used as an alternative regimen as it is less effective.

questions.text: A 24-year-old primiparous woman with Grade 2 genuine stress incontinence did not respond to conservative management. Which of the following surgeries will not be beneficial for her condition?
questions.raw_text: A 24-year-old primiparous woman with Grade 2 genuine stress incontinence did not respond to conservative management. Which of the following surgeries will not be beneficial for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Latzko procedure

Latzko procedure is not beneficial for a patient with genuine stress incontinence as it is done for vesicovaginal fistula.

The various surgeries done for genuine stress incontinence (GSI) are as follows:

  • Vaginal approach
    • Kelly repair
    • Pacey repair
  • Marshall-Marchetti-Krantz operation - abdominal approach. It is not done anymore as it causes osteitis of the pubis.
  • Burch colposuspension
  • Combined vaginal and abdominal suspension - Pereyra operation
  • Slings
    • Tension-free vaginal taping
    • Transobturator taping
  • Laparoscopic suspension of the bladder neck
  • Periurethral collagen injection

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: At which of the following locations does a Berry aneurysm have the highest risk of rupture?
questions.raw_text: At which of the following locations does a Berry aneurysm have the highest risk of rupture?
questions.correct_answer: A. Origin of posterior communicating artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Origin of posterior communicating artery

The size and site of aneurysm are important in predicting the risk of rupture. Aneurysms with the following features have a greater risk of rupture:

  • Size >7 mm in diameter 
  • Located at the top of the basilar artery (i.e origin of the posterior cerebral artery)
  • Located near the origin of the posterior communicating artery.

The most common location of Berry aneurysm is the anterior communicating artery.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: You are asked to conduct an autopsy of a person who was found dead at his home. You notice the given findings on the body. Which test can be used to differentiate this from antemortem bruising?
questions.raw_text: You are asked to conduct an autopsy of a person who was found dead at his home. You notice the given findings on the body. Which test can be used to differentiate this from antemortem bruising?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incision test

The given image shows postmortem hypostasis. The classic test used to differentiate a bruise from hypostasis is the incision test. 

The suspected area is incised to see if the underlying blood is intravascular (hypostasis) or infiltrating the tissues outside the vessels (contusion).

Option A: Gettler's chloride test is used to differentiate between freshwater and saltwater drowning. It is not widely used now. 

Option C: In the precipitin test, a specific antiserum is made to react with the seminal fluid, blood, or saliva. A positive test will confirm human origin.

Option D: Breslau's second life test is done to determine whether a child was born alive or not.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: At what age in women is a DEXA scan done routinely?
questions.raw_text: At what age in women is a DEXA scan done routinely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. At 65 years

Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA scan) is routinely done in women at 65 years of age to screen for osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is the most common metabolic bone disorder characterized by abnormally low bone mass, which makes the bone unusually fragile and increases the risk of fractures.

The criteria to screen for osteoporosis according to the national osteoporosis foundation is as follows:

  • Females aged 65 years or more 
  • Males aged 70 years or more
  • Post-menopausal females under the age of 65 years with risk factors
  • Fracture after the age of 50 years
  • Males aged 50-69 with risk factors

A DEXA scan is performed in the above patients to assess bone mineral density, and the results are reported in terms of T-score or Z-score.

Pearl: Z-score and T-score for osteoporosis:

Z-score:

It is the number of standard deviations a patient’s BMD(bone mass density) differs from the average BMD of their age, sex, and ethnicity.

A Z-score of -2 or below should trigger investigations for underlying disease.

T-score:

It is the BMD at the site when compared to the young normal reference mean. It is a comparison of a patient’s BMD to that of a healthy 30-year old.

  • Normal is a T-score of -1 or higher.
  • Osteopenia is defined as a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5.
  • Osteoporosis is defined as a T-score less than -2.5, that is a BMD which is two and a half standard deviations below the mean of a 30-year old man/woman.

Pearl: Risk factors for osteoporosis:

Risk factor for osteoporosis
Low BMI
Family history of osteoporosis
Old age
Previous fragility fracture
Chronic use of glucocorticoids
Family history of hip fractures
Smoking and alcohol intake
Drugs like anticonvulsants, anticoagulants and thyroid replacement therapy
Hyperparathyroidism, multiple myeloma, and malabsorption syndrome

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the condition represented in the image below.
questions.raw_text: Identify the condition represented in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Miliary tuberculosis

The above image represents "miliary tuberculosis". Individual lesions are small (2-mm) foci of yellow-white consolidation scattered through the lung parenchyma 

Miliary tuberculosis (TB) is the widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis via hematogenous spread. It occurs when organisms draining through the lymphatics enter the venous blood and circulate back to the lung. Miliary TB may infect any number of organs, including the lungs, liver and spleen.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of atropine in the management of organophosphate poisoning?
questions.raw_text: What is the mechanism of action of atropine in the management of organophosphate poisoning?

options.label: C
options.text: Binds with both nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors

options.label: D
options.text: Is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine

questions.correct_answer: D. Is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine

Atropine is useful in organophosphate poisoning because it is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine. 

An acetylcholinesterase enzyme has an esteratic and an anionic site. The organophosphates bind to the esteratic (active) site of AChEs (acetylcholine esterases) and deactivate them. This results in excessive Ach, causing increased muscarinic activity like increased tracheobronchial and salivary secretions, bronchoconstriction, miosis, bradycardia, and, to a lesser extent, peripheral ganglionic and CNS actions. It has relatively insignificant action on nicotinic receptors. 

Atropine antagonizes these parasympathetic effects by competitive inhibition of acetylcholine at the muscarinic receptors.

Pralidoxime reactivates the acetylcholinesterase, which had been deactivated in organophosphate poisoning. Pralidoxime attaches to the anionic site of the enzyme that remains unoccupied. Then it reacts with the phosphorus atom of the organophosphorous compound, which is attached to the esteric site to form a phospho-oxime complex. It then dissociates from the enzyme, regenerating the active enzyme.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of Thoracoscore?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not a component of Thoracoscore?
questions.explanation:

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 56-year-old man suffering from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus came for a routine checkup. His lipid profile revealed increased TG (triacylglycerol) and VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein). What is the cause of this abnormal lipid profile?
questions.raw_text: A 56-year-old man suffering from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus came for a routine checkup. His lipid profile revealed increased TG (triacylglycerol) and VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein). What is the cause of this abnormal lipid profile?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased activity of lipoprotein lipase and decreased activity of hormone sensitive lipase

options.label: B
options.text: Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity

options.label: C
options.text: Increase in peripheral function of LDL receptors

options.label: D
options.text: Increased in activity of hepatic lipase

questions.correct_answer: B. Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity

In chronic diabetes, the values of TG and VLDL are increased due to an increase in hormone-sensitive lipase and a decrease in lipoprotein lipase.

Insulin has an inhibitory effect on hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL). In diabetes, low insulin corresponds to an increase in HSL activity. This promotes the breakdown of lipids and the release of TG and free fatty acids from the adipose tissue.

Insulin induces the activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) which is present on the capillary walls. LPL promotes hydrolysis of TG and the degradation of the transport proteins, VLDL, and chylomicrons. In diabetes, low insulin leads to decreased LPL activity which corresponds to an increase in VLDL and TG.

Pearl: Hormone sensitive lipase Vs lipoprotein lipase

   HSL  Lipoprotein lipase
Location  Adipocyte  Capillaries
Action  Hydrolyse TAG in adipose   tissue  Hydrolyse TAG in chylomicron , VLDL
Acts in the state of  Fasting (Glucagon)  Fed (Insulin)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A player participating in an Under-12 tennis tournament suspects foul play by a rival player. He claims to fit the criteria for the age requirements for the tournament, but the opposing players do not agree. Which of the following sets of X-rays would be most useful to verify the claims of the player?
questions.raw_text: A player participating in an Under-12 tennis tournament suspects foul play by a rival player. He claims to fit the criteria for the age requirements for the tournament, but the opposing players do not agree. Which of the following sets of X-rays would be most useful to verify the claims of the player?

options.label: B
options.text: X-ray of the elbow and pelvis

options.label: D
options.text: X-ray of the hands and wrist

questions.correct_answer: D. X-ray of the hands and wrist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. X-ray of the hands and wrist

The X-ray of choice to determine the skeletal age of a player in an under-12 tennis tournament is the X-rays of the hands and wrist.

Skeletal radiographs, typically of the left hand and wrist, and dental examinations are frequently used for age estimation in sport disputes and medicolegal cases where documentary evidence of age is not available or questionable.

The Greulich and Pyle atlas, Tanner-Whitehouse (TW) method, and software such as boneXpert are standard tools used to radiologically assess skeletal maturity from hand and wrist radiographs.

These assessments evaluate skeletal maturation, which reflects the child's physiologic age rather than their exact chronologic age.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is not true regarding a Bochdalek hernia?
questions.raw_text: What is not true regarding a Bochdalek hernia?

options.label: A
options.text: Early respiratory distress leading to early diagnosis and treatment is a good prognostic sign

options.label: B
options.text: The contents of hernial sac commonly includes retroperitoneal fat, left kidney or spleen

options.label: C
options.text: The condition is diagnosed prenatally by ultrasonography.

options.label: D
options.text: Pericardial cyst is a differential diagnosis.

questions.correct_answer: A. Early respiratory distress leading to early diagnosis and treatment is a good prognostic sign
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Early respiratory distress leading to early diagnosis and treatment is a good prognostic sign

Early respiratory distress, within 6 hours of birth, is thought to be a poor prognostic sign.

Features of a Bochdalek hernia:

  • Respiratory distress is a cardinal sign in infants with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).
  • Early respiratory distress, within 6 hr after birth, is thought to be a poor prognostic sign.
  • Children with CDH may also have a scaphoid abdomen and increased chest wall diameter.
  • Bowel sounds may also be heard in the chest, with a bilateral decrease in breath sounds.
  • The point of maximal cardiac impulse may be displaced away from the side of a hernia if a mediastinal shift has occurred.
  • Retroperitoneal fat, left kidney, spleen or only the omentum commonly herniates through the defect. If the defect is large, most abdominal contents including stomach may herniate.

Diagnosis:

  • Chest radiography and passage of a nasal gastric tube confirm the diagnosis.
  • CDH can be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasonography (between 16 and 24 weeks of gestation)
  • High-speed fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can further define the lesion.

Ultrasonography findings:

  • Polyhydramnios
  • Chest mass
  • Mediastinal shift
  • Gastric bubble or a liver in the thoracic cavity
  • Fetal hydrops

Differential diagnosis:

  • Eventration
  • Cystic lung lesion (pulmonary sequestration or cystic adenomatoid Malformation)
  • Group B streptococcal sepsis: associated with delayed onset of symptoms and a CDH often on the right side.
  • Pneumothorax: always occurs on contralateral to the side of CDH.

Treatment:

Variable period of time (24-72 hours) to allow for stabilization before surgical repair

The viscera are reduced into the abdominal cavity, and the posterolateral defect in the diaphragm is closed using interrupted, nonabsorbable sutures.

In most cases (80%-90%), a hernia sac is not present. If identified, it is excised at the time of repair.

Conventional mechanical ventilation, high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV), and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) are the 3 main strategies to support respiratory failure in the newborn with CDH.

Good relative indicators of stability are as follows:

  • Requirement for conventional ventilation only
  • Low peak inspiratory pressure
  • Fio2 <50

If the defect is too large, a porous polytetrafluoroethylene (Gore-Tex) patch is used.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient with a history of cholelithiasis, presented with vomiting and abdominal pain. The abdominal radiograph showed Rigler’s triad. Which of these is not a component of Rigler’s triad?
questions.raw_text: A middle-aged female patient with a history of cholelithiasis, presented with vomiting and abdominal pain. The abdominal radiograph showed Rigler’s triad. Which of these is not a component of Rigler’s triad?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Large bowel obstruction

Rigler’s triad is seen in gallstone ileus and consists of

  • Pneumobilia
  • Small bowel obstruction
  • Ectopic gall stone (usually in the right iliac fossa)

This should not be confused with Rigler’s sign and Rigler's notch sign. 

Rigler's Sign:

Seen in pneumoperitoneum. Here, the air is seen on both sides of the bowel wall unlike normally, where the air is seen only in the intraluminal side of the bowel.

Rigler's notch sign:

Refers to indentation seen in the border of a solid lung mass, which is thought to represents a feeding vessel, thus suggesting the presence of bronchial carcinoma. But, this is not specific and can also be seen in granulomatous infections.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old patient is being evaluated for primary amenorrhea. Laboratory investigations reveal decreased estrogen, FSH, and LH. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 19-year-old patient is being evaluated for primary amenorrhea. Laboratory investigations reveal decreased estrogen, FSH, and LH. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kallman syndrome

Decreased levels of estrogen, FSH, and LH are suggestive of hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, which is caused by Kallman syndrome.

It is an X-linked disorder (KAL gene) that causes isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and anosmia.

Causes of hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism:

  • Congenital
    • Kallman's syndrome 
    • Isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (IHH)
    • Prader-Willi syndrome
    • CHARGE syndrome
  • Acquired
    • Pituitary tumors, apoplexy
    • Hyperprolactinemia
    • Anorexia nervosa, excess exercise
    • Irradiation
    • Infection
    • Trauma

Option A: Asherman syndrome causes secondary amenorrhea due to intrauterine synechiae.

Option B: Müllerian agenesis presents with primary amenorrhea with normal levels of all hormones.

Option D: Turner's syndrome causes primary amenorrhea due to hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The liver specimen obtained after the autopsy of a patient is given below. What could be the likely cause of this finding?
questions.raw_text: The liver specimen obtained after the autopsy of a patient is given below. What could be the likely cause of this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Heart failure

In the image, the liver specimen shows a nutmeg liver appearance, which occurs in congestive hepatomegaly. This is secondary to passive congestion due to right heart failure.

In right heart failure, congestion occurs in the hepatic and portal vessels, with the most significant congestion around the central veins. This results in an increased liver size and weight. The pericentral zones become congested and red-brown. The periportal regions usually are tan. This leads to a nutmeg liver appearance. With longstanding failure, the central areas can become fibrotic, eventually culminating in cardiac cirrhosis.

Pathological changes are also seen in the spleen and the gastrointestinal tract. Portal venous hypertension also causes the enlargement of the spleen, with platelet sequestration. This is known as congestive splenomegaly. This can also contribute to chronic congestion and oedema of the bowel.

Other options:

Option A: Liver cirrhosis would show a gross appearance of multiple regenerative nodules throughout the liver, separated by bridging fibrosis. The following image shows the gross appearance of the liver in alcoholic liver cirrhosis:

 

Option B: Haemochromatosis presents with a gross image of dark brown discoloration of the liver, as well as the other involved organs, with hepatomegaly.

Option D: Non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis is characterised by fibrosis around the portal vein without the architectural changes of cirrhosis and is due to increased portal pressure. Gross appearance may vary, ranging from normal to shrunken.

questions.correct_answer: D. Onset before 2nd year of life
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Onset before 2nd year of life

The patient most likely has Milroy disease which is the familial version of congenital lymphedema. It is inherited as a dominant trait.

Primary lymphedema is classified on the basis of age of onset and the presence of familial clustering.

  2. Lymphedema precox - most common type. onset between 2 to 35 years of age
  3. Lymphedema tarda - rare. onset after 35 years of age

Treatment includes conservative management such as massage, compression stockings, or bandaging.

Surgical management includes vascularized lymph node transfer (VLNT). It involves the transfer of functional lymph nodes from a healthy donor site to an area of the body with damaged or diseased lymphatic drainage.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Immunohistochemistry for HER2 protein expression is performed in 3 patients with breast carcinoma, with the following results. Which of the following patients should be subjected to fluorescence in-situ hybridization?
questions.raw_text: Immunohistochemistry for HER2 protein expression is performed in 3 patients with breast carcinoma, with the following results. Which of the following patients should be subjected to fluorescence in-situ hybridization?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Patient C

The immunohistochemistry (IHC) pattern of patient C reveals moderately strong circumferential staining (faint brown color) in >10 % of cells, which is classified as 2+ or equivocal staining. Hence, she should be subjected to fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to confirm HER2-positive gene amplification status.

The following are classified as HER2-positive tumors:

  • Tumors that show 3+ staining on IHC (here FISH is not needed).
  • Tumors with 2+ staining on IHC, followed by HER2-gene amplification confirmed by FISH

Once HER2-positive status is confirmed, targeted therapy against HER2 can be initiated with trastuzumab or lapatinib. 

Pearl: Newer molecular tests in breast cancer

Newer molecular tests for breast cancer have been developed, which help in predicting the advantage of adding chemotherapy. These are:

  • Oncotype Dx (21-geneassay)
  • Mammaprint (70-gene assay)
  • EndoPredict (12-gene assay)
  • PAM50 (50-gene assay)

Oncotype Dx can only be used in hormone (ER, PR) receptor-positive cancers, while mammaprint can be used in both hormone receptor (ER, PR) positive and hormone receptor-negative cancers. 

Using these molecular tests, a recurrence score (0 – 100) is calculated.

  • If the score is low, then there is no advantage of adding chemotherapy
  • If the score is high, then chemotherapy should be added

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What does the blood-gas partition coefficient of an inhaled anesthetic indicate?
questions.raw_text: What does the blood-gas partition coefficient of an inhaled anesthetic indicate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Solubility in blood

The blood gas (B:G) partition coefficient of an inhaled anesthetic is an indicator of solubility in blood which determines the speed of induction and recovery.

An inhalational anesthetic with a lower blood gas partition (B:G) coefficient would have lower solubility in blood. This would mean a higher alveolar concentration which will lead to faster induction and recovery.

Xenon with a blood-gas partition coefficient of 0.115 has the fastest induction and emergence from anesthesia.

Methoxyflurane with a blood gas partition coefficient of 12 has the slowest induction and emergence from anesthesia.

The speed of induction and emergence:

Xenon > Desflurane > Sevoflurane> Isoflurane > Enflurane > Halothane > Methoxyflurane

Pearl: Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC)

Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) is the minimum concentration of an inhaled anesthetic at 1 atm of pressure that prevents skeletal muscle movement in response to a surgical incision in 50% of patients. 

MAC of inhaled anesthetics

Isoflurane 1.2 1.4 
Enflurane 1.7 1.9

MAC is an indicator of potency. The lower the MAC, the higher is the potency.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A construction worker is brought to the casualty following a crush injury to his right lower limb. Which of the following scores can be used to decide between amputation and limb-salvage surgery?
questions.raw_text: A construction worker is brought to the casualty following a crush injury to his right lower limb. Which of the following scores can be used to decide between amputation and limb-salvage surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mangled Extremity Severity Score

Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS) score can be used to decide between amputation and limb salvage in crushing injuries.

Components of MESS are:

  • Shock
  • Ischemia
  • Velocity
  • Age

Total score is 11. Six or less is consistent with a salvageable limb.

Other scores to assess if the limb is salvageable or not are:

  • Limb salvage index
  • Ganga score

Option A: Gustilo Anderson Classification is used to classify open fractures. 

Option B: Revised Trauma Score (RTS) characterizes the injured patient’s condition by incorporating the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), systolic blood pressure, and respiratory rate. 

Option D: Trauma Injury Severity Score (TRISS) comprises Injury Severity Score (ISS), Revised Trauma Score (RTS), age of the patient and mechanism of Injury (blunt/penetrating).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate is found to have increased irritability, poor feeding, and 2 episodes of seizures. Lumbar puncture was done and the findings were suggestive of meningitis. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.raw_text: A neonate is found to have increased irritability, poor feeding, and 2 episodes of seizures. Lumbar puncture was done and the findings were suggestive of meningitis. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Escherichia coli

The given clinical scenario describes neonatal meningitis. E. coli > Streptococcus agalactiae, part of group B streptococci, are the most likely causative organism of neonatal meningitis.

Early features of meningitis include temperature instability (hypo or hyperthermia), lethargy, bradycardia, and feed intolerance. Late features include seizures, bulging fontanelle, and nuchal rigidity.

The most common cause of bacterial meningitis in a 0 to 2-month baby is E.coli. Earlier, group B streptococci was the most common cause of neonatal meningitis. However, in recent years, E.coli has emerged as the most common cause. In babies aged 2 to 24 months, Hemophilus influenzae type b are the primary causative pathogens, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae. For children older than 2 years, pneumococci remain a prominent cause of meningitis, with Neisseria meningitidis being the second most common pathogen.

The most common etiological agents of neonatal meningitis and sepsis are listed in the table below:

  India Worldwide
Neonatal meningitis E. coli, Klebsiella Group B Streptococci
Neonatal sepsis Klebsiella, S. aureus, E. coli Group B Streptococci

Neonates have immature cellular and humoral immunity. This makes them prone to meningitis and sepsis. Thus, an infant with a fever who is 28 days or younger, should be evaluated for sepsis.

Option C: Meningococcal infections are usually asymptomatic. If invasive disease occurs, then the clinical spectrum varies widely from meningococcal meningitis (highest proportion) to bacteremia without sepsis, meningococcal septicemia with or without meningitis, pneumonia, chronic meningococcemia, and occult bacteremia.

Option D: Meningitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes is rare but clinically significant. Infants can acquire the infection in utero or through an infected birth canal. Neonatal listeriosis can manifest as early-onset disease, typically within 1-2 days of birth, primarily as a septicemic form. Alternatively, it can present as a late-onset disease in infants older than 5 days, predominantly as a meningitic form.

The child in this scenario has some degree of dehydration, since the child is restless and irritable, drinks water readily, has sunken eyes, and the skin goes back slowly on the skin pinch test (<2 seconds) with sunken eyes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A doctor tells a 31-year-old woman, who is 20 weeks pregnant, that her baby has a developmental defect. She has come to you for a second opinion. The following USG finding is seen. Identify the defect.
questions.raw_text: A doctor tells a 31-year-old woman, who is 20 weeks pregnant, that her baby has a developmental defect. She has come to you for a second opinion. The following USG finding is seen. Identify the defect.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anencephaly

The given ultrasound image shows an open defect in the calvaria and skin leading to the exposure of the cranial neural tube. This is consistent with the diagnosis of anencephaly. 

Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. It is one of the earliest detectable congenital defects that can be detected as early as 10 to 11 weeks of gestation.  Screening can also be done by serum estimation of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP). The following are the radiological signs seen in anencephaly. 

  • Frog eye sign - Absence of cranial calvaria, prominent orbits thereby resembling the face of a frog. 
  • Shower cap sign - The absence of the cranium could lead to the protrusion of a disorganized mass of brain tissue. This resembles a shower cap giving rise to a characteristic triangular facial appearance.

Neural-tube defects can be prevented with pre-conceptional supplementation of folic acid. A dose of 4 mg daily is recommended in subsequent pregnancies.  

The frog eye and showercap signs are shown below:

 

Option B: Omphalocele is a midline anterior abdominal wall defect through which the solid abdominal viscera and/or bowel may herniate. The extruded abdominal contents are covered in a sac. Given below is an ultrasound image of the fetus suggestive of an omphalocele (asterix).

 

Cystic hygroma is a congenital multiloculated lymphatic lesion that is classically found in the left posterior triangle of the neck. It occurs as a result of sequestration or obstruction of developing lymph vessels. This defect can be picked up in a first-trimester ultrasound. The images below show the MRI and USG appearance of cystic hygroma, respectively:

 

Encephalocele is caused due to defects in the skull through which the meninges and/or neural tissue herniate. The squamous part of the occipital bone is the most frequently affected bone. 

The image shows a newborn with encephalocele.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is preferred in the management of primary progressive multiple sclerosis ?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following drugs is preferred in the management of primary progressive multiple sclerosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ocrelizumab

Ocrelizumab is preferred in the management of primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS). Natalizumab, fingolimod, and alemtuzumab are used in the management of relapsing multiple sclerosis and not PPMS.

Ocrelizumab is a monoclonal antibody against CD20 molecules present on B cells. It reduces the progression of the disease and improves other clinical parameters.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease characterized by chronic inflammation, demyelination, gliosis (scarring), and neuronal loss.

Based on clinical course, MS is classified as:

  • Relapsing or bout onset MS (RMS)
  • Secondary progressive MS (SPMS)
  • Primary progressive MS (PPMS)

The drugs used in the management of RMS are listed in the table below:

Highly effective Moderately effective Modestly effective
  • Anti CD20 antibodies: Ocrelizumab, Ofatumumab, Rituximab
  • Anti integrin antibody: Natalizumab
  • Anti CD 52 antibody: Alemtuzumab
  • Mitoxantrone
  • Sphingosine-1-phosphate inhibitor: Fingolimod
  • Dimethyl fumarate
  • Cladribine
  • Glatiramer acetate
  • Interferon beta
  • Teriflunomide

 Siponimod, a selective S1P1 S1P5 modulator, reduces the risk of progression of SPMS. Ocrelizumab, cladribine and high dose interferon beta can also be used.

Ocrelizumab is the first drug to alter the progression of disability in PPMS.

questions.text:
A 32-year-old male patient presents to the surgical emergency with a history of peptic ulcer disease and pain abdomen, bloating, and obstipation for 2 days. What is the next line in management?

A. IV fluids
B. CECT abdomen
C. Exploratory laparotomy
D. Upper GI endoscopy

The image of the x-ray film is given below:
questions.raw_text:
A 32-year-old male patient presents to the surgical emergency with a history of peptic ulcer disease and pain abdomen, bloating, and obstipation for 2 days. What is the next line in management?

A. IV fluids
B. CECT abdomen
C. Exploratory laparotomy
D. Upper GI endoscopy

The image of the x-ray film is given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A and C

The given clinical scenario and the chest X-ray showing air under the diaphragm is suggestive of a hollow viscus perforation occuring secondary to the peptic ulcer disease(PUD) in this patient. The next line of management in this condition is administration of IV fluids (option A) and exploratory laparotomy(option C).

Hollow viscus perforation is a life-threatening condition. In PUD, the perforation most commonly occurs as a complication of anterior duodenal ulcers and gastric ulcers.This results in leakage of gastric contents into the abdomen resulting in acute chemical peritonitis.

Clinical features of perforation include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, guarding & rigidity, rebound tenderness and decreased or absent bowel sounds. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

An erect xray abdomen shows gas under the diaphragm. If the patient can't stand an x-ray can be taken in lateral decubitus position and may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus.

The below image shows an x-ray radiograph of a hollow viscus perforation:

CECT (option B) is performed in hemodynamically stable patients and is the most sensitive investigation to detect minimal/ suspected pneumoperitoneum.

Management of a hollow viscous perforation is mainly resuscitation, IV fluids, analgesics, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency laparotomy. 

Upper GI endoscopy is done in a patient with upper GI hemorrhage (m/c variceal veins rupture) to diagnose and manage the source of bleeding with techniques such as banding and sclerotherapy (option D).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A 62-year-old male patient with heart failure is scheduled for a heart transplant. His renal function test is deranged and hemoglobin is 6 gm%. The physician ordered 2 units of whole blood. Four hours after transfusion, he developed severe respiratory distress. On examination, he is hypoxemic, has tachycardia and his mean arterial pressure is elevated. Which of the following are the best investigations for the above scenario?
  1. Chest X-ray
  2. Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level 
  3. Absolute neutrophil count
  4. Leucocyte antibodies
  5. Platelets
questions.raw_text:
A 62-year-old male patient with heart failure is scheduled for a heart transplant. His renal function test is deranged and hemoglobin is 6 gm%. The physician ordered 2 units of whole blood. Four hours after transfusion, he developed severe respiratory distress. On examination, he is hypoxemic, has tachycardia and his mean arterial pressure is elevated. Which of the following are the best investigations for the above scenario?
  1. Chest X-ray
  2. Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level 
  3. Absolute neutrophil count
  4. Leucocyte antibodies
  5. Platelets
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 2

The clinical scenario describes an elderly patient with heart failure who develops severe respiratory distress associated with hypoxia, tachycardia, and elevated mean arterial pressure following a blood transfusion. The most likely diagnosis is transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). The recommended investigations for suspected TACO include chest X-ray and BNP levels.

Chest X-ray in TACO may show bilateral and predominant alveolar infiltrates. BNP levels are usually elevated in TACO secondary to volume overload.

Anti-leukocyte antibodies are present in transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), not in TACO patients.

TACO is usually a clinical diagnosis suspected in any patient who has acute respiratory distress and/or hypertension during transfusion or within 6 hours of completion.

Risk factors include older age, pre-existing fluid overload, cardiac dysfunction, renal dysfunction, and transfusion of large volumes of blood components.
Management of TACO involves discontinuing the transfusion and providing oxygen and diuretics.

Identification of at-risk patients, a slow transfusion rate (1 PRBC over 3-4 hours), close monitoring, and the use of diuretics in hemodynamically stable patients with a history of TACO can prevent TACO.

questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true regarding the instrument shown below?

A. It is used in women not on thromboprophylaxis and planned for caesarean section.
B. It is used in women on thromboprophylaxis and planned for caesarean section.
C. It is removed once the patient starts ambulating.
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following statements is true regarding the instrument shown below?

A. It is used in women not on thromboprophylaxis and planned for caesarean section.
B. It is used in women on thromboprophylaxis and planned for caesarean section.
C. It is removed once the patient starts ambulating.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A and C

The given image shows a pneumatic compression device. It is used in women who are not on any thromboprophylaxis and planned for cesarean section (statement A), and it is removed once the patient starts ambulating after surgery (statement C).

The device is used because pregnancy and surgery increase the risk of thromboembolism.

According to recent guidelines, patients without additional risk factors are placed on pneumatic compression devices for thromboprophylaxis before cesarean delivery and are not given pharmacological agents.

Pneumatic compression devices with pharmacological therapy (unfractionated heparin or low molecular weight heparin) are given to patients undergoing cesarean delivery with additional risk factors.

Indications of pharmacological thromboprophylaxis:

  • Inherited coagulation disorder
  • Overweight or obese patient
  • Heart failure
  • Family history of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following should be the treatment of choice for renal cell carcinoma with tumor less than 4 cm in size?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following should be the treatment of choice for renal cell carcinoma with tumor less than 4 cm in size?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Partial nephrectomy

Partial nephrectomy (also known as nephron-sparing surgery) is the treatment of choice for tumors <4 cm.

Indications for partial nephrectomy:

  • Tumors < 4cm
  • Well-selected tumors between 4-7 cm
  • Bilateral tumors
  • Tumor in solitary kidneys
  • Patients with pre-existing renal dysfunction.

Recently, partial nephrectomy is also increasingly being performed for stage T1b tumors. 

Treatment of renal cell carcinoma: 

RCC is a radio and chemoresistant tumor.

Staging  Description  Management 
Stage 1  Tumor <7 cm, confined to the kidney Partial nephrectomy 
Stage 2  Tumor >7 cm, confined to the kidney Radical nephrectomy 
Stage 3  Tumor extends into the major veins or perinephric tissue but not into the adrenal gland and not beyond Gerota's fascia Radical nephrectomy 
Stage 4  Tumor invades beyond Gerota fascia (including contiguous extension into the ipsilateral adrenal gland) 
  • Debulking surgery
  • mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus, sirolimus
  • Tyrosine kinase inhibitors: sunitinib, sorafenib

Note: The above staging system is the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging of RCC.

Radical nephrectomy consists of the removal of the kidney, perirenal fat, adrenal gland, and regional lymph nodes. The adrenal gland is no longer removed except in cases of obvious tumor involvement. Lymphadenectomy is indicated only in high-risk patients with large primary tumors and enlarged lymph nodes.

Cryoablation is indicated in the T1a stage of RCC if surgery cannot be performed. It is also indicated in advanced/metastatic tumors. 

Note: Sunitinib and sorafenib are also used in GIST and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Pearl: Histologic subtypes of renal cell carcinoma

 Clear-cell type:

  • Most common type
  • Originates from proximal convoluted tubules
  • Caused by deletion of chromosomes 3p & 6p 
  • Associated with von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease and tuberous sclerosis

Papillary type:

  • Originates from proximal/distal convoluted tubules
  • Caused by c-met mutation
  • Histology shows Psammoma bodies
  • Associated with hereditary papillary renal cell carcinoma
  • Micropapillary variant is associated with long term dialysis

Chromophobe type:

  • Best prognosis
  • Originates from intercalated cells of collecting duct
  • Caused by loss of multiple chromosomes (1, 2, 6, 10, 13) and extreme hypodiploidy
  • Associated with Birt-Hogg- Dubé syndrome
  • Histology shows plant-like cells/ resin like nucleus
  • Cytokeratin positive on IHC 

Collecting (Bellini duct) type:

  • Worst prognosis
  • Originates from collecting tubules
  • Caused by deletion of 1q & monosomy of multiple chromosomes

Medullary type:

  • Poor prognosis
  • Originates from the distal nephron
  • Associated with sickle cell trait

Note: Sarcomatoid change can occur infrequently in all types of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and is an ominous feature.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A condition requires the surgery depicted in the image shown below. All the following are usually seen associated with this condition except?
questions.raw_text: A condition requires the surgery depicted in the image shown below. All the following are usually seen associated with this condition except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absent kidney

The given image shows a Roux-en-Y loop of the small intestine (jejunum) attached to an area of the liver capsule (Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy), which is suggestive of Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy procedure done for biliary atresia in infants. An absent kidney is not associated with this condition.

Extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA) is defined as a partial or total absence of permeable bile duct between porta hepatis and the duodenum. It is due to inflammatory fibrosis of the biliary tree. It leads to obstruction to bile flow thereby causing leaking of conjugated bilirubin into the circulation.

Associated anomalies include cardiac lesions, polysplenia, situs inversus, absent vena cava, and a preduodenal portal vein.

Management of extrahepatic biliary atresia
Type I

Atresia restricted to the common bile duct

Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
Type II

Atresia of the common hepatic duct

 Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y hepatoportoenterostomy)
Type III

Atresia of the right and left hepatic duct

In the Kasai procedure, the extrahepatic biliary tree is dissected proximally till the liver capsule, the porta hepatis is transected and a jejunal loop is anastomosed in order to provide a drainage pathway for bile. 

Infants with biliary atresia, who do not achieve successful drainage after Kasai's procedure, require liver transplantation within the first year of life. This is the most common reason for liver transplantation in children.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are correct about hair cells?
  1. There is 1 row of inner hair cells and 3 rows of outer hair cells
  2. Inner hair cells are responsible for transmitting auditory impulses
  3. Majority of the afferent fibres of spiral ganglion supply the inner hair cells.
  4. Outer hair cells primarily initiate the electrical signals sent to the brain in response to sound vibrations.
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following statements are correct about hair cells?
  1. There is 1 row of inner hair cells and 3 rows of outer hair cells
  2. Inner hair cells are responsible for transmitting auditory impulses
  3. Majority of the afferent fibres of spiral ganglion supply the inner hair cells.
  4. Outer hair cells primarily initiate the electrical signals sent to the brain in response to sound vibrations.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. i, ii, iii

Statements i, ii, and iii are correct.

Statement i: There is 1 row of inner hair cells and 3 rows of outer hair cells is a correct statement. 

Statement ii: Inner hair cells are responsible for transmitting auditory impulses is a correct statement. Inner hair cells are richly supplied by afferent cochlear fibres and are probably more important in the transmission of auditory impulses.

Statement iii: The majority of the afferent fibres of spiral ganglion supply the inner hair cells is a correct statement. Ninety-five percent of afferent fibres of spiral ganglion supply the inner hair cells while only five percent supply the outer hair cells. Efferent fibres to the hair cells come from the olivocochlear bundle.

Statement iv: Outer hair cells primarily initiate the electrical signals sent to the brain in response to sound vibrations is an incorrect statement. Outer hair cells mainly receive efferent innervation from the olivary complex and are concerned with modulating the function of inner hair cells.

questions.text: The test given below in the image is used for:
questions.raw_text: The test given below in the image is used for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stereopsis test

The given image is of Titmus stereotest, which is done for the assesment of stereopsis (perception of depth).

  • The pictures consist of a housefly for children and circular patterns for adults.
  • The picture is held in front of the eyes of the patient at a distance of about 16 inches and the patient is asked to wear polarized glasses. 
  • If the patient's perception of the depth is normal, the housefly appears to rise above the plane, like a 3D image. If the patient is asked to pinch the wings of the housefly, he/she will try to pinch in the air, above the plane of the image.
  • If the patient's perception of depth in either eye is defective, then the image appears just like normal 2D image.

Option A: Tests for ocular deviation include

  • Cover tests
  • Prism cover test- This will tell the amount of deviation in prism dioptres.
  • Maddox rod test
  • Hirschberg corneal reflex test

The below given image shows Maddox rod test.

Option C: Test for refractive error includes

  • Retinoscopy
  • Auto refractometry

The below given image shows the findings of Retinoscopy in different refractive errors.

Option D: Tests for colour blindness include

  • Ishihara test: It is frequently used to screen for a red–green colour vision deficit. It consists of a test plate followed by 16 plates, each with a series of dots arranged to show a shape or number that the subject is asked to identify.
  • Hardy–Rand–Rittler test: It is similar to ishihara test but is used to detect all three color vision defect.
  • Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue test: Is the most sensitive test for both acquired and congenital colour blindness. It consists of 85 caps of different hue that needs to be rearranged.

The below given image depicts the ishihara test.

Pearl: Grades of binocular vision

I - Simultaneous perception                       

  • Ability to see two dissimilar objects simultaneously

II - Fusion

  • Ability to superimpose two incomplete but similar images

III - Stereopsis

  • Ability to perceive depth

Pearl: Cover tests in ophthalmology

Cover–uncover test:

  • To detect the presence of heterophoria: Latent squint
  • One eye is covered with the occluder, and the other eye is made to fix an object.
  • In the presence of heterophoria, the eye under the cover will deviate.
  • When the cover is removed, the eye under the cover will return back to its normal.
  • This movement is observed.
  • The direction of movement determines the type of heterophoria.

Direct Cover test:

  • Confirms the presence of manifest squint.
  • Differentiates apparent squint from a manifest squint.
  • The patient is asked to fixate on the point light.
  • The normal-looking eye is covered.
  • In manifest squint, the uncovered eye will move in the opposite direction to take fixation.
  • In apparent squint, there will be no movement of the uncovered eye.

Alternate cover test:

  • In the below image, the patient has right exotropia with left eye fixating.
  • Both eyes move each time the cover alternates from one eye to the other.
  • It reveals if the squint is unilateral or alternate.
  • It differentiates between concomitant and paralytic squint.

questions.text: A 35-year-old male came to the OPD with complaints of an increase in his heart rate and palpitations. On examination, there was episodic tachycardia and occasional extrasystole. Ocular examination showed visual field defects. Which of the following is the likely cause?

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A boy presents with recurrent episodes of melena. On examination, there was eczema of the skin with multiple petechiae. His platelet count was low but RBC and WBC counts were within normal limits. Which of the following is the diagnostic investigation in this patient?
questions.raw_text: A boy presents with recurrent episodes of melena. On examination, there was eczema of the skin with multiple petechiae. His platelet count was low but RBC and WBC counts were within normal limits. Which of the following is the diagnostic investigation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. WASP gene mutation

The given scenario of recurrent episodes of melena, eczema, and multiple petechiae along with low platelet counts is suggestive of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. The diagnostic investigation in this patient is WASP gene mutation testing. 

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome(WAS) is an X-linked recessive immunodeficiency disorder. It is caused by mutations in the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) that primarily affects the T lymphocytes.

Normally, WASp regulates the actin cytoskeleton and thus helps in cell adhesion, migration, and the formation of synapses between antigen-presenting and target cells. In WAS, there is a progressive loss of T lymphocytes in the peripheral blood resulting in defects in cellular immunity. 

The clinical features of WAS are recurrent bacterial infections, eczema, and bleeding due to thrombocytopenia. Patients with WAS are prone to develop B-cell lymphomas and autoimmune disorders.

The image given below shows eczema seen in WAS

Diagnosis is based on intracellular immunofluorescence analysis of WAS protein (WASp) expression in blood cells. IgM levels in the serum are low, but levels of IgG are usually normal. Reduced-sized platelet is a typical feature of WAS.

Although prophylactic antibiotics, immunoglobulin G (IgG) supplementation, and topical treatment for eczema can be tried, the only curative treatment is an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Gene therapy trials are also under research.
