questions.text: A patient has complains of fever with chills. A throat examination reveals swollen glands and a thick, whitish membrane over his tonsils. Albert staining is to be done. What are the constituents of Albert's stain?
questions.raw_text: A patient has complains of fever with chills. A throat examination reveals swollen glands and a thick, whitish membrane over his tonsils. Albert staining is to be done. What are the constituents of Albert's stain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Toluidine and malachite green

The given scenario is suggestive of diphtheria caused by Corynebacterium diphtheria. This organism is stained using Albert's stain which contains toluidine blue 'O' and malachite green. Both these dyes have an affinity for acidic cytoplasm as they are basic dyes.

Albert’s, Neisser’s, and Ponder’s stain are used to demonstrate the metachromatic granules(Volutin / Babes Ernst granules) of Corynebacterium diphtheria.

Corynebacterium diphtheria appears as green-coloured bacilli with purple-blue-coloured metachromatic granules in cuneiform arrangement.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following principles is primarily used in polymerase chain reaction?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following principles is primarily used in polymerase chain reaction?

options.label: B
options.text: It can amplify small amounts of DNA

options.label: C
options.text: It can amplify small amounts of RNA

questions.correct_answer: B. It can amplify small amounts of DNA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It can amplify small amounts of DNA

The primary principle used in polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the amplification of small amounts of DNA. 

PCR is an automated process in which a single or a few copies of a DNA piece is amplified to generate of thousands to millions of copies of that particular DNA sequence. There are 3 basic steps are involved in PCR:

  • DNA extraction from microorganism
  • Amplification of extracted DNA - Denaturation (95°C), Primer annealing (55°C), Extension (72°C)
  • Gel electrophoresis of the amplified product

PCR is used in rapid diagnostic tests for infections (e.g. HIV DNA), forensic investigations etc. The founder of PCR is Karry B Mullis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 30-year-old married man complains of low energy and lack of motivation. He mentions that he feels useless and has no hope for the future. He is willing to take medication but is apprehensive about its side effects on his sexual life. Which of the following drugs would you prescribe to him?
questions.raw_text: A 30-year-old married man complains of low energy and lack of motivation. He mentions that he feels useless and has no hope for the future. He is willing to take medication but is apprehensive about its side effects on his sexual life. Which of the following drugs would you prescribe to him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mirtazapine

Low mood, lack of motivation, and hopelessness are suggestive of depression. Mirtazapine can be prescribed to this patient as sexual dysfunction is not a side effect associated with its use.

Mirtazapine blocks histamine (H1), 5­HT2A, 5HT2C and 5­HT3 receptors. It also blocks α2 autoreceptors on noradrenaline neurons­ and α2 heteroreceptors on serotonin neurons. It thus enhances both noradrenaline and serotonin release. Due to its sedative effect, mirtazapine is also used in depression with insomnia. Its side effects include increased appetite, weight gain, and rarely, agranulocytosis. It has minimal effects on sexual function. 

Other options:

Option A: Fluoxetine is an SSRI that can cause side effects like GI disturbances, risk of suicidal behavior, sexual dysfunction, and weight gain. Vilazodone is an SSRI that is not associated with sexual dysfunction or weight gain.

Option B: SNRIs like venlafaxine have side effects that include nausea, dizziness, sexual dysfunction, and risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior.

Option D: TCAs like imipramine have side effects like orthostatic hypotension, weight gain, GI disturbances, sexual dysfunction, seizures, and irregular heartbeats.

questions.text: A 33-year-old woman receiving treatment for TB presents to your OPD with complaints of blurry vision and pain on movement of the left eye for the past 2 days. Examination showed Marcus Gunn pupil. Which anti-tubercular drug is most likely associated with this condition?
questions.raw_text: A 33-year-old woman receiving treatment for TB presents to your OPD with complaints of blurry vision and pain on movement of the left eye for the past 2 days. Examination showed Marcus Gunn pupil. Which anti-tubercular drug is most likely associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ethambutol

The given clinical features, along with Marcus Gunn pupil, are suggestive of optic neuritis, which is a dose-dependent adverse effect associated with ethambutol.

Ethambutol’s major adverse effect is optic neuritis, causing reduced visual acuity and loss of red-green discrimination. Risk rises with dose and duration; it may affect one or both eyes. Symptoms usually reverse after drug withdrawal.

Tests of visual acuity and red-green discrimination before the start of therapy and periodically thereafter are recommended.

Kat G mutation- the most severe form of resistance.

Inh a gene overexpression-  confers cross-resistance with ethionamide.

Mutation in rpoB- the gene coding for the β subunit of RNA polymerase.

 Mutation of the Pnca gene.

Mutations in the embB gene.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A middle-aged man undergoing treatment for alcohol deaddiction was started on disulfiram. Which of the following statements is true regarding this drug?
questions.raw_text: A middle-aged man undergoing treatment for alcohol deaddiction was started on disulfiram. Which of the following statements is true regarding this drug?

options.label: A
options.text: When used with alcohol it causes respiratory difficulties

options.label: C
options.text: It can be initiated even in minimally motivated persons

options.label: D
options.text: Its action persists up to 2-3 days after stopping the drug

questions.correct_answer: A. When used with alcohol it causes respiratory difficulties
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. When used with alcohol it causes respiratory difficulties

Alcohol consumption during disulfiram therapy can result in respiratory difficulties.

Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits both the cytosolic and mitochondrial forms of aldehyde dehydrogenase. Consequently, when ethanol is ingested while on disulfiram, acetaldehyde levels rise significantly. This accumulation triggers aversive reactions characterized by redness of the skin, pounding headache, nausea, vomiting, breathing difficulties, chest heaviness, skin eruptions, hypotension, and sudden loss of consciousness. These effects may persist for up to 14 days(option D) after the last dose of disulfiram.

It is used for behavioural modification during alcohol de-addiction. The principle of action is aversive conditioning (not anti-craving) (option B). Due to its severe adverse effects, it should be given only to highly motivated individuals (option C) and requires careful medical supervision. Administration of disulfiram must be delayed until the patient has abstained from alcohol consumption for a minimum of 12 hours.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What does the Paul-Bunnell test diagnose?
questions.raw_text: What does the Paul-Bunnell test diagnose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kissing disease

Paul-Bunnell test is used to diagnose kissing disease.

Infectious mononucleosis (IM), or kissing disease, is caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). Patients present with fever, pharyngitis, bilateral symmetrical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. A drug-induced rash may develop on using beta-lactam antibiotics. Large, atypical lymphocytes are seen in the peripheral blood of affected patients. 

Paul-Bunnell test is a heterophile agglutination test used for diagnosis of IM. It identifies the heterophile antibodies produced in IM that agglutinate sheep erythrocytes. In this test, inactivated serum of a patient is mixed with 1% suspension of sheep erythrocytes in serial dilutions. After incubation at 37°C for four hours the tubes are examined for agglutination. An agglutination titre of 100 or above is suggestive of infectious mononucleosis. 

Pearl: Serological tests in microbiology

Precipitation test:

  • Ascoli's thermoprecipitin test: Anthrax
  • Streptococci grouping: Lancefield technique
  • VDRL test for syphilis (slide flocculation test)
  • Kahn test for syphilis (tube flocculation test)
  • Elek gel precipitation test for C.diphtheria

Agglutination test:

  • Widal test- typhoid
  • Weil- Felix reaction- Typhus fever
  • Streptococcus MG agglutination test- Mycoplasma pneumoniae
  • Paul Bunnel test- Infectious mononucleiosis
  • Coombs test
  • Rose Waaler test- Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Microscopic Agglutination test- Leptospirosis
  • Anti streptolysin O test

Complement fixation test:

  • Wasserman reaction(syphilis)
  • Treponema pallidum immobilization test

Neutralization test:

  • Schik test for diptheria
  • Anti streptolysin O test
  • Nagler's reaction (clostridium perfringens)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following eggs to the organism.
questions.raw_text: Match the following eggs to the organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A

The correct match is 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A.

The Hymenolepis nana egg is roughly spherical or ovoid. It has a thin colorless outer membrane and inner embryophore that encloses the hexacanth oncosphere. They are non bile-stained. The eggs float in saturated salt solution. 

The image below shows an egg of H. nana.

Ascaris lumbricoides (Roundworm) are round or oval in shape. They are always bile-stained which gives them golden-brown color. They have a thick smooth translucent shell with:

  • an outer coarsely mammillated albuminous coat
  • a thick transparent middle layer, and
  • an inner lipoidal vitelline membrane.

The eggs float in a saturated salt solution. The image below shows the egg of A. lumbricoides.

The unfertilized eggs of Ascaris are elliptical, narrower, and contain a small atrophied ovum. It has a mass of disorganized refractile granules. The shell is thinner and the egg does not float in a saturated salt solution.

The egg of Ancylostoma duodenale or hookworm is oval or elliptical. They are colorless, not bile-stained. The eggs are surrounded by a thin transparent hyaline shell membrane. It contains a segmented ovum, usually with 4-8 blastomeres. There is a clear space between the ovum and the shell. It floats in saturated salt solution. The image below shows the egg of A. duodenale.

The eggs of Taenia solium and Taenia saginata are indistinguishable. The egg is spherical. The inner embryophore is radially striated and is yellow-brown due to bile staining. A fully-developed embryo (oncosphere) with three pairs of hooklets (hexacanth embryo) is present in the center.

The eggs of T. saginata are infective only to cattle and not to humans, whereas the eggs of T. solium are infective to pigs and humans. The eggs do not float in a saturated salt solution. The image below shows the egg of Taenia.

Pearl: Eggs in parasitology

Pearl: Helminth eggs that float in saturated salt solution

The following are the helminths whose eggs float in a saturated salt solution. (mnemonic: THE FAN)

  • Trichuris trichiura
  • Hymenolepis nana
  • Enterobius vermicularis
  • Fertilized eggs of Ascaris lumbricoides
  • Ancylostoma duodenale
  • Necator americanus.

Pearl: Parasites with bile-stained eggs

The following are the parasites with bile-stained eggs. (mnemonic: FaT CAT)

  • Fasciola hepatica (sheep liver fluke)
  • Fasciolopsis buski (giant intestinal fluke)
  • Trichuris trichiura (whipworm)
  • Clonorchis sinensis (chinese liver fluke, oriental liver fluke)
  • Ascaris lumbricoides (round worm)
  • Taenia solium (pork tapeworm)
  • Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved in the hyperacute rejection of renal transplants?
questions.raw_text: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved in the hyperacute rejection of renal transplants?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type II

Hyperacute graft rejection is an example of type II hypersensitivity reaction.

It is mediated by preformed antibodies. It is a rare event that occurs in kidney transplantation.

Graft rejection Time taken for rejection Immune mechanisms involved Type of hypersensitivity
Hyperacute Minutes to hours Preformed antibodies II
Acute Weeks to months Cytotoxic T-cell mediated IV
Chronic  Months to years Chronic DTH mediated and Ab mediated IV

 

Pearl: Classification of Transplant Rejection Reactions

Hyperacute rejection (minutes to hours):

  • Mechanism: Antidonor antibodies present in the circulation of the recipient
  • Histopathological findings:
    • Grossly, cyanotic and mottled graft with pale white areas
    • Neutrophils accumulate
    • Acute fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls or complete occlusion by thrombi

Acute rejection (days to weeks):

  1. Acute cellular rejection (acute T cell-mediated rejection):  
    • Mechanism: CD8+ CTLs directly destroy graft or CD4+ cells secrete cytokines that damage graft.
    • Histopathological findings:
      • Tubulointerstitial pattern (type I): extensive interstitial and tubular inflammation associated with focal tubular injury
      • Vascular pattern - Inflammation (type II) and necrosis (type III): Endotheliitis (swollen endothelial cells with lymphocytes between endothelium and vessel wall)
  2. Acute antibody-mediated (humoral) rejection: 
    • Mechanism: antibodies bind to endothelium and activate complement causing damage and graft failure
    • Histopathological findings:
      • Inflammation of glomeruli and peritubular capillaries.
      • Activation of the antibody-dependent classical complement pathway.
      • Focal thrombosis in small vessels. 

Chronic rejection (months to years):

  • Mechanism: T-cells react against alloantigens and secrete cytokines which stimulate fibroblasts and vascular smooth muscle cells (graft arteriosclerosis). Chronic rejection may also be antibody-mediated.
  • Histopathological findings:
    • Predominantly vascular changes (intimal thickening and vascular occlusion)
    • Glomerulopathy with duplication of basement membrane
    • Interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy with loss of renal parenchyma

Pearl: Transplant Rejection and Hypersensitivity

Type of Rejection  Type of Hypersensitivity

Host vs Graft
Hyperacute Type 2
Acute Type 2 and 4
Chronic Type 2 and 4
Graft vs Host
Graft vs host reaction Type 4

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with headache, fever, and vomiting. On examination, you observe the following. He is diagnosed with herpangina. Which group of viruses causes the same?
questions.raw_text: A 5-year-old boy presents with headache, fever, and vomiting. On examination, you observe the following. He is diagnosed with herpangina. Which group of viruses causes the same?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enteroviruses

The given image shows palatal ulcers in herpangina. It is caused by the coxsackievirus A, a large subgroup of the enteroviruses.

Herpangina or vesicular pharyngitis is characterized by grayish- white papulovesicular lesions on an erythematous base that ulcerate. These are present on:

  • Soft palate
  • Anterior pillars of tonsils
  • Uvula
  • Posterior oropharynx

It is a common clinical manifestation of coxsackievirus A infection in children, but it can also be caused by coxsackievirus B, echoviruses, or enterovirus 71.

Treatment is usually only supportive, as the disease is self-limiting and usually runs its course in less than a week.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following findings will you not observe in a thyroid gland biopsy taken from a patient suffering from Hashimoto thyroiditis?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following findings will you not observe in a thyroid gland biopsy taken from a patient suffering from Hashimoto thyroiditis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Orphan Annie eye nuclei

Orphan-Annie eye nuclei are a feature of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid, not Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure.
It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in areas of the world where iodine levels are sufficient. 

The thyroid gland is often diffusely enlarged, painless, with some degree of hypothyroidism. This may be preceded by transient thyrotoxicosis (Hashitoxicosis). It is associated with an increased risk of:

  • Other autoimmune conditions 
  • Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphomas
  • Papillary carcinoma 

Histologically, the following findings are seen:

  • Intense lymphocytic infiltrate containing small lymphocytes, plasma cells, and well developed germinal centers
  • Atrophied thyroid follicles 
  • The epithelial cells lining the follicles contain eosinophilic granular cytoplasm
    • This is called oncocytic metaplasia
    • These cells are called Hurthle cells

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young man who got injured in the neck while diving is brought to the emergency. Which of the following classifications systems is unlikely to be used to classify his injury?
questions.raw_text: A young man who got injured in the neck while diving is brought to the emergency. Which of the following classifications systems is unlikely to be used to classify his injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. AO-Magerl classiﬁcation

In the given scenario, the patient has suffered a cervical spinal injury. The AO-Magerl classification is used for the classification of thoracolumbar spinal injuries.

In AO-Magerl classification, thoracolumbar injuries are classified into 3 types based on the primary force that caused injury:

  • Type A (compression force)
  • Type B (distraction force)
  • Type C (torsional/rotational force)

The various classification systems used to classify cervical spinal injuries include:

  • The Anderson and D'Alonzo classification is used for odontoid fracture in the C2 vertebra.
  • The Levine and Edwards classification is used for Hangman's fracture (traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 over C3). 
  • The Allen and Ferguson classification is used for subaxial cervical spine (C3-C7) injuries.

questions.text: The MR nephrogram of a patient with loin pain is given below. All of the following can be included in the differential diagnoses except:
questions.raw_text: The MR nephrogram of a patient with loin pain is given below. All of the following can be included in the differential diagnoses except:
questions.correct_answer: C. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

The given MR nephrogram shows linear bands of contrast extending from the medulla of the kidney towards the cortex of the kidney, called a striated nephrogram. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) does not show a striated nephrogram.

Whereas, Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) shows a striated nephrogram.

A striated nephrogram is usually seen in:

  • Medullary sponge kidney (MSK)
  • Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD)
  • Acute papillary necrosis
  • Acute pyelonephritis
  • Renal tuberculosis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy was referred to an otolaryngologist for subjective left-sided hearing loss. A hearing test revealed mild conductive hearing loss at low and middle frequencies. Otoendoscopy showed a mass with the appearance as shown below. Which of the following criteria is used to diagnose this condition?
questions.raw_text: An 8-year-old boy was referred to an otolaryngologist for subjective left-sided hearing loss. A hearing test revealed mild conductive hearing loss at low and middle frequencies. Otoendoscopy showed a mass with the appearance as shown below. Which of the following criteria is used to diagnose this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Levenson criteria

The given clinical scenario with the otoendoscopy showing a white pearly mass behind the intact eardrum in the anterosuperior quadrant is suggestive of congenital cholesteatoma. Levenson's criteria should be satisfied in order to diagnose this condition.

Levenson's criteria:

  1. A white mass behind the normal tympanic membrane
  2. Normal pars tensa and pars flaccida
  3. No prior history of otorrhoea or perforation
  4. No prior history of otological surgeries
  5. Exclusion of canal atresia, intramembranous, or giant cholesteatoma
  6. Episodes of otitis media should not be considered as exclusion criteria.

Another criterion, which is not used now, is Derlaki and Clemis.

questions.text: Which of the following diseases primarily involves the marked structure?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following diseases primarily involves the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paralysis agitans

The structure marked in this transverse section of the brain at the level of superior colliculus is substantia nigra. Degeneration of substantia nigra is seen in Parkinson's disease, also known as paralysis agitans.

Substantia nigra is pigmented due to the presence of neuromelanin granules, which help in the synthesis of dopamine. In Parkinson's disease, there is an absence/reduced pigmentation of the substantia nigra.

Bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor are classic features of Parkinson's disease. Because of motor disability, it is also referred to as paralysis agitans.

Other options:

Option B: Depression is often a comorbid finding with Parkinson's disease, but is not due to damage to the substantia nigra.

Option C: Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. It is due to atrophy of the entorhinal cortex, located in the medial temporal lobe.

Option D: Huntington’s chorea is an autosomal dominant disorder of movement and cognition primarily involving the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Your senior asks you to administer oxygen to a patient in order to avoid diffusion hypoxia. When is this phenomenon observed during anesthesia?
questions.raw_text: Your senior asks you to administer oxygen to a patient in order to avoid diffusion hypoxia. When is this phenomenon observed during anesthesia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Recovery from nitrous oxide

Diffusion hypoxia is observed in anesthesia during recovery from nitrous oxide anesthesia.

Due to low solubility (low blood gas partition coefficient), N2O diffuses from the blood to the alveoli and replaces the oxygen. This reduces alveolar O2 concentration, resulting in relative hypoxemia.

Diffusion hypoxia can be avoided by using 100% oxygen for 10 minutes during recovery from anesthesia.

Pearl: Unique features of Nitrous oxide

Concentration-effect

  • The blood gas partition coefficient of N2O is 35 times higher than O2 and N2, hence its rapid uptake diminishes its volume and concentrates the remaining anesthetics in the alveolus.

Second-gas effect

  • Concentration-effect of one gas over another is known as the second gas effect
  • Increase in the partial pressure of the 2nd gas (Oxygen and volatile agents) due to the rapid uptake of N2O during induction.

Diffusion hypoxia (Finks effect)

  • Rapid elimination of N2O during recovery causes a reduction in the partial pressure of oxygen leading to hypoxia
  • Avoided by using 100% oxygen for 10 minutes during recovery from anesthesia.

Nitrous oxide in gas-filled spaces

  • It diffuses into air-containing cavities more rapidly than air (principally nitrogen) can be absorbed by the bloodstream
  • If the walls surrounding the cavity are rigid, pressure rises instead of volume.

Hence N2O is contraindicated in:

  • Venous or arterial air embolism
  • Acute intestinal obstruction
  • Pneumocephalus, pneumothorax
  • Pulmonary air cysts
  • Intraocular air bubbles
  • Tympanic membrane grafting.

questions.raw_text:

Platelet count - 3,23,000 /μL

PT - elevated

aPTT - elevated

TT - elevated
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reptilase

Reptilase is a thrombin agonist which is used to differentiate heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and afibrinogenemia. It is resistant to the action of heparin.

The differential diagnosis for normal platelet count with elevated PT, aPTT and TT are HIT and afibrinogenemia. After adding reptilase, if the TT is corrected, it points to HIT. In afibrinogenemia, since there is an absence of fibrin, there is no change in the TT.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman visits the infertility clinic with a complaint of recurrent abortions. Upon investigations, she is found to have a septate uterus. Which of the following corrective procedures has the best obstetric outcome?
questions.raw_text: A 24-year-old woman visits the infertility clinic with a complaint of recurrent abortions. Upon investigations, she is found to have a septate uterus. Which of the following corrective procedures has the best obstetric outcome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Transcervical resection of septum

Transcervical hysteroscopic resection of the septum has the best obstetric outcome.

The procedure involves the resection of the septum under hysteroscopic guidance. Hence, it doesn't scar the uterus and avoids the necessity of cesarean sections for future pregnancies improving obstetric outcomes.

Metroplasty is the surgical resection of the intrauterine septum. This is done by approaching the uterus transabdominally via 3 methods:

  • Jones metroplasty
  • Strassmann metroplasty
  • Tompkins metroplasty

All of these methods are not preferred nowadays as they cause uterine scarring.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with hypercholesterolemia on statin therapy presents to your OPD for follow-up. You notice his cholesterol is still high and decide to add on another drug that directly inhibits the absorption of cholesterol. Which of the following will you prescribe?
questions.raw_text: A patient with hypercholesterolemia on statin therapy presents to your OPD for follow-up. You notice his cholesterol is still high and decide to add on another drug that directly inhibits the absorption of cholesterol. Which of the following will you prescribe?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ezetimibe

Ezetimibe is the drug that prevents hypercholesterolemia by directly inhibiting the absorption of cholesterol.

Ezetimibe acts by interfering with a specific cholesterol transport protein, NPC1L1, in the intestinal mucosa and reduces the absorption of both dietary and biliary cholesterol. It causes a compensatory increase in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, but LDL cholesterol is decreased. Statins block this enhanced cholesterol synthesis (cholesterol synthesis inhibitors) and so their combination has a synergistic effect.

Other options: 

Option B: Orlistat is an anti-obesity drug that acts by inhibiting pancreatic and gastric lipase and thus interferes with the digestion and absorption of dietary triglycerides.

Option C: Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant. The bile-acid sequestrants are highly positively charged and bind negatively charged bile acids. Because of their large size, the resins are not absorbed, and the bound bile acids are excreted in the stool.

Cholestyramine primarily reduces LDL levels by increasing hepatic bile acid synthesis, which results in increased LDL uptake and diversion of cholesterol to bile acid production. 

Option D: Niacin reduces lipolysis by hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) and reduces hepatic triglyceride synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with easy fatiguability. The mother also complains that the child has increased hunger between meals, which is relieved after food. Liver examination revealed no glycogen. The enzyme most likely deficient is _________.
questions.raw_text: A 4-year-old child presents with easy fatiguability. The mother also complains that the child has increased hunger between meals, which is relieved after food. Liver examination revealed no glycogen. The enzyme most likely deficient is _________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycogen synthase

The most likely enzyme deficiency in a child with fatigue, excessive hunger between meals, and absent liver glycogen is glycogen synthase deficiency.

Glycogen is a storage carbohydrate synthesized from glucose (glycogenesis) and is stored in the liver, muscles, and brain. Glycogen synthase is a regulating enzyme for glycogenesis.

Glycogen synthase exists in both phosphorylated (inactive) and dephosphorylated (active) forms. Phosphorylation is stimulated by epinephrine, norepinephrine, and glucagon via cAMP. Dephosphorylation is stimulated by insulin via phosphodiesterase.

A deficiency of glycogen synthase leads to glycogen storage disorder and presents in infancy with early morning drowsiness and fatigue, fasting hypoglycemia, pallor, emesis, and hypoglycemic convulsions. It leads to a marked decrease in liver glycogen stores. Hepatomegaly is absent.

Laboratory investigations reveal prolonged hyperglycemia, glycosuria, ketosis, lactic acidosis, low alanine levels, and normal insulin levels after glucose administration. A liver biopsy is diagnostic.

Treatment involves protein-rich frequent meals, and nighttime supplementation with cornstarch to prevent hypoglycemia and hyperketonemia.

 Other options:

Option A: Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, also known as McArdle's disease or glycogen storage disease type V, primarily affects skeletal muscle glycogen metabolism. Affected individuals experience muscle weakness, cramps, and exercise intolerance, but it doesn't typically cause the symptoms mentioned in the question.

Option C: Debranching enzyme deficiency, also known as Cori's disease or glycogen storage disease type III, presents with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and growth retardation. The liver would still contain glycogen, albeit with an abnormal structure.

Option D: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, known as von Gierke's disease or glycogen storage disease type I, is characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hepatomegaly. In this case, glycogen is present in the liver but cannot be broken down efficiently into glucose.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Pott’s puffy tumor is
questions.raw_text: Pott’s puffy tumor is
questions.correct_answer: A. Subperiosteal abscess of frontal bone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subperiosteal abscess of frontal bone

Pott's puffy tumor is the subperiosteal abscess of frontal bone. It is a complication of frontal sinusitis.

An acute infection of the frontal sinus can cause osteomyelitis of the frontal bone. Suppurative material then breaches the frontal bone leading to subperiosteal abscess formation in the tissues of the forehead. Pus may form externally under the periosteum as a soft boggy swelling with a doughy consistency called Pott’s puffy tumor. It may spread internally causing subdural, epidural, and periorbital abscesses as well as secondary septic thrombosis of the dural sinuses. It is more often seen in adults as frontal sinus is not developed in infants and children.

CT of the brain and paranasal sinuses is the most appropriate investigation. It can show the involvement of sinuses as well as intracranial or soft tissue spread of infection. 

Treatment consists of large doses of antibiotics, abscess drainage, and trephining of the frontal sinus through its floor. Sometimes, the removal of sequestra and necrotic bone may also be required. 

The images below show the clinical presentation and radiographic findings of the condition: red arrow - Pott's puffy tumor; blue arrow - intracranial spread

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The function of the Golgi tendon organ is to _________
questions.raw_text: The function of the Golgi tendon organ is to _________

options.label: C
options.text: Sense changes in position of the muscle

options.label: D
options.text: Sense changes in length of the muscle

questions.correct_answer: B. Sense changes in muscle tension
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sense changes in muscle tension

Golgi tendon organ sense changes in muscle tension.

Golgi tendon reflex (Inverse myotatic/ Inverse stretch reflex) is disynaptic, is the opposite of the stretch reflex.

When the tension in a contracted muscle is significantly elevated, the inhibitory effect from the Golgi tendon organ leads to instantaneous relaxation of the entire muscle. This effect is called the lengthening reaction.

It is a protective mechanism to prevent tearing of the muscle or avulsion of the tendon from its attachments to the bone.

Note: Muscle spindles senses changes in muscle length (stretch).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is undergoing modified radical neck dissection (MRND) for laryngeal malignancy. While ligating the internal jugular vein, his etCO2 dropped from 40 mmHg to 14 mmHg, and the patient developed hypotension along with cardiac arrhythmia. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.raw_text: A patient is undergoing modified radical neck dissection (MRND) for laryngeal malignancy. While ligating the internal jugular vein, his etCO2 dropped from 40 mmHg to 14 mmHg, and the patient developed hypotension along with cardiac arrhythmia. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Venous air embolism

A drastic fall in etCO2 with hypotension during neck surgery is most likely due to venous air embolism (VAE).

In modified radical neck dissection (MRND), a head-up position is given to provide a bloodless surgical field. VAE into severed vessels is likely to occur when the surgical site is above the right atrium and venous pressure at the incision site is below the atmospheric pressure. Pulmonary artery pressure will rise and etCO2 will fall after a venous air embolism.

In sympathetic overactivity and carotid body stimulation, blood pressure will rise.

In vagal stimulation, a drastic drop in etCO2 is unlikely.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An elderly woman on treatment for migraine presents with chest pain. She has a previous history of angina/MI. Which of the following mechanism of the prescribed drug for migraine might have caused this presentation?
questions.raw_text: An elderly woman on treatment for migraine presents with chest pain. She has a previous history of angina/MI. Which of the following mechanism of the prescribed drug for migraine might have caused this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5-HT agonist

The patient may have been given sumatriptan, a 5-HT1b/1d receptor agonist, which causes vasoconstriction and is used in migraine. Thus, sumatriptan will worsen angina by causing coronary vasoconstriction.

Angina will be worsened if the O2 demand of the heart is increased or there is reduced blood flow to the already ischemic areas. Triptans activate 5-HT1B receptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction of cranial arteries which is the therapeutic mechanism in migraine headaches. However, they can also constrict coronary arteries, reducing blood flow and triggering angina or even MI in susceptible patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is used for wound infection grading?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is used for wound infection grading?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Southampton grading

Southampton wound grading system is used to score the severity of wound site infection.

Southampton wound grading system:

  • Grade 0 - Normal healing
  • Grade I - Normal healing with different grades of erythema
  • Grade II - Erythema with other signs of inflammation at different parts of the wound.
  • Grade III - Clear or serosanguinous discharge at different sites
  • Grade IV - Pus discharge

Other options:

Option A: American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA)  grading is used in pre-anesthetic checkups to assess a patient's physical health and fitness for anesthesia and surgery.

Option B: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) is a set of clinical criteria used to identify and monitor critically ill patients with high-grade burns, severe trauma, and other major surgeries.

Option D: Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II)  is a scoring system used to assess the severity and predict the outcome of pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A middle-aged male patient presents with protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet. Which of the following is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition?
questions.raw_text: A middle-aged male patient presents with protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet. Which of the following is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pegvisomant

The clinical features of protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet are suggestive of acromegaly. Pegvisomant is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition.

Acromegaly is commonly caused due to growth hormone-secreting somatotroph adenoma. It occurs secondary to mutations of the pituitary-specific gene PIT-1.

Patients present with frontal bossing, increased hand and foot size, mandibular enlargement with prognathism, widened space between the lower incisor teeth, soft tissue swelling resulting in increased heel pad thickness, coarse facial features, and large fleshy nose.

Serum IGF-1 levels (elevated) and GH suppression test with oral glucose are useful in the diagnosis. The levels of GH do not reduce in response to the oral glucose load. 

Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the tumor, octreotide, and pegvisomant will be helpful in the management of this condition.

Other options:

Option A: Octreotide is a synthetic analog of somatostatin. It is used for the treatment of acromegaly and secretory diarrhea.

Option C: Cabergoline is a dopamine D2 receptor agonist. It is used as a first-line drug for the treatment of hyperprolactinemia.

Option D: Oglcegepant is a calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antagonist. It is used for the treatment of migraine.

Pearl: Tests for Acromegaly

Screening test:

The single best test for the diagnosis of acromegaly is the measurement of serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1). A normal serum IGF-1 concentration is strong evidence that the patient does not have acromegaly.

Confirmatory test:

GH suppression test: 75 g of oral glucose (OGTT- oral glucose tolerance test) is administered to the patient. Blood GH levels are checked at 30, 60, 90, 120 min (i.e over 2 hours) after the glucose load. Normally, glucose suppresses GH and it falls to <1 ng/mL. If GH >1 ng/mL, it is diagnostic of acromegaly.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl is admitted for evaluation for recurrent seizures. She has a large port-wine stain on the right side of her face as shown below.  The MRI of the head shows a leptomeningeal angioma. What is the most common ocular manifestation of the underlying condition?
questions.raw_text: A 6-year-old girl is admitted for evaluation for recurrent seizures. She has a large port-wine stain on the right side of her face as shown below.  The MRI of the head shows a leptomeningeal angioma. What is the most common ocular manifestation of the underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glaucoma

The given clinical picture of a young child presenting with unilateral port wine stain in the region of trigeminal nerve supply and leptomeningeal angioma as seen on MRI is indicative of Sturge-Webber syndrome (SWS). Glaucoma is the most common ocular manifestation of SWS.

Sturge weber syndrome is a neurocutaneous disorder(phakomatoses) that is characterized by unilateral capillary malformation at the region of trigeminal supply known as port wine stain or nevus flammeus, ipsilateral diffuse cavernous hemangioma of the choroid and ipsilateral leptomeningeal hemangiomatosis, which causes seizures and mental retardation.

Ocular manifestation of SWS include:

  • Glaucoma - most common ocular manifestation. It develops anywhere between infancy to adulthood. When developed in infancy it presents as buphthalmos.
  • Diffuse choroidal hemangioma
  • Serous retinal detachment
  • Visual field defects- Leptomeningeal hemangiomas affect the parietal and occipital lobes and lead to homonymous hemianopia 
  • Heterochromia of the iris
  • Episcleral and conjunctival lesions

Option A: Uveitis is the inflammation of the uveal tissue of the eyes. It can be associated with a number of systemic conditions such as sarcoidosis, behcet's disease, ankylosing spondylitis, reiter's syndrome,Toxoplasmosis and Posner–Schlossman syndrome (PSS).

Option B: Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited or acquired pigmentatory retinal dystrophy affecting the rods more. The earliest manifestation is worsening of night blindness which gradually progresses to tunnel vision and ultimately loss of central vision. The classic triad of findings in RP comprises bone-spicule retinal pigmentation, arteriolar attenuation and waxy disc pallor.

Systemic Associations of RP include:

  • Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome
  • Cockayne's syndrome
  • Refsum's syndrome
  • Usher's syndrome
  • Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome

The below given image shows the classical triad findings of Retinitis pigmentosa.

Option C:Keratitis is the inflammation of cornea which is characterised by corneal edema, cellular infiltration and ciliary congestion. It can be either infectious or non-infectious in nature which includes allergic keratitis, neurotrophic keratitis, exposure keratitis and peripheral ulcerative keratopathies such as Rosacea keratitis and Mooren's ulcer.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 23-year-old girl presents with the finding shown below. She has a history of multiple similar episodes in the past and reports that some of her family members have similar complaints. She has no itching. Which of the following is deficient in this patient?
questions.raw_text: A 23-year-old girl presents with the finding shown below. She has a history of multiple similar episodes in the past and reports that some of her family members have similar complaints. She has no itching. Which of the following is deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C1 inhibitor

This girl presents with features of hereditary angioneurotic edema, which is due to a deficiency of C1 inhibitor.

Hereditary angioedema follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. It is more common than complement deficiency states. A deficiency of C1 inhibitor leads to unregulated activation of kallikrein. This increases the production of vasoactive peptides such as bradykinin.

This condition is characterized by recurring episodes of angioedema, which can be life-threatening, affecting the subcutaneous tissues or the mucous membranes of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts. Acute attacks can be managed with fresh plasma infusions, which replenish the deficient inhibitor.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 26-year-old female presents to the ER with menorrhagia. She mentions that her father and sister also suffer from bleeding disorders. Which of the following is an autosomal dominant bleeding disorder?
questions.raw_text: A 26-year-old female presents to the ER with menorrhagia. She mentions that her father and sister also suffer from bleeding disorders. Which of the following is an autosomal dominant bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Von Willebrand Disease

This patient's clinical features are suggestive of von-Willebrand disease. It is caused by a deficiency of the von-Willebrand factor. 

They are present within cytoplasmic vesicles called Weibel-Palade bodies.

Normal Platelet count, Prolonged BT, Normal PT, and Prolonged aPTT are seen in von-Willebrand disease. Factor VIII is found bound to the Von-Willebrand factor (vWF)  in the blood. Deficiency of vWF results in Factor VIII deficiency and prolongation of aPTT in this disease. Prolonged BT is due to abnormal platelet-mediated hemostasis.

vWF is also found in

  • Platelet granules (Less as compared to endothelial cells)
  • Subendothelium, where it binds to collagen

Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder in humans. The bleeding tendency is usually mild and manifests during surgical or dental procedures. The most common presenting symptoms are spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes (epistaxis), excessive bleeding from wounds, or menorrhagia.

It is usually transmitted as an autosomal dominant disorder, but rare autosomal recessive variants can be seen.

Three types are recognized, with phenotypic variations:

Type 1 and type 3 von-Willebrand disease are associated with quantitative defects in vWF.

Type 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with a mild to moderate vWF deficiency; it is the most common among all subtypes. It is associated with mild disease.

Type 3 disease is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting in little to no vWF synthesis. Because vWF stabilizes factor VIII in the circulation, factor VIII levels are also reduced in type 3 disease and the associated bleeding disorder is often severe.

Type 2 von-Willebrand disease is associated with defects in the quality of vWF produced. Type 2A is the most common. It is inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder.

Other options:

Factor X, VIII and IX deficiencies are all causes of hemophilias. These conditions manifest as prolonged bleeding after injuries, dental treatment and hemarthrosis. They are also additionally X-linked conditions so the presence of this condition in her father and sister makes X-linked transmission impossible.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
Which of the following mothers can initiate breastfeeding?
  1. A mother with an active infection of herpes on both her breasts.
  2. A mother with positive serology for hepatitis B infection.
  3. A mother with active tuberculosis.
  4. A mother who is on treatment with chemotherapeutic agents for leukaemia.
  5. A mother with a history of chronic smoking.
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following mothers can initiate breastfeeding?
  1. A mother with an active infection of herpes on both her breasts.
  2. A mother with positive serology for hepatitis B infection.
  3. A mother with active tuberculosis.
  4. A mother who is on treatment with chemotherapeutic agents for leukaemia.
  5. A mother with a history of chronic smoking.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 and 5 only

The correct answer is 2 and 5 only. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated if the mother has hepatitis B infection or if she is a chronic smoker.

Infants born to an HbsAg positive mother routinely receive hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine. So, a delay in the initiation of breastfeeding is not required.

Contraindications of breastfeeding:

Do not Breastfeed

Do not give expressed breastmilk

Infant factors:

  • Classic galactosemia

Maternal factors:

  • Human T-cell lymphocyte virus (HTLV) infection
  • Ebola virus infection
  • PCP/cocaine abuse

Do not Breastfeed (Temporarily)

Do not give expressed breastmilk  (Temporarily)

Maternal factors:

  • Brucellosis
  • undergoing diagnostic imaging with radiopharmaceuticals
  • Active herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection with lesions on the breasts

Do not Breastfeed (Temporarily)

Can give expressed breastmilk

Maternal factors:

  • Untreated, active Tuberculosis
  • Active Varicella infection

Alcohol consumption and smoking are NOT contraindications of breastfeeding. However, smoking and alcohol consumption should be discouraged.

Note: In a mother with untreated, active tuberculosis:

  • Temporarily withhold breastfeeding but can feed with expressed breastmilk
  • Resume breastfeeding once she has been adequately treated for 2 weeks and is no longer contagious.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme, supplementary nutrition provided should cover at least _______
questions.raw_text: Under the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme, supplementary nutrition provided should cover at least _______

options.label: A
options.text: 1/3 of the total protein requirement + ½ of total energy requirement

options.label: B
options.text: 2/3 of the total protein requirement + ½ of total energy requirement

options.label: C
options.text: ½ of the total protein requirement + 1/3 of total energy requirement

options.label: D
options.text: ½ of the total protein requirement + 2/3 of total energy requirement

questions.correct_answer: C. ½ of the total protein requirement + 1/3 of total energy requirement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ½ of the total protein requirement + 1/3 of total energy requirement

Under the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme, supplementary nutrition provided must cover at least ½ of the total protein requirement and 1/3 of total energy requirement to children in schools.

The MDM scheme is also called School Lunch Programme and has been operational since 1961 in India. Currently, it functions under the broad coverage of the Minimum Needs Programme.

Some other principles of the MDM are:

  • The meal provided under the MDM should only be a supplement and not a substitute to home diets.
  • The cost of the meals should be reasonably low.
  • The meal should be easy to cook in schools.
  • Locally available foods must be used, for as far as possible.
  • The menu should be regularly changed to avoid monotony.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 48-year-old male presents to the ER with confusion and shaking of the entire body. He has a history of excessive alcohol consumption. What is the cause of delirium tremens in an alcoholic?
questions.raw_text: A 48-year-old male presents to the ER with confusion and shaking of the entire body. He has a history of excessive alcohol consumption. What is the cause of delirium tremens in an alcoholic?

options.label: D
options.text: Small doses of regular consumption of alcohol

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute infection

Among the given options, acute infection can be a cause of delirium tremens in an alcoholic patient.

Physical illness e.g., hepatitis or pancreatitis predisposes to the syndrome; a person in good physical health rarely has delirium tremens during alcohol withdrawal.

The syndrome usually develops on the third day of admission. A patient admitted for an unrelated condition may unexpectedly have an episode of delirium, which is the first sign of a previously undiagnosed alcohol-related disorder.

Episodes of delirium tremens usually begin at the age of 30-40 years, after 5 to 15 years of heavy drinking, and are typical after a binge. Gradual withdrawal of alcohol does not cause delirium tremens. However, sudden withdrawal can cause it.

Treatment of alcohol withdrawal: 

  • For patients showing withdrawal symptoms, chlordiazepoxide 25-50 mg every 2-4 hours can be administered orally. 
  • For patients with delirium tremens, 50-100 mg of chlordiazepoxide should be administered every 4 hours. 
  • If oral administration of drugs is not possible, intravenous lorazepam can be tried.

questions.text: The chance of passing a genetic disease X by affected parents to their first child is 0.16. If they plan to have two children, what is the probability that both the children will have the disease?
questions.raw_text: The chance of passing a genetic disease X by affected parents to their first child is 0.16. If they plan to have two children, what is the probability that both the children will have the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 0.0256

The probability of both children having the disease is 0.0256.

In this scenario, the chance of each child having the disease is 0.16. The second child having the disease is independent of the first child having it. So, the events are statistically independent.

Applying the multiplication rule of probability, the probability of both children having the disease is,

0.16 x 0.16 = 0.0256.
These are non-mutually exclusive events as the first child having the trait does not rule out the chance of the second child having it.   

On the other hand, the probability of one of the two children having the disease is given by,

p(A or B)= p(A) + p(B) - p(A and B)= 0.16 + 0.16 -(0.16 x 0.16)= 0.32- 0.0256= 0.2944

Pearl: Probability

  • Expressed as a decimal fraction never as a percentage. Denoted by p
  • Must lie between 0 (zero probability) and 1 (absolute certainty).
  • Probability of an event cannot be negative.
  • The probability of an event not occurring (q) is q= 1-p

Rule

Description

Example

The Addition Rule

(p) of any one of several particular events occurring = the sum of their individual probabilities, provided the events cannot both happen and are mutually exclusive.

Probability of picking a heart card from a deck is 0.25 and that of picking a club is 0.25. Thus the p (hearts or clubs) is 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.50.

The Multiplication Rule

(p) of two or more statistically independent events all occurring is = product of their individual probabilities.

If the lifetime probability of a person developing a lung neoplasm is 0.25 and the life time probability of developing dementia is 0.01, then the p (lung neoplasm and dementia) is 0.25 x 0.01 = 0.0025.

The Binomial Distribution

 

(p) of the occurrence of a specific combination of mutually exclusive independent events.

The events for which binomial distribution is used have only two outcomes like yes or no, tall or short, male or female, etc.

 

Widely used in genetic counseling.

questions.text: There is an outbreak of hookworm infection in your locality. On investigation, it is found that the outbreak is a result of open-air defecation. The district council decides to construct an RCA type of latrine in every household.  What is the optimum water seal required?
questions.raw_text: There is an outbreak of hookworm infection in your locality. On investigation, it is found that the outbreak is a result of open-air defecation. The district council decides to construct an RCA type of latrine in every household.  What is the optimum water seal required?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2.5 cm

The optimum water seal required for an RCA type of latrine is 2 – 2.5 cm.

It was designed by the Research-cum-Action Projects (RCA) in Environmental Sanitation of the Ministry of Health. Water seals aids in preventing flies and other organisms from reaching the waste. It also prevents the escape of odors and foul gases, eliminating the nuisance from the smell.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PGE1

Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) maintains the patency of ductus arteriosus (PDA). This is used in term neonates with underlying cyanotic congenital heart disease awaiting surgical intervention as they have duct-dependant circulation.

Indomethacin and Ibuprofen are the NSAID indicated for closing the ductus arteriosus in premature infants and neonates.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes with complaints of fever and increasing fatigue for the past week. On examination, he is febrile, hypotensive and tachycardic. The findings of microscopic examination of his peripheral blood smear is given below. What is the causative agent?
questions.raw_text: A 55-year-old man comes with complaints of fever and increasing fatigue for the past week. On examination, he is febrile, hypotensive and tachycardic. The findings of microscopic examination of his peripheral blood smear is given below. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium falciparum

Fever, fatigue, hypotension, tachycardia and the blood smear showing multiple ring forms in RBCs are suggestive of malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum.

Falciparum malaria, or malignant tertian malaria, is the most serious malaria. Plasmodium falciparum infects both young and mature erythrocytes, resulting in a large population of erythrocytes affected. Affected erythrocytes display cytoadherence, form rosettes and cause capillary plugging in vital organs like the brain, kidney, lungs etc. Diagnosis is by demonstration of P. falciparum in peripheral blood smear. The peripheral smear findings of falciparum malaria include:

  • Multiple ring forms: Multiple delicate rings are visible within the erythrocytes
  • Double chromatin: Binucleate ring forms resembling stereo headphones
  • Accole form or form applique: Ring forms are attached to the margins of red cells
  • Maurer's dots or clefts: Coarse brick red dots within erythrocytes
  • Banana shaped gametocytes within erythrocytes
  • Absent schizont

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are responsible for corneal transparency?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are responsible for corneal transparency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratan sulfate

The glycosaminoglycan (GAG) responsible for corneal transparency is keratan sulfate.

Glycosaminoglycans or mucopolysaccharides are complex carbohydrates made up of amino sugars and uronic acids. They may be attached to a protein molecule to form a proteoglycan. 

Keratan sulfate is a mucopolysaccharide that does not contain uronic acid. It is constituted by repeating disaccharide units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose.

Keratan sulfate is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal transparency.

 2 types of keratan sulfate are seen:

  • Keratan sulfate I is present in the cornea.
  • Keratan sulfate II is mainly present in the cartilage.

Keratin sulfate I and II differ in their linkage to the core proteins. Keratan sulfate I links to a core protein L-asparagine via N-acetylglucosamine and Keratan sulfate II to  L-Serine (or L-Threonine) via N-acetylgalactosamine.

The chemical structure of Keratan sulfate is shown in the image below.

 

Other options:

Option B: In chondroitin sulfates (chondroitin 4-Sulfate & chondroitin 6-Sulfate), the repeating disaccharide units are glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine.  They maintain the structure of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and are located in endochondral bone and cartilage. They are also found in the ECM of the central nervous system. They act as signaling molecules in the prevention of the repair of nerve endings after injury.

Option C: Heparan sulfate is found on many extracellular cell surfaces and contains glucosamine with fewer N-sulfates than heparin. The predominant uronic acid is d-glucuronic acid. In the plasma membrane of cells, they act as receptors and mediate cell growth and cell-cell communication. It is also found in the basement membrane of the kidney along with type IV collagen and laminin, where it determines the charge selectiveness of glomerular filtration.

Option D: Hyaluronic acid is present in synovial fluid. It is also found in skin, bone, cartilage, vitreous humor, and embryonic tissues. It contains repeating units of N Acetyl Glucosamine and glucuronic acid. It plays a role in morphogenesis and wound repair. The high concentrations of hyaluronic acid along with chondroitin sulfates in cartilage contribute to its compressibility.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the ER with a sudden-onset fever and the following painful rash over her face and upper limbs. CBC reveals neutrophilia. This presentation is associated with all of the following conditions except:
questions.raw_text: A patient presents to the ER with a sudden-onset fever and the following painful rash over her face and upper limbs. CBC reveals neutrophilia. This presentation is associated with all of the following conditions except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aplastic anemia

This clinical presentation with painful edematous plaques is suggestive of febrile neutrophilic dermatosis or Sweet syndrome. It is not associated with aplastic anemia. It is associated with the following conditions:

  • Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) - most common
  • Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
  • Solid malignancies of the genitourinary tract
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
  • Drugs - all-trans-retinoic acid, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF)
  • Idiopathic Sweet syndrome - common in women following respiratory tract infection

This condition presents with the following triad:

  • Fever
  • Neutrophilia
  • Dense dermal infiltrate of neutrophils: 
    • Pinkish-red to reddish-brown edematous painful plaques
    • Occur over the head, neck, extremities

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: When pharmacotherapy is necessary for managing delirium, which of the following is preferred as the first-line treatment?
questions.raw_text: When pharmacotherapy is necessary for managing delirium, which of the following is preferred as the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Haloperidol 0.5 mg PO

Haloperidol is commonly used for the first-line pharmacological treatment of delirium.

The two major symptoms of delirium that may require pharmacological treatment are psychosis and insomnia.

Options A, B: Benzodiazepines are often used as an adjunct in agitated patients, but should be used judiciously for insomnia as their sedative property can worsen confusion in delirium. 

Option C: The use of second-generation antipsychotics may be considered for delirium management, but clinical trial experience with these agents for delirium is limited. Clozapine itself is known to sometimes trigger delirium.

Note: IV regimens of haloperidol are mostly used in the ICU in the critically ill due to their fast onset of action and predictable pharmacokinetics. Oral haloperidol may be used as a maintenance regimen in patients with a functional GI tract. Intramuscular haloperidol is considered only in acutely combative patients without IV access.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient who was a known case of rheumatoid arthritis is brought to the ER due to dizziness. Her BP was 90/60mmHg. She was prescribed a medication by her local doctor which she stopped taking suddenly. Her blood sugar was low and serum potassium was 6mEq/L. Which of the following drugs should be given to her next?
questions.raw_text: A patient who was a known case of rheumatoid arthritis is brought to the ER due to dizziness. Her BP was 90/60mmHg. She was prescribed a medication by her local doctor which she stopped taking suddenly. Her blood sugar was low and serum potassium was 6mEq/L. Which of the following drugs should be given to her next?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrocortisone

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis. It is a life-threatening condition caused due to sudden insufficiency of adrenal hormones. If a patient displays features of adrenal insufficiency, treatment must immediately be commenced, before awaiting the biochemical diagnosis. Intravenous administration of hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours, >2 litres of saline is given in 6 hours under careful cardiovascular monitoring.

The symptoms of adrenal insufficiency are as follows:

  • Glucocorticoid deficiency leads to:
    • Fatigue, lack of energy
    • Weight loss, anorexia
    • Myalgia
    • Hypoglycemia 
    • Low blood pressure, postural hypotension
  • Mineralocorticoid deficiency leads to:
    • Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting
    • Dizziness, postural hypotension
    • Low blood pressure, postural hypotension
    • Hyponatremia
    • Hyperkalemia
  • Adrenal androgen deficiency leads to dry and itchy skin, loss of libido 
  • The hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed areas results from excess ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) secretion which occurs in response to decreased adrenal cortical hormones.

Primary causes of the Addisonian crisis include:

  • Adrenal haemorrhage
  • Acute infection

Secondary causes of the Addisonian crisis include:

  • Surgery
  • Cessation of steroid therapy
  • Postpartum pituitary necrosis.
 
 

Pearl: Causes of Adrenocortical Insufficiency

Primary adrenal insufficiency:

  • Anatomical destruction of gland
  • Autoimmune (Addison's disease)
  • Isolated autoimmune adrenalitis (polygenic)
  • Infections - HIV, tuberculosis, fungi
  • Surgical removal
  • Acute hemorrhagic necrosis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome)
  • Amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis
  • Metastatic carcinoma
  • Cytotoxic agents – mitotane
  • Enzyme inhibitors – metyrapone, ketoconazole
  • Congenital adrenal hypoplasia
  • Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1 (AIRE1 gene on 21q22)
  • Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 2 (polygenic)
  • X-linked adrenal hypoplasia (DAX1 gene on Xp21)
  • Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD gene on Xq28)

Secondary adrenal insufficiency:

Hypopituitarism due to hypothalamic or pituitary disease

  • Neoplasm
  • Infiltration (sarcoidosis)
  • Infection (tuberculosis, pyogenic, fungal)

Suppression of HPA axis

  • By endogenous steroids from tumor
  • By exogenous steroids

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the incision.
questions.raw_text: Identify the incision.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gibson incision

The image above shows a Gibson incision. Gibson incision is used for kidney transplantation or as an extraperitoneal approach to the distal ureter with low morbidity. 

The traditional pelvic Gibson incision is an oblique or curvilinear incision that starts 3 cm above and parallel to the inguinal ligament and extends vertically 3 centimeters medial to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) extending down toward the inguinal fold and terminating just lateral to the rectus muscle or continuing to above the symphysis pubis.

The Gibson incision is the traditional approach for renal transplant and transplant nephrectomy. This muscle-splitting incision provides great extraperitoneal access to pelvic vessels, the lower ureter, and the bladder for benign and malignant disease and is also utilized as a part of minimally invasive nephrectomy for specimen extraction or use of a hand port. 

The image below shows the gibson incision.

Other Options:

Option A: battle incision, a lower right paramedian incision, but placed more laterally than the standard paramedian incision. It is suitable for dealing with acute appendicitis and pathologies in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen.

Option C: Mayo Robson’s incision is a right upper paramedian incision extended like a hockey stick to the midline. It is indicated in cholecystectomy.

Option D: Lanz incision, a transverse or skin crease incision for appendicitis, 2 cm below the umbilicus, centered on the midclavicular–mid-inguinal line. Due to its continuation with Langer’s lines, the Lanz incision produces much more aesthetically pleasing results with reduced scarring.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with a Type 1 Choledochal cyst. All of the following statements are correct except?
questions.raw_text: A patient presented with a Type 1 Choledochal cyst. All of the following statements are correct except?

options.label: B
options.text: Cyst opened and drainage is done

questions.correct_answer: B. Cyst opened and drainage is done
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cyst opened and drainage is done

In the given clinical scenario, a patient presented with a Type 1 Choledochal cyst. Cyst opening and drainage will not be done in this patient. the preferred course of action involves the complete surgical excision of the cyst. Complete resection of the cyst is essential because there is a risk of malignant transformation (cholangiocarcinoma). (Option A)

Choledochal cysts are congenital cystic dilations of the intrahepatic and/or extrahepatic biliary tree. They present with a triad of jaundice, a palpable upper quadrant mass, and abdominal pain. 

The clinical triad (abdominal pain, mass, and jaundice) and the MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) findings suggest choledochal cyst. According to the Todani classification, the type III choledochal cyst opens into the duodenum. The treatment of choice for type III choledochal cyst is Endoscopic sphincterotomy followed by surveillance.

Choledochal cysts are congenital dilations of the intra and/or extrahepatic biliary system.

Pathogenesis involves an Anomalous Pancreaticobiliary Junction (APBJ) which may allow reflux into the biliary tract, leading to inflammation, increased biliary pressure, and cyst formation. (Option D)

Clinical features of choledochal cysts are as follows

  • 60% of cases are diagnosed before the age of 10 years
  • more common in females than in males (4:1)
  • The classic symptom triad includes abdominal pain, right upper quadrant mass, and jaundice (most consistent symptom)
  • Other symptoms- nausea, weight loss, fever, pruritus, etc

Complications include

  • Cholangitis (may lead to cirrhosis and portal hypertension) 
  • Pancreatitis
  • Bile peritonitis (due to cyst rupture) 
  • Cholangiocarcinoma

Diagnostic investigations for choledochal cysts are as follows:

  • Ultrasonography: 
    • Confirms the presence of an abnormal cyst 
    • Define the dimensions of the cyst 
    • Define its relationship to the vascular structures in the porta hepatis, as well as the intrahepatic ductal configuration
  • Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI/MRCP) is the investigation of choice. It reveals the anatomy of the ducts 
  • CT - delineates the extent of the intra- or extrahepatic dilatation       
  • ERCP - defines the distal biliary tree 

Todani classification (Option C) of the choledochal cysts along with their management is as shown below,

Type of choledochal cyst Surgical management
Type I -  fusiform dilatation of the bile duct (most common - seen in 75% of patients) complete surgical excision, cholecystectomy, and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
Type II - saccular diverticulum from the common bile duct Diverticulectomy, cholecystectomy, and common bile duct repair
Type III- diverticulum within the pancreas, also known as choledochoceles ERCP + sphincterotomy (Only cyst in which reconstruction is not required)
Type IV a - multiple cysts (both intrahepatic and extrahepatic) Liver transplant
b - multiple cysts limited to the extrahepatic biliary tree Kasai procedure (Portoenterostomy)
Type V - multiple cysts involving only intrahepatic ducts (Caroli's disease) Liver transplant

 

Biliary-enteric reconstruction is not required in Type III choledochal cyst as it has the lowest risk of malignancy, and it may not be associated with ABPJ (anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction). Therefore, endoscopic drainage is sufficient. 

Pearl: Classification of Choledochal Cysts

Type

Feature

Type I

The most common choledochal cyst type; it involves only the extrahepatic biliary tree and is generally a fusiform dilation.

Type II

Saccular diverticulum off the common bile duct and may be mistaken for an accessory gallbladder.

Type III

A cystic dilation of the intramural common bile duct, within the wall of the duodenum, known as choledochoceles.

Type IV

Type IVa: Cysts involving the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree

Type IVb: Multiple cysts limited to the extrahepatic biliary tree.

Type V

Also known as Caroli disease, involve the intrahepatic ducts only.

Pearl: Diagnostic Evaluation of the Bile Ducts

Diagnostic Evaluation of the Bile Ducts

  • Hepatobiliary ultrasound: Initial procedure of choice in investigating possible biliary tract obstruction
  • CT scan: Procedure of choice in investigating possible biliary obstruction if diagnostic limitations prevent HBUS
  • MRCP: Useful modality for visualizing pancreatic and biliary ducts
  • ERCP: Best visualisation of distal biliary tract
    • Endoscopic sphincterotomy and stone removal can also be done
  • PTC(Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography): Best visualisation of proximal biliary tract
    • Indicated when ERCP is contraindicated or failed
  • EUS: Most sensitive method to detect ampullary stones

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Smoking increases the risk of which of the following diseases?
  1. Duct ectasia
  2. Fibroadenoma
  3. Mondor's disease
  4. Breast carcinoma
questions.raw_text:
Smoking increases the risk of which of the following diseases?
  1. Duct ectasia
  2. Fibroadenoma
  3. Mondor's disease
  4. Breast carcinoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3, 4

Smoking increases the risk of which of duct ectasia, Mondor's disease, and breast carcinoma. 

Duct ectasia is defined as dilated major milk ducts. It is considered a disorder of involution as part of ANDI. Abnormally dilated ducts are filled with debris. This acts as an irritant and can lead to periductal inflammation and subsequent fibrosis, leading to nipple retraction. Duct ectasia appears to be associated with smoking and diabetes.

The thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the breast and anterior chest wall is called Mondor’s disease. The pathognomonic feature is a tender thrombosed subcutaneous cord, usually attached to the skin. When the skin over the breast is stretched by raising the arm, a narrow, shallow, subcutaneous groove alongside the cord becomes apparent. Smoking was found to be a potential factor involved in the pathogenesis of Mondor’s disease. Other risk factors include breast surgery, breast biopsy, an inflammatory process, breast cancer, and trauma.

The risk factors of breast cancer can be divided into modifiable (those that can be modified by adopting a healthy diet and lifestyle) and non-modifiable risk factors. The events increasing the oestrogenic exposure of the breast are said to be risk factors for breast cancer, such as early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy, and hormone replacement with high estrogen therapy. Smoking is a modifiable risk factor with a relative risk (RR) = 1.14 for smoking 25 or more cigarettes/day and RR = 1.07 for smoking for 20 years or more.

Fibroadenoma is the most common cause of a breast lump in women aged 15–25 years. It arises from the hyperplasia of a lobule and is surrounded by a well-defined capsule. Smoking is not a risk factor for fibroadenomas.

Pearl: Risk Factors and Protective Factors for Breast Carcinoma

Risk factors:

  • Age: Incidence increases with increasing age.
  • Sex: more common in females.
  • Family history of breast cancer
  • Race, ethnicity (white women have increased risk compared to women of other races)
  • History of radiation exposure
  • Mammographically dense breast
  • Genetic factors:
  • Mutations in tumor suppressor genes:
    • BRCA 1
    • BRCA 2
    • TP53
    • CHEK2
  • Hereditary syndromes:
    • Li Fraumeni syndrome
    • Cowden’s syndrome
    • HNPCC syndrome
    • Peutz-Jegher’s syndrome
    • Ataxia telangiectasia
  • Hormonal factors (hyperestrogenemia is the risk factor):
    • Early menarche
    • Late menopause
    • First full-term pregnancy >30 years
    • Nulliparity
    • Obesity (postmenopausal)
  • Higher socioeconomic status, high fat diet, alcohol intake

Protective factors:

  • Early age at first pregnancy
  • Multiparity
  • Breastfeeding
  • Oophorectomy
  • Exercise
  • Tamoxifen and Aromatase inhibitors
