questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: While crossing the road, a truck with dense exhaust fumes pass you by and you immediately cough. Which of the following receives sensory stimuli for the generation of the reflex involved?
questions.raw_text: While crossing the road, a truck with dense exhaust fumes pass you by and you immediately cough. Which of the following receives sensory stimuli for the generation of the reflex involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nucleus tractus solitarius

The nucleus tractus solitarius receives the sensory afferents in the cough reflex.

The cough reflex is a protective mechanism of the larynx to expel irritants and keep the airway clear. Chemical or mechanical irritation of the respiratory mucosa stimulates the afferent internal laryngeal nerve, which is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve of the vagus nerve. 

These sensory fibres synapse in the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla oblongata. Complex neural networks here generate the conscious 'urge to cough' while also sending efferent signals to the various muscles involved in generating an effective cough, which include the adductors of the vocal cord, the diaphragm, the external intercostals and the muscles of the anterior abdominal wall.

Alcohol can cause chemical irritation of the internal laryngeal nerve while also acting as a potent inhibitor of the central nervous system, which may cause inhibition of the cough and gag reflexes that increase the risk of aspiration.

Other options:

Option B: The nucleus ambiguus sends motor efferent fibres to the pharyngeal constrictors, intrinsic laryngeal muscles, and striated muscles of the palate and upper esophagus through the CN IX and CN X.

Option C: The inferior salivatory nucleus gives rise to the preganglionic parasympathetic fibres that enter the relay in the otic ganglion, as part of the secretomotor pathway of the parotid gland.

Option D: The rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) is the major excitatory source of the sympathetic nervous system that forms part of the baroreceptor reflex, responsible for causing a rise in BP.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old baby presented with seizures, developmental delay and failure to thrive. Following an MRI, a diagnosis of a neuronal migration disorder was made. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 9-month-old baby presented with seizures, developmental delay and failure to thrive. Following an MRI, a diagnosis of a neuronal migration disorder was made. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Schizencephaly

Among the given options, schizencephaly is a neuronal migration defect. MRI is the study of choice for elucidating schizencephaly and associated malformations.

Neuronal migration is the process during brain development, where the neuronal cells migrate to their proper designated site by various mechanisms, to form the 6-layered cerebral cortex. Any abnormality in the above process leads to neuronal migration defects.

Neuronal migration defect includes the following:

  • Schizencephaly: (schiz = split or cleavage) It is the presence of unilateral or bilateral clefts within the cerebral hemispheres. The patient can be severely intellectually challenged, with microcephaly, seizures, and spastic quadriparesis.

    The image below shows schizencephaly:

 

  • Lissencephaly (agyria): It is the absence of cerebral convolutions. Rather than the normal 6 layers of the cortex, there may be fewer layers. The child will have developmental delay, microcephaly, and seizures.

    The image below shows lissencephaly:

Myelomeningocele (Option B) is a neural tube defect that occurs due to defective closure of the neural tube.

Lhermitte–Duclos disease  (Option C) is the cerebellar dysplasia leading to focal enlargement of cerebellum and macrocephaly, cerebellar signs, and seizures.

Plagiocephaly  (Option D) is the asymmetry and flattening of the skull of the child, due to extrinsic moulding forces (consistent sleeping on the same side of the head).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-month-old infant was brought with complaints of jerking movement of limbs towards the body. On examination, there is a regression of developmental milestones. Electroencephalogram shows hypsarrythmia. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.raw_text: A 10-month-old infant was brought with complaints of jerking movement of limbs towards the body. On examination, there is a regression of developmental milestones. Electroencephalogram shows hypsarrythmia. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)

The clinical scenario along with the electroencephalogram showing hypsarrythmia is suggestive of the West syndrome. Adreno-corticotropic hormone (ACTH) is the drug of choice for this condition.

West syndrome is severe generalized epilepsy that begins between the ages of 2 and 12 months. It is characterized by a triad of: 

  1. Infantile epileptic spasms
  2. Developmental regression
  3. Hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalogram (EEG)

Hypsarrhythmia refers to a high voltage, slow, chaotic background with multifocal spikes as shown below.

West syndrome has been known by many names like infantile spasms, salaam attacks, salaam convulsions infantile spastic epilepsy, and jackknife convulsion syndrome. During an attack babies typically attain complete heaving of the head forward towards their knees, and then immediately relax into the upright position.

The image given below illustrates infantile spasms in a child.

Diagnosis is confirmed by EEG which typically shows hypsarrythmia.

The treatment of choice in West syndrome is either adreno-corticotropic hormone (ACTH) or corticosteroids. An antiseizure medication, mainly vigabatrin can be used when associated with tuberous sclerosis.

Note: The table given below shows the EEG features seen in various seizure disorders.

Disease Typical EEG feature
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome 1.5-2.5 Hz spike and polyspike bursts in sleep
Absence seizures 3 Hz spike and slow-wave (spike and dome pattern)
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy 4-5 Hz spike
West syndrome Hypsarrhythmia (high-voltage waves with chaotic background)

Options A and C: Phenytoin and levetiracetam are used in focal seizures and status epilepticus.

Option D: Phenobarbitone is used as an antiepileptic in neonatal seizures and as an enzyme inducer in Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II.

  • Lamotrigine
  • Levetiracetam
  • Phenytoin
GTCS

  • Levetiracetam 
  • Lamotrigine 
Typical absence seizures 
  • Ethosuximide (drug of choice)
  • Sodium valproate
  • Lamotrigine
Atypical absence seizures

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A firefighter presented with a chronic non-healing painless ulcer over his left leg. He gave a history of sustaining  2nd-degree burns injury to the leg 10 years back during a rescue mission. The examination finding is as shown below. All of the following are true about this condition, except ______.
questions.raw_text: A firefighter presented with a chronic non-healing painless ulcer over his left leg. He gave a history of sustaining  2nd-degree burns injury to the leg 10 years back during a rescue mission. The examination finding is as shown below. All of the following are true about this condition, except ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Highly vascular

The given scenario and image showing an irregular ulcer with cauliflower shaped granulation tissue points to a diagnosis of Marjolin’s ulcer. It is avascular.

Pearl: Marjolin’s Ulcer

  • Low-grade squamous cell carcinoma arising from:
    1. Long-standing ulcers like a venous ulcer
    2. Post-burn scar
    3. Chronic osteomyelitis
    4. Post-radiation ulcer
  • Slow growing since it is relatively avascular
  • Painless due to the absence of nerves in scar tissue
  • No secondary deposits since there are no lymphatics in scar tissue
  • Radioresistant due to avascularity

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient has come with sudden onset of chest pain and his CT scan shows the following picture. What is the diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 50-year-old patient has come with sudden onset of chest pain and his CT scan shows the following picture. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic dissection

The given CT scan showing a double lumen and dilatation of the aorta is suggestive of an aortic dissection. 

In this condition, blood enters the space below the intima of the aorta. This results in the formation of a true lumen and false lumen. The true lumen is often the smaller of the two because of being compressed by the false lumen, as shown below (2D MRI showing the dissection flap at peak systole and mid-diastole. The true lumen expands during systole and collapses during diastole due to pressure fluctuations from the false lumen).

 

Feature True Lumen False Lumen
Position Medial, smaller Lateral, larger
Enhancement Early, washes out Late or thrombosed
Behaviour May collapse Often dilates
Branch supply Coronaries, celiac, SMA, right renal Left renal artery
Signs — Cobweb sign, Beak sign


The cobweb sign refers to slender linear strands of incompletely sheared media within the false lumen.

The beak sign is a wedge of hematoma at the edge of the false lumen, forming an acute angle between the dissection flap and the outer aortic wall.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The image shows certain changes in the conjunctiva commonly found in a DNA repair defect syndrome. What is the first clinical manifestation of this disease?
questions.raw_text: The image shows certain changes in the conjunctiva commonly found in a DNA repair defect syndrome. What is the first clinical manifestation of this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Progressive cerebellar degeneration

The given image shows multiple telangiectasias of conjunctival vessels. This along with DNA repair defect point towards ataxia-telangiectasia (AT) or Louis–Bar syndrome. Progressive cerebellar degeneration is the first clinical manifestation in ataxia-telangiectasia, presenting at about 1 year of age.

AT is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. The disease shows chromosomal instability due to inactivating mutations in the ATM gene. The ATM protein kinase plays a key role in the control of double-strand break DNA repair.

It is a multisystem disorder characterized by ataxia and mucocutaneous telangiectasia. Cutaneous features include: 

  • Telangiectasias - initially conjunctival, most prominent on face
  • Premature hair greying
  • Café‐au‐lait spots
  • Pigmentary changes - poikiloderma.

Other cardinal features of AT are:

  • Immunodeficiency - increased susceptibility to infections
  • Hypogonadism
  • Sensitivity to ionizing radiation
  • Insulin resistance
  • Predisposition to cancer

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The peripheral smear of a patient diagnosed with multiple myeloma is shown below. What does the marked structure contain?
questions.raw_text: The peripheral smear of a patient diagnosed with multiple myeloma is shown below. What does the marked structure contain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immunoglobulin

The given image shows a Mott cell which is a plasma cell with globular cytoplasmic inclusions containing immunoglobulins called Russell bodies.

Inclusions containing Ig are frequently seen in the cytoplasm (Russell bodies) or the nucleus (Dutcher bodies) of some of the plasma cells in myeloma.

Pearl: Pathological Cells/Bodies in Multiple Myeloma

  • Dutcher bodies - pale-staining, PAS-positive intranuclear inclusions within plasma cells containing Ig, which are more common in IgA myeloma (Image below). 

Russell bodies - They are globular intracellular accumulations of immunoglobulins (Ig). Russell bodies are distended endoplasmic reticulum. Plasma cells filled with multiple Russell bodies are called Mott cells.

  • Flame cells - Plasma cells with fiery red cytoplasm due to vermillion-staining, glycogen-rich IgA in cytoplasmic projections

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which tumor does not cause osteomalacia and phosphaturia?
questions.raw_text: Which tumor does not cause osteomalacia and phosphaturia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Breast carcinoma

Breast carcinoma does not cause osteomalacia and phosphaturia.

Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) is a rare paraneoplastic syndrome which presents with hypophosphatemia, osteomalacia and renal phosphate wasting. It is most commonly seen with mesenchymal tumors.

Tumors associated with osteomalacia are:

  • Hemangiopericytoma (option B)
  • Non-ossifying fibroma
  • Osteosarcoma (option A)
  • Osteoblastoma
  • Fibrosarcoma (option C)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding carbamate poisoning is true when compared to organophosphorus poisoning?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements regarding carbamate poisoning is true when compared to organophosphorus poisoning?

options.label: A
options.text: It is associated with faster aging of the cholinesterase enzyme

options.label: B
options.text: It can also lead to the intermediate syndrome

options.label: C
options.text: Severe CNS toxicity can be seen

options.label: D
options.text: Pralidoxime is the mainstay in management

questions.correct_answer: B. It can also lead to the intermediate syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It can also lead to the intermediate syndrome

Carbamates can also lead to the intermediate syndrome.

Option A: Carbamate-cholinesterase bond undergoes rapid, spontaneous hydrolysis which leads to regeneration of the enzyme within a few hours. This is called reversible carbamylation. Hence, aging (conversion of the inhibited enzyme into a non-reactivable form) does not occur and the effect of carbamate toxicity is of a shorter duration.

Option C: Carbamates do not effectively penetrate the CNS in adults. Hence, there is less CNS toxicity.

Option D: Pralidoxime is contraindicated in carbamate poisoning because it may potentiate the toxicity of carbamates due to its transient oxime-induced cholinesterase inhibition.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presented to the clinic for a missed vaccination. His routine anthropometric measurements were noted. He was found to be 90 cm tall with a lower segment of 45 cm. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis in this child?
questions.raw_text: A 3-year-old boy presented to the clinic for a missed vaccination. His routine anthropometric measurements were noted. He was found to be 90 cm tall with a lower segment of 45 cm. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia

The upper segment to lower segment (U/L) ratio in this child is 1. The U/L ratio is low for his age which makes spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia most likely among the given options.

The lower segment is defined as the length from the symphysis pubis to the floor. The upper segment is measured by subtracting the lower segment from the height.

The U/L ratio is

  • 1.7 at birth
  • 1.3 at 3 years
  • 1 after 7 years
  • 0.9 in adults

High U/L ratio:

  • Rickets
  • Achondroplasia
  • Untreated congenital hypothyroidism 

Low U/L ratio:

  • Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia
  • Vertebral anomalies

Arm span:

  • Length between the tips of the middle finger of the outstretched hands is the arm span.
  • It is shorter than the length by 2.5 cm at birth; it equals height at 11 y and thereafter is slightly greater than height (usually<1 cm).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A dermatologist wants to prescribe acitretin to a patient with psoriasis. Which of the following statements is false regarding the drug?
questions.raw_text: A dermatologist wants to prescribe acitretin to a patient with psoriasis. Which of the following statements is false regarding the drug?

options.label: B
options.text: It can cause increased sensitivity to sunlight

options.label: C
options.text: Female patients should avoid getting pregnant for 6 months after therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Acitretin has a half life of about 50 hours

questions.correct_answer: C. Female patients should avoid getting pregnant for 6 months after therapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Female patients should avoid getting pregnant for 6 months after therapy

Female patients should avoid conception for 3 years after discontinuing acitretin treatment to prevent retinoid-induced embryopathy.

Acitretin is approved for use in the cutaneous manifestations of psoriasis.

Absolute contraindications:

  • Pregnant women
  • Women who are planning to get pregnant
  • Breastfeeding

Relative contraindications:

  • Leukopenia
  • Alcoholism
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Hypercholesterolemia
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Significant hepatic or renal disease

Note: Female patients should avoid conception for 1 month after discontinuation of isotretinoin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presented with symptoms of heart failure. He had undergone a coronary bypass procedure with a small-diameter graft 3 weeks ago.  What is the likely cause for his presentation?
questions.raw_text: A patient presented with symptoms of heart failure. He had undergone a coronary bypass procedure with a small-diameter graft 3 weeks ago.  What is the likely cause for his presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thrombosis

The above scenario is suggestive of an early failure of a small-diameter venous graft (≤8 mm). The likely mechanism for graft failure within the 1st month is acute thrombosis.

Based on the diameter of the synthetic or autologous vascular graft, it can be classified as:

  • Large diameter graft (12-18mm) -
    • Used in high-flow locations such as the aorta
  • Small diameter graft (≤8 mm) -
    • Includes the saphenous vein or left internal mammary artery
    • Used in coronary bypass surgeries 

Other options:

Option A, B and D: Atherosclerotic plaque, neointimal hyperplasia and aneurysms are all late complications of graft failure taking months or years to manifest.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 54-year-old woman comes to the diabetic clinic for follow up. Her lipid profile shows high LDL cholesterol. Which bile acid sequestrant would you prescribe for her?
questions.raw_text: A 54-year-old woman comes to the diabetic clinic for follow up. Her lipid profile shows high LDL cholesterol. Which bile acid sequestrant would you prescribe for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Colesevelam

Colesevelam can be prescribed for her as it is the only bile acid sequestrant that is specifically approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus. 

It lowers LDL by binding bile acids in the intestine, promoting hepatic conversion of cholesterol to bile acids. Additionally, it is approved for improving glycemic control in type 2 diabetes, though the exact mechanism of its glucose-lowering effect is not fully understood. Other bile acid sequestrants, such as cholestyramine and colestipol, are less preferred in diabetics due to a lack of glycemic benefit and higher gastrointestinal side effects.

NOTE: Colesevelam provides dual benefits-reducing LDL cholesterol and improving blood glucose in type 2 diabetes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old primigravida who conceived after in-vitro fertilization therapy came for an antenatal checkup at 38 weeks of gestation. Her obstetric history revealed that she was pregnant with DCDA twins. On examination, the first twin was found to be in a breech position and the maternal blood pressure was found to be greater than 140/90 mm Hg on two occasions with grade 1+ proteinuria. What should be done next?
questions.raw_text: A 35-year-old primigravida who conceived after in-vitro fertilization therapy came for an antenatal checkup at 38 weeks of gestation. Her obstetric history revealed that she was pregnant with DCDA twins. On examination, the first twin was found to be in a breech position and the maternal blood pressure was found to be greater than 140/90 mm Hg on two occasions with grade 1+ proteinuria. What should be done next?

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor BP and terminate pregnancy if BP rises

options.label: C
options.text: Terminate pregnancy at 40 weeks of gestation

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediate Caesarean section

Immediate cesarean section is done as the first twin is in breech presentation. Uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies are terminated at 38 weeks of gestation. 

Timing of delivery depends on the type of twin pregnancy:

Type of twin pregnancy Timing of delivery
Dichorionic diamniotic 38 weeks
Monochorionic diamniotic 34 - 37 weeks + 6 days
Monochorionic monoamniotic 32 - 34 weeks by Caesarean section

 The mode of delivery depends on the 1st twin:

1st twin presentation Mode of delivery
Vertex Vaginal
Breech Cesarean section
Transverse Cesarean section

After delivery of 1st twin, if the 2nd twin is in breech, assisted breech delivery is done. If the 2nd twin is in a transverse lie, the internal podalic version is done under GA in the OT followed by breech extraction.

Complications in attempting vaginal delivery in non-vertex presentation (i.e) transverse and breech:

  • Interlocking of twins
  • Fetal head trapping above the cervix
  • Umbilical cord prolapse

According to ACOG criteria (2019), preeclampsia requires proteinuria of grade 2+ or more. In the case of pre-eclampsia, termination of pregnancy must be done at 37 weeks. According to the updated criteria, this patient does not have pre-eclampsia. Hence, a Caesarean section can be done at 38 weeks as for any uncomplicated DCDA twin pregnancy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are used to stop esophageal variceal bleed?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following are used to stop esophageal variceal bleed?
questions.correct_answer: A. A, B, C and D
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A, B, C and D

All the given options can be used to stop esophageal variceal bleeding.

Image A shows the Sengstaken-Blakemore tube. It has 3 lumens - one aspiration port and 2 inflation balloons. They are:

  • Gastric aspiration port
  • Gastric balloon port
  • Esophageal balloon port

The gastric balloon is inflated and tension is applied to the gastroesophageal junction. If this does not control the haemorrhage, the esophageal balloon is inflated as well, compressing the venous plexus between them. Only gastric contents can be aspirated.

Image B shows the Minnesota tube. It has 4 openings - 2 inflation tubes and 2 suction tubes i.e. both gastric and oesophageal aspiration ports are present, which allows the aspiration of both gastric and esophageal contents.

Images C and D both show an upper GI endoscope. They are used to identify the source of bleeding and once identified, sclerotherapy and endoscopic variceal banding are performed, which have been shown to control hemorrhage effectively.

Banding has a lower rate of complications. If bleeding does not stop by banding/sclerotherapy, balloon tamponade should be tried.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The below-given image is characteristically seen in which of the following type of leprosy?
questions.raw_text: The below-given image is characteristically seen in which of the following type of leprosy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Borderline leprosy

The given image shows a case of borderline tuberculous leprosy, or dimorphous leprosy, as evidenced by the cutaneous, rash-like discoloration of the patient’s skin. This generally overlies the back, and crosses the midline. So, the best choice would be Borderline leprosy.

Microscopically, there is diffuse epithelioid cell granuloma with very scanty lymphocytes and no giant cells; the papillary zone is clear and the nerves are swollen slightly by cellular infiltrate. Acid-fast bacilli are present in moderate numbers.

The borderline leprosy patients are immunologically unstable and are at an increased risk of developing immune-mediated reactions. Type 1 lepra reactions that occur most commonly in mid-borderline leprosy patients, are delayed hypersensitivity reactions caused by increased recognition of mycobacterial leprae antigens in skin and nerve sites.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient was treated with TCA for a major depressive episode in the hospital for 4 weeks. What is the main concern while considering his discharge from the hospital?
questions.raw_text: A patient was treated with TCA for a major depressive episode in the hospital for 4 weeks. What is the main concern while considering his discharge from the hospital?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Suicidal risk

Suicidal thoughts or behavior are a side effect of TCAs. Therefore, the attendants of the patient should be warned regarding this when a patient gets discharged after being treated with TCAs for a major depressive episode.

Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are drugs that act by inhibiting the reuptake of noradrenaline and serotonin from the synaptic clefts. 

The side effects of TCAs are due to blockade of other receptors:

  • Muscarinic M receptors- constipation, dry mouth, arrhythmia
  • Histamine H1 receptors- sedation
  • 5HT receptors - weight gain due to increased appetite
  • Alpha1 receptors - postural hypotension.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is not used for induction of anaesthesia in pediatric patients?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not used for induction of anaesthesia in pediatric patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Desflurane

Desflurane is a highly pungent gas and can produce laryngospasm if used for inhalational induction. Hence it is not used as an induction agent.

The incidence of laryngospasm following desflurane induction is almost 50%. It is usually used for maintenance of anaesthesia only and is of particular value in obese patients, neurosurgical and spinal fusion procedures where rapid awakening is required for neurological function assessment.

Option A: Halothane is hepatotoxic but can be used (Sevoflurane is preferred)

Option B: Sevoflurane is the preferred inhalational agent for induction in the pediatric age group. Cardiovascular depression, bradycardia, and arrhythmias are less frequent with sevoflurane than with halothane and hence the former is preferred.

Option D: Nitrous oxide has the highest minimum alveolar concentration and so it is the least potent. It is used in combination with other potent inhaled anaesthetics to reduce their dose. It can be used to hasten the induction of anaesthesia along with other induction agents.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs increases the uveoscleral outflow?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following drugs increases the uveoscleral outflow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Latanoprost

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin drug, which acts by increasing the uveoscleral outflow and thereby lowers the intraocular pressure. 

Mechanism of action: Latanoprost is a prodrug and gets activated during its passage through the cornea. It acts by stimulating the prostanoid receptors on the ciliary muscles. This leads to the release of matrix metalloproteinases, which increases the uveoscleral outflow.

Pearl: Antiglaucoma drugs: Mechanism of lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) at a glance

Drugs that increase trabecular outflow

  • Miotics (e.g., pilocarpine)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
The X-rays of two patients are given below. Patient 1 is a 5-year-old boy with cyanosis and breathlessness worsening on exertion. He squats after physical activity for relief. Patient 2 is a 3-day-old neonate with severe cyanosis since birth, unresponsive to oxygen supplementation. What are the most likely diagnoses?

TGA: Transposition of great arteries

TAPVR: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return

TOF: Tetralogy of Fallot
questions.raw_text:
The X-rays of two patients are given below. Patient 1 is a 5-year-old boy with cyanosis and breathlessness worsening on exertion. He squats after physical activity for relief. Patient 2 is a 3-day-old neonate with severe cyanosis since birth, unresponsive to oxygen supplementation. What are the most likely diagnoses?

TGA: Transposition of great arteries

TAPVR: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return

TOF: Tetralogy of Fallot
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 - TOF, 2 - TAPVR

The correct answer is B. 1 - Tetralogy of Fallot, 2 - TAPVR.

In patient 1, cyanosis on exertion with squatting for relief is classic for TOF. Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance and venous return, increasing flow through the obstructed RV outflow tract.

The chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) due to right ventricular hypertrophy with a concavity in the region of the pulmonary artery, and the lung fields are oligaemic.


Patient 2, a neonate with cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen indicates cyanotic congenital heart disease. TAPVR is associated with total mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous blood flow within the heart, producing cyanosis.

The chest X-ray shows a figure-of-eight or snowman appearance due to the supracardiac shadow formed by the anomalous pulmonary veins draining via the left superior vena cava and innominate vein. The heart is enlarged with increased pulmonary vascularity.

Pearl: Radiological findings in some congenital heart defects

Boot shaped heart - Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

 

Egg on string appearance - Transposition of Great Arteries (TGA)

 

Snowman's heart appearance or figure of 8 appearance - Supracardiac TAPVC

 

Box Shaped Heart - Ebstein's Anomaly

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient came with complaints of hair loss. His wife mentions that she has noticed some behavioral changes. The doctor notices that there is a loss of eyebrows on the lateral side. He then comes to a conclusion by examining the nails. What is the type of poisoning in this case?
questions.raw_text: A patient came with complaints of hair loss. His wife mentions that she has noticed some behavioral changes. The doctor notices that there is a loss of eyebrows on the lateral side. He then comes to a conclusion by examining the nails. What is the type of poisoning in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thallium

The given scenario of hair loss, loss of eyebrows on the lateral side along with behavioral and nail changes point to thallium poisoning. 

Thallium poisoning occurs due to an overdose or idiosyncrasy. Thallium sulfate and thallium acetate are the two salts of thallium used in dyes, in the glass industry, and as rodenticides and pesticides. 

Mild cases of poisoning have features of joint pain, loss of appetite, and drowsiness. Severe cases present with colic, vomiting, muscle pain, convulsions, psychosis, tremors, delirium, and coma are seen in severe cases. Hair loss is seen after 2 weeks and a characteristic feature is loss of the outer thirds of the eyebrows. Mees lines are seen on the nails. Maculopapular rashes in a butterfly pattern on the face are characteristic. 

In chronic poisoning, alopecia, skin rashes, peripheral neuropathy, and mental confusion are present.

Treatment is mainly by stomach wash with potassium iodide or Prussian blue, activated charcoal. Hemodialysis is useful and forced diuresis can be given.

The image below shows Mees lines.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of Syndrome Z?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not a component of Syndrome Z?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. LDL more than 100mg/dl

Syndrome Z is defined as a combination of obstructive sleep apnea syndrome with metabolic syndrome. LDL more than 100 mg/dL is not a criterion for the diagnosis of metabolic syndrome.

Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed based on The NCEP: ATP III Criteria. Three or more of the following must be present :

  • Central obesity: waist circumference >102 cm (M), >88 cm (F)
  • Hypertriglyceridemia: triglyceride level ≥150 mg/dL or specific medication
  • Low HDL cholesterol: <40 mg/dL and <50 mg/dL for men and women, respectively, or specific medication
  • Hypertension: blood pressure ≥130 mmHg systolic or ≥85 mmHg diastolic or specific medication
  • Fasting plasma glucose level ≥100 mg/dL or specific medication or previously diagnosed type 2 diabetes

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following  co-enzyme deficiencies makes a patient prone to lactic acidosis?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following  co-enzyme deficiencies makes a patient prone to lactic acidosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thiamine

Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency makes a patient prone to lactic acidosis.

Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) serves as a coenzyme for the pyruvate dehydrogenase enzyme. In a state of thiamine deficiency, there is an impaired conversion of pyruvate to acetyl CoA. When the patient consumes a high carbohydate diet, there is thus an accumulation of pyruvate. Pyruvate then gets converted into lactate by the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase. This results in increased plasma concentrations of lactate and pyruvate, leading to a state of lactic acidosis.

Converts alanine to pyruvate and vise-versa.
2 Pyruvate carboxylase Formation of oxaloacetate from pyruvate to be used in the TCA cycle
3 Pyruvate dehydrogenase Pyruvate to acetyl Co-A to be used in the TCA cycle
4 Lactic acid dehydrogenase Pyruvate to lactate(Anaerobic glycolysis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman with a long history of dyspnea, chronic cough with sputum, and wheezing died of respiratory failure following a bout of lobar pneumonia. She was not a smoker or an alcoholic. The lung at autopsy is shown in the image below. Which of the following is most likely to cause the pathological changes shown?
questions.raw_text: A 30-year-old woman with a long history of dyspnea, chronic cough with sputum, and wheezing died of respiratory failure following a bout of lobar pneumonia. She was not a smoker or an alcoholic. The lung at autopsy is shown in the image below. Which of the following is most likely to cause the pathological changes shown?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency

The above gross specimen shows emphysematous damage involving enlargement of the entire acinus, suggestive of panacinar emphysema. It is caused by alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency.

In panacinar (panlobular) emphysema, the acini are uniformly enlarged from the level of the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal blind alveoli. It commonly occurs in the lower zones and at the anterior margins of the lung, and is most severe at the bases.

The image below shows panacinar emphysema.

Pearl: Types of emphysema

Emphysema is classified according to its anatomic distribution within the lobule.

  • Central part of acinus (respiratory bronchiole)
  • Upper lobes of lung
  • Commonly seen in smokers
Panacinar
  • Entire acinus (respiratory bronchiole + alveoli)
  • Lower lobes of lung
  • Commonly seen in young non-smokers
  • Associated with α-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Paraseptal
  • Distal part of acinus (alveoli)
  • Subpleural region
  • Commonly seen in young adults 
  • Increased risk for spontaneous pneumothorax 
Irregular
  • Focal and irregular involvement of acinus
  • Areas of the lung near scar tissue 
  • Not usually seen in COPD

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young woman with a distant breast cancer relative comes to you in the clinic. You are advising her to practice self-examination of her breasts. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding this practice?
questions.raw_text: A young woman with a distant breast cancer relative comes to you in the clinic. You are advising her to practice self-examination of her breasts. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding this practice?

options.label: A
options.text: It should be done once a month, every month

options.label: B
options.text: Ideally, be done between the 3rd to 6th day of the menstrual cycle

options.label: C
options.text: It should only be done while standing

options.label: D
options.text: The examination should be done by using the middle three fingerpads

questions.correct_answer: C. It should only be done while standing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It should only be done while standing

Self-examination of breasts can be done while standing or lying down.

It should be ideally be done once a month, every month between the 3rd to 6th day of the menstrual cycle. If the periods are irregular or the patient is post-menopausal, then the patient can pick any day of the month. 

It can be done any time of the day while showering, dressing, standing, or lying down at night.

Steps of the self-examination:

  1. Visual inspection: See for any abnormalities, like shape, size, dimpling, puckering of the skin, nipple discharge, etc.
  2. Manual inspection: It is done by using the middle three fingerpads. Feel for any lumps. Techniques used are (either one of them): 
    • Horizontal stripes method
    • Vertical stripes method
    • Dial clock method

Be sure to check under the areola and press the nipple gently to check for any discharge.

Correct answer: C. Total duration is for 20 months

All oral longer MDR-TB regimen is used for the treatment of XDR-TB patients for a duration of 20 months.

Regimen class Drugs
All oral longer MDR TB regimen Bdq(6 months) Lfx Lzd Cfz Cs for 18-20 months

 

Pearl: ATT Regimen for TB Patients

As per the latest recommendations from National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP), treatment of TB is now based primarily on drug susceptibility testing. This is irrespective of new cases, previously treated cases or recurrent TB cases. 
All cases of TB are treated with Drug Sensitive TB Regimen, as long as the patient is sensitive to isoniazid and rifampicin. (No classification into category I or II)

Type of TB Case Intensive Phase Continuation Phase
New and previously treated cases (H and R sensitive) 2 months HRZE 4 months HRE (Only HR as per WHO guidelines)

Classification based on drug resistance. 

The cases are classified as:

  • Mono-resistant (MR): A TB patient who is resistant to one 1st line anti-TB drug only.
  • Poly-Drug Resistant (PDR): A TB patient, who is resistant to more than one 1st line anti-TB drug, other than Rifampicin and isoniazid. 
  • Rifampicin Resistant (RR): A TB patient who is resistant to rifampicin with or without resistance to other drugs. Patients, who have rifampicin resistance, should be managed as if they are an MDR TB case.
  • Multi-Drug Resistant (MDR): A TB patient who is resistant to both isoniazid and rifampicin.
  • Extensively Drug-Resistant (XDR): A MDR TB patient who is additionally resistant to a fluoroquinolone (ofloxacin, levofloxacin, or moxifloxacin) and at least one additional group A drug (as of 2021, these are bedaquiline and linezolid)

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Hawkin's classification is used for which fractures?
questions.raw_text: Hawkin's classification is used for which fractures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Talus

Hawkin's classification is used for the fracture of the neck of the talus.

The fracture of the neck of the talus most commonly occur following a high-energy injury causing forced dorsiflexion with axial load. They can be further classified using Hawkin's classification:

  • Type I - Undisplaced
  • Type II - Subtalar dislocation
  • Type III - Subtalar and tibiotalar dislocation
  • Type IV - Subtalar, tibiotalar, and talonavicular dislocation

Undisplaced fractures are managed conservatively in a short leg cast for 8-12 weeks and a non-weight bearing cast for 6 weeks. Hawkin's type II-IV are managed by open reduction with internal fixation (ORIF).

The below image shows the Hawkins classification of talar neck fractures.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A woman is planning a trip to Morocco, which is endemic for yellow fever. As per travel regulations, she receives the yellow fever vaccine. After how many days following vaccination is she eligible to travel?
questions.raw_text: A woman is planning a trip to Morocco, which is endemic for yellow fever. As per travel regulations, she receives the yellow fever vaccine. After how many days following vaccination is she eligible to travel?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 10

This woman is eligible to travel to the endemic area 10 days after being vaccinated for yellow fever. This period is required for the majority of vaccine recipients to develop immunity.

The 17D vaccine for yellow fever is given subcutaneously. Unvaccinated people are required to remain quarantined for 6 days (maximum period of incubation).

questions.text: Identify the layer of skin (in the image given below) in which desmosomes are abundant.
questions.raw_text: Identify the layer of skin (in the image given below) in which desmosomes are abundant.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. D

Desmosomes are abundant in the stratum spinosum (Option C, label D in the image) layer of the epidermis of the skin.

Desmosomes are adhesion complexes in epidermis which link adjacent keratinocytes. They appear like spines on microscopy and hence this layer is also called the prickle layer. Defects of desmosomal proteins, inherited or acquired, result in blistering disorders.

questions.text:
What is the correct sequence of visualizing regions while performing FAST in a patient suspected to have abdominal trauma?
  1. Subxiphoid
  2. Left upper quadrant
  3. Right upper quadrant
  4. Suprapubic
questions.raw_text:
What is the correct sequence of visualizing regions while performing FAST in a patient suspected to have abdominal trauma?
  1. Subxiphoid
  2. Left upper quadrant
  3. Right upper quadrant
  4. Suprapubic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-3-2-4

The correct sequence to visualize regions in FAST is subxiphoid → right upper quadrant → left upper quadrant → suprapubic.

Focussed assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) is a non-invasive investigation that can be performed rapidly in the emergency room. It helps identify an abnormal collection of fluid or blood.

FAST is indicated in:

  • Haemodynamically unstable patients who had a blunt abdominal trauma
  • Patients who sustained penetrating abdominal trauma with no other indications for immediate laparotomy (signs of hemodynamic instability, peritoneal irritation, peritoneal penetration, and gunshot wound with transperitoneal trajectory).

Technique:

  • The patient is placed in a supine position.
  • With a 3.5-5.0 MHz convex transducer, the following regions are scanned:
    • Subxiphoid transverse view is used to assess pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries.
    • A longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant is used to assess right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison's pouch.
    • A longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant is used to assess splenic injury and left kidney injury.
    • Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region are used to assess Douglas's pouch and bladder.

An "extended FAST or eFAST" scan: Assess left and right thoracic views, in addition to the FAST assessed regions, to look for pneumothorax and hemothorax.

 

The image demonstrates pericardial effusion on FAST ultrasound, characterized by hypoechoic fluid surrounding the myocardium.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young child with congenital hydrocephalus was treated with a successful ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. Four months post surgical repair, the child presented with fever, nuchal rigidity, and irritability. You suspect meningitis. What is the next best step?
questions.raw_text: A young child with congenital hydrocephalus was treated with a successful ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. Four months post surgical repair, the child presented with fever, nuchal rigidity, and irritability. You suspect meningitis. What is the next best step?

options.label: B
options.text: Check shunt patency by nuclear study

options.label: C
options.text: Blood culture and take CSF sample from shunt tap

options.label: D
options.text: Blood culture and take CSF sample by lumbar puncture

questions.correct_answer: C. Blood culture and take CSF sample from shunt tap
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blood culture and take CSF sample from shunt tap

In a child with suspected shunt-associated meningitis, the next best step to confirm the diagnosis is a blood culture and a CSF sample from a shunt tap.

Shunt aspiration is the preferred method for obtaining VP shunt fluid, as it allows for better detection of microbes and reduces the risk of contamination by avoiding the need for a separate procedure. Fluid is typically collected from a subcutaneous reservoir using a 25-gauge needle. This method is preferred over lumbar puncture (Option D).

Bacterial meningitis may be caused due to meningococcus, streptococcus pneumoniae, or Haemophilus influenzae type b. The clinical presentation of meningitis in children with VP shunts is similar to acute bacterial meningitis in other children. These include fever, rash, vomiting, and refusal to feed. Clinical signs of meningeal irritation (Kernig and Brudzinski signs) are not usually seen in infants. 

Blood cultures should be done in all cases of suspected meningitis. Treatment is aggressive with systemic antibiotics. Third-generation cephalosporins along with vancomycin can be used. Wait and watch policy is not followed (option A).

A ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is used to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) due to an obstruction in the normal outflow or there is a decreased absorption of the fluid. A silicone rubber device with a proximal portion inserted into the ventricle, a unidirectional valve, and a distal segment is commonly used for shunt placement. 

Complications of the shunting procedure include infection due to skin flora entering the shunt (Staphylococcus epidermidis), intracerebral or intraventricular hemorrhage, shunt over drainage, shunt nephritis, shunt disconnection, obstruction, inguinal hernia, and seizures. 

Shunt patency studies are performed to determine whether shunt revision surgery is needed in the malfunctioned ventriculoperitoneal shunt. This is done using radionucleotides (option B)

Hydrocephalus represents a group of conditions that result from impaired circulation or absorption of CSF.

Causes of communicating hydrocephalus (increased production or reduced absorption) includes choroid plexus papilloma, meningeal malignancy, and meningitis. Causes of noncommunicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus include aqueductal stenosis, infectious (toxoplasmosis, mumps), Chiari malformation, Dandy-Walker malformation, and mass lesions. 

In infants, signs include rapid head enlargement, bulging fontanel, and downward eye deviation. Long-tract signs and dilated scalp veins may also be observed. Older children may experience irritability, lethargy, poor appetite, vomiting, and headaches. Diagnosis can be done using MRI, ultrasound, and measurement of ICP. 

Medical management with medications like acetazolamide and furosemide can provide temporary relief, but long-term outcomes are often unsatisfactory. Most cases require surgical intervention, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a subcentre area with a crude birth rate (CBR) of 20, what would be the expected number of antenatal care (ANC) registrations by the village health nurse (VHN) in a year?
questions.raw_text: In a subcentre area with a crude birth rate (CBR) of 20, what would be the expected number of antenatal care (ANC) registrations by the village health nurse (VHN) in a year?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 60

  • According to the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) laid down by the Government of India, a subcentre is to serve a population of 5000 in plains.
  • In this scenario, the CBR is 20.
  • Probable number of pregnancies (Y) = Birth rate x population of the area / 1000 = 20 x 5000/1000 = 100.
  • But, we add a correction factor of 10% to adjust for pregnancy wastage in the form of abortions or stillbirths. 
  • Thus, total number of expected pregnancies= Y + 10% of Y= 110
  • As all the pregnancies are not registered, and at any given time an ANM should have atleast half the expected pregnancies registered with her, the number of ANC registrations is taken as 50% of the expected pregnancies.
  • Therefore, Total ANC registrations = total number of expected pregnancies/2 = 55
  • Hence, the closest answer is 60.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Nomogram used for vancomycin dosing is?
questions.raw_text: Nomogram used for vancomycin dosing is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Matzke

The nomogram used for vancomycin dosing is the Matzke nomogram.

The Matzke nomogram includes dosing intervals ranging from 0.5 to 12 days on a continuum of CLcr(Creatinine clearance) values from 0 to 120 mL/min. It is designed to guide the determination of the initial empiric dose and interval of intravenous (IV) vancomycin in hospitalized adults who are not receiving hemodialysis. The nomogram does not apply to patients who exhibit highly variable vancomycin pharmacokinetics. These patients include the critically ill, those with burn injuries affecting more than 20 percent of their body surface, patients with rapidly changing renal function, pregnant women, those with liver failure/ascites, individuals at the extremes of weight, patients who are acutely post-transplant, and those with cystic fibrosis

The Rumack-Matthew nomogram uses the serum acetaminophen concentration, in relation to the time after ingestion, to assess potential hepatotoxicity after a single, acute ingestion of acetaminophen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below :
questions.raw_text: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Purkinje cells

The cells marked in the above histological image are Purkinje cells.

Characteristics of Purkinje cells:

  • Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum.
  • The cells are evenly spaced and are arranged in a single layer.
  • A dendrite arises from the neck of each flask-shaped cell, which passes upward to enter the molecular layer, which then branches extensively to form a dendritic tree.
  • The axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer to enter the white matter.
  • Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex.
  • The initial segment of the axon receives synaptic contacts from basket cell axons.
  • The main axon terminates in one of the cerebellar or vestibular nuclei.
  • Purkinje cells are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Pathological significance:

  • Negri bodies in rabies, are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells.
  • Loss of Purkinje cells and granule cells is seen in ataxia-telangiectasia.
  • In patients with subacute cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells. Some patients show circulating PCA­1 antibody (anti­Yo) against Purkinje cells.
  • Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia, and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

Pearl: Layers of the cerebellar cortex

The cerebellar cortex is divided into 3 layers. They are:

  • Molecular layer - It is the outermost layer. It contains stellate cells and basket cells. They receive excitatory input from the parallel fibers and form inhibitory synapses on the Purkinje cells. It contains many myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers giving it a pale appearance in H and E staining.
  • Purkinje layer - It is the middle layer. It contain flask-shaped cell bodies of Purkinje cells. Their dendrites pass into the molecular layer. The axons of the Purkinje cells passes through the granular layer into the white matter and synapses with the cerebellar nuclei.
  • Granular layer - It is the innermost layer. It contains the cell bodies of the granule cells as well as Golgi cells. It receives excitatory input from the mossy fibers. They end on the dendrites of the granule cells and these complexes are called glomeruli. The axon from the granule cells travels to the molecular layer and bifurcates in a T-shape. These branches form the T and are called parallel fibers. These parallel fibers form excitatory synapses with the Purkinje cells. The granule cells form the only excitatory neurons in the cerebellar cortex. Golgi cells receive input from parallel fibers and mossy fibers. They send inhibitory output to the granule cells.

Neurotransmitters released:

  • Stellate, basket, Golgi and Purkinje cells- GABA
  • Granule cells - Glutamate

The only output from the cerebellar cortex is inhibitory from the Purkinje cells to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old lactating female with an 18-month-old child comes with a history of irregular, heavy bleeding seeking contraceptive advice. Which is the contraceptive of choice?
questions.raw_text: A 24-year-old lactating female with an 18-month-old child comes with a history of irregular, heavy bleeding seeking contraceptive advice. Which is the contraceptive of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mala N

Among the given options, the contraceptive of choice in this lactating mother with heavy irregular bleeding is MALA N. 

MALA N is a combined oral contraceptive (COC) that contains ethinyloestradiol (EE2) in a dose of 20–30 mcg and 0.15 mg of Levonorgesterol. It acts by suppressing ovulation by suppression of pituitary hormones FSH AND LH.

COC has the lowest failure rates and helps in controlling polymenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, and menorrhagia. The risk of thromboembolism is established during the first 6 weeks postpartum (puerperal period) with COC and they are known to suppress lactation. In this clinical scenario, since the child is 18 months old (complementary feeds are usually started at 6 months and child is not entirely dependant on breastmilk for nutrition) and the woman is way past the puerperal period, it can be safely administered.  

Other options:

Option A: Progestasert is a hormone-containing IUCD that acts by forming a thick mucus plug at the cervix and prevents the entry of sperms. Its usage is limited in cases with heavy unexplained bleeding. 

Option B: Copper T is not used in this patient as it might worsen the symptoms of menorrhagia and may result in anemia.

Option D: Norethisterone enanthate depot is an intramuscular injection given once in 2 months. Though it is suitable for lactating women, it has an increased risk of menstrual irregularity and osteopenia and so not preferred in this case.

  • Combined oral contraceptive pills (COC)

    • Mala N - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate (Govt. supply, free of cost)
  • Progesterone only pills (POP) - suitable for lactating women

    • Norgestrel 75 μg
    • Levonorgestrel (LNG) 30 μg
  • Once a month or long-acting pills - highly disappointing results
    • Quinestrol (long-acting estrogen) + short-acting progesterone
  • Gossypol - male pill : Cottonseed derivative and causes azoospermia and severe oligospermia
  • Post-coital pills or interceptive

    • Mifepristone 10-600 mg
    • Ulipristal 30 mg, within 5 days of intercourse
    • Centchroman 60 mg, 2 tablets, within 24 hrs of intercourse
    • GnRH agonists  
    • CuT IUCD, inserted within 5 days

  • Vaginal ring or Nuvaring - Etonogestrel + ethinyl estradiol daily release, use for 3 weeks with withdrawal for 1 week

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text:
A radiograph of the wrist is given below. Identify the true statements regarding this condition.
  1. The age of occurrence is 40-60 years.
  2. Ground-glass appearance on X-ray is diagnostic.
  3. It has an epiphyseal origin.
  4. 30% of cases undergo malignant transformation.
questions.raw_text:
A radiograph of the wrist is given below. Identify the true statements regarding this condition.
  1. The age of occurrence is 40-60 years.
  2. Ground-glass appearance on X-ray is diagnostic.
  3. It has an epiphyseal origin.
  4. 30% of cases undergo malignant transformation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 only

The given x-ray showing a lytic lesion at the end of a long bone is suggestive of a giant cell tumor (GCT)/osteoclastoma. It affects the ends of long bones, involving metaphysis/epiphysis (statement 3). GCT is most commonly seen in the distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus, and distal radius. 

GCTs usually affect young adults of age 20 to 40 years (statement 1), with slight female predominance. It is a benign but locally aggressive tumor. They present with swelling, vague pain, or pathological fracture through the lesion.

A solitary eccentric, expansile, lobulated lytic lesion in the epiphysis/metaphysis is seen on a plain X-ray, which is diagnostic (statement 2). The tumor is homogeneously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance called a soap bubble appearance (shown below). Soft-tissue extension with a mass can also be observed. They usually lack calcification, new bone formation, or periosteal reaction.

 

Histologically, GCTs display a mixture of meaty, reddish-purple tissue with soft yellow areas. They are characterized by numerous osteoclast-like giant cells dispersed among round or spindle-shaped mononuclear cells (shown below). The tumor stroma is well-vascularized with bands of cellular or collagenous fibrous tissue. 

 

Malignancy transformation is rare (<1%) in GCTs, though possible (statement 4).

The treatment of choice for GCT is extended curettage and bone grafting. GCT in the relatively insignificant bone like the distal ulna, clavicle, and proximal fibula is treated by resection without reconstruction. Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce the proliferation of osteoclasts and hence have been shown to stabilize local and metastatic disease. Radiation can be used for spinal or sacral tumors.

Denosumab is an anti-RANKL antibody that can be used to stop the osteolytic process. It can be used in advanced stage 3 lesions or lesions in inoperable locations.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: All of the following can lead to an increase in temperature of the body in the first two hours following death except:
questions.raw_text: All of the following can lead to an increase in temperature of the body in the first two hours following death except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cyanide poisoning

Cholera, septicemia, and sunstroke lead to an increase in body temperature in the first two hours following death.

Postmortem caloricity is the condition in which the temperature of the body remains raised for about the first two hours after death.

It occurs:

  • When the regulation of body temperature has been severely disturbed before death as in sunstroke, pontine hemorrhage
  • Increased heat production in muscles due to convulsions as in tetanus and strychnine poisoning
  • When there has been increased bacterial activity as in septicemia, cholera

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents with heat intolerance and weight loss for the past few weeks. He has lost 10 kgs despite having an increased appetite. On examination, he has a fine tremor of the hands, and his thyroid is enlarged. Lab investigations reveal low TSH and elevated T3 and T4. What is the most common ocular motility defect seen in this condition?
questions.raw_text: A 40-year-old male presents with heat intolerance and weight loss for the past few weeks. He has lost 10 kgs despite having an increased appetite. On examination, he has a fine tremor of the hands, and his thyroid is enlarged. Lab investigations reveal low TSH and elevated T3 and T4. What is the most common ocular motility defect seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Elevator restriction

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Grave's disease. The most common ocular motility defect seen in Grave's disease is elevator restriction.

It occurs due to the fibrotic contracture of the inferior rectus muscle. The inferior rectus muscle has to relax during the elevation of the eye. The fibrosis of the muscle restricts its relaxation and thus elevation of the eye is restricted.

There is an inability to look up (in both adducted and abducted positions) along with esotropia (fibrosis of the medial rectus). 

Only the belly of the muscle is involved in thyroid myopathy; the tendon is characteristically spared.

Ocular motility restriction in order of frequency is as follows:

  • Elevation defect
  • Abduction defect, due to fibrosis of the medial rectus
  • Depression defect, due to fibrosis of the superior rectus
  • Adduction defect, due to fibrosis of the lateral rectus
