questions.text: A 45-year-old man has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus. When should you refer him to an ophthalmologist?
questions.raw_text: A 45-year-old man has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus. When should you refer him to an ophthalmologist?

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately at the time of diagnosis

questions.correct_answer: B. Immediately at the time of diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediately at the time of diagnosis

Patients with type 2 diabetes should undergo a comprehensive ophthalmological examination to screen for diabetic retinopathy at diagnosis, followed by an annual examination of the fundus.

In patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus, screening for retinopathy is recommended 3 to 5 years after diagnosis. Annual fundal examination is recommended thereafter.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presented to the psychiatric outpatient department with a 2-year history of repetitive involuntary blinking, shoulder shrugging, sniffing, vocalization, and whistling. Which of the following drugs is not used in the treatment of this disorder?
questions.raw_text: A 16-year-old boy presented to the psychiatric outpatient department with a 2-year history of repetitive involuntary blinking, shoulder shrugging, sniffing, vocalization, and whistling. Which of the following drugs is not used in the treatment of this disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clozapine

The given history is suggestive of Tourette's syndrome. Clozapine, contrary to many other atypical antipsychotics, has not been found to be useful in the treatment of tics (including Tourette's syndrome).

Treatment modalities used for Tourette's syndrome (in order of preference):

  • Detection and treatment of co-morbidities like OCD, ADHD, depression, and anxiety. 
  • Education and behavioral treatments -  habit reversal, exposure, and response prevention are the behavioral treatments of choice. 
  • Adrenergic alpha-2 agonists (always to be tried first before starting antipsychotics) - clonidine and guanfacine are found to be effective. 
  • Antipsychotics - aripiprazole and risperidone are effective and preferred over typical antipsychotics. Pimozide and haloperidol may be more efficient but are often poorly tolerated and need constant monitoring.

Note: Botulinum toxin has been used to treat painful focal motor tics affecting the neck muscles.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is involved in recognition and clearance of necrotic cells?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is involved in recognition and clearance of necrotic cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inflammasome

Inflammasomes are involved in the recognition and clearance of necrotic cells.

Inflammasomes are involved in pyroptosis, a process of programmed cell death distinct from apoptosis and necrosis. This process is dependent on caspases 1, 4, and 5 and is responsible for killing infected cells. It occurs in the following sequence:

  • Activation of the inflammasome complex by infected cells
  • This causes activation of caspase-1
  • This results in the generation of IL-1, which is responsible for fever, inflammation, and leukocyte recruitment

Other options :

Option B: Toll-like receptors (TLR)- recognize molecules shared by pathogens

Option C: P-selectins - an important role in the initial recruitment of WBCs at the site of inflammation & in platelet recruitment and aggregation at the site of injury.      

Option D: Mannose receptor - C-type lectin receptor involved in the recognition of glycosylated pathogens and apoptotic cells, not primarily necrotic cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
What is the correct sequence of events that occur during necrosis?

1) Cell swelling
2) Karyolysis
3) Karyorrhexis
4) Pyknosis
questions.raw_text:
What is the correct sequence of events that occur during necrosis?

1) Cell swelling
2) Karyolysis
3) Karyorrhexis
4) Pyknosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 4, 3, 2

The sequence of events in necrosis is: cellular swelling → pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis

Necrosis is defined as the spectrum of morphological changes that follow cell death due to the progressive degradative action of enzymes.

Morphological changes that occur in necrosis are as follows:

Cytoplasmic changes -

  • Increased eosinophilic staining on H&E specimens
  • Moth-eaten appearance of the cytoplasm - due to vacuolated cytoplasmic organelles formed by enzymatic degradation
  • Glassy and homogenous cytoplasm - due to loss of glycogen in the cytoplasm

Nuclear changes -

  • Pyknosis - the nucleus first shrinks and becomes more condensed
  • Karyorrhexis - fragmentation of the pyknotic nucleus
  • Karyolysis - the nucleus fades away, leaving behind only the cell membrane or empty cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Anaplasia refers to:
questions.raw_text: Anaplasia refers to:

options.label: B
options.text: Variation in cell size and shape

options.label: C
options.text: Replacement of one type of cell by other

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lack of differentiation

Anaplasia refers to a lack of differentiation.

The term anaplasia means to form backward implying a reversal of differentiation to a more primitive level. The extent to which neoplastic cells resemble normal cells, both morphologically and functionally, is called differentiation.

Anaplasia is an important morphological feature of malignant transformation.

The morphological features of malignancy include:

  • Anaplasia
  • Pleomorphism - variation in the size and shape of cells
  • Increased N: C ratio (nucleus: cytoplasmic ratio) - around 1:4 in normal cells, increases to 1:1 in malignant cells
  • Hyperchromasia - coarsely clumped and darkly stained chromatin within irregular nuclei
  • Increased mitosis - atypical, bizarre mitotic figures
  • Loss of polarity - sheets or large masses of tumor cells grow in an anarchic, disorganized fashion

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Deficiency in which of the following vitamins can lead to metaplastic transformation in the lung?
questions.raw_text: Deficiency in which of the following vitamins can lead to metaplastic transformation in the lung?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin A

The deficiency of vitamin A (retinoic acid) induces squamous metaplasia in the respiratory epithelium.

This occurs because vitamin A is essential for maintaining the normal differentiation of epithelial cells. Without it, the normal columnar ciliated epithelium can transform into a stratified squamous epithelium, impairing mucociliary function and increasing susceptibility to infection and damage.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following does not usually undergo hyperplasia?
questions.raw_text: Which among the following does not usually undergo hyperplasia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Skeletal and heart muscle

Skeletal muscle and heart muscle usually undergo hypertrophy, not hyperplasia.

Hyperplasia = increase in the number of cells.
Hypertrophy = increase in size of cells.

The table below shows a comparison of skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle based on their ability to undergo hyperplasia and hypertrophy:

Muscle Type       Hyperplasia Hypertrophy 
Skeletal Muscle No Yes
Cardiac Muscle  No Yes
Smooth Muscle    Yes Yes

 

Examples of physiologic hyperplasia:

  • Female breast during puberty and pregnancy (hormonal hyperplasia)
  • Uterine smooth muscle during early pregnancy
  • Compensatory hyperplasia of liver cells after partial resection

Examples of pathologic hyperplasia:

  • Endometrial hyperplasia
  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Both physiological hyperplasia and hypertrophy are simultaneously seen in which of the following individuals?
questions.raw_text: Both physiological hyperplasia and hypertrophy are simultaneously seen in which of the following individuals?

options.label: A
options.text: A 24-year-old man vigorously training for an athletic race

options.label: B
options.text: A 35-year-old woman regularly taking combined oral contraceptive pills

options.label: C
options.text: A 50-year-old man with proliferation of liver cells following transplantation

options.label: D
options.text: A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks of gestation

questions.correct_answer: D. A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks of gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks of gestation

Physiological hypertrophy and hyperplasia can be simultaneously seen in the uterus during pregnancy.

In early pregnancy, uterine growth is due to hyperplasia of uterine smooth muscle cells; however, the predominant growth of the uterus during pregnancy occurs after mid-gestation, by way of stretch‐induced myometrial hypertrophy.

Simultaneous physiological hypertrophy and hyperplasia also occur in the female breast during puberty and pregnancy.

Other options:

Option A: Enlargement of skeletal muscles in athletes is an example of physiological hypertrophy.

Option B: Combined oral contraceptive pills, causing endometrial hyperplasia, is an example of pathological hyperplasia.

Option C: Following transplantation of a liver lobe, the remaining liver cells proliferate so that the organ grows back to its original size (compensatory hyperplasia).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with long-standing hypertension develops left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following transcription factors do not play a role in this?
questions.raw_text: A patient with long-standing hypertension develops left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following transcription factors do not play a role in this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HNF

HNF (Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor)is a transcription factor primarily involved in the development and function of the liver and pancreas. It plays a crucial role in regulating genes related to glucose metabolism and is notably associated with Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY).

The transcription factors involved in cardiac muscle hypertrophy are:

  • GATA4 (GATA-binding protein 4)-activated by hypertrophic stimuli (e.g., mechanical stress, neurohormonal signals)
  • MEF2(Myocyte Enhancer Factor 2 )- activated by pressure and volume overload
  • NFAT (Nuclear Factor for Activated T-cells)-activated by calcineurin signaling; involved in the hypertrophic response

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about cellular adaptations is correct?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements about cellular adaptations is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Hyperplasia involves synthesis of intracellular components

options.label: B
options.text: Atrophy is defined as decrease in cell size only

options.label: C
options.text: Atrophy is the decrease in number and size of cells

options.label: D
options.text: Metaplasia is an irreversible replacement of a cell by another cell type

questions.correct_answer: C. Atrophy is the decrease in number and size of cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Atrophy is the decrease in number and size of cells

Atrophy is a reduction in the size of an organ or tissue due to a decrease in cell size and number.

Cellular adaptations are reversible changes in the size, number, phenotype, metabolic activity, or functions of cells in response to changes in their environment. There are 4 types:

  • Hypertrophy -
    • Increase in organ size due to an increase in the size of cells
    • Involves synthesis and assembly of intracellular structural components
  • Hyperplasia - 
    • Increase in organ size due to an increase in the number of cells
    • It is due to division and proliferation of stem cells
  • Atrophy - reduction in organ size due to a decrease in cell size and number.
  • Metaplasia - one differentiated cell type (epithelial or mesenchymal) is replaced by another cell type

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Micro-RNA are involved during which of the following stages?
questions.raw_text: Micro-RNA are involved during which of the following stages?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Post transcriptional

Micro-RNAs (miRNA) act during the post-transcriptional stage.

It is a type of non-coding RNA. The primary function of miRNA is to modulate the translation of target mRNAs into their corresponding proteins. After the target RNA is transcribed from its gene (post-transcriptional), the miRNA may either induce mRNA cleavage or repress its translation. This is referred to as gene silencing because it stops the gene from making its protein.

Note: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) are short RNA sequences that can be introduced experimentally into cells. They have functions similar to endogenous miRNA (serve as substrates for the Dicer enzyme and interact with the RNA-induced silencing complex). They may have a therapeutic role in silencing certain oncogenes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the study of heritable changes in gene expression that are not caused by alterations in DNA sequence?
questions.raw_text: What is the study of heritable changes in gene expression that are not caused by alterations in DNA sequence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epigenetics

Epigenetics is the branch of molecular biology that deals with the study of heritable changes in gene function not involving changes in the DNA sequence.

These heritable changes involve factors that mediate processes such as:

  • Histone organization 
  • DNA methylation 
  • Chromatin organization

These, in turn, regulate the genomic organization and gene expression in a cell-type-specific fashion. The dysregulation of these epigenomic factors plays a major role in the development of malignancy.

Other options:

  • Option A: Genomics is the study of the entire genome, including its structure, function, evolution, and mapping.
  • Option B: Phylogenetics is the study of evolutionary relationships among biological species or organisms.
  • Option D: Molecular genetics focuses on the structure and function of genes at a molecular level.

Note: Green tea catechins have been reported to modulate epigenetic processes. They can reverse the DNA methylation of tumor suppressor genes and increase the transcription of these genes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Angiography of the upper limb vessels in a patient shows a blockage in the brachial artery. All of the following vessels will have decreased flow, except:
questions.raw_text: Angiography of the upper limb vessels in a patient shows a blockage in the brachial artery. All of the following vessels will have decreased flow, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anterior circumflex humeral artery

The anterior circumflex humeral artery is a branch of the axillary artery. Hence, it is unlikely to have a decreased flow due to blockage in the brachial artery. 

The brachial artery has 3 branches: 

  • Profunda brachii (accompanies radial nerve in the spiral groove) gives off nutrient artery to the humerus and an ascending branch which anastomoses with posterior circumflex humeral artery. It then divides into: 
    • Anterior descending artery (Radial collateral artery)  
    • Posterior descending artery (Middle collateral artery) 
  • Superior ulnar collateral artery (accompanies ulnar nerve)
  • Inferior ulnar collateral (supratrochlear) artery

The image given below shows branches of the brachial artery.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug decreases Lipoprotein(a)?
questions.raw_text: Which drug decreases Lipoprotein(a)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Niacin

The drug that decreases lipoprotein(a) is niacin.

Niacin is the only lipid-lowering agent that significantly lowers lipoprotein(a) levels. However, its side effects limit its use. Niacin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, reducing free fatty acids (FFA) release into circulation. It also decreases LDL, VLDL, and triglycerides and increases HDL cholesterol. It could be used in statin-intolerant patients. 

The main adverse effects of niacin are cutaneous flushing and pruritus, which can be controlled by pretreatment with aspirin. Niacin can also cause hepatotoxicity (a medically serious side effect manifesting as an increase in serum transaminases), GI toxicity (dyspepsia), hyperuricemia, and hyperglycemia. Concurrent use of niacin with statins can cause myopathy. 

Other options: 

Options A and C: Fenofibrate and Gemfibrozil belong to the fibrate group of drugs. Fibrates bind to peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) and reduce triglyceride levels by PPARα-mediated stimulation of fatty acid oxidation, increased lipoprotein lipase (LPL) synthesis, and reduced expression of apo C-III. Fibrates increase the HDL by PPARα-mediated stimulation of apo A-I and apo A-II expression.

Fibrates are the drugs of choice for treating type III hyperlipoproteinemia, as well as mild hypertriglyceridemia.

Option D: Colestipol is a bile acid sequestrant, i.e., it binds to the bile acid in the intestine and gets excreted in the stools. This depletion in bile acid increases bile acid production, which utilises the hepatic cholesterol. This increases the LDL receptors, thereby increasing the LDL-cholesterol clearance. Severe hypertriglyceridemia is a contraindication to the use of colestipol.

It can be used as a second-line agent if statins do not lower the LDL levels sufficiently or in patients who can not tolerate statins.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient has a fever, cough, and cold. The chest x-ray is given below. What will be the examination finding in the infrascapular region?
questions.raw_text: The patient has a fever, cough, and cold. The chest x-ray is given below. What will be the examination finding in the infrascapular region?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dull note on percussion

The above X-ray and symptoms are suggestive of pleural effusion secondary to a lower respiratory tract infection. On examination, dullness to percussion will be observed.

Pleural effusion refers to the pathological accumulation of fluid in the pleural space due to

  • excess fluid formation from the interstitial spaces of the lung, parietal pleura, or peritoneal cavity
  • decreased fluid removal by the lymphatics

Pleural effusion may present with dyspnea, pleuritic pain, dry cough, and associated symptoms like fever, weight loss, edema, and ascites depending on the etiology. On examination, there may be tachypnea, dullness on percussion and decreased/absent breath sounds at the base(s).

The etiology of pleural effusion can be of two types:

  • Exudative: disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage because of local factors. Examples include malignancy, infections, and pulmonary embolism.
  • Transudative: disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage due to systemic factors. Examples include congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome.

Option A: Hyperresonance is a sign of pneumothorax or emphysema.

Option B: Crackles are heard in cases of pulmonary edema or pneumonia.

Option D: Stridor is due to a lesion in the upper airways, usually tracheal or laryngeal.

Pearl: Types of pleural effusion

Transudative Pleural effusion

  • Congestive heart failure (most common)
  • Cirrhosis
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Myxedema 
  • Peritoneal dialysis
  • Urinothorax
  • Hypoalbuminemia
  • Constrictive pericarditis
  • Superior vena cava obstruction

Exudative Pleural effusion 

  • Infections: Tuberculosis, pneumonia, intraabdominal abscess (like- liver abscess)
  • Malignancy: Pleural mesothelioma, metastasis, lymphoma
  • Connective tissue diseases: SLE, rheumatoid arthritis
  • Drugs: Amiodarone, bromocriptine, dantrolene, dasatinib, methysergide, nitrofurantoin
  • Others:
    • Pancreatitis
    • Asbestosis
    • Pulmonary embolism
    • Hemothorax
    • Chylothorax
    • Meigs' syndrome 
    • Dressler syndrome (post-myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery)
    • Yellow nail syndrome

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A man with FUO has a job that requires traveling around the world. The bone marrow picture is shown below. Which of the following investigation would be the most appropriate in this case?
questions.raw_text: A man with FUO has a job that requires traveling around the world. The bone marrow picture is shown below. Which of the following investigation would be the most appropriate in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. rk 39 antigen test, Leishmaniasis

The given clinical vignette of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) / Fever of unknown origin (FUO) with a history of frequent travel is suggestive of an infectious cause of FUO. The given slide shows macrophages infested with intracellular Leishmania donovani bodies (arrows) characterized by a kinetoplast and characteristic double dot appearance (Leishman stain). The most likely diagnosis is leishmaniasis and it can be established by the rk 39 antigen test.

Pyrexia/ Fever of unknown origin - criteria:

  • Fever >38.3 degrees C (101 F) on 2 occasions
  • Duration > 3 weeks
  • Diagnosis is not certain after history, physical examination, and routine and obligatory investigations in spite of three OPD visits or after 3 days of hospitalization. 

Causes of FUO are enlisted in the table.

Infectious cause Non-infectious cause

Bacterial:

  • M.tuberculosis
  • Salmonella spp
  • Brucella spp
  • Chlamydia psittaci
  • Leptospira spp
  • Rickettsia spp
  • Coxiella burnetti
  • Mycoplasma spp
  • Atypical mycobacteria

Viral:

  • Cytomegalovirus
  • Epstein - Barr virus
  • Arboviruses
  • Enteroviruses
  • HIV

Fungal:

  • Candida albicans
  • Cryptococcus neoformans
  • Histoplasma capsulatum
  • Aspergillus spp
  • Coccidiodes immitis 

Parasitic:

  • Plasmodium spp
  • Leishmania spp
  • Trypanosoma spp
  • Toxoplasma gondii
  • Wuchereria bancrofti
  • Brugia malayi

Neoplasm:

  • Lymphoma
  • Leukemia
  • Myeloma
  • Renal cancer
  • Colon cancer
  • Liver cancer
  • Metabolic disorder
  • Gout
  • Porphyria

Connective tissue disorder:

  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
  • Polyarteritis nodosa 

Granulomatous disease:

  • Crohn's disease
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Polymyositis

 

Leishmaniasis is a slowly progressing indigenous disease caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Leishmania. It is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Phlebotomus sandfly which inoculates the flagellated promastigotes into the skin of the host in developing countries.

In human beings, the disease presents in four different forms with a broad range of clinical manifestations:

  • Visceral leishmaniasis, or kala-azar,
  • Cutaneous leishmaniasis,
  • Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, and
  • Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis.

The life cycle of Leishmania involves two forms,

  • The promastigote which develops and lives extracellularly in the sandfly vector and
  • The amastigote multiplies intracellularly in the reticuloendothelial cells of the host.

It lowers immunity, causes persistent fever, anemia, liver and spleen enlargement, and if left untreated, death may occur due to opportunistic infection.

The microscopic demonstration of amastigotes from bone marrow is the gold standard for the diagnosis of Kala-azar.

For microscopic demonstration of the parasite, the materials collected are:

-Peripheral blood

-Bone marrow

-Splenic aspirate

-Enlarged lymph node. 

Other diagnostic tests are: 

  • Rapid diagnostic test: rK39 Rapid diagnostic test and Kala-azar dipstick test strip. This is recommended by National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) in India.
  • Parasitological diagnosis: Demonstration of LD bodies in buffy coat smear - confirmatory.
  • Aldehyde test of Napier: Widely used for surveillance.
  • Serological tests for diagnosis: Rapid dipstick test, Direct agglutination test, ELISA, Indirect Fluorescent Antibody Test
  • Leishmanin (Montenegro) test: Induration of 5mm or more is considered positive, usually positive 4-6 weeks (delayed-hypersensitivity) after onset in cutaneous leishmaniasis, valuable for distinguishing immune from nonimmune subjects and endemicity.

The given images show amastigotes in the bone marrow. 

Drugs used in the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis are sodium stibogluconate, miltefosine, and amphotericin. Liposomal amphotericin single dose 10mg/Kg IV is the first line of treatment in India.

Pearl: Important serological tests for the diagnosis of parasitic infections

Serological tests are helpful for the detection and surveillance of many protozoal and helminthic infections.

These tests are basically of 2 types:

  • Tests for antigen detection
  • Tests for antibody detection

Antigen Detection:

Antibody detection:

  • Complement fixation test (CFT)
  • Indirect hemagglutination test (IHA)
  • Indirect immunofluorescent antibody test (IFA)
  • Rapid immunochromatography test
  • ELISA test

Pearl: AIDS-defining opportunistic infections and neoplasm

Infections:

  • Protozoal and helminthic infections-
    • Cryptosporidiosis or Isosporiasis (cystoisosporiasis) - Chronic intestinal
    • Toxoplasmosis (pneumonia or CNS infection)
  • Fungal infections-
    • Candidiasis (esophageal, tracheal, or pulmonary)
    • Cryptococcosis (CNS infection)
    • Coccidioidomycosis (disseminated)
    • Pneumocystosis (pneumonia or disseminated infection)
    • Histoplasmosis (disseminated)
  • Bacterial infections-
    • Mycobacteriosis (“atypical,” e.g., Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare) disseminated or extrapulmonary
    • Mycobacterium tuberculosis (pulmonary or extrapulmonary)
    • Nocardiosis (pneumonia, meningitis, disseminated)
    • Salmonella infections, disseminated
  • Viral infections-
    • Cytomegalovirus (pulmonary, intestinal, retinitis, or CNS infections)
    • Herpes simplex virus (localized or disseminated infection)
    • Varicella-zoster virus (localized or disseminated infection)
    • Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

Neoplasms:

  • Kaposi sarcoma
  • Primary lymphoma of brain
  • Invasive cancer of uterine cervix

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A concerned mother of an infant, known case of cystic fibrosis, presents to your OPD with complaints of abdominal pain, loose stools not settling with antibiotics, and other medications. She recently stopped breastfeeding and switched to formula feeds. On examination, you find petechial rashes. Which of the following below mentioned causes would not prompt you to suspect a deficiency of Vitamin K in this child?
questions.raw_text: A concerned mother of an infant, known case of cystic fibrosis, presents to your OPD with complaints of abdominal pain, loose stools not settling with antibiotics, and other medications. She recently stopped breastfeeding and switched to formula feeds. On examination, you find petechial rashes. Which of the following below mentioned causes would not prompt you to suspect a deficiency of Vitamin K in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Artificial milk feeds

Vitamin K deficiency occurs mostly in breastfed infants not in artificial milk-fed babies, as the formula milk is fortified.

The use of broad-spectrum antibiotics that eliminate the intestinal vitamin K2- producing bacteria can cause vitamin K deficiency. Biliary obstruction causes malabsorption of the fat-soluble vitamin K.

There are 3 forms of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) of the newborn:

  Secondary to maternal intake of medications Early VKDB (classic hemorrhagic disease of the newborn)  Late VKDB
Onset At birth 1 to 14 days 2 to 12 weeks
Cause Drugs that cross the placenta and interferes with Vit K function eg. phenobarbital, phenytoin, warfarin Low stores of Vitamin K at birth, poor transfer of Vitamin K across the placenta, Inadequate intake during the first few days of life.  In breastfed babies and in those with malabsorption of vitamin K (cystic fibrosis, biliary atresia)

Early VKBD of the newborn is prevented by the administration of a single intramuscular (IM) injection of vitamin K (1 mg) at birth.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient comes with complaints of progressive weakness as the day progresses. He is found to have antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Which is the most common ocular finding in this disease?
questions.raw_text: A 45-year-old patient comes with complaints of progressive weakness as the day progresses. He is found to have antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Which is the most common ocular finding in this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ptosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myasthenia gravis and ptosis is the most common ocular feature of the disease.

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction most commonly caused by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The disorder is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles where the weakness increases during repeated use and may improve following rest.

Ptosis and diplopia are common initial complaints due to early involvement of the lids and extraocular muscles (EOMs). Of them, Ptosis is a more common manifestation than diplopia. Ptosis in myasthenia gravis is insidious, bilateral, and frequently asymmetrical.

Investigations of myasthenia gravis include:

  1. Ice pack test -This tests for a transient improvement of the ptotic eyelid on placing an ice pack for 2 minutes, as  the cold inhibits the breakdown of acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase.
  2. Tensilon (Edrophonium) test - This tests for a transient improvement in the weakness on administration of a short-acting anticholinesterase such as edrophonium.
  3. Antibody testing - for Acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies, MuSK protein antibodies helps support a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes catalyze the rate-limiting step of glycogenolysis?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following enzymes catalyze the rate-limiting step of glycogenolysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycogen phosphorylase

The rate-limiting step in glycogenolysis is catalyzed by the enzyme, glycogen phosphorylase.

The process of phosphorolytic cleavage of the α1 → 4 linkages of glycogen to yield single units of glucose 1-phosphate, is catalyzed by the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase.

Glycogen phosphorylase requires pyridoxal phosphate as the coenzyme The phosphate group is catalytically active. There are different isoenzymes of glycogen phosphorylase in the liver, muscle, and brain.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50 -year-old woman presents with a gradual loss of visual acuity in the right eye. A CT head post-contrast reveals thickening of the optic nerve-sheath complex with a tram-track appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 50 -year-old woman presents with a gradual loss of visual acuity in the right eye. A CT head post-contrast reveals thickening of the optic nerve-sheath complex with a tram-track appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Optic nerve sheath meningioma

Based on the given clinical scenario and radiologic finding, the most likely diagnosis is optic nerve sheath meningioma, a benign tumour arising from the arachnoid cap cells of the optic nerve sheath. It is most frequently seen in middle-aged women, with bilateral cases linked to neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF-2). Post-contrast CT or MRI show tram-track sign.

The post-contrast T1 weighted axial MRI image below shows a hypoattenuating optic nerve surrounded by the peripheral enhancement of the tumour(tram-track sign):


Optic nerve glioma is intrinsic to optic nerve, commonly seen in children, often associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1). It presents as fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve on imaging. The tram-track sign is useful in differentiating between optic nerve sheath meningioma and optic nerve gliomas.

Pearl: Tram Track Appearance in Various Conditions

Tram tracks or tram track signs are medical signs that bear some resemblance to tramway tracks (Railway Track).

1. Pulmonology

  • When found in the lungs, tram tracks are radiologic signs that are usually accompanied by pulmonary edema in cases of congestive heart failure and bronchiectasis.
  • Tram tracks are caused by bronchial wall thickening, and can be detected on a lateral chest X-ray.

2. Nephrology

  • The term "tram tracks" is also used to describe the basement membrane duplication found on light microscopy that is characteristic of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) type I.
  • It is less commonly associated with types II and III.

3. Neurology

  • The term has also been used to describe findings associated with optic nerve sheath meningioma.
  • Tram track-shaped calcifications in the cerebral cortex indicate Sturge-Weber syndrome.

4. Mammary glands:

  • Tram track appearance in mammography/USG indicates Duct Ectasia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Fimbriectomy is also known as:
questions.raw_text: Fimbriectomy is also known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kroener's procedure

Fimbriectomy is also known as Kroener's procedure. This procedure involves ligation of the distal ampulla of the tube with two permanent sutures. Then, resection of the infundibulum of the tube is done.

Some more techniques of permanent sterilization include:

Pomeroy method - The fallopian tube is identified on each side, brought out through the incision. The middle portion is formed into a loop which is tied at the base with catgut and excised. This is the most commonly used technique.

Uchida's method - The tubal serosa is stripped off the muscular layer in the midsegment of the tube. The muscle layer is excised. The proximal end is ligated and buried in the broad ligament. This minimal excision of the tube preserves the potential for tuboplasty.

Irving's procedure - The mid-portion of the tube is ligated and the intervening portion is excised. The proximal end is buried in the myometrium and the distal end is buried in the broad ligament. It is a reliable method but irreversible and may require a laparotomy incision.

Madlener's procedure - A loop of the fallopian tube is crushed and then ligated with a nonabsorbable suture.

Pearl: Classification Of Contraceptives Based On Effectiveness

Category Failure rate in first year Contraceptive
First tier  < 2 % IUCD, Implants, Sterilization
Second tier  3-9 % Hormonal - oral, injected, transdermal patches, transvaginal rings
Third tier  10-20 % Barrier, Fertility awareness method
Fourth tier  21-30 % Spermicidal preparations

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: You have a 55-year-old male patient with a history of infective endocarditis presents with high-grade fever, new-onset murmurs, and splinter hemorrhages. What is the correct way to collect blood culture samples?
questions.raw_text: You have a 55-year-old male patient with a history of infective endocarditis presents with high-grade fever, new-onset murmurs, and splinter hemorrhages. What is the correct way to collect blood culture samples?

options.label: A
options.text: 3 sets of culture samples, 2 from the peripheral lines and 1 from the affected valve with a gap of 30 minutes between the collection of each

options.label: B
options.text: 2 samples, 1 from the periphery and 1 from atrium, with a gap of 30 minutes between the collection of each

options.label: D
options.text: 1 from the blood and 1 from the urinary catheter

questions.correct_answer: A. 3 sets of culture samples, 2 from the peripheral lines and 1 from the affected valve with a gap of 30 minutes between the collection of each
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3 sets of culture samples, 2 from the peripheral lines and 1 from the affected valve with a gap of 30 minutes between the collection of each

Correct way to collect sample is 3 sets of culture samples, 2 from the peripheral lines and 1 from the affected valve with a gap of 30 minutes between the collection of each

The American Heart Association recommends collecting three sets of blood culture samples for patients with suspected infective endocarditis. One set should be collected from the affected valve, if possible. The other two sets should be collected from peripheral veins. There should be a gap of at least 30 minutes between the collection of each set.

Note: The 2023 Duke-ISCVID guidelines considers blood culture as the gold standard for diagnosing infective endocarditis. While collecting three samples from different sites and at specific time intervals is still recommended, it is no longer strictly necessary. 

Pearl: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

  1. Pathologic criteria
  2. Clinical criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

The presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established either when:

  • Symptoms resolve and do not recur with <4 days of antibiotic therapy OR
  • If surgery or autopsy yields no pathologic or macroscopic evidence of endocarditis in <4 days of antimicrobial therapy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A baby was delivered at home in a village. Until which day of life should an ASHA worker visit this baby?
questions.raw_text: A baby was delivered at home in a village. Until which day of life should an ASHA worker visit this baby?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 42

Under the Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK) guidelines, ASHA workers should visit all newborns up to 42 days of life, according to the following schedule. 

  • 4 visits after institutional delivery (healthy newborn): Day of discharge/Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, and Day 42.
  • 5 visits after home delivery (healthy newborn): Day 1 (within 24 hours), Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, and Day 42.
  • 9 visits for 'At-risk' newborn: Day 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 14, 21, 28, and 42. This is a newly defined risk category under SSBSK.

During her visits, ASHA workers must record weight, ensure vaccination, and register births. ASHA is entitled to financial incentives for completed home visits under SSBSK, and additional incentives for 'At-risk' identification/follow-up and timely referrals.

Pearl: ASHA

ASHA stands for Accredited Social Health Activist.

General norms with respect to ASHA workers:

  • Must be a woman in the age group of 25-45 years - married/divorced/widow
  • Must be a resident of that village
  • Formal education of up to 10th standard 
    • If no candidates are available, the requirement can be relaxed to the 8th standard
  • At least 1 ASHA for a population of 1000 
    • In tribal, hilly, and desert areas, the norm can be relaxed to 1 ASHA per habitation

States can relax the norms on population and educational qualifications on a case-to-case basis, depending on the local conditions. However, these are exceptions and not the general norm.

Responsibilities of ASHA:

    • Health education and awareness
    • Reproductive and child health and family planning
    • Facilitate the access to health services
    • Promotion of sanitation and household toilet construction
    • Provision of primary medical care for minor ailments
    • Provider of DOTS
    • Depot holder of essentials like ORS, iron and folic acid tablets, condoms, disposable delivery kits, etc.
    • Dispersal of health information on her community to higher centres
    • Some responsibilities are integrated with Anganwadi workers and Auxiliary Nurse Midwife

Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK) unifies HBNC and HBYC into a single continuum-of-care programme (birth to 36 months), with a formal risk-stratification approach.

Category Visits Schedule
Healthy newborn, institutional delivery 4 visits Day of discharge/Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, Day 42
Healthy newborn, home delivery 5 visits Day 1 (within 24 h), Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, Day 42
'At-risk' newborn (LBW < 2.5 kg, preterm <37wks, congenital anomaly, not breastfed, SNCU/NICU discharge) 9 visits Day 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 14, 21, 28, 42
Young child (6 weeks–36 months), quarterly Home visits 8 visits 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 months

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: All of the following increases gastric acid secretion except:
questions.raw_text: All of the following increases gastric acid secretion except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serotonin

All of the above increase gastric acid secretion except serotonin.

Serotonin is localized in the enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa and within neurons of the GI tract. Serotonin inhibits gastric acid secretion. It stimulates the production and release of gastric and colonic mucus. Serotonin acts as an enteric neurotransmitter and increases intestinal motility.

The main factors that stimulate gastric secretion are acetylcholine, gastrin, and histamine. Parasympathetic stimulation releases Ach which stimulates the secretion of

  • pepsinogen by peptic cells
  • hydrochloric acid by parietal cells
  • mucus by mucous cells.

Both gastrin and histamine strongly stimulate acid secretion by parietal cells but have little effect on other cells.

The stomach mucosa has two important types of tubular glands:

  • The oxyntic (gastric) glands secrete hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, and mucus.
  • The pyloric glands secrete mainly mucus for protection of the pyloric mucosa from the stomach acid. They also secrete the hormone gastrin.

Note- Serotonin released from the small intestine triggers vomiting by stimulation of 5HT3 receptors. Therefore, 5HT3 antagonists like ondansetron are used as antiemetics.

Pearl: Stimuli that affect gastrin secretion

Stimuli that increase gastrin secretion

  • Luminal - Peptides and amino acids
  • Neural - Increased vagal discharge via GRP
  • Bloodborne
    • Ca 2+
    • Epinephrine

Stimuli that inhibit gastrin secretion

  • Luminal
    • Acid
    • Somatostatin 
  • Bloodborne- Secretin, GIP, VIP, glucagon, calcitonin

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the length of the eustachian tube?
questions.raw_text: What is the length of the eustachian tube?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 36 mm

The length of the eustachian tube is 36 mm.

The eustachian tube is also called the auditory or pharyngotympanic tube. It connects the nasopharynx with the tympanic cavity. It is directed forward, downward, and medially with an angle of 45° to the horizontal axis.

It is 36 mm long in adults and is divided into two parts:

  • Bony part - forms the outer one-third of the tube as it is located near the middle ear and is 12 mm in size.
  • Fibrocartilaginous part - forms the inner two-thirds as it is located near the nasopharynx and is 24 mm in size.

In the middle ear, it opens in the anterior wall, and in the nasopharynx, it opens 1-1.25 cm posterior to the posterior end of the inferior turbinate.

Note: The eustachian tube in infants is 18 mm, i.e., about half the size of an adult eustachian tube.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following malignancies, a liver transplantation is not contraindicated?
questions.raw_text: In which of the following malignancies, a liver transplantation is not contraindicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Testicular cancer

Liver transplantation is relatively not contraindicated in testicular cancer. Past history of malignancy is a relative contraindication to transplantation, because the effect of surgery and resulting immunosuppression may predispose the patient to early recurrence of the tumor.

Testicular carcinoma has a relatively low risk of recurrence (0%-10%) following transplantation. In contrast, renal carcinoma, breast carcinoma, and melanoma pose a higher risk of recurrence, exceeding 10%.

The left and right images below show her current appearance and her appearance last month, respectively. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?
questions.raw_text: A 50-year-old woman was diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis and was started on levothyroxine 2 weeks ago. She now presents to your clinic with abdominal pain and dizziness. The left and right images below show her current appearance and her appearance last month, respectively. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperglycemia

The given image showing skin hyperpigmentation in a patient with severe dizziness and a history of autoimmune thyroiditis points to a diagnosis of Addison’s disease. Hyperglycemia is not a feature of this condition. Hypocortisolism leads to hypoglycemia in these patients.

Addison’s disease is primary adrenal insufficiency characterized by the disruption of glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and androgen secretion. Primary adrenal insufficiency is most commonly caused by autoimmune adrenalitis and coincident autoimmune disease occurring in these patients most frequently includes thyroid autoimmune disease, vitiligo, and premature ovarian failure.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Attributable risk calculated to understand the relation between smoking and lung cancer is 90%. Which of the following is true?
questions.raw_text: Attributable risk calculated to understand the relation between smoking and lung cancer is 90%. Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: 10% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated

options.label: B
options.text: 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in population if smoking is eliminated

options.label: C
options.text: 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated

options.label: D
options.text: 10% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in population if smoking is eliminated

questions.correct_answer: C. 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated

Attributable risk (AR) describes the extent of outcome (lung cancer) that can be attributed to exposure (smoking). In the given scenario, an AR of 90% means that 90% of lung cancer cases among smokers are attributable to smoking. Therefore, 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated.

AR is the difference in incidence rates of disease between an exposed group and an unexposed group. AR is indicative of the extent of the disease attributed to the exposure. It also refers to the amount of disease that could be eliminated in the exposed persons if the exposure is controlled or eliminated. It also helps to determine the impact a successful preventive or public health program might have in case the exposure to cause is reduced or eliminated.

Population-attributable risk (PAR) is the difference in the incidence of disease in the total population and the incidence of disease among those not exposed to the supposed cause. PAR is useful in providing an estimate of the amount by which the disease could be reduced in that whole population if the suspected factor was eliminated or modified.

For example, a PAR of 90% in the context of smoking and lung cancer means that 90% cases of lung cancer in the population can be attributed to smoking.

Relative risk is defined as the ratio of incidence of the disease (outcome) among exposed and unexposed groups. It helps in establishing the association between a cause and a disease. However, it does not help in assessing the extent of the cause bringing about the disease (outcome).

Pearl: Relative and Attributable Risk

Relative Risk:

  • Ratio of incidence of disease or death among exposed to that among the non-exposed is called relative risk (RR).
  • It is also called risk ratio.
  • It is the direct measure of the strength of association between suspected cause and effect in cohort studies.
  • RR < 1 indicates inverse association(protective effect)
  • RR = 1 indicates no association.
  • RR > 1 indicates positive association.
  • RR of 2 indicates a 100% increase in risk.
  • Relative risk calculation (RR) = [ a/(a+b) ]/ [ c/(c+d) ] where, 
  Cancer
Exposure   yes no
yes a b
no c d

 

Attributable Risk:

  • Attributable risk (AR) is the difference in incidence rates or proportions of disease or death between an exposed and non-exposed group.
  • It is expressed in percentage and gives the extent to which the disease can be attributed to the exposure in a cohort study.

questions.text: While discharging a patient who underwent a  vesicovaginal fistula repair, which of the following would you recommend?
questions.raw_text: While discharging a patient who underwent a  vesicovaginal fistula repair, which of the following would you recommend?

options.label: A
options.text: Sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoid pregnancy for a year

options.label: B
options.text: Sexual abstinence  for 3 weeks and avoid pregnancy for 6 months

options.label: C
options.text: Sexual abstinence  for 6 weeks and avoid pregnancy for a year

options.label: D
options.text: Sexual abstinence for 6 months and avoid pregnancy for 6 years

questions.correct_answer: A. Sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoid pregnancy for a year
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoid pregnancy for a year

While discharging a patient who underwent vesicovaginal fistula repair, sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoiding pregnancy for a year would be recommended. 

Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of urinary fistula which commonly arises due to obstetric trauma. Small fistulas due to difficult childbirth can heal spontaneously. Most established fistulas need to be repaired vaginally usually after 3 months to allow the inflammation to subside. Post-operatively, continuous bladder drainage for 14 days along with antibiotics is recommended. Vaginal or speculum examination and intercourse are not advised for 3 months. Avoiding pregnancy for a year is also recommended. A cesarean section is usually done for future pregnancies.

Presenting features of VVF include constant dribbling of urine/ true incontinence. Excoriation of the vagina, vulva, and thighs can occur due to constant contact with urine. Few patients might develop bladder stones. Vaginal urine collection can be seen on retraction of the posterior vaginal wall with a speculum. A bimanual examination can be used to assess the fixity and scarring of the surrounding tissues. A cystourethroscopy can be used for localization and assessing bladder mucosa viability.

Pearl: Indications & contraindications for induction of labor

Indications:
  • Uncontrolled maternal diabetes mellitus
  • Gestational hypertension
  • Pre-eclampsia
  • Post-term pregnancy
  • Abruption placentae
  • Premature rupture of membranes
  • Rh-isoimmunization
  • Intra-uterine growth restriction (IUGR)
  • Intra-uterine death (IUD)
  • Oligohydramnios
Contraindications:
  • Contracted/distorted pelvis and cephalopelvic disproportion
  • Placenta previa or vasa previa
  • Active genital herpes
  • Pelvic tumor & carcinoma cervix
  • Transverse lie or footling breech
  • Appreciable macrosomia
  • Severe hydrocephalus
  • Umbilical cord prolapse
  • High-risk pregnancy with fetal compromise
  • Previous classical cesarean or hysterotomy
  • Previous history of uterine rupture
  • Pelvic surgeries like vesicovaginal fistula/rectovaginal fistula/pelvic floor repair (third or fourth-degree perineal tears repair)
  • Previous 3 or more lower transverse cesarian sections.

questions.text: A farmer from the sub-Himalayan belt had a thorn prick injury a year back and developed a warty, verrucous growth at the site of prick. A skin biopsy sample was taken and sent for histopathological examination. The characteristic microscopic body as shown in the image was seen. questions.raw_text: A farmer from the sub-Himalayan belt had a thorn prick injury a year back and developed a warty, verrucous growth at the site of prick. A skin biopsy sample was taken and sent for histopathological examination. The characteristic microscopic body as shown in the image was seen. Which of the following could be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chromoblastomycosis

The history of a slowly spreading warty, verrucous lesion following a thorn prick injury and the histopathological image showing medlar bodies is suggestive of chromoblastomycosis.

Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a subcutaneous mycotic infection that is usually caused by traumatic inoculation. Over months to years, the primary lesion becomes verrucous and wart-like with extension along the draining lymphatics. 

Histologically, the lesions are granulomatous and the dark sclerotic bodies may be seen within leukocytes or giant cells called medlar/copper penny bodies.

questions.text: The following clinical examination was performed. What lesion would cause an exaggerated reflex?
questions.raw_text: The following clinical examination was performed. What lesion would cause an exaggerated reflex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Upper motor neuron

The examination being performed is the ankle jerk reflex, also known as the Achilles reflex. Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions are associated with exaggerated deep tendon reflexes.

Hyperreflexia is a feature of UMN nerve injury. There may be an acute decrease in reflexes, but this is normally followed by hyperreflexia. LMN lesions on the other hand will present with depressed reflexes.

UMNs refer to corticospinal tract neurons and brainstem neurons that control spinal motor neurons. Injury to UMNs leads to:
  • Spasticity
  • Hypertonia 
  • Hyperreflexia
  • Abnormal plantar extensor reflex (positive Babinski sign). 

Other options:

Options A, B and D: Polyneuropathy/ neuropathic weakness and radiculopathy are types of lower motor neuron weakness and will not cause exaggerated reflexes.

The following image shows the Babinski reflex:

questions.text: What is the amount of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 litres of water if the 4th, 5th, and 6th cups of a Horrock’s apparatus show distinct blue color?
questions.raw_text: What is the amount of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 litres of water if the 4th, 5th, and 6th cups of a Horrock’s apparatus show distinct blue color?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 8 grams

The dose of bleaching powder required is 8 grams.

It is given by (n x 2) gms for 455 litres of water, where n is the number of the first cup that shows distinct blue color. In this scenario, the dose of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 litres of water is (4 x 2) = 8grams.

Pearl: Horrock’s Apparatus

  • Horrock’s Apparatus is used to estimate the chlorine demand of water.
  • This is widely used in the disinfection of wells to find out how much bleaching powder is required.
  • Contents of this water-testing apparatus:
    • 6 white cups of 200 ml each and one black cup with a circular mark
    • 2 metal spoons (each holds 2g of bleaching powder)
    • 7 glass stirring rods and 1 special pipette
    • Two droppers
    • Starch-iodide indicator solution
  • Procedure:
    • Use 2g of bleaching powder to create a thin paste in the black cup. It is now called the Chlorine stock solution.
    • The six white cups are filled with the water to be tested
    • Add one drop of the stock solution to the 1st cup, two drops to the 2nd cup, three drops to the 3rd cup, and so on till adding six drops to the 6th cup.
    • Stir the cups and wait for half an hour.
    • Add 3 drops of starch-iodide indicator to each cup
    • Development of blue color in the apparatus indicates free residual chlorine. 
    • The first cup which develops this color gives an estimate of the amount of bleaching powder needed to disinfect 455 Litres of the sample water.
  • Chlorine demand or the dose of bleaching powder required is given by (n x 2) g for 455 liters of water, i.e., (n x 2) g of bleaching powder is required to disinfect 455 liters of water. Here, n represents the position of the cup (1, 2, 3, etc.) that was first to show a distinct blue color.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young lady presented with a tingling sensation in her legs and hands. On examination, she had fissured tongue, lips, and lesions in the angle of the mouth. On investigation, she had low RBC glutathione reductase activity. Which vitamin is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.raw_text: A young lady presented with a tingling sensation in her legs and hands. On examination, she had fissured tongue, lips, and lesions in the angle of the mouth. On investigation, she had low RBC glutathione reductase activity. Which vitamin is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Riboflavin

Tingling sensation of legs and hands, fissured tongue and lips, and lesions in the angle of the mouth combined with low RBC glutathione reductase activity is consistent with riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency.

Deficiency state of riboflavin, a water soluble vitamin, is characterized by the following signs and symptoms:

  1. Cheilosis: Pallor in the angle of mouth and fissuring of lips, which extends radially to skin
  2. Glossitis: Tongue becomes smooth, loss of papilla causing magenta-colored tongue
  3. Eyes: Keratitis, conjunctivitis and corneal vascularisation
  4. Other features: Seborrheic dermatitis, anemia

The nutritional status of riboflavin can be assessed by measuring the activity of the RBC glutathione reductase, by FAD added in vitro. This test is specific for riboflavin deficiency.

The image below shows cheilosis and stomatitis due to riboflavin deficiency.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with a past history of pulmonary tuberculosis undergoes a CT scan, and the image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A patient with a past history of pulmonary tuberculosis undergoes a CT scan, and the image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspergilloma

The most likely diagnosis is aspergilloma. The CT images show the Monod sign, which refers to gas surrounding an intracavitary fungal ball, with the ball changing position between supine and decubitus views, confirming mobility. 

Aspergilloma is a fungus ball of Aspergillus fumigatus forming in pre-existing cavities in lungs, most commonly post-tuberculous cavities. The air crescent sign (a crescent of air surrounding the fungus ball within the cavity ) is the classic CT finding. The ball is mobile and shifts on decubitus positioning (Monod sign).

The image below shows the fungal-ball at the posterior position when the patient is supine, and at the anterior portion of the cavity when the patient is prone, showing it shifting with gravity.


Other pulmonary manifestations of Aspergillus:

  • Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity reaction in asthmatics, showing finger-in-glove sign (mucoid impaction in dilated bronchi) and central bronchiectasis.

 

  • Angioinvasive aspergillosis occurs in immunocompromised patients. HRCT shows the halo sign: ground-glass opacity surrounding a nodule, representing hemorrhage. The air crescent sign in angioinvasive aspergillosis is a late finding, usually seen around 2 weeks after onset as the white blood cell count recovers. Since it can look like an intracavitary fungal ball, it may resemble an aspergilloma on imaging without showing the positional mobility.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following can be determined using the cephalic index?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following can be determined using the cephalic index?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Race

Cephalic index is used to determine the race of the individual.

Formula to calculate cranial index = maximum skull breadth x 100 / maximum skull length

The skull offers the best evidence on racial origins. There are three main racial groups, namely, Caucasian, Mongoloid and Negroid. 

Type of skull Cephalic index Race
Dolichocephalic 70-74.9 Pure Aryans, Aborigines, Negroes
Mesaticephalic 75-79.9 Europeans, Chinese, Indians
Brachycephalic 80-84.9 Mongolian

All the skulls cannot be accurately differentiated into the 3 broad categories because of racial mixing. The skull of an Indian is caucasian with a few negroid features. 

Race determination indices from other bones:

  • Upper limb bones - Brachial index
  • Lower limb bones - Crural index
  • Both upper and lower limb - Intermembral index

Krogman's degree of accuracy in sexing adult skeletal remains:

  • Pelvis alone – 95%
  • Skull alone – 90%
  • Pelvis plus skull – 98%

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the adult representation of the location of anterior neuropore?
questions.raw_text: What is the adult representation of the location of anterior neuropore?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lamina terminalis

The location of the anterior neuropore is represented in adults as lamina terminalis. 

The anterior neuropore closes around the 25th day of intrauterine life. Its location in adults is represented by the lamina terminalis. The lamina terminalis forms the anterior boundary of the third ventricle.

The posterior neuropore closes around the 28th day of intrauterine life. Its location in adults is represented by the terminal ventricle. The terminal ventricle is present in the proximal 5 to 6 mm of filum terminale.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a splenectomized patient, there is an increased risk of infection by all capsulated organisms. Which of the following is least likely to cause an infection in such patients?
questions.raw_text: In a splenectomized patient, there is an increased risk of infection by all capsulated organisms. Which of the following is least likely to cause an infection in such patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Staphylococcus aureus

In splenectomized patients, there is an increased risk of infection by capsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and some Gram negative enteric bacteria such as Klebsiella pneumoniae. 

Although Staphylococcus aureus strains have capsules, these organisms are less likely to cause infections in a splenectomized patient, as these organisms are primarily eliminated by neutrophil-associated phagocytosis.

Pearl: Overwhelming Post-splenectomy Infection (OPSI)

It is the most common fatal infection following splenectomy. 

Certain components called opsonins attach to the encapsulated organisms, and then they are delivered to the spleen, where their uptake is facilitated by receptors present on the surface of splenic phagocytes. After splenectomy, this defence mechanism is lost leaving patients susceptible to infection from these bacteria.

Most common within 2-3 years following splenectomy. 

Causative agents: Usually capsulated organisms like

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae (Most common)
  • Haemophilus influenzae
  • Neisseria meningitidis
  • Streptococcus species
  • Salmonella species
  • Capnocytophaga canimorsus, implicated in OPSI as a result of dog bites

Clinical features

  • Prodromal features like fever, chills, sore throat, malaise, diarrhea, and vomiting
  • Rapid progression to hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagula­tion, respiratory distress, coma, and death within hours of presen­tation
  • High-grade bacteremia with no identifiable foci of infection
  • Poor response to antibiotics

If an elective splenectomy is planned, prophylactic vaccinations against pneumococcus, meningococcus C (both repeated every 5 years), and H. influenzae type B (Hib) must be given atleast 2 weeks before the elective surgery.

In case of an emergency splenectomy, patients should be given vaccines at least two weeks after surgery but before discharge from the hospital.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following factors is responsible for the draughtsman appearance of pneumococcal colonies?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following factors is responsible for the draughtsman appearance of pneumococcal colonies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autolysin

The factor responsible for the draughtsman appearance of pneumococcal colonies is autolysin.

When pneumococci are incubated on blood agar for a prolonged duration, the resultant colonies are surrounded with concentric rings and have a central umbonation. This appearance of pneumococcal colonies is known as carrom coin appearance or draughtsman appearance.

Autolysin is an amidase enzyme produced by pneumococci that cleaves peptidoglycan, leading to the autolysis of cells. It is also responsible for the bile solubility of pneumococci.

The below image shows the characteristic draughtsman appearance of pneumococcal colonies.

questions.text: Oral examination of a young patient shows the following finding. Which bacteria belonging to viridans group is most commonly implicated in this condition?
questions.raw_text: Oral examination of a young patient shows the following finding. Which bacteria belonging to viridans group is most commonly implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Streptococcus mutans

The above image shows dental caries which are commonly caused by Streptococcus mutans. It belongs to the viridans group/α-hemolytic streptococci.

Streptococcus mutans breaks down the dietary sucrose producing acid and a tough adhesive dextran. The acid damages dentine while the dextrans bind together with food debris, epithelial cells, mucus, and bacteria to form dental plaques, leading to formation of dental caries.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient admitted to an ICU spiked a fever and his blood culture was positive for gram-positive cocci in chains, which are catalase-negative. He was being given ceftazidime and amikacin via a central venous line for the past week. Following this, you started him on vancomycin but his blood culture remained positive for the same organism even after 2 weeks of therapy. Which of the following is the most likely organism causing the infection?
questions.raw_text: A patient admitted to an ICU spiked a fever and his blood culture was positive for gram-positive cocci in chains, which are catalase-negative. He was being given ceftazidime and amikacin via a central venous line for the past week. Following this, you started him on vancomycin but his blood culture remained positive for the same organism even after 2 weeks of therapy. Which of the following is the most likely organism causing the infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enterococcus faecium

The given scenario is suggestive of vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) infection.

Gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase-negative suggest that the organism belongs to Streptococcaceae family. Positive culture after 2 weeks of vancomycin therapy suggests resistance to vancomycin.

Option A: Streptococcus pyogenes are sensitive to vancomycin and are not commonly implicated in central venous line infections.

Option B: Viridans streptococci are usually mouth commensals and are sensitive to vancomycin.

Option D: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are gram-positive cocci in clusters which are catalase-positive. Hence, they can be ruled out.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following bacteria is associated with the causation of colorectal carcinoma, rectal polyp, endocarditis and septicaemia and is pyrrolidinyl arylamidase test negative?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following bacteria is associated with the causation of colorectal carcinoma, rectal polyp, endocarditis and septicaemia and is pyrrolidinyl arylamidase test negative?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Streptococcus gallolyticus

Streptococcus gallolyticus is associated with the causation of colorectal CA, rectal polyp, endocarditis, and septicemia and is pyrrolidinyl arylamidase test (PYR test) negative.

Streptococcus gallolyticus, formerly called Streptococcus bovis, is a non-enterococcal Group D streptococci. It is bile insoluble, esculin hydrolysis positive, PYR negative and shows no growth in 6.5% NaCl.

questions.text: Which of the following types of streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins is bacteriophage mediated?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following types of streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins is bacteriophage mediated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. type A & type C

Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins type A and type C are bacteriophage-mediated toxins.

The streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin(SPE) is so named because the primary effect of the toxin is the induction of fever. It is also known as erythrogenic toxin because its intra-dermal injection into susceptible individuals produced an erythematous reaction (Dick Test).

There are 3 types of streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins namely:

  • type A - phage mediated.
  • type B - chromosome mediated.
  • type C - phage mediated.

A throat swab was taken and sent to the lab for culture on blood agar. Which of the following factors is responsible for the zones of hemolysis seen in the culture below?

The given case scenario o a patient with fever, sore throat, and a scarlatiniform rash is suggestive of scarlet fever caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. Streptolysin S is the factor responsible for the zones of hemolysis seen around streptococcal colonies on blood agar.

Streptococci produces two hemolysins:

  • Streptolysin S is called so because it is soluble in serum. It is also oxygen-stable hemolysin. It is a protein but is not antigenic.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following methods of sterilization involves exposure to 100 °C for 20 minutes on 3 successive days?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following methods of sterilization involves exposure to 100 °C for 20 minutes on 3 successive days?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tyndallization

The method of sterilization that involves exposure at 100°C for 20 minutes for 3 successive days is called tyndallization or intermittent sterilization. 

Tyndallization, which utilizes steam, was used for sterilization of media containing gelatin, egg, serum, or sugar. This method may not kill spores of certain anaerobes and thermophiles. Autoclaving has replaced this method now. 

Other options:

Option A: Autoclaving involves heating at 121°C for 15 minutes at a pressure of 15psi. This is the used for intruments, linen, laboratory ware.

Option C: In pasteurization, milk is heated at either 63°C for 30 minutes (the holder method) or at 72°C for 15–20 seconds (the flash process), followed by cooling quickly to 13°C or lower. 

Option D: Heating an article at 80–85 °C for 30 minutes on 3 consecutive days is called inspissation.

Autoclaving All Linen, surgical instruments, laboratory ware, media and pharmaceutical products

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Pasteurization is done at  ______.
questions.raw_text: Pasteurization is done at  ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 63 degree Celsius for 30 minutes

Pasteurization is done at 63 degree Celsius for 30 minutes.

Pasteurization is the process of applying heat to milk to kill or stunt the growth of pathogenic bacteria. It was developed by Louis Pasteur. There are two methods for pasteurization:

  • Holder method: Milk is heated at 63°C for 30 minutes
  • Flash process: Milk is heated to 72°C for 15–20 seconds

Once heated appropriately, the milk is cooled quickly to 13°C or lower. All the non-sporing pathogens (mycobacteria, brucellae, salmonellae) are killed in pasteurization. In the Holder method, heat resistant Coxiella burnetti may survive. 

Note: Louis Pasteur pioneered the techniques of pasteurization and sterilization. He also first advanced the germ theory of disease which states that most diseases were caused by microorganisms. Furthermore, he disproved the theory of spontaneous generation and developed vaccines for rabies and fowl cholera. He is thus known as the father of modern microbiology.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following methods will not help you visualize the bacterial cell wall?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following methods will not help you visualize the bacterial cell wall?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Simple staining

The cell wall of bacteria cannot be seen with simple stains or direct light microscopy.

The bacterial cell wall is present outside the plasma membrane and confers strength and shape to the cell. It is composed of peptidoglycans. The cell wall can be demonstrated by the following methods:

  • Plasmolysis
  • Microdissection
  • Reaction with specific antibodies
  • Mechanical rupture of the cell
  • Differential staining procedures (E.g. Chance's method)
  • Electron microscopy
  • Fluorescence microscopy

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old sex worker presented with a painless ulcer on her vulva. On examination, inguinal lymphadenopathy is present. Which of the following methods has been used to demonstrate the causative agent as per the given image?
questions.raw_text: A 28-year-old sex worker presented with a painless ulcer on her vulva. On examination, inguinal lymphadenopathy is present. Which of the following methods has been used to demonstrate the causative agent as per the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dark-field microscopy

A painless genital ulcer with inguinal lymphadenopathy with the presence of spiral organisms on microscopy is suggestive of syphilis. It is caused by Treponema pallidum, demonstrated by dark-field microscopy. 

Dark-field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism. The dark ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies. It uses reflected light and has a higher resolving power than the light microscope. Dark-field microscopy is the the most specific and sensitive technique to visualize Treponema pallidum when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present.

Other options:

Option B: Phase contrast microscopy improves the contrast to delineate structures within cells. A dark image is formed on a light background.

Option C: Fluorescent microscopy uses fluorescent dyes like auramine-rhodamine to appreciate Mycobacterial species and malarial parasites. 

Option D: The electron microscope, invented by Ernst Ruska, helps in appreciating viral structures. It has a very high resolving power. 

Pearl: Stages of syphilis

Primary syphilis:

  • Chancre - Painless, indurated, usually single. The chancre self heals in 1-4 months.
  • Lymphadenopathy - Painless, unilateral or bilateral, shotty and rubbery inguinal nodes
  • Dory flop sign - As the chancre is too hard to fold, it will flip over once the prepuce is retracted back.

Secondary syphilis:

  • A & B: Generalized non-itchy rash with no vesicles present on the palm and sole. This is the most common lesion.
  • C & D: Condyloma lata.
  • E: Moth-eaten non-scarring alopecia
  • F: Mucous patches are flat erosions on the tongue that can coalesce to form snail track ulcers. These are the most infectious lesions.
  • G: Pigmentary plaques
  • H: Psoriasiform syphilitic lesions
  • Generalized diffuse non-tender lymphadenopathy

Tertiary syphilis:

  • Gummatous syphilis are deep punched-out ulcers, with gum-like secretions on the floor
  • Pseudo-chancre redux is a gumma occurring at the site of a previously healed ulcer  
  • CVS - Aortitis and aneurysm of the ascending aorta
  • CNS - General paresis of the insane and tabes dorsalis 

Latent syphilis is the period between secondary and tertiary syphilis. In this period the patient is asymptomatic clinically and only serological evidence of the infection is present. It is classified into:

  • Early latent syphilis - Within 1 year of infection
  • Late latent syphilis - After 1 year of infection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement regarding Micrococci.
questions.raw_text: Choose the incorrect statement regarding Micrococci.

options.label: C
options.text: It is rarely associated with disease.

questions.correct_answer: D. It is arranged in chains.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is arranged in chains.

Micrococci are arranged in pairs, tetrads or clusters of eight. 

Micrococci are Gram-positive cocci that are often mistaken for S. aureus. However, they are larger in size and mostly occur in pairs, tetrads or clusters of eight. They form smaller colonies in culture in comparison to S. aureus. Hugh-Leifson oxidation-fermentation test can be used to differentiate between micrococci (oxidative pattern) and staphylococci (fermentative pattern).

Micrococci are catalase-positive and modified oxidase-positive. They are ordinarily non-pathogenic but can rarely cause infections in an immunocompromised host. They are part of normal bacterial flora in the body.

The following image shows the tetrad arrangement of micrococci:

Different bacteria with their typical arrangements are given below:

1. Staphylococcus: Clusters
2. Streptococcus: Chains
3. Pneumococcus: Pairs/lanceolate shaped
4. Micrococcus: Tetrads

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with a history of vomiting within 3 hours of consumption of food at a party. Which of the following organism is most likely to cause these symptoms?
questions.raw_text: A 14-year-old boy presents with a history of vomiting within 3 hours of consumption of food at a party. Which of the following organism is most likely to cause these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Staphylococcus aureus

Vomiting 2 hours after the consumption of food is likely food poisoning by Staphylococcus aureus. 

Staphylococcus aureus can grow in carbohydrate and protein food sources, producing enterotoxins. There are 15 types, all of which are superantigens. They are preformed toxins that are relatively heat stable. They stimulate the vagus nerve,  vomiting centre of the brain and intestinal peristaltic activity. Type A enterotoxin is responsible for most cases of food poisoning. 

The common sources of infection are the foods that are not cooked after handling. These include sliced meats, puddings, pastries, and sandwiches. Ingestion of such contaminated food causes food poisoning within 30 minutes to 6 hours after consumption. Patients present with nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and diarrhoea.
