questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An outbreak of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection was reported in the surgical ward of a hospital. Which of the following precautionary measures would you recommend to best curb its spread?
questions.raw_text: An outbreak of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection was reported in the surgical ward of a hospital. Which of the following precautionary measures would you recommend to best curb its spread?

options.label: A
options.text: Administration of vancomycin empirically to all the patients

options.label: C
options.text: Wearing masks before performing invasive procedures

options.label: D
options.text: Washing of hands before & after treating the patients

questions.correct_answer: D. Washing of hands before & after treating the patients
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Washing of hands before & after treating the patients

Among the given options, washing hands before and after treating the patients is the most effective way to curb the spread of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections.

In addition to this, personnel with active S. aureus lesions and carriers should be excluded from areas having patients at highest risk for severe staphylococcal infections like newborn nurseries, intensive care units, operating rooms, and cancer chemotherapy wards. In such individuals, the application of topical antiseptics such as mupirocin to nasal or perineal carriage sites may diminish the shedding of MRSA.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The specimen obtained by performing incision and drainage of a breast abscess was sent for culture on nutrient agar.  An image of the culture plate is given below. Microscopy of the isolated organism revealed gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters. Which of the following is a false statement regarding this organism?
questions.raw_text: The specimen obtained by performing incision and drainage of a breast abscess was sent for culture on nutrient agar.  An image of the culture plate is given below. Microscopy of the isolated organism revealed gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters. Which of the following is a false statement regarding this organism?

options.label: B
options.text: Golden yellow pigmentation  is due to β-carotene

options.label: C
options.text: Pigment production is enhanced by adding milk to culture media

options.label: D
options.text: Confluent growth presents a characteristic  'oil-paint appearance'

questions.correct_answer: A. Pigment production occurs optimally at 35°C.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pigment production occurs optimally at 35°C.

Gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters that produce golden-yellow pigment on nutrient agar is suggestive of Staphylococcus aureus. The pigment production occurs optimally at 22°C.

Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive coccus. On nutrient agar, its colonies are large (2-4 mm in diameter), convex, smooth, shiny, opaque and easily emulsifiable. The colonies appear golden yellow due to the presence of staphyloxanthin (carotenoid). Pigment production occurs optimally at 22°C and in aerobic conditions. It is enhanced when 1% glycerol or milk is incorporated in the medium.

On a nutrient agar slope, there is confluent growth of Staphylococcus, which appears as a characteristic oil-paint appearance.

questions.raw_text: The drug shown in the image below is administered for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malaria

The image given below shows artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), which is used in the treatment of falciparum malaria.

ACT consists of artesunate given for 3 days and sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine given for 1 day. It is supplied by the government of India under the national vector-borne disease control program (NVDCP).

It is given to all confirmed cases of Plasmodium falciparum infection, found positive by microscopy or rapid diagnostic tests. Primaquine with dose of 0.75 mg/kg of body weight is given on day 2 along with it. Artemether-lumefantrine is used for the treatment of falciparum malaria in the northeastern states of India. 

This drug is not given in pregnancy and in children less than 5 kg of body weight.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following methods of antibiotic susceptibility testing cannot be used to calculate the minimum inhibitory concentration of an antimicrobial drug?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following methods of antibiotic susceptibility testing cannot be used to calculate the minimum inhibitory concentration of an antimicrobial drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kirby–Bauer method

Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) cannot be calculated using Kirby-Bauer's disk diffusion method and Stokes disk diffusion method as they are semi-quantitative methods.

MIC is the lowest concentration of an antimicrobial agent that will inhibit the visible growth of a microorganism. Methods to determine MIC include:

  • Tube dilution method
  • Agar dilution method
  • E-test method

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman with fever and lower abdominal pain is diagnosed to have PID. Which is the most common cause for this condition?
questions.raw_text: A young woman with fever and lower abdominal pain is diagnosed to have PID. Which is the most common cause for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlamydia

Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of PID.

PID is an infection of the upper genital tract. It is generally transmitted sexually as an ascending infection along with sperms. It is usually a polymicrobial infection,

Organisms causing PID include:

Sexually transmitted:

  • Chlamydia (most common)
  • Gonococcus
  • Mycoplasma
  • Trichomonas

Pyogenic Aerobes:

  • Staphylococci
  • Streptococci
  • E Coli

Anaerobes:

  • Bacteroides fragilis
  • Peptostreptococcus 
  • Clostridium 
  • Actinomyces (most common in IUD users)

Other: 

  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Note: Genital tuberculosis is the only PID that does not spread sexually. It has a hematogenous spread. Thus, it is the most common PID in virgin girls.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A young lady who is on oral contraceptive pills refrains from taking any drug even for minor ailments due to the fear of contraceptive failure. Which of the following drugs can be taken safely?
questions.raw_text: A young lady who is on oral contraceptive pills refrains from taking any drug even for minor ailments due to the fear of contraceptive failure. Which of the following drugs can be taken safely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aspirin

Among the given drugs, aspirin use is least likely to cause contraceptive failure.

Other options:

Option B: Broad-spectrum antibiotics like tetracycline suppress the intestinal flora and interfere with the enterohepatic circulation of estrogen. This leads to lowering of plasma estrogen levels and can result in contraceptive failure.

Options C and D: Enzyme inducers like phenytoin and rifampicin increase the metabolism of oral contraceptives and can cause contraceptive failure.
subtopics: Oral Contraceptive Pills / OCPs - Interactions & Contraindications

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 21-year-old young man presents with a neck mass. Past history is significant for surgical removal of a pheochromocytoma 6 months ago. On examination, a marfanoid habitus is noted along with the following finding. Which of the following should the patient be screened for?
questions.raw_text: A 21-year-old young man presents with a neck mass. Past history is significant for surgical removal of a pheochromocytoma 6 months ago. On examination, a marfanoid habitus is noted along with the following finding. Which of the following should the patient be screened for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medullary thyroid carcinoma

This clinical scenario and image showing mucosal neuromas are suggestive of MEN2B syndrome. This condition is associated with medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. 

The MEN syndromes are a group of inherited diseases of multiple endocrine organs. Tumors occur at a younger age than sporadic tumors, either synchronously (at the same time) or metachronously (at different times).

MEN2 syndrome occurs due to abnormal activation of the RET gene. Medullary carcinoma is seen in both MEN 2A and 2B syndromes. However, it tends to be more aggressive and metastasizes more frequently in MEN2B syndrome.

Note: RET gene is deactivated in Hirschsprung disease.

Pearl: MEN 2 Syndrome Features

MEN 2A

  • Known as Sipple’s syndrome
  • Chromosome 10 / RET gene
  • Associated conditions are:
    • Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (90%)
    • Pheochromocytoma (>50%)
    • Parathyroid adenoma (10–25%)

MEN 2B

  • Known commonly as MEN 3
  • Chromosome 10/ RET gene
  • Associated conditions are:
    • Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (>90%)
    • Pheochromocytoma (>50%)
    • Other associated abnormalities include: (40–50%)
      • Mucosal neuromas
      • Marfanoid habitus
      • Medullated corneal nerve fibers
      • Megacolon
subtopics: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Syndromes / MEN Syndromes

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Flow volume given below indicates_____
questions.raw_text: Flow volume given below indicates_____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extrathoracic obstruction

The inspiratory flow-volume curve is truncated in patients with variable extrathoracic obstructions.

  • During a forced expiration, the cross-sectional area of a variable extrathoracic obstruction increases as the pressure inside the airway increases.
  • The expiratory flow-volume curve is therefore nearly normal or not affected.
  • However, during a forced inspiration, the pressure inside the upper airway decreases below atmospheric pressure, and unless the stability of the upper airway is maintained by reflex contraction of the pharyngeal muscles or by other structures, the cross-sectional area of the upper airway will decrease. Therefore, the inspiratory flow-volume curve is truncated in patients with variable extrathoracic obstructions.
  • Flow-volume curves are very useful in assessing obstructions of upper airways and the trachea (refer figure and flowchart).

Pearl: Flow-volume graph/Loop

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient was transfused 4 units of blood 2 hours ago, and now she complains of chest discomfort. X-ray shows bilateral fissural thickening. Which of the following is the most probable cause?
questions.raw_text: A patient was transfused 4 units of blood 2 hours ago, and now she complains of chest discomfort. X-ray shows bilateral fissural thickening. Which of the following is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fluid overload

The given clinical condition is most likely due to fluid overload.

Fluid overload also called transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is the main cause of death from transfusion. Risk factors include older age, renal failure, preexisting fluid overload, cardiac dysfunction, administration of a large volume of RBCs, and an excessive rate of transfusion in relation to the patient’s hemodynamic tolerance.

TACO results in dyspnea, hypoxia, bilateral and predominantly alveolar infiltrates on chest x-ray, frequent systolic hypertension, and elevated brain natriuretic peptide. Fever may also present.

Prevention involves identifying at-risk patients, close monitoring, a slow transfusion rate, and the use of diuretics in hemodynamically stable patients with a history of TACO. Treatment requires stopping the transfusion and administrating oxygen and diuretics.

Other options:

Option A: ABO incompatibility reactions may present with hypotension, tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, chills, chest, and back pain, hemoglobinuria, and hemoglobinemia. In the most severe cases, DIC, acute renal failure, shock, and death may occur.

Option C: Hypocalcemia can be caused by citrate, which is used as an anticoagulant. It manifests as circumoral paresthesia, and changes in cardiac function may result from multiple rapid transfusions.

Option D: Graft-versus-host disease typically presents 5–10 days after transfusion, and it manifests as cytopenia, fever, a characteristic skin rash, diarrhea, and abnormal liver function.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Gastric lavage can be performed in case of poisoning by:
questions.raw_text: Gastric lavage can be performed in case of poisoning by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carbolic acid

Gastric lavage can be performed in case of carbolic poisoning.

In carbolic acid poisoning, if the patient survives for 48 hrs, there will be carboluria followed by anuria. The victim will pass dark, smoky urine which soon turns olive green on standing due to oxidation of hydroquinone and pyrocatechol. 

It is a corrosive acid, however, it hardens the GI mucosa producing a leather bottle stomach and anesthetizes the nerve endings. This allows for gastric lavage. 

Contraindications of gastric lavage:

  • Corrosives poisoning (except carbolic acid)
  • Convulsants/CNS stimulants
  • Comatose patients
  • Volatile poison
  • Upper GI pathology (eg. esophageal varices)
  • Hypothermic patient
  • Severe heart disease
  • Advanced pregnancy

Sulphuric acid and kerosene are corrosives and strychnine is a convulsant. Hence gastric lavage is not done in these poisonings.

Pearl: Mechanism of action of corrosives

Corrosive Mechanism of Action Type of necrosis
Strong acids Hydrogen ions penetrate tissues and lead to cell death and eschar formation. This prevents further hydrogen ion penetration and protects against deeper injury. Coagulation necrosis
Carbolic acid Same as other strong acids, but also hardens the GI mucosa. Produces a leather bottle stomach and anesthetizes the nerve endings. This allows for gastric lavage. Coagulation necrosis 
Oxalic acid Same as other strong acids, but also scavenges calcium ions, leading to hypocalcemia and Calcium oxalate renal stones.  Coagulation necrosis
Hydrofluoric acid Fluoride ions scavenge intracellular cations, such as calcium and magnesium and inhibit Na/K ATPase, disrupting cell membranes. This leads to hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia. Liquefactive necrosis
Strong alkalis Hydroxide ions easily penetrate tissues, leading to the dissolution of cell membranes. It is associated with deep tissue injury. Liquefactive necrosis

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 32-year-old lady presented with dry, itchy eyes, blurred vision, and sensitivity to light. She says there are black dots floating around in her visual field. She denies wearing any spectacles or contact lenses. On fundoscopy, the following image is obtained. What is the diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 32-year-old lady presented with dry, itchy eyes, blurred vision, and sensitivity to light. She says there are black dots floating around in her visual field. She denies wearing any spectacles or contact lenses. On fundoscopy, the following image is obtained. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sarcoidosis

Dry, itchy eyes, blurred vision, sensitivity to light with candle wax dripping on fundus examination points to a diagnosis of sarcoidosis.

Sarcoidosis is a chronic granulomatous multi-system disease. Ocular inflammation occurs in 25–70% of sarcoid patients, which includes uveitis, conjuctival and lacrimal gland involvement. Chronic granulomatous panuveitis may be seen. Anterior uveitis is the most common manifestation.

In anterior uveitis due to sarcoidosis, the following features can be seen:

  • "Mutton fat" keratic precipitates 
  • Iris nodules (Koeppe and/or Busacca) 
  • Trabecular meshwork nodules 
  • Tent-shaped peripheral anterior synechiae 

In intermediate uveitis, vitreous cells with snowbanking and snowball opacities/string of pearl appearance are seen. Posterior uveitis presents with candle-wax dripping (thick venous sheathing and periphlebitis), pre-retinal nodules (Lander’s sign), choroidal granulomata and sarcoid infiltration. Other ocular features seen are interstitial keratitis and band-shaped keratopathy. Steroids are the mainstay of treatment in sarcoidosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Following total thyroidectomy, a patient started having difficulty in breathing, and repeated attempts to extubate were unsuccessful. The most probable cause is ___
questions.raw_text: Following total thyroidectomy, a patient started having difficulty in breathing, and repeated attempts to extubate were unsuccessful. The most probable cause is ___
questions.correct_answer: C. Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury

The clinical picture of breathing difficulty and unsuccessful attempts at extubation after total thyroidectomy is suggestive of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

Thyroid surgery may cause injury to both external (ELN) and recurrent laryngeal nerves (RLN). The upper part of the RLN is closely related to the inferior thyroid artery. Unilateral RLN injury may be asymptomatic but in a few may cause hoarseness of voice.

The relation of RLN with the inferior thyroid artery is shown in the image below:

Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy can also occur postoperatively and the presentation is acute. Other causes of it include carcinoma of the cervical esophagus, carcinoma thyroid, and cervical lymphadenopathy. All the intrinsic muscles are paralyzed in this condition.

The vocal cords lie in the median or paramedian position due to the unopposed action of the cricothyroid muscles. This leads to dyspnoea and stridor, necessitating emergency tracheostomy.

For long-standing cases of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, there are two main treatment options. One approach involves performing a tracheostomy with a speaking valve. Alternatively, cord lateralizing procedures can be considered, such as transverse cordotomy, partial arytenoidectomy, injection of botulinum toxin, thyroplasty type II, or re-innervation procedures.

Transverse cordotomy (Kashima operation) involves excising laterally the soft tissue at the junction of the membranous cord and the vocal process of the arytenoid with laser.

Partial arytenoidectomy involves excising the medial part of the arytenoid with a laser.

Thyroplasty type II creates a lateral expansion of the larynx which is similar to vocal cord lateralization.

Reinnervation procedures innervate paralyzed posterior cricoarytenoid muscle by implanting a nerve-muscle pedicle of sternohyoid or omohyoid muscle with its nerve supply from ansa hypoglossi.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presented with a low-grade fever associated with loss of appetite and weight loss. A barium meal follow-through was done and is as shown. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 30-year-old woman presented with a low-grade fever associated with loss of appetite and weight loss. A barium meal follow-through was done and is as shown. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ileocecal TB

The given clinical scenario, along with the barium study findings, is suggestive of ileocecal tuberculosis. The given image shows dilated proximal ileum, narrowed terminal ileum and ileocecal junction, and shrunken cecum.

The ileocecal junction is the commonest site of tuberculosis in the gastrointestinal tract. Other sites involved in the abdomen are the liver, spleen, and peritoneum.

Barium meal follow-through study findings in ileocecal tuberculosis are:

  • Dilatation of the proximal ileum
  • Narrowed terminal ileum (string sign) and ileocecal junction
  • Gooseneck ileus – ileum hanging from the pulled-up cecum
  • The ileocecal angle becomes obtuse
  • The cecum appears shrunken and pulled up away from the right iliac fossa
  • Conical cecum
  • Fleischner sign

 

On barium enema, ileocecal tuberculosis typically shows narrowing of the terminal ileum, thickening and gaping of the ileocecal valve, and a contracted, hypermotile cecum. In contrast, carcinoma of the colon classically produces an “apple-core” appearance due to an annular constricting lesion.

Pearl: Barium studies in GI tuberculosis

  • Earliest feature is spasm and hypermotility, with edema of the valve.
  • Thickening of the valve lips, with narrowing of the terminal ileum: Fleischner or inverted umbrella sign is characteristic of TB.
  • In advance disease, the characteristic deformity includes symmetric, annular, napkin-ring stenosis and obstruction or shortening and pouch formation.
  • The cecum is shrunken and retracts out of the iliac fossa due to contraction of the mesocolon: Pulled-up cecum
  • Loss of ileocecal angle with dilated terminal ileum: Gooseneck deformity
  • Narrowing of the terminal ileum due to irritability, along with shortened rigid cecum: Sterlein sign
  • Persistent narrow stream of barium in the bowel indicates stenosis: String sign

options.label: C

Correct answer: B. Calcified cartilage at metaphysis

Calcified cartilage at metaphysis is known as the white line of Frankel and it is seen in scurvy.

Pearl: Radiological Features of Scurvy

Radiological features of scurvy:

  • Generalised osteopenia
  • Pencil-point cortex: Cortical thinning
  • Periosteal reaction due to subperiosteal hemorrhage
  • Scorbutic rosary: Expansion of the costochondral junctions

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old female patient is undergoing focussed parathyroidectomy for parathyroid adenoma. According to the Miami criteria, for the resection to be considered adequate, the intraoperative drop in parathyroid hormone should be ______.
questions.raw_text: A 32-year-old female patient is undergoing focussed parathyroidectomy for parathyroid adenoma. According to the Miami criteria, for the resection to be considered adequate, the intraoperative drop in parathyroid hormone should be ______.

options.label: A
options.text: More than one third  the maximum preoperative value in 10min

options.label: B
options.text: More than one third  the maximum preoperative value in half an 30 min

options.label: C
options.text: More than half  the maximum preoperative value in 10min

options.label: D
options.text: More than half  the maximum preoperative value in 30 min

questions.correct_answer: C. More than half  the maximum preoperative value in 10min
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. More than half the maximum preoperative value in 10min

Drop of parathyroid hormone to more than half the maximum value at 10 min postresection is considered an adequate resection in a parathyroid adenoma by the Miami criteria.

Most of the patients with primary hyperparathyroidism have single adenoma, and therefore undergo a focused or minimally invasive parathyroidectomy, where the localized abnormal parathyroid gland is removed. Once the gland is removed, the surgeon can ensure that there is no other hyperactive gland remaining by performing an intraoperative PTH assay for Miami criteria.

It is based on the principle that the half-life of the PTH is 3-5 minutes. In a single-gland disease, once the gland is removed the PTH levels should drop to >50% of the preoperative PTH level within 10 minutes. However, if there is no drop in PTH level, then a multi-gland disease is suspected and the surgery is converted to a bilateral neck exploration.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While studying a community, the researcher found 30% of the population to be below 15 years of age, and 10% was over 65 years of age. What is the total dependency ratio of this population?
questions.raw_text: While studying a community, the researcher found 30% of the population to be below 15 years of age, and 10% was over 65 years of age. What is the total dependency ratio of this population?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 66.6%

The total dependency ratio in this population is 66.6%. 

This can be calculated as follows.

Here, the total population below 15 years of age is = 30%

Total population above 65 years of age = 10%

So, total population between 15-65 years of age = 100 - (30 + 10) = 60%

Hence, dependency ratio in this population = 100* (30% + 10%)/60% = 66.6%

questions.text: A female patient presents with active genital warts with a history of recurrence, but her husband doesn't have it. What advice will you give to prevent transmission?
questions.raw_text: A female patient presents with active genital warts with a history of recurrence, but her husband doesn't have it. What advice will you give to prevent transmission?

options.label: B
options.text: Give prophylactic anti-virals to the husband

options.label: C
options.text: Give anti-virals whenever active lesions are present

options.label: D
options.text: Don't involve in intercourse when active lesions are present

questions.correct_answer: D. Don't involve in intercourse when active lesions are present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Don't involve in intercourse when active lesions are present

The advice to prevent transmission is to not involve in intercourse when active genital warts are present.

Genital warts are caused by HPV and transmitted through the sexual route. Antivirals are not very effective against anogenital warts. Biological treatment options like podophyllin, imiquimod, 5-fluorouracil are given. The best way to prevent transmission of infection is by avoiding sexual intercourse when active lesions are present.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: At what level does the spinal cord end in adults?
questions.raw_text: At what level does the spinal cord end in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. L1-L2

The distal termination of the spinal cord is the lower border of L1 in adults.

Because the spinal cord ends at L1, lower nerve roots course some distance before exiting the intervertebral foramina. These lower spinal nerves form the cauda equina.

Note:

In children, the spinal cord ends at L3 and moves up with age.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who is a known case of cirrhosis of the liver presents with abdominal distension and swelling of the lower limbs. The preferred diuretic for this patient would be
questions.raw_text: A patient who is a known case of cirrhosis of the liver presents with abdominal distension and swelling of the lower limbs. The preferred diuretic for this patient would be
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Eplerenone

The preferred diuretic for this patient with cirrhosis presenting with abdominal distension and lower limb swelling is eplerenone.

Eplerenone is a mineralocorticoid receptor/aldosterone antagonist. High doses of mineralocorticoid receptor/aldosterone antagonists decrease total body sodium in cirrhotic patients with ascites by natriuresis. 

Patients with liver cirrhosis have a decreased effective arterial blood volume because of splanchnic vasodilatation. This stimulates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and results in hyperaldosteronism. This causes increased sodium and water retention and leads to the development of ascites. This also contributes to resistance to loop diuretics. 

Normally, aldosterone (AL) enters the cells of the late distal tubule and collecting ducts by diffusion and binds to a specific mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in the cytoplasm. This AL-MR complex mediates Na+ reabsorption, which drives the secretion of K+ and H+into the tubules.

Eplerenone competitively blocks this MR, preventing it from binding with aldosterone. The net effect is sodium diuresis and potassium retention. It is a potassium-sparing diuretic. Other mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists include spironolactone, canrenone, potassium canrenoate.

Some clinical uses of MR antagonists are - 

  • Hypertension due to primary hyperaldosteronism 
  • Edema associated with liver cirrhosis, congestive cardiac failure, chronic kidney disease
  • They may reduce mortality in patients with myocardial infarction

Side effects of MR antagonists are - 

  • Hyperkalemia- most important
  • Decreased libido- specific for spironolactone
  • Gynecomastia- specific for spironolactone

Other options : 

Option A- Triamterene directly inhibits renal epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the late distal tubule and collecting duct. It is a potassium-sparing diuretic and is generally used along with other diuretics in the treatment of hypertension and edema. Triamterene is metabolized in the liver, hence triamterene toxicity may be enhanced in patients with hepatic disease. It is used in the management of Liddle syndrome.

Option C- Chlorthalidone is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits Na+-Cl- symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride. Thiazide diuretics may be used for the treatment of hypertension, heart failure, nephrolithiasis due to idiopathic hypercalciuria, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Option D- Furosemide is a loop diuretic. It acts by inhibiting the Na+-K+-2Cl- symporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle resulting in increased excretion of sodium and chloride. It also has mild carbonic anhydrase inhibitory activity and also increases urinary excretion of bicarbonate and phosphate. Cirrhotic patients are often resistant to loop diuretics due to decreased secretion of the drug into tubular fluid and high aldosterone levels. Furosemide may be given along with eplerenone, but the best answer here is eplerenone since aldosterone antagonists are the main therapy for cirrhotic edema.

questions.text: A patient with liver cirrhosis is scheduled to undergo a laparotomy for a perforated appendix. According to the Child-Turcotte-Pugh score, which of the following parameters will you not use for this patient?

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Frotteurism is __________
questions.raw_text: Frotteurism is __________

options.label: A
options.text: Obtaining sexual pleasure by wearing clothes of opposite sex

options.label: B
options.text: Desire to seek surgery to become member of opposite sex

options.label: C
options.text: Sexual gratification by rubbing his private parts against another person

options.label: D
options.text: Exposure of one’s genitals to an unsuspecting stranger

questions.correct_answer: C. Sexual gratification by rubbing his private parts against another person
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sexual gratification by rubbing his private parts against another person

  • Frotteurism is a paraphilia which involves obtaining sexual gratification by contact with a non-consenting individual (rubbing his private parts against another person’s buttocks, breasts, thighs etc., sometimes in public places). There is very often a fantasy element to the practice, in which the offender believes their victim also finds it pleasurable. It is punishable under BNS Section 75, which pertains to sexual harassment. It carries a potential sentence of rigorous imprisonment upto 3 years, or fine, or both.
  • Eonism (also known as Transvestism) is a sexual paraphilia in which a person obtains sexual pleasure by wearing clothes of the opposite sex. There is no hormonal or genital abnormality.
  • Transsexualism: It is the desire to become a member of the opposite sex and seek surgery for anatomical alterations.
  • Exhibitionism is a paraphilia involving the exposure of one’s genitals to unsuspecting strangers. This is a punishable offence under BNS Section 296 (obscene acts) and BNS 292 (public nuisance), with the possibility of imprisonment up to 3 months, or a fine of Rs. 1000, or with both.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the rate-limiting step for hepatic bilirubin metabolism?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is the rate-limiting step for hepatic bilirubin metabolism?

options.label: D
options.text: Secretion of conjugated bilirubin into the bile

questions.correct_answer: D. Secretion of conjugated bilirubin into the bile
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Secretion of conjugated bilirubin into the bile

The rate-limiting step for hepatic bilirubin metabolism is the secretion of conjugated bilirubin into the bile.

Conjugated bilirubin is actively transported from hepatocytes into bile via the multispecific organic anion transporter (MOAT), also known as multidrug resistance-associated protein 2 (MRP-2), located on the canalicular membrane. Drugs such as phenobarbitone can induce this transport process.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The brace shown in the given image is _____.
questions.raw_text: The brace shown in the given image is _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Milwaukee brace

The brace shown in the image is the Milwaukee brace.

The Milwaukee brace is an active corrective spinal orthosis primarily used in the ambulatory treatment of structural scoliosis. Designed as a cervico-thoracic-lumbar-sacral orthosis (CTLSO), the main objective of the Milwaukee brace is to delay or eliminate the need for surgery. However, in recent years, the use of the Milwaukee brace has declined due to the availability and convenience of modern braces. Nonetheless, it is still employed for scoliosis cases characterized by high thoracic and cervical spine curves.

Option A: Boston brace is a type of thoraco-lumbo-sacral-orthosis (TLSO brace). It has a hard polypropylene outer shell with a soft foam lining inside. It is used in patients whose scoliosis curve apex is at T7 or lower. The below image shows a Boston brace.

Option C: Taylor brace is designed to control the upper and lower regions of the spinal column and support your spine whilst standing, sitting, and walking after spinal surgery.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are using the Kuppuswamy scale to calculate the socio-economic status of 10 families in the railway staff quarters. You find that every family has a total monthly income of Rs. 73,355. What is the standard deviation of this sample?
questions.raw_text: You are using the Kuppuswamy scale to calculate the socio-economic status of 10 families in the railway staff quarters. You find that every family has a total monthly income of Rs. 73,355. What is the standard deviation of this sample?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 0

In this scenario, the standard deviation will be zero.

The monthly income of every family is Rs. 73,355. So, all the elements in this distribution are the same. Hence, there is no variability. Both the standard deviation and variance which is the square of standard deviation will be zero.

Pearl: Variance, Deviation Scores and Standard Deviation

  • Deviation Scores: 
    • The deviation score of an element in distribution is the difference between the mean of the distribution and the element itself, i.e., subtracting the distribution’s mean from the element.
    • Denoted by the letter x
    • For example, if 29 and 15 are elements in a distribution that has a mean of 22, the deviation score of 29 would be (29 – 22) = 7 and the deviation score of 15 would be (15 – 22) = - 7.
    • Sum of all the deviation scores of elements in distribution will be zero
  • Variance (also called mean square) 
    • The mean of the squares of all the deviation scores of the distribution
    • Used to measure how far data is spread out
    • If the variance is zero, it indicates that all the elements in the distribution are the same and that there is no variability.
    • Population variance (σ2) is calculated as:
      • Find the deviation score of each element in the distribution
      • Square each of the deviation scores.
      • Obtain the mean of all these squared deviation scores
  •  
    • Sample variance (s2): 
      • more commonly used in statistics than population variance
      • The denominator is n-1 (and not N as it is in population variance)
      • For small samples, it is better to use n-1 in the denominator.
      • For a very large sample, like a population, subtracting 1 from a huge number will not make much of a significant correction. Hence, we may choose to ignore subtracting 1.
  • Standard Deviation (SD)
    • It is the square root of variance.
    • The standard deviation of a population is denoted by σ and the standard deviation of a sample is denoted by just s.
    • The formula for the standard deviation of a sample (usually <30):
    • For a population (large sample), the denominator would be replaced by just N.
    • It is particularly useful for normal distributions but can be used in skewed distributions
    • It is used to calculate the proportion of the population within the given SD
    • A low SD means that the data are close to the mean but a high SD would mean that the data are more spread out.
    • The empirical rule of a normal distribution states that:
      • Approximately 68% of the distribution falls within one standard deviation of the mean.
      • Approximately 95% of the distribution falls within two standard deviations of the mean.
      • Approximately 99.7% of the distribution falls within three standard deviations of the mean.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.raw_text: The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6th arch

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the left 6th arch artery.

During the development, the laryngeal nerves initially arise below the 6th arch artery and cross here to innervate the intrinsic muscles of the larynx. As the larynx moves cranially relative to the aortic arch arteries, the recurrent laryngeal nerves on the right and left sides are caught under the 6th arch arteries.

On the right side, the distal 6th arch artery disappears. Since there is no 5th arch artery, the right recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under the 4th arch artery which becomes the future right subclavian artery.

On the left side, the 6th arch artery persists, which develops into ductus arteriosus, which later forms ligamentum arteriosum. Due to the persistence of the 6th arch artery, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under it and therefore, has a relatively long course.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency room with complaints of sudden onset chest pain that radiates to the left arm and jaw. He is profusely sweating. An ECG was taken immediately. Interpret his ECG.
questions.raw_text: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency room with complaints of sudden onset chest pain that radiates to the left arm and jaw. He is profusely sweating. An ECG was taken immediately. Interpret his ECG.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left bundle-branch block

The patient has a myocardial infarction (MI) with ECG changes of a left bundle-branch block (LBBB), which can be identified by the following classical features:

  • Wide QRS complex- QRS ≥120 ms 
  • Predominantly negative (QS) complexes in lead V1 and entirely positive (R) complexes in lead V6.
  • M pattern seen in left chest leads (V5, V6) 

MI can have the following ECG changes:

  • ST-segment elevation- zone of injury
  • T wave depression
  • Deep Q waves- late sign to develop
  • New left bundle branch block (LBBB)

The ECG findings below are characteristic of LBBB: Mnemonic WILLIAM (W pattern in V1-V2; L-LBBB; M pattern in V3-V6)

The ECG findings below are characteristic of RBBB: Mnemonic MARROW (M pattern in V1-V2; R-RBBB; W pattern in V3-V6)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following side effects are more commonly seen with carbamazepine than oxcarbazepine, except_____.
questions.raw_text: All of the following side effects are more commonly seen with carbamazepine than oxcarbazepine, except_____.

options.label: D
options.text: Elevated levels of gamma glutamyl transpeptidases

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyponatremia

Hyponatremia occurs more frequently in the case of oxcarbazepine than carbamazepine.

Both carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are sodium-channel blockers. 

Carbamazepine is most effective in complex partial seizures. It is also used in GTCS and simple partial seizures, trigeminal and related neuralgias, and manic depressive psychosis.

Carbamazepine potentiates the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). It can result in water retention with decreased osmolarity and hyponatremia, especially in elderly patients with cardiac disease. Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine can cause leukopenia, aplastic anemia, hepato-toxicity and hyponatremia in the elderly. 

Oxcarbazepine shows lesser hypersensitivity reaction. Hence, rashes are more commonly seen with carbamazepine than with oxcarbazepine.

Studies have shown that carbamazepine elevates enzyme gamma-glutamyl transpeptidases (GGT) more frequently than oxcarbazepine because of enzyme P450 induction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Photostress test is used to differentiate between:
questions.raw_text: Photostress test is used to differentiate between:
questions.correct_answer: A. Macula and optic nerve disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Macula and optic nerve disease

Photostress test is used to differentiate between the disease involving the macula and optic nerve.

This test is of particular use in early macular diseases such as central serous retinopathy.

In this test, one eye is covered and the patient is asked to read the smallest line on the near chart. A bright light is then shone into the eye for 15 seconds, and the patient is asked to read the line again, and the time taken to recover is noted. The test is repeated with the other eye.

In normal people and in patients with optic nerve disease, the recovery time is not affected. Whereas, in patients with macular disease the recovery time is prolonged and is usually more than one-third of the normal recovery time. This is because, in macular disease, the photoreceptors are damaged, and there is a delay in the visual pigment regeneration process.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with congestive heart failure. Which of the following is not prescribed to prevent progression and revert cardiac remodelling?
questions.raw_text: A patient is diagnosed with congestive heart failure. Which of the following is not prescribed to prevent progression and revert cardiac remodelling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Digoxin

Digoxin has no role in preventing cardiac remodelling. It increases cardiac contractility and is indicated for the symptomatic management of congestive heart failure.

Drugs preventing ventricular remodelling:

  • ACE inhibitors/ ARBS
  • Beta-blockers
  • Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone)

The activation of RAAS and the sympathetic nervous system leads to the remodelling and progressive LV dysfunction. The RAAS activation is prevented by the ACE inhibitors/ARBs and the aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone), while the overactive sympathetic system is inhibited by the beta-blockers.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about non-invasive prenatal testing?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements is false about non-invasive prenatal testing?

options.label: A
options.text: It uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum

options.label: B
options.text: It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21

options.label: C
options.text: It can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation

options.label: D
options.text: It is done after the routine first trimester ultrasound assessment

questions.correct_answer: B. It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21

Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is used for the screening of trisomy 13, 18 and 21 and Turner's syndrome. It is not a diagnostic test.

It is a novel genetic test that uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum for screening of chromosomal anomalies. 

DNA from the fetus is found circulating in the maternal blood in two forms - either inside the intact fetal cells or as cell-free DNA from the breakdown of placental fetal cells. In NIPT, the cell-free chromosome fragments are measured and the quantitative differences from normal fetuses are noted.

NIPT can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation and is recommended after the routine first-trimester ultrasound assessment in high-risk pregnancies or if either 1st or 2nd-trimester screening becomes positive. Its disadvantage is that it is very expensive and it can be used for screening of only a few chromosomal anomalies such as trisomy 13, 18, and 21 and it doesn't analyse the entire karyotype.
subtopics: Antenatal Care - NIPT, Triple Test, & Quadruple Test

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a differentiating feature between cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is a differentiating feature between cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Breath sounds

The differentiating feature between cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax is breath sounds. The breath sounds are absent in tension pneumothorax while they are present in cardiac tamponade.

The presence of hypotension, distended jugular veins, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) suggest a cardiac tamponade. These features can also be seen in tension pneumothorax. Other clinical features pointing towards tension pneumothorax are absent breath sounds, hyper resonance to percussion, and shift of the mediastinum to the contralateral side. 

Heart sounds can be muffled by structures between the stethoscope and the heart, eg, adipose tissue deposition (obesity), fluid accumulation (pericardial effusion, pleural effusion), gas accumulation (pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema), soft tissue masses can lead to attenuation of heart sounds.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Choanal atresia is not associated with which of the following defects?
questions.raw_text: Choanal atresia is not associated with which of the following defects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal angiomyolipoma

Choanal atresia may be associated with CHARGE syndrome. Renal angiomyolipoma is not a part of CHARGE syndrome.

  • C- Coloboma of the eye
  • H- Heart defects
  • A- Atresia of the choana
  • R- Retarded growth and development
  • G- Genital anomalies
  • E- Ear anomalies and hearing loss.

Renal angiomyolipoma - It is one of the major features of tuberous sclerosis complex.

Pearl: Choanal atresia

It is due to the persistence of bucconasal membrane which separates primitive oropharynx from the primitive nasopharynx. It has the following features:

  • Bony obstruction is more common than membranous
  • Unilateral > bilateral
  • Unilateral cases may be asymptomatic and present in adult life
  • Bilateral cases are life-threatening and present with respiratory distress
  • Associated with CHARGE syndrome
    • C- Coloboma of the eye
    • H- Heart defects
    • A- Atresia of choana
    • R- Retarded growth and development
    • G- Genital anomalies
    • E- Ear anomalies and hearing loss.

CT scan is the investigation of choice

Image: Membranous, bilateral choanal atresia in a newborn

Immediate management involves placing a feeding nipple with a large hole at the mouth to force the baby to mouth-breathe - McGoverns technique.

Definitive treatment consists of correction of atresia by a trans-nasal or trans-palatal approach.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: On finding a congenital heart block in a fetus, which of the following conditions would you evaluate for in the mother?
questions.raw_text: On finding a congenital heart block in a fetus, which of the following conditions would you evaluate for in the mother?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. SLE

On finding a congenital heart block in the fetus, the mother should be evaluated for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

Fetal and neonatal heart blocks occur due to myocarditis and fibrosis in the region between the AV node and the bundle of His. Congenital heart block primarily develops in fetuses of women with antibodies to the SS-A or SS-B antigens, and up to 50 percent of women with SLE test positive for these antibodies. So in pregnancies with either of these antibodies, fetal cardiac monitoring is performed between 18 and 26 weeks of gestation.

The cardiac lesion is permanent, and in most cases, a pacemaker is required. Maternal hydroxychloroquine therapy is associated with a reduced incidence of fetal heart block, particularly in women who have previously had an affected child.

Neonatal lupus erythematosus occurs when the fetus passively acquires maternal antibodies, especially IgG, through the placenta. It is characterized by skin lesions known as lupus dermatitis in newborns, as well as various hematological and systemic abnormalities. In some cases, congenital heart block may also occur. Thrombocytopenia and hepatic involvement are also seen. 

The most common cutaneous finding in neonatal lupus erythematosus is an erythematous, slightly scaly eruption on the face and periorbital skin (raccoon sign/owl eye/eye mask). The eruption can be exacerbated by UV exposure. The rash improves over the first few months of life and usually resolves without scarring by 12 months of age.

Avoidance of sunlight should be advised, and low‐potency topical steroids may be of benefit.

The pregnancy outcomes are best in women with:

  •  Dormant lupus activity for at least 6 months before conception
  •  No lupus nephritis manifestation in the form of proteinuria or renal dysfunction
  •  Absent anti-phospholipid syndrome or lupus anticoagulant 
  •  Superimposed preeclampsia does not develop

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient with severe resistant depression is planned for electroconvulsive therapy. You ask the nurse to load atropine, a muscle relaxant, and an anesthetic drug as a part of pre-procedure preparation. Which of the following anesthetic agents should he load?
questions.raw_text: A patient with severe resistant depression is planned for electroconvulsive therapy. You ask the nurse to load atropine, a muscle relaxant, and an anesthetic drug as a part of pre-procedure preparation. Which of the following anesthetic agents should he load?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Methohexital

Methohexital is the most commonly used anesthetic agent for electroconvulsive therapy, because of its shorter duration of action and lower association with post-ictal arrythmias. Methohexital is the only anesthetic agent with no intrinsic antiepileptic property.

Pearl: Key points on electroconvulsive therapy

Produces grand mal seizure in an anesthetized patient.

Mechanism of action:

  • Neuroplasticity: Ability of the brain to form and reorganize synaptic connections.
  • Increases levels of Brain-Derived Growth Factor and Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor

Indications:

  • Treatment-resistant depression
  • Severe depression with suicidal risk (most common indication)
  • Depression with psychotic features
  • Depressed suicidal pregnant women
  • Refusal to eat or drink
  • Imminent risk for suicide
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
  • Catatonia and catatonic schizophrenia
  • Severe agitated depression

Electrode placement: Bifrontotemporal, right unilateral.

Anesthetic agent: Methohexital (most common)

Adverse effects:

  • Retrograde amnesia (most common)
  • Partial anterograde amnesia
  • Disorientation
  • Temporary headache

Memory disturbances recover within 1-6 months. Safe in pregnancy. ECT can reverse extrapyramidal symptoms of neuroleptics.

Contraindications: No absolute contraindication (raised intracranial tension is considered as a relative contraindication).

Increased risk of adverse effects in:

  • Severe cardiovascular disease, recent myocardial infarction
  • Space occupying brain lesion
  • Recent stroke, unstable aneurysm

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with generalized exfoliative erythroderma. The peripheral blood smear shows the following cell. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A patient presents with generalized exfoliative erythroderma. The peripheral blood smear shows the following cell. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sezary syndrome

The image shows a classical Sezary cell with cerebriform nuclei which points towards a diagnosis of Sezary syndrome. These are neoplastic T cells.

Sezary syndrome and mycosis fungoides are different manifestations of tumors of CD4+ helper T cells that are home to the skin.

Sezary syndrome is a variant presenting as generalized exfoliative erythroderma. It rarely goes into tumefaction and there is associated leukemia of Sezary cells.

In Mycosis fungoides, only the epidermis and upper dermis are infiltrated by neoplastic T cells with the characteristic cerebriform appearance. In the later stages of the disease, progression occurs to lymph nodes and bone marrow. Tumour cells are not seen in blood. The disease progresses through the premycotic phase, plaque phase, and tumour phase.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Where is the signaling sequence in a type 2 membrane protein located?
questions.raw_text: Where is the signaling sequence in a type 2 membrane protein located?

options.label: A
options.text: Inside the membrane at the N-terminal end

options.label: B
options.text: Inside the membrane at the C-terminal end

options.label: C
options.text: Outside the membrane at the N-terminal end

options.label: D
options.text: Outside the membrane at the C-terminal end

questions.correct_answer: A. Inside the membrane at the N-terminal end
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inside the membrane at the N-terminal end

The signaling sequence in a type 2 membrane protein is located inside the membrane (transmembrane region).

A membrane protein can be either integral protein (spans the thickness of the cell membrane) or peripheral protein (attached to the peripheral side of the membrane). 

Integral membrane proteins or transmembrane proteins are embedded in the cell membrane, spanning through the entire thickness. They are anchored by hydrophobic interactions and require the use of detergent for solubility.  Examples are ligand-binding receptors for hormones or neurotransmitters, transport proteins like Na+-K+ ATPase, pores, ion channels, cell adhesion molecules, and GTP-binding proteins (G proteins). 

Peripheral proteins are attached only to one surface of the cell membrane and do not penetrate all the way through. They are often attached to integral proteins. Examples are cell surface receptors, enzymes, ankyrin.

Signaling sequences are 16 to 30 amino acid residues in length and located at the N-terminal extension of the membrane proteins. After an appropriate trigger, they are either cleaved (and bind to MHC class I of the endoplasmic reticulum) or act as a membrane anchor (transporting proteins across the membrane).

Integral proteins can be divided into:

  • Type I integral proteins have a cleavable N-terminal signal sequence (towards the cytosol). Examples include histocompatibility antigens, glycophorin, and membrane immunoglobulin.
  • Type II integral proteins have a non-cleavable N terminal combined signal/anchor sequence. Examples include transferrin receptors and glycosyl transferases.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A 30-year-old female patient, on treatment for infertility, came with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and mild vaginal bleeding. Her beta hCG level was 2800 mIU/mL. On ultrasound, a 3cm mass was seen in the left adnexa. It contained a gestational sac with no fetal cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
questions.raw_text:
A 30-year-old female patient, on treatment for infertility, came with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and mild vaginal bleeding. Her beta hCG level was 2800 mIU/mL. On ultrasound, a 3cm mass was seen in the left adnexa. It contained a gestational sac with no fetal cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Single dose methotrexate

A patient on infertility treatment, with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding with beta hCG levels of 2800 mIU/mL, and a gestational sac in the left adnexa points to the diagnosis of unruptured ectopic pregnancy and the most appropriate management is single-dose methotrexate.

A pregnancy is considered ectopic if implantation occurs at a site outside the uterine cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.

Management of ectopic pregnancy: 

Expectant management: Ectopic pregnancies measuring <3 cm and with declining beta hCG levels initially <1500 mIU/mL may resolve without inter­vention and can be managed expectantly. 

Medical management with single or multiple-dose methotrexate is preferred if:

  • Hemodynamic stability
  • Serum beta-hCG ≥1500 mIU/ml and ≤5000 mIU/mL
  • Mean sac diameter <3.5cm with no fetal cardiac activity detected on transvaginal ultrasound.
  • Patients are willing to comply with post-treatment follow-up.
  • Patients have timely access to emergency medical services if their condition deteriorates.

Methotrexate(MTX) can be given as a single IM dose of 50 mg/m2 or as a multiple-dose regimen of 1mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, and 7.

Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

  • Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met
  • Gestational sac >3.5 cm
  • Fetal cardiac activity present
  • Beta hCG > 5000 mIU/mL
  • Significant pain and hemoperitoneum 
  • Failure of expectant or medical management
  • Clinical status of patient warrants urgent intervention
  • Doubtful compliance with medical management 

Milking of the tube through the fimbriae carries a high risk of bleeding, damage to the tube, the persistence of trophoblastic tissue, and recurrence of ectopic pregnancy. 

Pearl: Beta hCG in pregnancy

The pattern of beta hCG :

First detectable in plasma 7 to 9 days post-LH surge
          ⇓
Doubles every 2 days
          ⇓
Peaks at 8 to 10 weeks of gestation(~100 IU/mL)
          ⇓
Begins to decline at 10 to 12 weeks
          ⇓
Plateau at 16 weeks till term
 
  • Higher maternal plasma hCG levels- Multifetal pregnancy, erythroblastosis fetalis, gestational trophoblastic disease, Down syndrome.
  • Lower hCG plasma levels -early pregnancy wastage and ectopic pregnancy.

questions.text: In which of the following nerve injuries is the instrument shown below used?

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Radial nerve

The image shown above is that of a cock-up splint. It is used to manage radial nerve palsy. 

Radial nerve palsy manifests as an inability to dorsiflex the wrist and digits (wrist drop and finger drop). Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits. 

Other options: 

Option B: Median nerve injury happens in carpel tunnel syndrome where a nocturnal wrist splinting that helps to maintain the hand in neutral position could be of help during the initial therapy to alleviate symptoms.

Option C: Ulnar nerve injury / ulnar claw hand could be managed with a  knuckle bender splint if nerve recovery is anticipated. The splint can be used to correct and prevent metacarpophalangeal hyperextension.

Option D: Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture (VIN) is most commonly seen following supracondylar humeral fractures. Mild cases of VIN are treated with a Volkmann's splint (Turnbuckle splint).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A forest officer develops the lesion as shown in the image. Which of the following is not a differential to consider?
questions.raw_text: A forest officer develops the lesion as shown in the image. Which of the following is not a differential to consider?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. KFD

The given image shows the presence of eschar and Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD) is not a differential diagnosis for the presence of eschar.

Kyasanur Forest Disease is a hemorrhagic fever found in the state of Karnataka, India. KFD has an abrupt onset of fever, headache, conjunctivitis, myalgia, and severe prostration. Characteristic skin lesions that are associated with KFD are petechial lesions. Some cases may develop hemorrhages in the skin, mucosa, and viscera, but there is no eschar formation.

Infection is transmitted by the bite of ticks, the principal vector being Haemaphysalis spinigera

Other options:

 A) Scrub typhus:

  • Scrub Typhus is also known as chigger-borne typhus.
  • Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. 
  • The vector is trombiculid mite.
  • Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers.

The incubation period is 1- 3 weeks. The patient typically develops a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite as shown in the image below, with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash.

C) Cutaneous anthrax:

  • In cutaneous anthrax, the lesion starts as a papule 1-3 days after infection and becomes vesicular, containing fluid that may be clear or blood-stained.
  • The whole area is congested and edematous and several satellite lesions filled with serum or yellow fluid are arranged around a central necrotic lesion which is covered by a black eschar.
  • This lesion is called a malignant pustule.
  • The disease used to be common in dock workers, carrying loads of hides and skins on their bare backs and hence known as hide porter’s disease.

D) Healing brown recluse spider bite:

  • The bite of the Loxosceles reclusa, the brown recluse spider is usually relatively painless.
  • After minutes or hours, severe pain develops at the site, accompanied by erythema, edema, and a central bulla.
  • In severe envenomation, a ‘target lesion’ is seen- central blue/ purple discoloration surrounded by an ischemic halo and an outer ring of erythema (the ‘red, white and blue’ sign).
  • After 3-4 days, the central area becomes necrotic and an eschar develops.
  • The eschar sheds eventually, leaving behind an ulcer, which takes time to heal.

questions.text: A 48-year-old woman with a lump in her right breast was advised to undergo mammography which was reported as BIRADS 3. What will be the appropriate next step of management in this patient?
questions.raw_text: A 48-year-old woman with a lump in her right breast was advised to undergo mammography which was reported as BIRADS 3. What will be the appropriate next step of management in this patient?
questions.correct_answer: D. Follow-up every 6 months for 2 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Follow-up every 6 months for 2 years

A BIRADS score of 3 means that it is probably a benign lesion. The next appropriate step is to follow up with this patient every 6 months for the next 2 years.

During this period, the score can either downgrade to BIRADS 2 or upgrade to BIRADS 4 or 5.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A man was brought in for questioning after a teenager was found dead at a Goan rave party. He reveals that he runs a nightclub in the city and that he has noticed anonymous people selling certain drugs that can enhance energy, endurance, and sociability in the clubbers who take them. Which of the following drugs is he most likely referring to?
questions.raw_text: A man was brought in for questioning after a teenager was found dead at a Goan rave party. He reveals that he runs a nightclub in the city and that he has noticed anonymous people selling certain drugs that can enhance energy, endurance, and sociability in the clubbers who take them. Which of the following drugs is he most likely referring to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Methamphetamine

Methamphetamine is a rave drug among the given options. Few substances are commonly used in all-night dance parties (raves) and in clubs to increase energy, endurance, sociability, and arousal. These substances are not all in the same drug class, and they do not produce the same physical or subjective effects.

This includes:

  • Methamphetamine
  • Methylenedioxymethamphetamine- MDMA
  • LSD
  • Gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB)
  • Ketamine
  • Flunitrazepam (Rohypnol)

GHB, Ketamine, and Rohypnol have been called date rape drugs because they produce disorienting and sedating effects, and often users cannot recall what occurred under the influence of the drug.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the most common drawback of the given device?
questions.raw_text: What is the most common drawback of the given device?
questions.correct_answer: C. Drug deposition in the oropharynx
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Drug deposition in the oropharynx

The given image shows a metered-dose inhaler (MDI). The most common side effect of this device is drug deposition in the oropharynx. 

Most material inhaled using this device will be swallowed and absorbed, entering systemic circulation after undergoing the first-pass effect in the liver. Some drug will also be absorbed into the systemic circulation from the lungs.

The use of a large-volume spacer will reduce the amount of drug deposited in the oropharynx, thereby reducing the amount swallowed and absorbed from the GI tract, thus limiting the systemic effects of the drug.

The given image shows the use of spacer with MDI:

 

Spacers reduce the velocity and size of particles entering the upper airways. This reduces the amount of drug that impinges on the oropharynx and increases the proportion of the drug inhaled into the lower airways.

Spacer devices are useful in delivering inhaled drugs to small children, as young as 3 years of age, who are not able to use a pMDI (pressurized MDI), as seen in the image below:

 

Pressurized metered-dose inhalers: Drugs are propelled from a canister in the pMDI with the aid of a propellant. These devices are convenient, portable, and typically deliver 50–200 doses of the drug.

Dry powder inhalers: Drugs may also be delivered as a dry powder using devices that scatter a fine powder dispersed by air turbulence on inhalation. Children less than 7 years of age find it difficult to use a DPI. DPIs have been developed to deliver peptides and proteins, such as insulin, systemically but have proved to be problematic because of the consistency of dosing.

The given image shows various types of dry powder inhalers:

 

Nebulizers: Two types of nebulizers are available. Jet nebulizers are driven by a stream of gas (air or oxygen), whereas ultrasonic nebulizers use a rapidly vibrating piezoelectric crystal and thus do not require a source of compressed gas.

The nebulized drug may be inspired during tidal breathing, and it is possible to deliver much higher doses of the drug as compared to pMDI. Nebulizers are therefore useful in treating acute exacerbations of asthma and COPD, for delivering drugs when airway obstruction is extreme (e.g., in severe COPD), for delivering inhaled drugs to infants and small children who cannot use the other inhalation devices, and for giving drugs such as antibiotics when relatively high doses must be delivered.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Sympathetic ophthalmia is seen after ____________.
questions.raw_text: Sympathetic ophthalmia is seen after ____________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Penetrating trauma

Sympathetic ophthalmia is seen after a penetrating trauma.

Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis seen after a penetrating trauma or less frequently, following intraocular surgery, usually multiple vitreoretinal procedures. Patients present between 2 weeks and 3 months after initial injury. 

The earliest symptom is blurred near vision in the sympathizing (uninjured) eye. The earliest sign is a retrolental flare in the sympathizing eye. Anterior uveitis develops in both eyes. The fundus shows multifocal choroidal infiltrates in the mid-periphery. Sub-retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) infiltrates corresponding to Dalen–Fuchs nodules (image)(a granuloma situated between Bruch membrane and the RPE) are also present. 

Steroids are the basis of treatment. High-dose oral prednisolone is given for several months. Immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, cyclosporine, and methotrexate can be used in resistant cases or as steroid-sparing agents. Enucleation of a severely injured eye with no visual potential within 2 weeks of injury prevents the occurrence of sympathetic ophthalmia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with palpitations. She informs you that a urine pregnancy test done one week ago was positive. Her investigations reveal hyperthyroidism. Which of the following antithyroid drugs can be prescribed for her?
questions.raw_text: A 25-year-old woman presents with palpitations. She informs you that a urine pregnancy test done one week ago was positive. Her investigations reveal hyperthyroidism. Which of the following antithyroid drugs can be prescribed for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Propylthiouracil

The patient in the given clinical scenario is in the 1st trimester of pregnancy. Propylthiouracil is used in the 1st trimester of gestation because it has lower teratogenic effects than carbimazole.

Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with teratogenic effects such as

  • Aplasia cutis congenita  
  • Choanal atresia
  • Treacheosopageal fistula
  • Fetal goiter

However, propylthiouracil use is limited to the first trimester due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. It is replaced with carbimazole or methimazole in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters of the pregnancy.

The lowest effective antithyroid drug dose should be used throughout gestation. This is to maintain the maternal serum-free T4 level in the upper limit of the non-pregnant normal reference range.

Pearl: Drug of choice for hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy

In the 1st trimester: Propylthiouracil

In the 2nd and 3rd trimester: Methimazole

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common complication of mastectomy?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is the most common complication of mastectomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seroma

The most common complication post-mastectomy is the development of a seroma.

Seroma is a collection of clear, yellow, viscous fluid in a surgically created cavity, resulting from the transection of lymphatics and blood vessels. It typically presents as a well-circumscribed, localized swelling with discomfort. Prevention involves placement of closed suction drains to obliterate the space between the pectoralis major and skin flap, effectively reducing seroma formation.

Other complications include:

  1. Wound infection
  2. Skin flap breakdown or necrosis
  3. Lymphedema
  4. Hemorrhage

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What sweat excretion rate in acclimatized, healthy young men is indicative of intolerable air temperature?
questions.raw_text: What sweat excretion rate in acclimatized, healthy young men is indicative of intolerable air temperature?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. > 4.5 litres/4 hours

A sweat excretion rate of > 4.5 L /4 hours in acclimatized, healthy young men is indicative of intolerable air temperature. This is known as McArdle’s maximum allowable sweat rate.

This is the maximum allowable sweat rate that is compatible with the normal physiological reaction of acclimatized, healthy young men who are exposed to heat. The predicted four-hour sweat rate (P4SR) is obtained from readings of air and mean radiant temperature and air velocity under different work intensities. Based on this value, the zone of comfort can be determined.

Zone of comfort    Predicted P4SR
Comfort zone 1 – 3 litres
Just tolerable 3 – 4.5 litres
Intolerable 4.5 + litres

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following zymogens requires gamma-glutamyl carboxylase?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following zymogens requires gamma-glutamyl carboxylase?

options.label: B
options.text: Factors II, VII, IX, and X

questions.correct_answer: B. Factors II, VII, IX, and X
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factors II, VII, IX, and X

Clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X are zymogens of serine proteases that contain glutamic acid residues. These residues undergo vitamin-K-dependent carboxylation via gamma-glutamyl carboxylase to form gamma-carboxyglutamic acid residues. These residues chelate calcium ions, allowing the binding of clotting factors to the platelet surface.

Zymogens are the proprotein form of enzymes (proenzymes) that require proteolytic activation to carry out their function.

The reduced form of vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the post-synthetic modification of these zymogens and their activation. This reduced form of vitamin K is recycled back from its oxidized form by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is inhibited by warfarin.

The absence of vitamin K or the presence of warfarin inhibits carboxylation of the glutamate residues, leading to the release of abnormal precursors of clotting factors in the blood.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A chronic smoker who worked in a cement factory for the past 20 years developed mesothelioma. The association is likely to be due to ______.
questions.raw_text: A chronic smoker who worked in a cement factory for the past 20 years developed mesothelioma. The association is likely to be due to ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asbestosis

The association in this case is between occupational exposure to cement for 20 years and the occurrence of mesothelioma, which is mediated by the development of asbestosis as a result of prolonged inhalation of asbestos.

Asbestosis occurs due to the inhalation of crystalline hydrated silicates (asbestos). It occurs in two distinct geometric forms, serpentine and amphibole. It is characterized by diffuse parenchymal interstitial fibrosis. It usually begins in the lower lobes of the lungs and may present with dyspnea and cough, usually after 20-30 years of exposure.

Asbestos exposure causes other lung diseases like:

  • Pleural plaques
  • Recurrent pleural effusions
  • Lung carcinoma
  • Mesothelioma

Asbestos bodies are a hallmark finding. They appear as golden brown, fusiform, or beaded rods. These are formed when the asbestos fibers are phagocytosed by the macrophages and are coated by iron-containing proteinaceous material derived from phagocyte ferritin.

The image below shows asbestos bodies.

Other options:

Option A: Silicosis is due to the inhalation of crystalline silicon dioxide (silica) as seen in individuals employed in sandblasting or rock mining. Macrophages phagocytose inhaled silica particles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators, like IL-1 and IL-8.

Histopathology reveals coalescent nodules of whorled collagen fibers surrounded by a peripheral zone of dust-laden macrophages. Radiologically, egg-shell calcification of the lymph nodes is seen.

Shown below is an image of a silicotic nodule with collagen whorls as seen in this condition.

Option C: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. On prolonged exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis, which is called complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved.

Microscopic features consist of coal-laden macrophages, black pigment, and dense collagenous interstitial fibrosis. 

The image below shows anthracosis—black pigment engulfed within macrophages as well as in the form of deposits.

Option D: Bagassosis is an occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of bagasse or sugarcane dust. A thermophilic actinomycete, Thermoactinomyces sacchari, is the causative organism. The symptoms are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis, and fever. Initially, it can result in acute diffuse bronchiolitis. If left untreated, it can progress to diffuse fibrosis, emphysema, and bronchiectasis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the rationale for choosing an inhaled anesthetic with the lowest MAC value?
questions.raw_text: What is the rationale for choosing an inhaled anesthetic with the lowest MAC value?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Highest potency

A drug with the lowest MAC would have the highest potency.

The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) value of an inhaled anesthetic is a measure of the potency of the anesthetic agent.

Least potent: nitrous oxide (MAC-104%). 1 MAC with nitrous oxide is practically impossible and thus it is always combined with other agents.

Most potent: methoxyflurane (MAC-0.16%) > trilene (MAC-0.2%), both of which are obsolete now.

Among the inhaled agents in clinical use, halothane is the most potent.

Pearl: Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC)

Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) is the minimum concentration of an inhaled anesthetic at 1 atm of pressure that prevents skeletal muscle movement in response to a surgical incision in 50% of patients. 

MAC of inhaled anesthetics

Anesthetic Agents
